This page is the landing point for KE's posture toward open scholarly standards — what the platform commits to, what ships today, and what is honestly still on the way. Read it if you are a librarian or data curator asking whether exports will outlive the platform, an institutional reviewer or grants office looking for the interoperability story, an environment administrator deciding what your knowledge environment inherits without configuration, or a research team weighing the platform for a future project. Each section deepens progressively; the table is the heart of the page. Standards adoption matters here because three things are true at once. Interoperability with the FAIR data ecosystem — findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable — is non-negotiable for an academic platform. Research data will outlast the platform that produced it, so the formats it lives in must be readable by tools the platform does not control. And scholarly citation depends on identifiers, vocabularies, and packaging that the wider research community already trusts — an identifier only the platform understands is not a citation, it is a private bookmark. Standards are the shared foundation; a research team's interpretation rides on top of it. Voice, vocabulary, and scholarly choices stay specific to each knowledge environment — the standards layer is what makes those choices legible outside the environment's own walls.

The platform distinguishes four maturity tiers, so that "we comply with X" never has to be read on faith: Built — shipped in production code and exercised by at least one feature you can see today. Removing it would break something visible. Active — partially implemented and in real use. You can configure against the standard, but the full export or rendering pipeline is not yet complete end to end. Validated — the platform has researched the standard, committed to its shape in a recorded design decision, and can defend the choice in front of a partner — but no implementation ships yet. Validated means committed, not built. Deferred — recognised as relevant; no commitment and no implementation until a research project or a partner contract makes the need concrete. Listed openly so the absence is visible rather than silent. The selection of standards in the table is itself deliberate. KE's scope spans text, structured data, geographic and temporal modelling, persistent identity, accessibility, and data protection — each with its own established body of standards. The table covers the standards the platform has committed to, surveyed in depth, or recognised as a near-future need. Standards outside this scope (medical imaging's DICOM, financial reporting's XBRL, music encoding's MEI) are not listed; if a future research project requires one, the same sequence applies before it enters this table — research first, then a recorded decision, then implementation. Standard What it covers Where the platform stands today Maturity TEI (P5) Text encoding for scholarly editions; manuscript description; critical apparatus Fields can declare TEI conformance, and annotations can target TEI element identifiers in encoded texts. A full TEI export of published records is committed but not yet built. Validated CIDOC-CRM Cultural-heritage modelling of events, people, and objects Fields can declare CIDOC-CRM conformance today, and drafted shared definitions for places and periods reference CIDOC-CRM classes. An export profile is designed; the platform will not claim CIDOC conformance publicly until its validation test suites pass. Validated GeoSPARQL (OGC) Geographic vocabulary for linked data; geospatial query Adoption is recorded in the platform's drafted place-modelling design; geographic storage and query support is not yet built. Validated PeriodO Gazetteer of historical period definitions A live lookup connector grounds an environment's period vocabulary against PeriodO's published definitions; AI-proposed matches are reviewed and confirmed by a person before they apply. Active Darwin Core Biodiversity taxa, occurrences, specimens Surveyed; no current research project requires it. The conditions for adopting it are recorded openly — see Pending and deferred. Deferred RO-Crate Research-object packaging with provenance On the platform's accepted standards list; the packaging contract for published records is drafted but not yet built. Validated IIIF (Presentation 3.0, Image 3.0, 3D) Image, audio-visual, and 3D interoperability; annotation targets Annotation targets follow the W3C Web Annotation model with IIIF-aligned shapes, and the platform validates those shapes when records are published. Integration of IIIF viewers — deep-zoom image viewing and annotation display — is designed but not yet built. Built (annotation targets); Validated (viewer integration) CSL (Citation Style Language) Citation styles for scholarly references Each environment selects a citation style defined in CSL; the platform renders citations through a standard CSL processor in publication, citation checking, search, and bibliographic export. Built ICU (Unicode collation and folding) Sorting and accent or case handling across scripts Multi-script sorting and folding currently use per-field rules over the database's and the search engine's built-in facilities; a first-class ICU integration is not adopted. Deferred Wikidata External authority for vocabulary grounding A live lookup connector matches an environment's vocabulary to Wikidata identifiers; environment administrators review and confirm proposed matches before they apply. Active JSON-LD Linked-data export Committed as the export format for published records. Export payloads are shape-checked today; the full linked-data export is not yet built. Validated GraphQL Application interface contract The platform's primary interface for reading and writing data is a GraphQL contract, in production for both the research workspace and environment administration. Built OpenAPI (REST) REST interface contract Not adopted as a top-level contract; GraphQL is the platform's primary interface. May be added for a narrow harvesting endpoint if a partner institution requires it. Deferred WCAG 2.2 AA Web accessibility Reader-facing accessibility controls ship today: colour presets, font size, line height, and font family. A full, recorded WCAG 2.2 AA audit has not yet been performed — Active here means real but partial, not certified. Active GDPR Data protection for personal data A documented data-protection impact assessment process is maintained. The platform's activity log redacts personal data before anything is written, and the log is tamper-evident — each entry is cryptographically chained to the one before it. Active Pleiades Gazetteer of ancient places On the platform's accepted standards list as a place-identity authority; live lookup is not yet built. Validated ORCID Researcher identity On the platform's accepted standards list; planned for researcher identity and contribution attribution on published work. Validated DOI / Crossref / DataCite Persistent identifiers; bibliographic registration Published records are designed to carry a stable, citable identity against which a DOI can be registered with an external agency. The platform does not mint DOIs itself. Validated

Compliance here is structural, not declarative. Any platform can claim conformance on a slide deck; what matters is whether drift from a declared standard fails visibly or hides as documentation rot. KE's posture is that drift should fail loudly — when data is saved, when a record is published, or when it is exported. Five mechanisms carry that posture: Standards declarations on fields. Fields in an environment's data model can declare the standards they conform to — a TEI element, a CIDOC-CRM class, an IIIF presentation shape. The declaration travels with the data through publication and export, so an outside reader can see what the data claims about itself without guessing. A vetted standards list. Environments declare conformance only against standards the platform has actually surveyed. Adding a new standard follows a fixed sequence: research first, then a recorded decision, then implementation. A coverage matrix. Every surveyed standard is mapped against every family of concepts the platform models, cell by cell, so each conformance statement traces back to recorded evidence rather than to a slogan. Validation at publication time. Before a published record's export goes out, automated checks refuse any claim of full coverage of a standard that the platform cannot actually validate. These checks run today for citation, image-annotation, and linked-data shapes; machine-runnable validation suites for TEI and CIDOC are planned, and they gate any public conformance claim for those two standards. Gates in the development process. Automated checks keep environment-specific vocabulary out of shared platform code, so the conformance machinery every environment relies on stays identical for all of them.

If you are a researcher. Your knowledge environment inherits scholarly citation and standards-grade export commitments without any configuration on your part. Your interpretive decisions are preserved when your source data is re-imported, citations render in your environment's chosen style, and the export formats in the table above are how your data is designed to travel to your institutional repository. See Citation Integrity and DOI Safety for the citation guarantee and Voice and Vocabulary for how your wording stays yours. If you are an environment administrator. Standards and Citations covers what your environment gets without configuration, what you can configure — citation style, vocabulary grounding against external authorities, standards declarations — and how your data exports. Vocabulary Grounding carries the operational steps. If you are a librarian, data curator, or institutional reviewer. The table above and the Pending and deferred section together are the honest inventory: what ships, what is committed, and what is recognised but not started. The versioning rules below explain how an export made today stays legible in ten years. If you are a research team evaluating the platform. The maturity tags tell you what you can rely on today versus what is planned. If a standard your project requires is at Validated or Deferred, ask the platform operator for an explicit timeline; the openly recorded gap is the basis for that conversation.

When a research team's environment is set up, the adoption decisions in the table are already made. The environment's fields can declare conformance against the accepted standards list; its published records flow through the same publication pipeline as every other environment's; its vocabulary can ground against the same external authorities — Wikidata and PeriodO — as everyone else's. What the environment configures is layered on top: citation style, vocabulary grounding choices, standards declarations, and its own voice and wording. The foundation is shared; the interpretation belongs to the research team. The practical sequence for a new environment: The environment's concept families are configured from the platform's shared field types. Fields can optionally declare which accepted standards they conform to. Vocabulary grounding — Wikidata for entities, PeriodO for periods — is offered as a guided workflow; the environment administrator reviews proposed matches and confirms the ones that fit. A citation style is selected; the choice flows into every surface where the platform renders citations. Published records flow through the shared publication pipeline. As each export format — JSON-LD, RO-Crate, TEI — reaches Built maturity, it becomes available to every environment at once, with no environment-specific code.
documents.s: What a new knowledge environment inherits

documents.t: No single standard covers everything a research collection needs to express. A place record may carry CIDOC-CRM for cultural-heritage modelling, GeoSPARQL for geometry, schema.org markup for search-engine visibility, Pleiades or Wikidata identifiers for external identity, and a JSON-LD context for serialisation — all at once. The platform's shared definitions are designed around composition: a single definition can declare conformance with several standards at once, and the export pipeline is designed to carry each conformance statement alongside the others. When two standards model the same thing with different shapes — a historical period as a CIDOC-CRM period, a Dublin Core period of time, or a SKOS concept — the platform is designed to express each shape from the same underlying record rather than picking one and discarding the others. A researcher does not have to choose which standard their data complies with. When a standard is silent on something the platform needs to express, the gap is recorded explicitly, and the extension lives as a clearly separate field rather than as a falsified conformance claim.

Standards themselves evolve. TEI is on P5; IIIF Presentation is on 3.0; CIDOC-CRM is on 7.1.3; WCAG is on 2.2. KE pins each adoption to a specific version of the standard, recorded with the adoption decision, and exported data is designed to carry that version pin in its conformance statements — so a future reader can resolve the exact specification the data was produced against. This is what keeps a 2026 export legible in 2036: the version pin is the contract.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Where to escalate You want to declare conformance with a standard that is not in the table The platform deliberately accepts declarations only against standards it has surveyed Ask for the adoption sequence to be opened: research first, then a recorded decision, then implementation Your platform operator A standard your project needs is marked Validated, not Built The commitment is recorded but the implementation has not shipped; the maturity tags describe what ships, not what is promised Treat the tag as the honest answer for today, and ask for an explicit timeline Your platform operator A standard you rely on publishes a new major version (for example, a future TEI P6) Each adoption is pinned to a specific version; an upgrade is treated like a new adoption The platform evaluates the new version through the same sequence and keeps both versions pinned during any transition Your platform operator A reviewer asks whether the platform validates conformance or only declares it Validation coverage varies by standard Citation, image-annotation, and linked-data shapes are validated when records are published; validation suites for TEI and CIDOC are planned and gate those claims. Ask for the current per-standard coverage in writing Your platform operator An export claims full coverage of a standard but appears incomplete Publication-time checks are designed to refuse full-coverage claims the platform cannot validate, so this would be a defect Report the record and the standard concerned Your environment administrator, who can escalate to the platform operator

Standards and Citations — what your environment inherits, what you configure, and what exports look like. Citation Integrity and DOI Safety — the citation guarantee for published records. Vocabulary Grounding — matching your vocabulary to external authorities. Voice and Vocabulary — how your wording stays yours.

Items where adoption is recognised as relevant but not yet committed, or committed but not yet finished — listed openly so the absence is visible: Darwin Core — no current research project requires biodiversity-grade modelling of taxa and specimens. It becomes a candidate when a project with specimen-level or species-level data joins the platform and the evidence review supports adoption. ICU (Unicode collation and folding) — sorting and accent handling currently use per-field folding rules over the database's and the search engine's built-in facilities. ICU becomes a candidate when a project needs Unicode-grade case or accent folding beyond those facilities, or when a partner requires ICU conformance in a contract. OpenAPI — GraphQL is the platform's primary interface. OpenAPI becomes a candidate if a partner institution requires it for automated harvesting of a specific endpoint. Full WCAG 2.2 AA audit — the accessibility controls ship today; the recorded end-to-end audit is queued until the public reading surface is stable, so that the audit measures a fixed target rather than a moving one. Until that audit is recorded, the platform does not present itself as WCAG-certified. CIDOC / Linked Art validation suites — machine-runnable validation tests are a precondition the platform set for itself: no public claim of CIDOC conformance until they pass. The suites are not yet written; holding the claim until they pass is deliberate. TEI conformance bundle — a runnable, version-pinned validation bundle is planned once published exports are stable enough to validate against TEI. When complete, it will be published alongside this overview. These gaps are recorded openly so that anyone evaluating the platform can read what it does not yet do alongside what it does. A known conformance gap beats an unverified conformance claim.

Two readers arrive at this page with different questions but a shared need for an honest answer. An institutional reviewer — a grants office, a research data manager, a data protection officer — is filling in a checklist and needs to know what the platform records, how long it keeps it, which data-protection rights it honours, where the data lives, and whether its accessibility and export claims hold up. A researcher or librarian is planning a deposit and needs to know which standards they can rely on today versus which are committed but not yet shipped, so that a deposit plan does not promise a repository something the platform cannot yet deliver. Both questions have the same answer shape: the platform states what ships, what is committed, and what is recognised but not started — and never lets a commitment read as a delivery. This page explains how to read that posture for a compliance review or a deposit plan. It is a guide to the answers, not a separate set of guarantees; the Standards and Compliance Overview carries the authoritative maturity table, and everything here points back to it. The single rule that governs every answer below: a maturity tag describes what ships, not what is promised. When a reviewer asks "do you comply with X?", the honest answer is the tag, plus the explicit gap where the tag is below Built.
A standard onboarding review tends to walk the same sequence. Here is where each answer comes from, and what the honest answer is today.
documents.s: For institutional reviewers: the checklist in the order it is asked

documents.t: The platform records a deliberately small set of operational signals about how it runs — never a copy of research content. For each AI call, each import run, and each suggestion-review decision, it keeps a structured record: the task, counts, timings, outcome flags, and one-way fingerprints of any text involved, never the raw text. Text matching a high-risk personal-data pattern — an email address, a phone number, an identification number — is dropped entirely, with no record and no fingerprint kept. The full inventory of signal classes, with what each contains and excludes, is in Telemetry and Privacy; the researcher-facing view of the same posture is in Privacy and Safety. The default posture is capture-off: AI-call, import-run, and review-decision capture record nothing until switched on for an environment, and switching on review-decision capture additionally requires a recorded privacy acknowledgment first. The one capture class that starts on is tip-activity, which carries no researcher identity at all.

Retention is set per data class, with defaults calibrated against operational-log guidance from data-protection regulators and the relevant information-security control set. AI-call records are kept in full for a short window, then only as a hashed aggregate; import-run records and security-relevant audit records have their own longer windows, with quarantined abuse material held shortest. The current default table — and the basis for each window — is in Telemetry and Privacy. Shorter, environment-specific retention is arranged through the platform operator.

GDPR support is Active: real and in use, with the mechanics documented per right. Access and portability are served by an operator-produced export scoped to a single environment, with a manifest. Erasure pseudonymizes user-identifying telemetry rows in place and keeps only small-count-suppressed aggregates as anonymous data. Restriction and objection are handled by per-person suppression, or by turning a signal class off at the environment level. The platform makes no automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects on a person: AI output is advisory, and researcher review gates any change to environment data. The lawful basis is legitimate interest, with a documented assessment per signal class and a data-protection impact assessment that precedes production capture and is refreshed annually. The right-by-right table and the lawful-basis detail are in Telemetry and Privacy.

Each environment's data lives in its own separate compartment of the database — its own schema — and the database itself enforces that isolation. Telemetry honours the same boundary: telemetry tables refuse to be read from outside an environment's schema. The platform operator holds read-only access to an environment's schema for support, and platform-level operational metrics (cost, latency, model name) that identify an environment only by an internal identifier and carry no content. No third-party analytics, advertising, or external telemetry service sees anything. Residency questions beyond this — where the underlying infrastructure runs for a given deployment — go to the platform operator, because they depend on the deployment, not on the platform code.

The honest answer is Active, not certified. Reader-facing accessibility controls ship today: a control panel for font size, line height, font family, and background-colour presets on the reading and browsing pages, plus keyboard navigation, visible keyboard-only focus rings, and screen-reader-announced hints on fields that are not yet editable. What has not happened is a recorded, end-to-end WCAG 2.2 AA audit — and until it has, the platform does not present itself as WCAG-certified. The audit is deliberately held until the public reading surface is stable, so that it measures a fixed target. The full picture of what works today, and what is still expanding (screen-reader announcement coverage, for example), is in Accessibility. For a compliance review, the correct line to record is: accessibility controls present and in use; formal AA audit not yet performed.
This is where deposit planning and compliance review meet, and where the maturity distinction matters most. Reading the export answer correctly is the next section.

Published records are designed to carry a stable, citable identity against which an external agency can register a persistent identifier. The platform does not mint those identifiers itself, and adoption of the researcher-identity and bibliographic-registration authorities is committed, not yet shipped. Research-object packaging that bundles a record with its provenance for long-term preservation is likewise committed but not yet built. The maturity tags in the Standards and Compliance Overview state exactly where each of these stands; treat the tag as the answer, and ask the platform operator for a timeline where a tag is below Built.

A deposit plan should distinguish what you can rely on now from what you can list as committed-pending. The line runs through the maturity tag. What you can rely on today (Built). Citation rendering through a standard processor, in your environment's chosen citation style, across publication, citation checking, search, and bibliographic export. The platform's primary read-and-write interface is a production application contract. Annotation targets on published records follow a shared web-annotation model and are shape-checked at publication time. These behave today; a deposit plan can lean on them. What is committed but not yet shipped (Validated). The linked-data export of published records, the research-object packaging that wraps a record with its provenance, and the full text-encoding export of published records are all committed in recorded design decisions but not yet built. The same is true of the persistent-identifier and researcher-identity authorities. Validated means committed, not built — list these in a deposit plan as committed-pending, not as available formats, and confirm a timeline with the platform operator before a repository or funder depends on a date. What is recognised but not started (Deferred). A standard listed as Deferred is recognised as potentially relevant but carries no commitment until a concrete project need or a partner contract makes it real. If a deposit depends on a Deferred standard, that is the opening for an explicit conversation with the platform operator, not an assumption to plan around.
documents.s: For researchers and librarians: planning a deposit

documents.t: A reasonable deposit plan can name a Validated export format as the intended destination — but it must not assume the format produces a file today. Validated means the platform has researched the standard, committed to a specific version of it in a recorded decision, and can defend that choice — but the export pipeline that emits a conforming file is not yet complete end to end. For a deposit plan, the practical reading is: design the deposit toward the committed format, keep the plan's promised-formats list to what is Built, and treat each Validated format as a near-future addition whose date comes from the platform operator. A second guard sits behind this. Before any published record's export goes out, automated checks refuse to claim full coverage of a standard the platform cannot actually validate. Those checks run today for citation, image-annotation, and linked-data shapes; machine-runnable validation suites for the heavier text-encoding and cultural-heritage standards are planned, and they gate any public conformance claim for those two. So an export will not silently overclaim conformance it cannot back — which is exactly the property a deposit plan needs.
documents.s: What "Validated" means before an export reaches Built

documents.t: When a committed export format reaches Built, it becomes available to every environment at once, with no per-environment work — published records already flow through the shared publication pipeline, and the new format joins that pipeline for everyone. For an in-flight deposit plan, this means the moment of change is the format reaching Built, not a per-environment migration. The sequence to expect: The format is committed (Validated) — list it as committed-pending, design toward it. The validation suite that gates its public conformance claim is completed — at that point a full conformance claim becomes possible rather than refused. The export reaches Built — it produces a conforming file, and the deposit plan can move the format from committed-pending to available. Each adoption is pinned to a specific version of the standard, recorded with the decision and carried in the exported data's conformance statements. A future reader can resolve the exact specification the data was produced against — which is what keeps a deposit legible long after the platform that produced it. When a standard publishes a new major version, the platform evaluates it through the same research-then-decision sequence and keeps both versions pinned during any transition, so an in-flight deposit pinned to the earlier version stays valid.
documents.s: When a format matures: what changes for an in-flight plan

documents.t: Most of these answers are read straight off the maturity table; a few require the platform operator because they depend on the deployment or on documents held outside the published docs. Question Who answers it Why Which standards ship, which are committed, which are deferred The maturity table in the Standards and Compliance Overview — self-serve The tag is the answer; nothing on this page upgrades it A timeline for a Validated or Deferred standard The platform operator Tags describe what ships, not when the rest will; a date is a commitment the operator makes, not a doc claim The legitimate-interest assessment, per signal class The platform operator Maintained as platform documentation, supplied on request A GDPR access, erasure, restriction, or objection request The environment administrator, who routes it through the platform operator The export and pseudonymization actions run on the operator side Where the infrastructure physically runs (residency) The platform operator Depends on the deployment, not on the platform code Whether a deposit can claim full conformance with a heavier standard today The maturity table, then the platform operator Public full-conformance claims for the text-encoding and cultural-heritage standards are gated on validation suites that are not yet written The division of labour to expect: reading the posture — which tag applies, what a signal class records, what a right entitles a person to — is self-serve from these pages. Producing artefacts that touch stored data — a GDPR export, a per-person suppression, a change to an environment's capture posture, a residency confirmation — is operator-mediated, because those actions run against the live environment and its platform record. An environment administrator initiates and routes such requests; the platform operator performs them.
documents.s: Who to ask, and how the tags map to answers

documents.t: Standards and Compliance Overview — the authoritative maturity table and the enforcement, composition, and versioning posture behind it. This page never upgrades a tag there; read it as the source of truth. Telemetry and Privacy — the full signal inventory, retention table, GDPR right-by-right handling, and third-party exposure. Privacy and Safety — the researcher-facing account of what is recorded and what is deliberately not. Accessibility — what accessibility controls ship today and what is still expanding, the basis for the honest "Active, not certified" answer. Standards and Citations — what an environment inherits, what it configures, and how its data exports.

You operate one knowledge environment on a multi-tenant platform. This area of the documentation tells you what you configure, where each control lives, and how to verify changes reach the surfaces you expect. Read this if you are onboarding a new environment, revising a configuration after researcher feedback, or auditing what your environment is doing. The platform ships generic. Your job is to shape four things: how the platform speaks, who can do what, what data comes in, and what the platform records about how it is being used.

Ordered by how often a typical administrator uses each. Voice and vocabulary substitution — the words the platform uses across every researcher-facing surface. Maturity: Active. Limit: scoped to platform-emitted wording; never rewrites researcher-authored content. See Voice and Vocabulary. Permissions panel — contributors, role composition, project rules, ownership transfers, and the audit trail. Maturity: Active. Limit: the permissions that make up each standard role are fixed; custom roles compose from the same building blocks. See Permissions Panel. Data import wizard — guided review of import proposals from Imports & AI → Imports, across Excel (.xlsx), MySQL, CSV bundle, and Coda sources. The platform parses your source first and asks AI for help second. Maturity: Active. See Data Import Wizard. Workspace configuration — table labels, display fields, source-table scoping, default visible columns, and the saved views researchers share. Maturity: Active. Limit: after a large cold import, review each table's default view before handing it to researchers, because field definitions can still be broader than one source table. See Workspace configuration. Field settings — a searchable inventory of every collection's fields at Workspace account menu → Manage structure → Field settings. Each link opens the collection's existing field editor, including required-before-activation behavior. Browse all fields, including unassigned fields keeps fields outside every collection discoverable in the retained advanced list. Maturity: Built. Limit: four advanced settings still need the older administrator view; the page lists them explicitly. See Field configuration. Vocabulary grounding — link your environment's vocabulary to external authorities such as Wikidata and PeriodO. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the tenant administrator role can confirm a grounding. See Vocabulary Grounding. AI-assisted vocabulary bootstrap — a one-pass onboarding workflow that proposes an initial vocabulary set for your review, so the platform speaks your domain's language sooner. Maturity: Built. Limit: the proposal review screen is not yet available, so the workflow cannot be run end-to-end today; until it ships, vocabulary entries are authored directly on the live vocabulary surface. See AI-Assisted Bootstrap. Efficiency tips — short contextual nudges shown to researchers in the import wizard and workspace; switch them on or off per environment and review aggregate acceptance numbers. Maturity: Active. Limit: tips never block a researcher's action; aggregate numbers are only reported when enough activity exists to keep individual researchers unidentifiable. See Efficiency Tips. Citation integrity — structural guarantees behind citable editions and stable artifact versions. Maturity: Active. Limit: the platform does not mint DOIs itself; it exposes the stable identity an external DOI minter relies on. See Citation Integrity. Media review surface — a single page to review everything the platform extracted from one version of a media artifact, with manual additions, a re-extraction dry run, and promotion to a citable edition. Maturity: Active. Limit: promoting an edition requires the administrator role. See Media Review Surface. Entry Surface readiness — a review of your public search and browsing controls before you launch them, run through your platform operator until the admin-tier review page ships. Maturity: Active (operator-mediated). Limit: a review, never an auto-apply; making a control public is a separate, explicit step. See Entry Surface Readiness. AI usage — your project's AI activity at Workspace account menu → Project monitoring → AI usage (/app/workspace/manage/ai-usage): calls, tokens, latency, and a per-model breakdown, with honest notes on what the figures cover and why no cost is shown yet. Existing /admin/ai-usage/ bookmarks redirect there after the same administrator check. Maturity: Active. Limit: AI-call metering is off by default, so a zero can mean "not measured" — the panel says so. See AI Usage. Citation console — the citation-style workflow's screen at /admin/citations/: active-style detail, catalog, test-corpus pinning, propose → scholar review → apply. Maturity: Active. Limit: installing a style outside the shipped catalog stays operator-mediated. See Citation Style Administration. Telemetry and privacy posture — what the platform records, what it does not, where the data lives, how long it is kept, and the data-protection rights it supports. Maturity: Active. Limit: capture is off by default; enabling it is an explicit, recorded decision. See Telemetry. Standards and citations — what the platform's standards support gives your environment without configuration, what you can configure on top, and what exports produce. Maturity: Built. Limit: some export profiles are still maturing; the standards overview carries per-item maturity. See Standards and Citations and the standards overview. User and access management — an older overview of the standard roles; the Permissions Panel is the live source of truth. Maturity: Built (legacy summary). Limit: role composition and custom-role authoring live in the Permissions Panel. See User and Access Management.

The most common administrator paths: Onboarding a new environment: configure voice and vocabulary by authoring entries directly on the vocabulary surface; confirm a few groundings if external authorities apply to your domain; compose permission roles and invite contributors; choose your citation style and have your platform operator apply it — a dedicated configuration screen is not yet available (see Standards and Citations); decide whether efficiency tips are on. Bringing in new source data: open Imports & AI → Imports and use the upload button for your source type (Excel, MySQL, CSV bundle, or Coda). The wizard parses the source, classifies risk, generates proposals, and routes each proposal through a two-step review: a scholar approves it, then an administrator applies it. Curating the workspace after import: open the workspace tables the import created, set or confirm their labels and display fields, hide irrelevant columns in the default view, and check which view is marked as default before inviting researchers in. Reviewing fields across collections: open the workspace account menu and choose Manage structure → Field settings. Search by field name, key, or type, then select Edit field name to open that field in its collection's existing editor. If a field is not assigned to any collection, use Browse all fields, including unassigned fields to find it in the retained advanced list. Reviewing media attestations: open the record from the workspace Media view and use the detail pane's Mesh→term tab — approve, reassign, or strip each part's term binding — and its Version tab to re-extract or pin a revision as a citable Edition (see Media Review Surface). Auditing recent activity: open the Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/ and use the Audit tab. Permission changes, ownership transfers, vocabulary edits, and reviewed AI-assisted changes all appear there. Checking what the platform is recording: Workspace → Manage → Telemetry at /app/workspace/manage/telemetry shows your environment's telemetry summary — which signals are being captured and in what volume. Existing /admin/monitoring/telemetry/ bookmarks redirect there after the same administrator check. Checking AI activity: open the workspace account menu and choose Project monitoring → AI usage. The panel separates recorded activity from capture coverage and explains why cost is not shown when no rate table exists.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The wording on a researcher-facing surface is still the platform default No vocabulary entry exists for that wording, or the entry has not been confirmed Open the vocabulary surface (see Voice and Vocabulary), find the matching key, and add or confirm an entry. Reload the surface to confirm the new wording. The Permissions Panel shows a banner of vocabulary findings The vocabulary check that runs when the panel loads found missing entries, broken grounding references, or inconsistencies Click into the surfaced rows. The check is read-only — acting on the findings is your decision. An import proposal is marked as parser-only because AI was unavailable AI assistance is not configured, or not reachable, in your platform deployment Parser-only proposals are still fully reviewable. To enable AI assistance, contact your platform operator. A re-import overwrote a researcher's manual edits The run used full refresh, which reloads rows from scratch, instead of edit-preserving refresh Restore the affected records from your environment's backup, then re-run as an edit-preserving refresh. If your platform operator runs imports for you, ask them to use the edit-preserving behaviour. If a failure mode is well documented in a specific feature page, that page owns the deeper troubleshooting; this overview only flags the top-level cases.

Researcher tier: Researcher guide — what researchers see in the workspace, public reader, and accessibility panel. Standards overview: Standards overview — the cross-audience standards overview. Platform operations — tenant lifecycle, deployment configuration, incident response, and backups are handled outside your environment. For anything in that category, contact your platform operator.

A new environment opens with the platform's standard wording: the labels that title records in the workspace, and the confirmation phrases researchers approve before high-impact operations. Researchers are not blocked while that wording is still generic — the platform adapts its standard phrasing using the labels from your environment's own configuration. The AI-assisted bootstrap shortens the path to wording that speaks your researchers' domain language. It generates a starter set of wording proposals tuned to the research discipline your environment declares and its concept families (the kinds of records your environment defines), for you to review — accept, reject, or edit — in one pass during onboarding. Bootstrap is a one-pass onboarding tool. After onboarding, Voice and Vocabulary describes how your environment's wording resolves and the paths for shaping it. Note the availability limit below: the in-product screen for reviewing bootstrap proposals is not yet available, so the workflow cannot be run end-to-end today.

Proposal generation — Maturity: Built. Generates a starter list of suggested wording entries from your declared research discipline and concept families: suggested titles for records of each concept family, plus suggested phrasings for the four confirmation prompts researchers approve before high-impact operations (reorganising entries into a connected structure, permanently removing duplicate entries, updating the same identifier across already-saved entries, and applying a batch of structural changes as one step). Each proposal carries the suggested wording, a short explanation of why it is proposed, and a confidence score. Proposals come from built-in rules today; model-generated proposals are not yet available. All-or-nothing commit — Maturity: Built. Accepted proposals are written to your environment's vocabulary in a single transaction. If any write fails, nothing is written; you can resolve the cause and retry without partial results to clean up. AI-reviewed status with provenance — Maturity: Built. Every committed entry is recorded with AI-reviewed status and carries a tamper-evident cryptographic reference back to the proposal that produced it, so an entry's bootstrap origin stays provable. An explicit wording override for the same phrase takes precedence — explicit wording always wins over AI-reviewed wording. Proposal review screen — Maturity: Deferred. The screen where you accept, reject, or edit each proposal is not yet available in the environment admin interface. Until it ships, your environment's wording is shaped through the paths described in Voice and Vocabulary — naming your concept families, renaming roles, and asking your platform operator about a specific phrase.

Because the proposal review screen is not yet available: Name your concept families well — the highest-leverage wording move available today. The platform substitutes those labels into its standard phrases automatically, so a good set of names improves many phrases at once. See Voice and Vocabulary for where to set them and for the other wording paths. Rely on the standard wording in the meantime: record titles and confirmation prompts render from the platform's standard templates, adapted with your environment's own labels where available. An incomplete vocabulary does not block your researchers. Review the vocabulary arriving in your data through Vocabulary Grounding — a separate surface for the values found in your imported records, not for the platform's wording.

Symptom Likely cause Fix You cannot find a bootstrap or proposal-review option in your environment's admin interface The proposal review screen is not yet available Shape your environment's wording through the paths in Voice and Vocabulary. If you expected bootstrap to be enabled for your environment, contact your platform operator. Confirmation prompts show standard platform wording rather than your domain's terms No environment-specific wording exists for those prompts, so the standard templates render with your labels substituted This does not block researchers. Check that your concept-family labels are set — the prompts substitute them automatically. For phrasing beyond that, contact your platform operator; see Voice and Vocabulary. An entry's wording carries AI-reviewed status and you want different wording AI-reviewed entries keep their wording until an explicit override replaces it An explicit override takes precedence over an AI-reviewed entry, but there is no self-service screen for editing an individual wording entry today — contact your platform operator.

Voice and Vocabulary — how platform wording resolves in your environment, and the paths for shaping it. Vocabulary Grounding — review the vocabulary values arriving in your imported data, with optional links to external authorities; a separate surface from platform wording. Permissions Panel — role and permission wording, and the wording review prompt for your environment.

Turning on an AI feature means some of your project's information is sent to an AI provider outside the platform. This page states, for each feature listed here, exactly what that is — so the decision is made with the facts rather than an assumption. Do not read this page as a complete list of what is active. It documents the features described below and no others, and the defaults are not uniform: reader names and AI grounding both start switched off and wait for an administrator, while the import assistant starts switched ON for a newly provisioned project. If you are compiling a record of what leaves your project, treat this page as covering the features it names, and ask your platform operator about any AI surface not documented here. Read it before enabling any AI feature, and again if your institution asks you what leaves the platform on your project's behalf. The two features on this page differ on the question that matters most, so there is no single rule to carry between them. Reader names for collections sends only the shape of your data: the names you gave your tables and columns, and one word chosen for readers. No value from inside a record is sent. Vocabulary grounding suggestions is the exception, and it is the reason this page cannot state one rule for both. Grounding exists to ask what a particular value in your records means, so the value itself is what is sent — a word or phrase a researcher typed into a field. If your reason for reading this page is to know whether record content leaves the platform, the answer is yes for this one feature, under the limits its section sets out.

Enabling an AI feature makes the configured AI provider a sub-processor of whatever that feature sends. If your institution keeps a record of sub-processors, or your project works under a data-protection agreement, the enabling decision belongs in that record, and this page is the description of what the sub-processor receives. Which provider is configured, and whether it is your own account or the platform's, is an environment decision — see Environment settings. Turning a feature on does not change the provider; it changes what the provider is given.

What it does. During the import wizard, this feature asks the AI provider what one record of a collection should be called for readers — "Specimen" rather than specimens_tbl. It proposes; nothing is written until a researcher accepts. See Voice and vocabulary for how an accepted name is used. What is sent. For each collection in one import session, and nothing else: What Where it comes from Source table names The names of the tables you imported Source column names The column names in those tables, capped per collection Structural type The archetype the platform assigned to the collection Role identifier The platform's own internal name for the collection's role A per-request handle Generated for the request; means nothing outside it The reader name in use today See below — this one can be text a person wrote Why the last row matters. The name readers currently see is sent so the model can leave a collection alone when its name is already right — it cannot make that judgement without knowing the current name. Usually that name was derived by the platform. But it can also be a name your project set by hand, or one a researcher accepted and edited on an earlier import. In those cases the text a person typed is part of what is sent. A disclosure that said only "table and column names" would understate this, so it is stated plainly instead: the current reader name is sent, and it may be your own wording. What is not sent. No rows. No field values. No record content of any kind. Nothing about who is in your project or who ran the import. How often. Once per collection when a suggestion reaches you, and re-opening the wizard does not send again, because the first answer is reused. Three is the limit on suggestions you SEE, not on collections sent. A session shows at most three reader-name suggestions. But when the AI answers for a collection and the platform then withholds the suggestion — because it matches the name already in use, or is not confident enough — that collection's place is released rather than counted, so further collections can still be sent. This is deliberate: a withheld suggestion should not use up one of your three. It does mean the number of collections described to the provider in one session can exceed three. What actually bounds it is the session's token budget, which your administrator sets and which refuses a request before the provider is contacted. If you need a hard ceiling on what leaves the project, that budget is the control — not the count of suggestions on screen. A request that fails is the exception, and it matters for this page. When the provider does not answer, or answers unusably, nothing is remembered — so the collection becomes eligible again and each use of Try again sends the same table names, column names and current reader name once more. What bounds that is the session's token budget, not a count of attempts: once the budget cannot cover another request, the platform refuses it before contacting the provider. So the honest ceiling on a failing session is the budget your administrator set, not "once". Turning it off. A project administrator can disable it at any time, and the switch takes effect immediately: a suggestion already on screen can no longer be accepted after the feature is switched off.

What it does. Some values in your records have no grounded reading — a term the platform cannot match to any vocabulary it knows. This feature asks what such a value might mean: first a public authority service, then the AI provider. It proposes; nothing is written until a researcher accepts. What is sent — including record content. The ungrounded value itself, which is text from inside a record: What Where it goes The ungrounded value The public authority service, as the search query The ungrounded value, or a stand-in for it The AI provider, in the prompt — see below The kind of value it is The AI provider, as the platform's own category name Candidate matches the authority returned The AI provider, to be judged What the model receives depends on a gate. Before the value reaches the prompt it is checked, and only a value that passes is sent as written. A value that does not pass is replaced by a keyed one-way hash of itself, or by [redacted] when it is classified as unsafe to send. The gate refuses a value when its kind is not on the allowlist, when it is empty or longer than the permitted length, when it carries a signal associated with personal data, or when it is an internal platform key rather than something a person wrote. The authority lookup is gated too, inside the connector that performs it, and a refused lookup is not attempted. But treat the plain reading as the operative one for a consent decision: when the gate allows a value, that value leaves your project verbatim, to a public service and to the AI provider. What is not sent. Whole rows. Other fields of the record the value came from. Your schema's identity — the platform's internal name for your project is used only as the key for the hash and does not itself reach the prompt. How often. Once per suggestion request. What bounds it is a rolling 24-hour token budget your administrator sets; when the budget cannot cover another request the platform refuses it before the provider is contacted. Turning it off. A project administrator can disable it at any time.

AI usage — how many AI calls your project has made, and what they cost in tokens. Telemetry — what the platform records about its own operation, and how capture is decided. Environment settings — which AI provider is configured for your environment. Voice and vocabulary — how reader names are used once accepted.

The AI usage panel at /app/workspace/manage/ai-usage shows what AI has been doing on behalf of your project: how many calls ran, how many tokens went in and out, how much was served from cache, average latency, and a per-model breakdown. Read it when you want a sense of your project's AI activity, or before a conversation with your platform operator about usage and cost. The page is also where the project's AI features are switched on and off, and where each one's token budget is set — so it is both the record of what AI has done and the control over what it may do next.

Activity summary — total calls, calls this month, tokens in, tokens out, cached tokens, and average latency, scoped to your project only. Maturity: Active. Limit: requires the project admin role; the counters cover your project's own recorded calls, never other projects'. Per-model breakdown — the same counters split by AI model and provider, so you can see which models your project's workflows actually used. Maturity: Active. Honest coverage note — AI-call metering is off by default. The panel always states what its figures cover: while metering is off, that the numbers reflect only periods when it was on; once metering is on, that they reflect only successfully recorded calls (privacy-filtered calls and earlier unmetered periods are not included). A zero here can mean "not measured", and the panel says so rather than presenting it as "no usage". Maturity: Active. AI feature switches — one card per AI feature the project can use: Reader name suggestions and Vocabulary grounding suggestions. Each carries a switch to use the feature in this project and a token budget that bounds what it may spend. Both start switched off. Turning one on sends some of your project's information outside the platform, and what each one sends differs — read What AI features send before enabling either, because grounding sends values from inside your records and reader names does not. Maturity: Active. Limit: requires the project admin role. Honest cost note — no cost figure is shown yet, and the panel says why: the per-model rate table has not been built for your project. The platform never guesses a cost. Maturity: Active. Limit: cost display arrives with the bring-your-own-key rate substrate.

Sign in with a project-admin account. In the workspace, open the account menu, then choose Project monitoring → AI usage, or go directly to /app/workspace/manage/ai-usage. Existing /admin/ai-usage/ bookmarks take you to the same page after the same administrator check. The panel loads your project's current totals, and below them the switch and token budget for each AI feature. Changing either takes effect for the project immediately. Two things on this page are not the same control, and only one of them is yours. The feature switches decide whether an AI feature runs at all. Enabling or disabling AI-call metering — whether the platform records the calls this page counts — is a privacy-relevant, recorded decision made with your platform operator, and is not set here; see Telemetry.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Every number reads zero No successfully recorded calls exist for this project, or AI-call metering is off and activity was not captured Read the coverage note on the panel before interpreting the zero. If metering is off, ask your platform operator about enabling capture; see Telemetry. No cost figure appears The per-model rate table does not exist yet Current behavior, stated on the panel — cost display arrives with the rate-table substrate. The page refuses to open Your account does not hold the project admin role in this project Ask a project admin to check your role in the Permissions Panel.
Telemetry — what the platform records, the capture defaults, and how enabling capture is decided and recorded. Permissions Panel — roles, including who can open operations pages like this one.

When a researcher in your environment ratifies a binding set on a media artifact — saying "these terms correctly describe these regions of this artifact" — and a DOI is minted on top of that ratified state, the platform guarantees the cited data cannot silently change. A re-extraction run against a citable Edition is refused outright: it stops before any binding is touched. False-positive bindings a reviewer rejects stay rejected across re-runs. Read this when evaluating the platform for a peer-reviewed publication or a DOI-minted scholarly artifact, or when answering an institution's editorial, DPO, or library question about how citation integrity is enforced. This page explains the guarantees in plain language. The actions that produce the ratified state live on the Media Review Surface.

Three-layer artifact identity — every cited artifact carries three kinds of identity: a citable identity (the publishable artifact name plus an optional DOI, Zotero, or institutional handle); platform-internal identifiers that are never published; and the artifact's own natural self-description as the machine selector — glTF node names for 3D models, IIIF region selectors for images, TEI xml:id values for texts. When a specific part is cited, the printed locator is the resolved scholarly label that part maps to (e.g. the term a mesh region is bound to), not the raw selector string; the selector stays internal as the machine pointer · Maturity: Active · Limit: the platform never rewrites the artifact file at ingest; internal identifiers and raw selectors stay internal. Working versions and citable Editions — every binding set belongs to an artifact version that is either a Revision (a working copy that can still change) or an Edition (frozen, citable, peer-review-targetable) · Maturity: Active · Limit: an environment may carry many Revisions of the same artifact; promoting one to an Edition is a deliberate, separate action. Explicit promotion to Edition — promoting a Revision to an Edition is a single confirmed action on the Media Review Surface; once promoted, the version is protected against re-extraction · Maturity: Active · Limit: requires the admin role. Edition freeze against re-extraction — the platform refuses any ingest run that would change the bindings of an Edition; the run stops with an error before any binding is touched · Maturity: Active · Limit: structural — not a warning, not a log entry. Durable rejection (Strip) — when a reviewer strips a false-positive binding, the platform keeps the record as a tombstone — a retained marker of the rejection — instead of deleting it, so later re-extraction recognises the rejection and refuses to re-propose the same binding · Maturity: Active. Reviewer-edit preservation in working versions — bindings a reviewer has approved or amended are marked as reviewer-owned; re-extraction never overwrites them, even while the version is still a Revision · Maturity: Active · Limit: bindings no reviewer has touched remain refreshable in a Revision. Per-action attribution — every review action records who acted, what the action was, when, and an optional note; this record is stored with the binding and is never deleted or rewritten by re-processing · Maturity: Active · Limit: the trail lives on each binding record; the platform does not keep a separate consolidated audit log of these review actions.

The guarantees described here are produced by actions on the Media Review Surface; this page describes what those actions mean for citation. Pin a citation-ready Revision as an Edition: open the record from the workspace Media view, confirm the bindings are correct on its detail pane's Mesh→term tab, then on the Version tab pin the revision as an Edition with an Edition label (requires the admin role); a confirmation step precedes the pinning. Attach a DOI to an Edition (forthcoming — no workspace control yet): the platform does not mint DOIs. DOI adoption — binding an existing, externally-minted DOI (from your institutional library, a repository system, or a Crossref or DataCite membership) to the media object so the platform records it and surfaces it in the citation — is a gated capability whose workspace control is not yet built; it lands when DOI adoption is enabled for an environment. By default, and until then, the Edition is fully citable by its stable canonical identity, no DOI required — adoption adds a DOI to an already-citable Edition, it never gates citeability. Strip a false-positive binding durably: in the workspace Media detail pane's Mesh→term tab, choose Strip on the wrong binding and confirm. The rejection is permanent across re-extractions: future runs recognise it and do not re-propose the binding. Update the artifact file under an active citation: ask your platform operator to ingest the updated file under a new version label. The original Edition's data — and any DOI adopted on it — stay intact; the new Revision is reviewed on its own merits and can be pinned as a new Edition later. The platform does not: Mint DOIs. DOI minting belongs to your institution's library or repository system; the platform provides the stable target. Host published papers. The platform holds the cited data, not the publication. Count citations. How often a published Edition is cited is a question for your institution's bibliometric tools. Embargo by date. There is no embargo or paywall workflow. If you need an embargo, hold the promotion to Edition until you are ready to publish, then promote.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A re-ingest of an artifact file was refused with a message that the version "is frozen for citation" The artifact version is an Edition; the platform refused to change it This is the guarantee working as designed. Ask your platform operator to ingest the file under a new version label; the original Edition stays intact. A reviewer stripped a binding last week, but the latest re-extraction proposed it again This should not happen — a stripped binding is preserved as a rejection across re-runs Contact your platform operator, identifying the artifact and the affected binding. Durable rejection is a structural guarantee; a recurrence is a platform defect. Promote to Edition is missing or disabled The artifact has not been ingested with a version yet, or your role lacks admin Confirm the artifact has been ingested (ingest creates the first version); verify your role assignment in the Permissions Panel. You need to embargo an Edition until publication The platform does not implement embargo workflows Keep the version a Revision in a private workflow until the embargo lifts, then promote. The platform does not restrict access to Editions by date. An audit reviewer asks for a formal audit log separate from the per-binding attribution Per-binding attribution is durable but lives on each binding record The per-binding attribution records — who acted, what the action was, when, and any note — are the audit trail, and re-processing never deletes or rewrites them. The platform does not keep a separate consolidated log of binding review actions; if the reviewer needs the records gathered into one export, contact your platform operator.

Tenant admin companions: Media Review Surface — the operational surface that produces the ratified state these guarantees protect; Telemetry — what operational signals the platform records and the privacy controls around them; Standards and Citations — what your environment inherits without configuration. Cross-audience standards overview: Standards.

This page is the operating reference for the citation-style service behind the propose → review → apply workflow. It names the administrative endpoints that drive that workflow, explains what the detail view tells you, and explains the pinned test corpus and the blast-radius measurement that decides how risky a proposed style change is. Read it when you are about to refine a citation style and want to know exactly what each step does, what numbers the platform reports back, and why a proposal lands in one risk class rather than another. This is the companion to Standards and Citations, which describes the citation framework and the propose → review → apply workflow as a working procedure. That page is where to start; this one goes deeper into the service the workflow runs through. It does not replace it — the workflow narrative lives there and is not repeated here. The service now has a dedicated screen: the citation console at /admin/citations/ (Citations group in the admin sidebar). The console shows your project's active style — its identifier, version, and who applied it — alongside the counts of pinned test citations and proposals awaiting review, and it drives the workflow: adopt any style from the standard catalog, propose a refinement by pasting sample citations (the console shows the returned risk class, blast-radius percentage, the pinned citations that would change, and a plain-language explanation), apply a proposal after reviewing that report, recording your review notes with the apply, and curate the reader formats — the venue formats a reader's citation switcher offers on your published entries, chosen from the standard catalog; leaving that list empty inherits the platform default. Style selection is project-wide: adopting or applying a style makes it the single active style for the whole environment. The console's review queue lists proposals created or tracked in your session; a proposal created elsewhere can be acted on by entering its proposal id. Pinning has two doors: the citation binding section in the workspace — where a previewed citation pins into the regression corpus with one click — and the administrative endpoints, which also carry the bounded automatic sweep and the switch that turns a pinned case on or off. Every path, screen and endpoint alike, requires an active admin membership in this project; an account's staff status alone is not enough. Applying a proposal is protected against a moved baseline: if another admin switched the active style after a proposal was drafted, the apply is refused rather than silently rebasing onto a style the proposer never reviewed — the console surfaces that refusal as a plain message asking you to propose again against the current style.
The service exposes a small set of administrative endpoints, each scoped to one entry type. The two read paths report state; the write paths drive the workflow and the test corpus.

Style detail — the read view for one entry type. It reports the entry type's active style (its identifier, version, when it was applied, and by whom), the number of active citation test cases pinned for that entry type, and how many style proposals are currently pending review. Call this first: it tells you what is live, how much test coverage exists, and whether anyone has a refinement waiting · Maturity: Built. Catalog browse — lists the citation styles that ship with the platform, so you can adopt one directly instead of refining. A catalog of more than seventy standard styles ships with the platform · Maturity: Built.
documents.s: Reading the active style and pending work

documents.t: These two carry the propose → apply path. The risk report the proposal returns is the review: the same administrator reads it and decides, and the platform's protection is evidence (the pinned-corpus measurement and the moved-baseline refusal), not a second signature. Propose — you submit a list of sample citations you want the rendered output to match. The platform generates a proposed style, measures it against the pinned test corpus, and returns a risk class, a blast-radius percentage, the specific test cases that would change, and a plain-language explanation of what the proposal does. The proposal is recorded as pending; nothing is applied · Maturity: Built. Apply — an administrator reviews the proposal's risk report and applies it, optionally recording review notes. The style is stored in your environment as the new active style, recorded with the applying administrator and a version stamp. From then on, citations render against the new active style; existing published pages pick it up the next time they are rebuilt. Only a pending proposal can apply; an already-applied one is refused · Maturity: Built. Adopting a catalog style directly (through the catalog browse endpoint) skips the propose-and-review path: the chosen style is stored as the active style straight away, stamped with a checksum of the style file and the administrator who selected it. Use the review path when you are refining how citations read for your own material; use direct adoption when an off-the-shelf venue or institution style already fits. A proposal can also be refused at the propose step itself when the base style it refines is too large to regenerate safely. The refusal message says to adopt a closer catalog style first — do that, then propose the refinement against the closer base.

The style detail (and the console) reports a per-rule compliance line: which citation rules render with schema checking on, and which have it switched off. A rule with schema checking off still renders, but its structured citation data is not being validated against the citation standard — treat that as a temporary state while a mapping is being shaped, not a resting place. Relatedly, the platform's citation-profile analysis reports when a mapping would publish citations missing the core findability fields (author or editor, title, and the container or date where the citation's type expects one), so a gap is named before readers meet it.

The active style renders the citation of the published page itself, and it stays the authoritative default for every reader. Each published entry also offers a citation format selector: alongside your style — shown as the project style — a reader can re-render the entry's citation in the venue formats your environment offers. That offered list is curated in the console's Formats offered to readers section, a checkbox list over the standard catalog; an environment that has not curated one inherits the platform default (APA, MLA, Chicago author-date, Chicago notes & bibliography, Harvard). Reader-facing changes to the offered list can take up to an hour to appear, because the reader's catalog is cached. The switch itself happens in the reader's own browser, from the citation's structured data; it does not change the active style, what other readers see, or the pinned test corpus — proposals are always measured against your active style. The evidence rows on a published entry are outside the active style's reach altogether: they render through your environment's declared reference conventions and read the same for every reader. For how those conventions are built up from your own tables, see the worked example in Standards and Citations.
documents.s: What the active style governs on a published page

documents.t: The risk numbers a proposal reports are only as meaningful as the test corpus they are measured against. A pinned citation test case is one published citation, frozen as the expected rendered text plus the structured citation data behind it, kept as a regression check for one entry type. What pinning does — the platform reads citations off your already-published entries and records each one as an expected result. After pinning, any future style proposal is rendered against these frozen citations; if the proposal would change one of them, that change is counted as a regression · Maturity: Built. How pinning is scoped — pinning draws only from published entries for the entry type. You can pin a previewed citation with one click from the citation binding section in the workspace, pin a single citation (by naming the published entry and the citation's position on it), or let the platform sweep your published entries and pin a representative sample automatically. The automatic sweep is deliberately bounded so the corpus stays a representative regression check rather than an exhaustive copy: it pins at most three citations of any one structural shape and at most forty in total, and it skips citations that are not well-formed enough to pin reliably. The response reports how many candidates it saw, how many it skipped, the shape breakdown, and every case it pinned · Maturity: Built. Turning a case on or off — a pinned case can be deactivated and reactivated. Only active cases count toward the blast-radius measurement, so deactivating a case removes it from the regression baseline without deleting it · Maturity: Built.

When you propose a style, the platform renders it against every active pinned test case for that entry type and counts how many would change. From that it computes two things: Blast-radius percentage — the share of pinned test cases the proposal would change. It is the count of changed cases divided by the total active cases, as a percentage. With no pinned cases the blast radius is zero, which is why the test corpus matters: a proposal measured against an empty corpus carries no evidence about its real reach. Risk class — a plain label derived from the blast-radius percentage, used to route the proposal: Low — at or below five percent of pinned cases change. A small, contained refinement. Medium — between five and twenty-five percent change. Read the changed cases before applying. High — more than twenty-five percent change. A wide-reaching change that warrants careful second-eyes review; nothing is applied automatically. The proposal also returns the specific test cases that would change — each with its expected text and what the proposed style would render instead — so a reviewer is looking at concrete before-and-after citations, not just a number.

The typical sequence — steps 1, 3, and 4 run in the citation console; step 2 runs from the citation binding section in the workspace or through the administrative endpoints: Check the current state — read the style detail to see the active style, how many test cases are pinned, and whether a proposal is already pending. Build a baseline, if you have not — pin citations from your published entries so a proposal can be measured against real output: one click on a previewed citation in the citation binding section, or the endpoints for a single named citation or the automatic sweep. Without pinned cases, every proposal reports a zero blast radius and tells you nothing about its reach. Propose a refinement — submit the sample citations you want the output to match. Read the returned risk class, blast-radius percentage, and the list of cases that would change. Apply — after reading that report, apply the style with your review notes; it becomes the active style, and citations render against it from then on. If an off-the-shelf style already fits, skip steps 3 and 4 and adopt a catalog style directly through the catalog browse path. Which actions are administrator-self-serve and which involve your platform operator: Self-serve (environment administrator role): what the citation console at /admin/citations/ shows and does — reading the active style and its counts, browsing the standard catalog, adopting a catalog style, proposing a refinement from sample citations, applying a proposal after reviewing its risk report, and curating the reader-format list — plus, in the workspace's citation binding section, declaring citation bindings and pinning previewed citations into the regression corpus. Endpoint-run (no console screen): the bounded automatic pin sweep, pinning a single named citation, turning a pinned case on or off, and the draft preview — rendering a handful of real citations for one entry role (optionally with a draft citation field mapping) through the same rendering path publication uses, without changing anything. The endpoints are admin-gated; the console does not call them. Operator-mediated: installing a citation style that is not in the shipped catalog — provide the style file or a published style URL to your platform operator.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A proposal reports a zero blast radius even for a big change No active test cases are pinned for the entry type, so there is nothing to measure against Pin a representative sample of citations from your published entries first, then re-propose. The risk numbers only mean something against a baseline. Applying a proposal is refused because "the active style moved" Another administrator switched the active style after this proposal was drafted, so the proposal's measurements no longer describe the change that would actually happen This refusal is deliberate. Re-run the proposal against the current active style and review the fresh numbers before applying. A proposal cannot be applied It was already applied, or the active style moved after it was drafted Only a pending proposal applies. If the style moved, propose again against the current style — the refusal message says so. A previewed citation refuses to pin ("not well formed enough") The rendered citation lacks the structure the regression corpus requires — usually a thin mapping that produces only a title Bind the missing parts (author, date, or locators) and preview again; pin once the citation carries real structure. The automatic pin sweep recorded fewer cases than expected The sweep is bounded to keep the corpus representative — at most three citations of any one shape and forty in total — and it skips citations that are not well-formed enough to pin This is expected. The response reports candidates seen, cases skipped, and the shape breakdown; the sample is meant to be representative, not exhaustive. A blast-radius number looks too low to trust The corpus is thin, or relevant cases were deactivated Check the active test-case count in the style detail, and reactivate any deactivated cases that belong in the baseline before re-proposing. A style your researchers need is not in the catalog The catalog ships standard styles only Ask your platform operator to install it; provide the style file or a published style URL. Proposing a refinement is refused because the base style is too large The style being refined is too large to regenerate safely, so the platform declines rather than producing an unreliable proposal Adopt a closer catalog style first — the refusal message says so — then propose your refinement against that closer base.
