You cannot run any of these steps The acting account lacks the environment administrator role Ask an environment administrator to act, or to grant your role administrator access — see Permissions Panel.

Start here: Standards and Citations — the citation framework and the propose → review → apply workflow as a procedure. Companion: Citation Integrity — the guarantees that protect a citation once an entry is published. Roles: Permissions Panel — the administrator role these endpoints require. Cross-audience parent: Standards & Compliance Overview.

A saved connection is your environment's named reference to an outside service — a Coda account, a live MySQL database, or another recognized provider. The connection stores where the secret lives, never the secret itself: the platform reads the actual key or password from its storage place only at the moment a feature uses it, and never writes it to the database, to logs, or to background-job records. Read this page when you prepare a background import that reads from a live source, when an import fails with a credential error, or when you need to know exactly what the platform does and does not store. Saved connections are an operator-mediated surface. You view, edit, scope, and validate your environment's connections yourself; creating a connection, deleting one, and placing the secret value itself are done by your platform operator. The split is stated action by action below.

Saved connection records — each connection carries a label (unique per provider within your environment), a provider, an authentication scheme, a secret reference with its backend, a status, an allowed-features list, and non-secret connection details. Maturity: Active. Limit: the record holds a reference to the secret, never the value — saving is refused when a value-like entry is detected in the reference or the details. Import wizard reads through saved connections — Coda and MySQL imports can run through a saved connection; background reads of a live source require one, because a background job cannot carry a one-time key. Maturity: Active. Limit: of the credentialed providers, the wizard reads source data only from Coda and MySQL. Credential-only providers — Airtable and Notion connections can be stored and validated; the platform checks their status, feature scope, and authentication scheme, but the import wizard does not read source data from them. Maturity: Built. Limit: storing the connection registers it for credential checks only — there is no import path behind it. Validate without using — a list action confirms that a stored reference still resolves to a secret, without using the credential: no usage is recorded and the secret is not kept. The outcome (time, result, and a failure class on error) is written to the connection. Maturity: Active. Feature scoping — the allowed-features list names which platform features may use the connection; a feature is refused unless its key is listed. Maturity: Active. Usage record — each real use stamps the connection's last-used time and increases its usage count; both are read-only on the form, alongside the last validation outcome. Maturity: Active. Secret backends — environment variables and AWS Secrets Manager are read at use time; "No stored secret" is supported for federated schemes. Maturity: Active. Limit: HashiCorp Vault and GCP Secret Manager are selectable when saving, but the platform does not read secrets from them — validating such a connection reports it as unavailable.

Action Who View your environment's saved connections You. The list shows only your own environment's connections. Edit a connection — label, scheme, backend, reference, allowed features, details, status You, subject to your account's permissions. Validate connections You — the Validate selected credential references action on the list. Create a new connection Platform operator. The screen offers no add control inside an environment. Delete a connection Platform operator. Deletion is not offered inside an environment. Place or rotate the secret value itself (a server environment variable, a cloud-stored secret) Platform operator — the value lives outside the platform. Configure AI providers Platform operator. AI features are configured at platform level, not through saved connections.

The saved-connections screen is titled External Service Credentials in your environment's admin. It does not appear in the admin sidebar; open it by its address, /admin/customers/externalservicecredential/. The list shows each connection's label, provider, authentication scheme, status, secret backend, usage count, last-used time, and last update, with filters for provider, scheme, status, and backend, and a search box that matches labels and secret references.

Provider Import wizard Saved-connection role Coda Reads through it Required for background Coda imports and for loading source rows again at final import or re-import; an inline read uses a one-time API key instead, which is never saved. The import check accepts only the static API / bearer token scheme. MySQL Reads through it Required for reading a live database in the background. Connection details (host or socket, database, username, port, SSL) live on the connection as non-secret details; the secret reference supplies only the password, at run time. The import check accepts only the database username/password scheme. Airtable Does not read from it Store and validate only. The credential check accepts the static token, both OAuth 2.0 flows, and the service-account scheme. Notion Does not read from it Store and validate only. The credential check accepts the static token and both OAuth 2.0 flows. AWS Bedrock Not an import source A catalog entry. No platform feature currently reads it — AI providers are configured by your platform operator, not through saved connections. Generic API Not an import source A catalog entry for any other service. No platform feature currently reads it.

Ten schemes are available. The form's guidance: prefer OAuth, OIDC, IAM, or federated schemes when the provider supports them; static tokens are the fallback. Scheme Notes Static API / bearer token The default. The only scheme the Coda import check accepts. Database username/password The only scheme the MySQL live-import check accepts. OAuth 2.0 authorization code Accepted by the Airtable and Notion credential checks. OAuth 2.0 client credentials Accepted by the Airtable and Notion credential checks. OIDC federation May be saved with No stored secret. SAML SSO / federation May be saved with No stored secret. AWS IAM role / STS May be saved with No stored secret. IAM database authentication May be saved with No stored secret. Kerberos May be saved with No stored secret. Service account Accepted by the Airtable credential check.

The backend names where the secret value lives. The connection's Secret ref field holds the pointer into that place — never the value. Backend What the reference is Read at use time? Environment variable The name of an environment variable on the platform server — uppercase letters, digits, and underscores. The default backend. Saving is refused if the reference does not look like a variable name. Yes. Setting the variable's value is operator work. AWS Secrets Manager The secret's identifier in AWS Secrets Manager. Optional non-secret details on the connection can select a region, a specific secret version, or one field inside a JSON secret. Yes, fetched server-side. No stored secret Nothing. Allowed only for the five federated schemes marked above, where the platform's own runtime identity carries authentication. Saving is refused for any other scheme. Resolves to no secret material. HashiCorp Vault An identifier in Vault. No — the platform does not read secrets from this backend; validation reports the connection as unavailable. GCP Secret Manager An identifier in GCP Secret Manager. No — same as Vault. Two further save-time guards apply everywhere: a reference may not embed a user:password@ address form, and the connection's details area refuses credential-like keys (passwords, tokens, API keys) outright — details are for non-secret values such as a host name or a region.

Status Meaning Needs review The starting status of every new connection. Features will not use it, and validation reports it as not allowed. Active The only status features use. Disabled Kept on record; features will not use it.

The Allowed features field is a list of feature keys, for example ["import_wizard_coda"]. A feature resolves a connection only when its key is listed — an Active connection with an empty list is usable by nothing and fails validation. The import feature keys: Feature key Used by import_wizard_coda Coda imports — background runs and source-row loading. import_wizard_mysql MySQL live-database imports. import_wizard_airtable The Airtable credential check (no import path). import_wizard_notion The Notion credential check (no import path).

Validate your connections: open the list, select the connections, and run Validate selected credential references. The result message reports how many resolved and how many failed; each connection's last validation time, outcome, and failure class are recorded on its form. Validation does not use the credential and does not count as usage. Make a connection usable: a feature uses a connection only when all three hold — status is Active, the feature's key appears in Allowed features, and the scheme is one the feature accepts. A new connection starts at Needs review, so reviewing and activating it is your explicit step. Run a live MySQL read in the background: with an Active MySQL connection in place, the import wizard's first step has a Saved MySQL connection for background reads field — enter the connection's label there. It is required only when reading a live database in the background; an inline read takes the credentials directly and does not keep them. Run a Coda import in the background: a background Coda import requires a saved connection name — the wizard refuses to queue one without it. Inline Coda reads use a one-time API key instead. At final import and on re-import, when a saved connection is present the platform loads source rows through it. Scope a connection narrowly: list only the feature keys the connection should serve. The wizard names the reason when a connection is refused — not active, not allowed for that import feature, or an unsupported scheme for that source.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A connection your platform operator created for you fails validation New connections start at Needs review; only Active connections resolve Set the status to Active, confirm Allowed features lists the right key, and validate again. Validation result is "not allowed" The feature key is missing from Allowed features, or the list is empty Add the matching feature key from the table above. Validation result is "unavailable" The environment variable is not set on the platform server, the cloud secret store could not be reached, or the backend is one the platform does not read (HashiCorp Vault, GCP Secret Manager) Contact your platform operator — the secret's storage place needs attention, or the connection should move to a supported backend. Saving is refused: the reference "must reference an env var name … not a raw value" A secret value was pasted into Secret ref on an environment-variable connection Enter the variable's name; ask your platform operator to set its value on the server. Saving is refused: details "cannot persist credential-like keys" A password, token, or key was placed in the connection's details area Move the secret behind a secret backend; keep only non-secret values (host, database, region) in the details. The wizard says the import "supports these auth schemes only" The connection's scheme is not one that source accepts Coda imports accept the static API / bearer token scheme only; MySQL live imports accept database username/password only. Adjust the connection's scheme. A MySQL connection is refused over its details The details must include a host (or socket) and a database name Add host (or unix_socket) and database to the connection's details; username, port, and ssl are optional. There is no add or delete control on the screen Creating and deleting saved connections is operator-mediated Contact your platform operator. A Coda or saved-database re-import fails with a credential error The connection's secret reference no longer resolves See the credential rows in Data Import Wizard troubleshooting; validate the connection here first to read the recorded failure class.

Data Import Wizard — the feature that reads through saved connections; its troubleshooting covers credential errors as they appear mid-import. Telemetry — import telemetry records that a saved connection was used, never its reference or secret. Platform-level operations — creating and deleting connections, placing secret values, and configuring AI providers are handled by your platform operator.

The Data Import Wizard brings source data into your environment without bypassing review. It reads an uploaded source (an Excel workbook, a MySQL dump or live connection, a set of CSV files, or a Coda document), proposes how each table and column should land in your environment, routes every proposal through a two-step approval, and writes records only after you start the final import. Read this when you bring in a new corpus, re-import a source whose shape you already know, or a researcher reports that an import did the wrong thing. The wizard is the supported path for getting data into an environment. For repair work or bulk operations outside the wizard, contact your platform operator.

Ordered roughly by what you touch first. Guided entry from the sidebar — Imports & AI → Imports opens the first wizard step with your recent imports and saved setups. All imports lists every import, with shortcut buttons (Start import, Excel, Database, CSV files, Coda) in its top-right toolbar. Pending Review is a flat queue of suggestions awaiting review across imports. Import status (/admin/imports/) lists every import — including background uploads — with its current stage and a Resume link back into it. Maturity: Active. Limit: the plain admin "Add" form does not read a source — always start from an upload route. At-a-glance import state on the list — the All imports list carries a Current stop column and a per-import proposal tally (approved / rejected / pending / total), so you can see which imports are waiting on you and at which step (for example, "Stage 4 — Needs choices") without opening each one. Maturity: Active. Excel upload — a project name, an optional description, and an .xlsx file. Files up to 5 MB import inline; larger files, up to 100 MB, run in the background. Maturity: Active. MySQL upload — two modes: a dump file (.sql or .sql.gz; 50 MB inline, up to 500 MB in the background) or a live connection address with optional credentials. Live-connection reads always run inline, and the credentials are held only for that request — they are never saved. A saved connection can reference a secret kept in the platform's managed secret store instead of carrying a password; the secret is resolved at run time. Maturity: Active. CSV upload — several files in one submission; each file becomes a table named after the file. Limits: 10 MB per file and 30 MB total inline; 50 MB per file and 250 MB total in the background. The wizard can suggest connections between files by matching overlapping values; these suggestions are deliberately more cautious than connections declared inside a single workbook. Maturity: Active. Coda upload — a project name, the Coda document name, a one-time API key, and an optional subset of tables. The key is held only for the upload/materialize request path and is not saved with the import or job payload. If rows have already been retained for replay, a retry can use that retained copy; otherwise the wizard asks for the key again instead of failing silently. Maturity: Active. Background imports — an upload that exceeds its inline limit is refused before processing, with a message telling you the limit. Resubmit with the background option: a status page refreshes while the job runs and links to the wizard when it is ready. You can close the tab; the job keeps working. Maturity: Active. Six-step review flow — Step 1 Bring in your data, Step 2 Here's what we found, Step 3 What we'll do, Step 4 A few things to confirm, Step 5 Practice run, Step 6 Ready when you are. Nothing is written to your environment until you press Start import in Step 6. Maturity: Active. Autonomy setting (Step 3) — "How involved do you want to be?": Hands off, Stay informed, Ask if unsure, or Confirm everything, saved per import. The setting controls how many of the wizard's confident structural readings are applied for you — always with an undo window — versus held for your decision. At the two most hands-off settings this can include a change to an existing setup that has no imported records yet; at Ask if unsure, only additive changes the wizard is highly confident about move ahead; Confirm everything holds every suggestion for you. High-risk suggestions and restructure suggestions wait for explicit review whatever the setting. For a first import of an unfamiliar corpus, use Confirm everything when table meanings must be checked one by one before the final import. Maturity: Active. Suggestion cards with reasons (Step 3) — each card shows what would change, how confident the wizard is in plain words (Very confident, Confident, Worth a look, Needs your eyes), the evidence behind the reading, and plain-language reasons. No raw percentage is shown. Respond with Looks good, or open Change this to say why. A table-meaning card carries its own picker in the card itself (see below). Card actions are protected form submissions; a stray link click cannot alter a suggestion. Maturity: Active. Change a table's meaning — a table-meaning card reads as four things: your own table name with its row count, the meaning it is read as, what that meaning is, and what the source says links to the table. The meaning itself is the picker — choose another and its definition follows your choice. Choosing one opens a short confirmation beside the card's actions — Read this table as Annotation? — with an optional Why box, and Read it that way applies the change and your reason together. Where the wizard weighed other meanings for the table, the card names them under Also considered, and it states what the choice decides. The suggestion retargets cleanly: risk is re-assessed against the new meaning, and every card, preview, and the final import follow the correction. A card carrying an older unapplied change request shows a "requested, not applied yet" banner with Apply change and Keep original actions, and a plain confirmation cannot approve a stale meaning. Maturity: Active. Limit: a completed import is closed — to reinterpret its tables, start a new import. What you said about this — a reason you give when asking for a change is kept with that match and shown back on its card, under its own heading and set apart from the wizard's own account of what it saw in your data. The same block does this in Step 3 and Step 4, so a reason reads the same way wherever you gave it. It stays there after the match is decided, so anyone revisiting the decision — including you, later — can see why it was made. Maturity: Active. Limit: the reason travels with this import; a later re-import carries your decision forward, not the words explaining it. Undo for automatic decisions — when the wizard applies a suggestion for you, a toast names exactly what was decided, and "applied for you" always names its cause. The undo window pauses while you hover or focus the toast, and the paused time genuinely extends the window. When a setting change applies several suggestions at once, you get one combined toast with Undo all. Maturity: Active. Limit: undo reverses review decisions before the final import; it does not undo records written in Step 6. Confirmations that are remembered (Step 4) — your answers to the wizard's clarifying questions are saved with the import. Where retained source rows are available, a "show me" view displays the surrounding source cells so you can answer from evidence rather than memory. Later imports of the same shape reuse your answers. Maturity: Active. Practice run (Step 5) — a full dry run before anything is saved. Issues are grouped by cause rather than by row, with a good/warning/error breakdown, and each group links back to the review queue or exports a summary of the affected rows. Maturity: Active. Draft reader preview — an admin-only preview of how approved rows will read on your public entry surface, rendered by the same machinery the real import uses. Restructured fields are marked in the preview, including "keep both" companion fields. The preview publishes nothing. Maturity: Active. Saved setups and format recognition — a successful import creates or updates a saved setup. When you upload a familiar shape again, Step 2 shows "We've seen this format before" with a confidence figure, and every choice stays editable. Saved setups store structure, never your source rows. Maturity: Active. Decisions carried forward on re-import — when you re-import over already-imported data, decisions that are structurally unchanged from your prior import are carried forward instead of re-asked. Anything new, changed, or ambiguous goes back to review; uncertainty always routes to review, never to a silent carry-over. Maturity: Active. Two-step approval with risk levels — every suggestion gets a risk level (low, medium, or high) with visible reasons. A suggestion held for review goes through two steps: a reviewer approves first, then an administrator applies. When your autonomy setting lets a confident structural reading move ahead for you, the decision is system-mediated and the undo window applies; for audit-sensitive imports, ask your platform operator to check the auto-apply markers and status reason rather than relying only on a visible reviewer name. Suggestions refined by AI always go through human review; AI never changes your environment directly. If the risk level changed while a suggestion sat in review — because the environment changed around it — apply is blocked until you read and acknowledge the new level. Maturity: Active. Needs revision — a reviewer can send a suggestion back with a required note instead of rejecting it outright. The suggestion blocks the final import until it is revised, and the note travels with it. Maturity: Active. Restructure suggestions — the wizard can propose shape improvements it detects in your source: a lookup column becomes a picker field, a supporting table becomes the option list behind a picker, or sibling language columns merge into one multilingual field. You choose Keep both (the original field plus a typed companion field) or Replace, under Choose how it comes in where the source already declares the shape and See what this change would do where accepting alters it. The card heads its bullets "How this column works" in the first case and "What changes if you accept" in the second, so a declared link is not described as a change it does not make. Beside the chooser, Add a note records a comment for review; it corrects nothing on its own. Approved restructures are carried through the final import. These suggestions never apply automatically, whatever their confidence. Maturity: Active. Honest receipts, with progress still being hardened — the final run records per-table outcomes and the completion receipt leads with what happened: record and connection counts, "references not linked yet" with a per-link breakdown, and an Open your workspace action. Every table in the plan produces exactly one outcome row — "created N records", or "will create 0 records" with the reason — predicted in the practice run and confirmed after the run. The linking pass can be much longer than the table-write steps; the wait/progress view is still being hardened for that long phase. Maturity: Active. Live cold-import proof — a 2026-06-29 browser walk ran a fresh Coda import through the wizard and completed the final import into the workspace: 10 workspace tables, 10,080 records, and 29,696 relationships. The receipt led to browsable workspace tables. Maturity: Built for that import class; keep using the practice run and receipt for each new source because source shape still matters. Resolve a "nothing will import" stop from inside the wizard — when the practice run finds that your approved choices would bring in zero rows, Step 5 names the situation ("Nothing will import yet") and offers only the action it can honestly deliver for that cause, rather than a dead end: fix the conflicting columns (it deep-links you back to Step 3), return to the review queue, or align/restructure the flagged columns. You never lose your work — there is no new upload and no re-run from scratch. Maturity: Active. Keep non-standard values as-is (import as text) — when the source checks flagged a column only for advisory reasons (its values don't match the type or script the wizard expected, which can be intentional), Step 5 offers Import these as-is (keep non-standard values). The column is brought in as text with its values stored exactly as they appear — nothing is coerced or dropped. A DRY RUN card previews the change before you commit: the flagged column moves from skipped to kept, a note states the values are kept as text, a Won't touch list bounds what stays unchanged, and a seal states "No source rows are written until you run the import." This is offered only for advisory flags; a structural problem (a duplicate key, a missing column) must be corrected and is never offered as keep-as-is. If you later undo the decision, it is fully reversed — a subsequent normal approval will not silently re-apply it. Maturity: Active. Limit: a transformation history of the kept column and in-place cell correction are planned, not yet present. Import assistant chat — a chat control on each wizard step that knows where you are in the flow. It can explain what it sees and propose actions, but a proposed action is never executed until you confirm it. Each import session has a chat budget; when the budget runs out the chat pauses and every import control keeps working. Your environment's AI settings can turn the assistant off. Maturity: Active. AI refinement is optional — when no AI provider is configured for your platform, the wizard still works end to end: the structural reading produces the suggestions, and the import is marked that AI refinement was unavailable. To enable AI refinement, contact your platform operator. Maturity: Active. Efficiency tips (Step 3) — short tip cards can appear alongside suggestion cards when tips are enabled for your environment. Tips never block an action. See Efficiency Tips. Maturity: Active. Import telemetry — when capture is enabled, import steps emit operational counts that carry no source content: no rows, filenames, document or table names, credentials, or tokens. See Telemetry. Maturity: Active. Limit: collection runs in the platform; a dedicated screen for browsing these metrics is not yet available.

Start in the sidebar at Imports & AI → Imports. Step 1 shows the source choices, your recent imports, and your saved setups. The All imports list offers the same upload routes as toolbar buttons. Submit the source that matches your shape — Excel, database, CSV files, or Coda. Within the inline size limit, the wizard reads the source immediately and opens the review. Above it, choose the background option and follow the status page; it links to the wizard when the job completes. Walk the six steps. Review what was found (Step 2), decide on suggestions and set how involved you want to be (Step 3), answer the clarifying questions (Step 4), and read the practice run (Step 5). Approve in two steps. A reviewer approves each suggestion, then an administrator applies it. If the risk level shifted while the suggestion waited, read the new level and acknowledge it before applying. Start the import (Step 6). Once every suggestion is approved or rejected, Start import becomes available. If your source needs a credential to read rows at import time — a Coda key or a live database password — Step 6 asks for it again and uses it only for that request path. Read the receipt when the run completes, and use Open your workspace to see the results. If a run is interrupted, your setup, approvals, and practice run are kept; starting again resumes from the stopped table, and completed tables are not written twice. For a Coda import that already fetched its rows before being interrupted, retrying replays the saved copy of those rows and does not ask for the one-time key again; if that saved copy is unreadable, the wizard asks for the key rather than failing silently. Risk levels in plain terms: Level What it means What happens Low The change is additive — a new table meaning, a new field, or no change to anything that exists. Quick lane. Confident low-risk suggestions can move ahead for you, with undo, depending on your autonomy setting. Medium The change alters an existing setup that has no imported records yet. Held for review by default. At the two most hands-off autonomy settings, a confident structural reading at this level can also move ahead for you, with undo. High The change alters a setup that already has imported records, or removes or merges whole tables. Held for explicit confirmation even after reviewer approval. Never applied automatically. A second pair of eyes is expected.

Re-importing a source you have brought in before is a normal operation: The wizard recognizes the saved setup, carries your unchanged decisions forward, and asks only about what is new or changed. For refreshing the records themselves, the platform supports two behaviours. Edit-preserving refresh matches incoming rows to existing records by their source identity, refreshes the values the source manages, and keeps researcher edits to fields the source does not manage — the right default for routine re-runs. Full refresh wipes the existing rows and reloads from scratch — destructive to researcher edits, only for genuine start-over situations. If you are unsure which behaviour a planned re-import will use, check with your platform operator before running it.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The imports list is empty No imports have been started yet Start from Imports & AI → Imports, or use the upload buttons on the All imports toolbar. The wizard only opens for imports created through an upload. The wizard says AI suggestions were unavailable No AI provider is configured for your platform The structural reading still produced suggestions — review them as usual. To enable AI refinement, contact your platform operator. A Coda or saved-database re-import fails with a credential error The saved connection's secret reference could not be resolved Check the saved connection in your environment. If the secret is held in the platform's secret store, contact your platform operator. Several suggestion cards target the same finding Each finding should produce exactly one suggestion This should not happen. Contact your platform operator. The practice run says "Nothing will import yet" Your approved choices would bring in zero rows — a column collision, everything set aside, no importable rows, source values the checks flagged, or rows not yet attached Use the action the stop offers: fix the conflicting columns, return to review, align/restructure the flagged columns, or — for advisory flags — Import these as-is (keep non-standard values). Your work is preserved; no re-upload is needed. The final import looks paused or the wait area is blank while linking records The relationship pass can be much longer than the table-write steps on large, relationship-heavy sources, and the wait/progress view can fail to render even when backend progress data exists. Keep the page open or return later from the import list. Restart only after the run reports failure or your platform operator confirms the worker stopped. Imported workspace tables expose more columns than one source table had Table records are separated by source table, but field definitions can still be shared at the concept-family level. Review the table's visible columns and saved views before inviting researchers in. Hide irrelevant columns in the default view, and escalate if per-source-table field scoping is required.

For researchers: Adding and editing rows — what researchers see once imported data lands in the workspace. Environment admin companions: Voice and Vocabulary — the wizard's on-screen wording follows your environment's voice settings; Efficiency Tips — the Step 3 tip cards; Permissions Panel — who can review and who can apply; Telemetry — what import telemetry captures.

Serve your environment's public site from your own domain (an apex or any host outside the platform's shared wildcard). This page covers Domain settings at /app/workspace/manage/domain, reached from the workspace account menu: what you can do from it, what stays with your platform operator, and how to read each domain's progress. The former /admin/domain/ bookmark redirects to this workspace page. Permanent citation URLs stay platform-hosted regardless of the domain you serve from — a custom domain changes where readers browse, never what published work is cited as.

Request a domain — enter the hostname you want (for example atlas.example.org). The platform records the request and issues a DNS ownership proof: one TXT record, whose name and value the screen shows for each requested host · Maturity: Built. Ownership proof by DNS TXT record — publish the shown value at the shown name (a dedicated _ke-verify.<host> label — the host itself is CNAME'd to the platform edge, and a CNAME cannot coexist with a TXT record). Nothing routes until ownership is verified, by design: an unverified host has no routing row at all · Maturity: Built. Progress ladder per domain — each requested host shows where it stands: awaiting DNS proof → ownership verified — awaiting TLS → TLS provisioned — awaiting reachability → live. A domain only reads "live" once TLS is provisioned and the host actually serves · Maturity: Built. Operator-side completion — verification, TLS provisioning, and activation are platform-operator actions; this screen deliberately has no control for them. You publish the record and your operator completes the chain · Maturity: Built.

Check entitlement — custom domains are a subscription feature. If the screen says they are not enabled for this environment, ask your platform operator to enable them; the request form appears once they do. Request — enter the hostname and press Request, or press Enter from the hostname field. A refusal (a malformed or already-requested hostname) comes back as a plain message without clearing what you entered. Publish the TXT record — copy the shown record name and value into your DNS. Hand off — tell your platform operator the record is published; they verify ownership and provision TLS. Watch the domain's stage line move to live. If you start a request and navigate to another workspace page before submitting it, the workspace asks whether to discard the draft. Cancel keeps both the page and the hostname you entered.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The request form is missing; the screen says custom domains are not enabled The environment lacks the subscription entitlement Ask your platform operator to enable custom domains for this environment. A request is refused with "already requested" or similar The hostname is malformed or already has a pending/verified row Check the domains list below the form — the host may already be in progress. The domain has been "awaiting DNS proof" for a long time The TXT record is not published at the exact name shown, or DNS has not propagated Verify the record name is the dedicated _ke-verify.<host> label (not the host itself) and the value matches exactly; then ask your operator to re-check. Ownership verified but not live TLS is not yet provisioned, or the host is not reachable through the platform edge This is the operator-side half of the chain — no action available here; ask your platform operator for status. You cannot open the page The acting account lacks the environment administrator role Ask an environment administrator to act — see Permissions Panel.

Roles: Permissions Panel — the administrator role this screen requires. Citations stay put: Standards and Citations — why permanent citation URLs are platform-hosted regardless of your serving domain.

Tips are short, contextual suggestions the platform shows researchers while they work — in the review step of the import wizard and in the workspace — pointing out a faster way to do what they are already doing, or a field worth filling in. Tips are advisory: they never change data and never block anyone. As environment administrator, you decide whether tips appear in your environment at all, and the names tips use for your record types and fields come from your environment's vocabulary. Read this page when deciding whether to leave tips on at onboarding, when a researcher reports an unwanted or oddly worded suggestion, or when a kind of tip stops appearing.

Environment-wide tips switch — one setting turns tips on or off for your whole environment. It is on by default for new environments; off means no tips appear anywhere, regardless of any other setting. Maturity: Active. Tips during import review — when a researcher makes the same correction repeatedly while reviewing an import, a tip suggests fixing the underlying rule once instead of correcting the remaining rows by hand. Tip cards appear beside the correction cards in the review step. Maturity: Active. Tips in the workspace — when a selected record has noticeably fewer filled fields than similar records in your environment, a tip names a field worth adding. Maturity: Active. Confidence-tiered display — the most confident suggestions appear directly beside the researcher's work; middling ones wait under a collapsed "More suggestions" heading; anything below the confidence bar is not shown at all. Maturity: Active. Wording through your vocabulary — tip sentences are written by the platform, and the names they use for your record types and fields resolve through your environment's vocabulary. You adjust those names through vocabulary entries; you do not edit tip text directly. Maturity: Active. Per-family acceptance figures — the platform keeps aggregate figures per kind of tip — how often that kind was shown and how researchers responded — for your environment only, over a rolling 30-day window. Individual researcher actions are not reported. Maturity: Built; a self-service view of these figures is not yet available — contact your platform operator if you need them. Automatic quiet-down — a kind of tip your researchers consistently pass over can pause itself in your environment. The pause requires sustained low uptake (around four weeks) and a minimum number of researcher responses, so a quiet week does not silence a useful tip. Your platform operator is notified when a kind of tip pauses. Maturity: Built. Separate measurement switch — whether tip activity is measured is a separate per-environment setting from whether tips display, so tips can be shown without their activity being measured. When tips are off, nothing is shown, so there is no tip activity to measure. Measurement records which tips appeared and how researchers responded, without recording who. Maturity: Built. See Telemetry for what your environment records.

Decide at onboarding: tips are on by default for a new environment. Review how tips will read to your researchers — the record-type and field names come from your vocabulary (see Voice and Vocabulary) — and either leave tips on or have them switched off until your vocabulary is ready. Turn tips off for your environment: the environment-wide setting lives on your environment's platform record — contact your platform operator to change it. Once tips are off, no new tips are served anywhere; anything already on a researcher's screen clears the next time the page or wizard step loads. Change how a tip is worded: adjust the matching vocabulary entry, and the new name appears the next time the tip is shown. If the problem is in the sentence around the names rather than the names themselves, contact your platform operator. When a kind of tip goes quiet: this may be the automatic quiet-down. Re-enabling a quieted kind of tip is not self-service — contact your platform operator.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Researchers see no tips even though tips are switched on No tip pattern currently applies — tips fire only after repeated same-shape corrections during import review, or when a record clearly lags similar records — or a kind of tip has been quieted Tips are deliberately conservative; silence usually means no pattern was found. If a kind of tip that used to appear has stopped, contact your platform operator to confirm whether it was quieted. The import review step shows no tips panel Nothing cleared the confidence bar for that session Nothing to fix — low-confidence suggestions are held back by design, and the panel does not render when there is nothing to show. A researcher reports an unwanted or oddly worded suggestion The tip draws your record-type and field names from your environment's vocabulary, and the entry it found reads poorly in context Adjust the matching vocabulary entry — see Voice and Vocabulary. If the wording problem is in the surrounding sentence, contact your platform operator. A kind of tip stopped appearing after weeks of normal use It may have paused automatically because researchers consistently passed it over Contact your platform operator to review and re-enable it. Consider whether different vocabulary wording would help it land better.

Researcher tier: Tips and guidance — what researchers see and how tips behave for them. Tenant admin companions: Voice and Vocabulary — controls the names tip wording draws on; Data Import Wizard — the review step is the main place tips appear; Telemetry — what your environment measures and records. For platform-side questions — switching tips or tip measurement on or off, re-enabling a quieted kind of tip, requesting your environment's acceptance figures, or anything affecting other environments — contact your platform operator.

The Entry Surface role configuration is the record that defines a public reading surface for your environment: which of your records become public pages, what the public route looks like, how the index is ordered, and what title each page carries. It is the configuration behind the readiness review — the review covers the controls that would go public, while this record declares the surface itself. Read this when you want to understand what a public Entry role controls before asking your platform operator to change one, when you are reviewing why a record did or did not appear on the public surface, or when you need to read the meaning of the fields on the role configuration record. The companion review surface is Entry Surface Readiness.

The role configuration record lives in your environment's admin area and is owned by your environment — your platform operator's seeding never overwrites a role you have edited. Inspecting a role and understanding its settings is something you do yourself. Applying a change so that it takes effect on the public surface — launching a role, promoting public controls, or rebuilding published pages — is operator-mediated. Recording a readiness decision does not promote anything, and editing a role configuration does not by itself republish the public surface. The safe sequence is: understand the record (yourself), then ask your platform operator to apply and rebuild. The fields below are written so you can read and reason about a role before that conversation.
A single role configuration declares one public reading surface. Its fields fall into five groups, matching how they are arranged in the admin record.

Role key — the platform-stable name for the role, such as primary. It is internal and stable; it does not change when you rename the public-facing noun. Display noun — the reader-facing noun for what this role publishes (for example, "entry" or "record"). This is the word readers see, separate from the internal role key. Active — whether the role is in use. An inactive role declares no public surface.

The selector decides which of your records this role publishes, without reclassifying those records: Archetype — the record family (the kind of records, such as people or works) the role draws from. Canonical type — an optional narrowing to a single type within that family. Left empty, the role takes the whole family. Primary selector — marks this selector as the primary one for the role. Allow multiple primary selectors — when off, a role must have exactly one primary selector; turning it on lets a role publish from more than one primary selector. Blast radius of editing a live role's selector. A selector edit applies lazily. Already-published pages keep serving their last good version until the next publish or rebuild. At the next rebuild, any record the edited selector no longer matches is removed from the public surface — whether or not that record is itself still published. An invalid selector set fails before any pages are written, so a bad selector cannot silently corrupt the surface; it stops the rebuild instead. Because a selector edit can remove live public pages, treat selector changes as the change you most want to review with your platform operator before it is applied.

These three settings are dotted source paths (for example, data.title) that point at a value in each record. They derive the public-facing identity of each page: Slug source — derives the public route for each record. A record where the slug source resolves to nothing has no public identity and is skipped by the page builder — it will not get a public page. Sort key source — derives the value the public surface sorts records by. Index key source — derives the value the browsable public index is keyed on. The public route for a page takes the form /entry/<role key>/<route reference>, where the route reference comes from the slug source.

The rules group carries finer selector and display settings: Selector rules — additional selector and display rules. Two keys you will encounter: display_label_source sets which value becomes the public page title, and seed records how the default for the role was derived (it documents the starting point, so you can see whether a setting is a seeded default or your own edit). Route aliases — additional route segments the surface accepts for this role, for example an older path a reader might still have bookmarked. These are accepted routes only; they do not change which record family a record belongs to. Search engine — an optional search-engine choice for this role. Left as the default, the role uses your environment's search profile. The other choices select a specific search backend for this role only; the role key stays local to your environment.

Config version — bump this when the public Entry Surface behavior for the role changes. Changing it signals that stale published pages should rebuild at the next publish. Record version and content hash — read-only bookkeeping the platform maintains for the record.

Editing the role configuration record stores your intent; it does not redraw the public pages on its own. When a published surface is rebuilt, a change to the role's selector, public identity sources, display noun, route aliases, selector rules, config version, or active flag is what causes the builder to recompute the affected pages. A record whose slug source resolves to nothing is skipped; a record the selector no longer matches is removed. Your platform operator runs the rebuild — see the operator-mediated note above.
documents.s: How a change reaches the public surface

documents.t: For a selector change: confirm which records currently match and which would match after the edit, because records that stop matching are removed from the public surface at the next rebuild. For a public identity change: confirm the dotted source path resolves to a value on the records you expect to publish; a path that resolves empty means no public page for that record. For a route alias change: confirm you are adding a route a reader might use, not asserting a record type. Before launch: confirm the readiness review reads clean — see Entry Surface Readiness — then hand off to your platform operator to apply and rebuild.
documents.s: What to check before requesting a change

documents.t: Entry Surface Readiness — the companion review surface, where you review and record decisions about the public controls a role would expose. Public reader — what researchers and external readers see once a public Entry surface launches.

Status (slice 8): the standalone readiness panel and its /app/admin/entry-surface-readiness/ endpoint were retired with the /app/admin/ shell. The readiness audit itself — the report engine, the stored review decisions, and the operator CLI — remains live substrate; only the prototype review surface was removed. A tenant review UI is being redesigned in the KE-admin tier; until it ships, readiness review runs through your platform operator as described below.

Before your environment exposes a public Entry surface — the published layer external readers will see — the readiness review lets you review the filter ("facet") and autocomplete controls that would become public, record a decision about each one, and confirm or defer each candidate. Read this when preparing for a public launch, when a readiness report flags a compact-control warning, or when activating an additional public role. The review stores review state only, never applies anything. Recording a decision stores review state for your environment; promoting a public control or confirming your environment's search configuration is a separate, explicit step performed with your platform operator.

Readiness report — for every active public Entry role in your environment, the report lists the reviewed filter and autocomplete fields, candidate fields, compact-control warnings, blockers, and all stored decisions, along with how many records were sampled to produce it. Maturity: Active. Viewing the report requires admin access in your environment. Durable review decisions — each decision is stored with its action, your reason (required, up to 500 characters), your username, the time, and a snapshot of the evidence the report showed you. Maturity: Active. A decision is a review checkpoint; it does not change the public surface itself. Fixed decision actions — review candidate before promotion; choose shorter public label; defer candidate with reason; defer public control with reason; acknowledge long-value exclusion. The action list is fixed; the reason is free text. Maturity: Active. Environment isolation — the report and your decisions are always scoped to the environment you are signed in to. You cannot read another environment's report or record decisions for it. Maturity: Active. Durable, re-reportable decisions — a recorded decision is confirmed back with its stored details, and the next readiness report includes it alongside confirmation that your environment's search configuration was untouched. Maturity: Active.

Until the KE-admin tier review UI ships, the readiness review is an operator-run workflow rather than a self-service page: Request the report. Your platform operator runs the readiness audit for your environment (the audit_entry_surface_facets operator command in its machine-readable --json mode — the mode whose output carries every stored decision with its action, reason, actor, and time) and shares the report: overall status — "Ready for scalar probe" once at least one public role has reviewed single-value filter fields, "Needs review" otherwise — plus each role's blockers, reviewed fields, candidate fields, compact-control warnings, and every previously recorded decision. The report is read-only: producing it never writes tenant configuration and never marks a search profile ratified. Review compact-control warnings. The report flags fields where some values are too long to show in a compact public filter control. Decide, per field, which action applies (the fixed action list above) and give a reason for each decision. Record decisions through your operator. Send your decisions — field, action, reason — to your platform operator, who records each one against your environment (the record_entry_surface_decision operator command, which stores the decision in your name). Each stored decision is durable and appears in the next report; recording a different decision for the same field replaces the earlier one. Hand off for launch. When the report reads clean and your environment is ready, your platform operator performs the public launch. Recording decisions is the review checkpoint that precedes the launch — it is not the launch itself.
documents.s: Usability — how you use it today

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Your review request is refused Your account does not have admin access in this environment Ask an existing environment administrator to grant admin access, or route the review through an admin account. Recording a decision fails with a validation message The reason is missing, or the chosen action is not valid for that field Your operator relays the server's message. Add a reason, or choose one of the actions valid for that field. The report shows no active public Entry roles Your environment does not have a public Entry role configured yet Public Entry roles are set up as part of preparing your environment for launch. Contact your platform operator. The report reads clean but the public Entry surface has not appeared Recording decisions does not promote public controls or launch the surface Confirm with your platform operator that the launch step was run. The readiness review is a checkpoint only. The report's "ratification unchanged" line worried you This is by design — recording decisions never changes your environment's search configuration Confirming the search configuration is a separate explicit operation performed with your platform operator. The line exists so you can verify nothing changed as a side effect of your review. You need to undo a recorded decision Decisions are durable review state Record a new decision for the same field. It replaces the earlier one; the report then shows the latest decision with its reason and time.
Public reader — what researchers and external readers see once your public Entry surface launches.

A small set of defaults live on your environment as a whole, rather than on any one import, field, or record. Each one shapes how a recurring activity starts out: how involved you are by default when new data arrives, how much AI assistance a single import-wizard session may use, and whether your environment's not-yet-reviewed vocabulary takes part in cross-environment summaries. Read this when you want to understand what these environment-wide defaults do, what their limits are, and who can change them today. These three settings are not edited from your own admin interface. They sit on the environment record that the platform operator manages, so changing any of them is an operator-mediated action — you decide what you want and ask your platform operator to apply it. The sections below mark each setting accordingly, so you know what to request and what to expect once it changes.

Default import autonomy — your environment carries a default answer to the import wizard's "How involved do you want to be?" question, used to pre-select the starting autonomy level for every new import. The four levels are Hands off, Stay informed, Ask if unsure, and Confirm everything; the environment default is Stay informed unless your operator sets it otherwise. The default only chooses the starting point — you can still change the level on any individual import, and your per-import choice always wins. Maturity: Active. Limit: this default is applied by your platform operator; there is no self-serve control for it in your admin interface today. AI chat session budget — the import wizard's assistant chat runs against a per-session token budget drawn from this environment-wide figure. The default is 50,000 tokens per session, and the platform allows a value up to 500,000. A value of zero means no cap — the chat is unbudgeted. When a session reaches the budget, the chat pauses for that session; every import control keeps working, so the pause never blocks the import itself. Maturity: Active. Limit: this budget governs the import-wizard assistant chat only; it is separate from the rolling budget that governs AI vocabulary-grounding suggestions, which is configured elsewhere. The figure is applied by your platform operator. Federation exposure for ungrounded vocabulary — by default, vocabulary values your environment has not yet reviewed can be included in future cross-environment summaries. Turning this off keeps your environment's not-yet-grounded values out of those summaries while your grounding work is still in progress, so only vocabulary you have reviewed represents your environment outside it. Maturity: Active. Limit: the control is on by default, applies to ungrounded values specifically, and is set by your platform operator.

None of these three settings is edited from the environment admin interface you work in day to day. To change one, decide the value you want and ask your platform operator to apply it on the environment record. Default import autonomy — if your team consistently overrides the per-import autonomy setting to the same level, that is the signal to change the environment default. Tell your operator which of the four levels you want as the starting point. The change affects only imports started afterward; imports already in progress keep the level they were given. For what each level does inside a single import, see Data Import Wizard. AI chat session budget — raise the figure if researchers report the wizard chat pausing before they are done in a session; lower it (or set zero for no cap) to suit your platform's posture. Because the budget is per session, a researcher who hits it can continue working immediately — only the chat pauses — and a fresh session starts again from the full budget. Confirm the new value with your operator. Federation exposure for ungrounded vocabulary — turn this off while your environment still has a meaningful queue of unreviewed vocabulary and you would rather that queue not represent you in cross-environment summaries. As your grounding work catches up, you can ask your operator to turn it back on. For the review work this setting interacts with, see Vocabulary Grounding.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A new import opened at an autonomy level you did not expect A new import starts at the environment default, not at the level you used last time Change the level on that import directly — your per-import choice always wins. If the default itself is wrong for your team, ask your platform operator to change the environment default. The wizard assistant chat keeps pausing before researchers finish The per-session token budget is being reached within a working session Researchers can continue — only the chat pauses, not the import. To allow more chat per session, ask your platform operator to raise the AI chat session budget (up to the platform maximum), or set it to zero to remove the cap. You cannot find a control for any of these settings in your admin interface These three settings live on the environment record managed by the platform operator, not in your admin surface Decide the value you want and ask your platform operator to apply it. There is no self-serve control for them today. Not-yet-reviewed vocabulary appears to be included in cross-environment summaries Federation exposure for ungrounded vocabulary is on by default Ask your platform operator to turn it off while your grounding work is in progress; turn it back on once your review queue is caught up.

Data Import Wizard — where the per-import autonomy setting and the assistant chat appear, and what each autonomy level does inside one import. Vocabulary Grounding — the review work that the federation-exposure setting interacts with, and the separate AI controls for grounding suggestions.

Every field in every table of your environment is described by one field definition: what kind of value the field holds, what it is called, where its data is read from, who can see it on published pages, how a connecting field finds the record it points to (its resolution rule — internally, a "resolver"), and how searches treat its script and accents. This page is the reference for those definitions. Read it when adding a field, choosing between a link and a lookup, restricting a field from published pages, or tuning accent behavior for a multilingual corpus. A field definition is configuration, not code. Renaming a field, reordering the field list, or restricting a field's visibility is an edit you make in the workspace, and it takes effect without platform changes.

A single definition drives the same field everywhere it appears · Maturity: Active. In the workspace — the definition is the column and the form field. Adding a definition adds a column to the table grid and a field to the editing form. The displayed name, the field description (the tooltip researchers see), and the field's position in the list all come from the definition. In editing — the field kind decides which editor control researchers get, and fields marked required gate the completion of a new row. Date fields use native date inputs in workspace editing surfaces and date-aware filtering in the table. In search matching — the definition's language settings (script, accent folding, language, multilingual) shape how searches match the field's values. Whether the field is searched, faceted, or suggested at all is a separate set of controls — see Making fields searchable. On published pages — the field's visibility level decides whether it appears on published pages; its display name and position carry over when it does.

Every field has exactly one kind · Maturity: Active. Kind Holds Plain text A text value Rich text Formatted text with a full text editor Number A numeric value, displayed per its numeric format Date A calendar date, edited with a native date input and filtered by calendar date Boolean Yes / no Select (single) One value from the field's option list Select (multi) Several values from the field's option list Relation A live link to one or more records in another table Lookup A read-only value pulled through a link field Media A reference to a media item The kind decides which detail settings apply (formats, roles, options — see below). Definitions are validated when saved: settings that do not fit the field's kind are rejected with a validation message rather than silently ignored. Changing a text-shaped timestamp column to Date runs the platform's explicit conversion path. Values that fit are normalized and counted as converted; values that do not fit remain raw and are marked for correction. The workspace shows that report. If at least one cell was rewritten, the conversion cannot be undone from local field-definition history and that table's Undo/Redo bucket is cleared.

Rich-text fields use one editor in both its popup and fullscreen presentations · Maturity: Built. Researchers can write headings and ordinary text, lists, links, callouts, tables, code, mentions, footnotes, equations, and accessible figures chosen from existing image media. The complete researcher workflow is Write formatted text. Link, equation, and figure forms use explicit Apply and Cancel actions. While one of those forms is open, document Save and popup/fullscreen changes wait for it. Ctrl+S or Cmd+S applies a valid focused form before saving; an incomplete form remains open so its draft is not silently discarded. Existing links offer Copy, Edit, and Remove. Edit and Remove participate in the editor's Undo and Redo history; copying a URL does not create an undo step. This history covers content in the open editor, not field-definition changes, publishing or unpublishing, or media attachment operations elsewhere in the workspace. Viewing is read-only. Switching to it cancels an unapplied contextual draft and hides block gutters and other mutation controls. Saving updates the workspace rich-text value; it does not publish the record. Publication remains a separate operation that creates the public snapshot. A mention is masked when its target is not publicly available, and a figure appears publicly only when its selected image media is also admitted to publication.

Source path — each ordinary field names the place its values are read from in your environment's record store (a path such as data.title). Fields added in the workspace default to a path derived from the field key. The source path belongs to your source: every re-import refreshes it, so a hand-edit to the path does not survive the next re-import. Maturity: Active. Field key and label — the field key is the field's stable identity. It survives source renames and label changes; renaming a field's displayed name never touches the key. Labels for imported fields default to your source's own column names, verbatim — your renames are then preserved. Maturity: Active. Imported or workspace-added — fields arrive through import or are added directly in the workspace. Field keys beginning with x_ mark a field as an environment extension. The table's Details view badges each field's capabilities — multilingual, linkable, rtl/script, lookup, and rich text. It does not badge a field's scope or provenance: a field's scope is not something the platform can read from the field's name, so it is not asserted on the badge row. Maturity: Active. What a re-import can and cannot change — every setting on a definition falls into one of three behaviors · Maturity: Active: Refreshed from source — source path, storage layer (which internal store holds the field's values), and connection rules. The source is the truth; re-imports overwrite these. Filled once if empty — field kind, script, language, multilingual, position, and choice options. Detection and import fill blanks; they never overwrite a value that is already set. Yours after creation — display name, field description, required, accent folding, formats and roles, formula templates, link and lookup configuration, and standards declarations. No automatic process overwrites these; they survive every re-import.
documents.s: Where a field's data comes from

documents.t: When a field points at records in another table, its definition records how the connection is resolved — the rule the platform follows, each time a record is read, to turn the stored value into the connected record · Maturity: Active. Direct — no connection; the value is read as-is. The default for ordinary fields. Foreign-key walk — follows a true foreign-key relationship carried over from your source database. String match — for a soft foreign key: no declared relationship exists in the source, but a value in this field equals a value in a named column of the target table. The rule names the two columns. Composed — multi-step or computed matching, performed by a named function from the platform's function library with parameters — for example, matching the part of a value before a comma against a bibliography table. Choosing one for a soft foreign key: when two tables relate only by matching values, the rule is string match. When the match needs computation first — splitting, prefixes, normalization — it is a composed rule. Connection rules are established during import analysis. The analyzer detects candidate connections from your data's structure and from value overlap between tables; an AI assistant proposes a rule only where the analysis is uncertain; a person approves before anything is written. From then on the rule runs identically on every read — no AI is involved when records are read. Re-imports refresh these rules from the source's structure; correcting one by hand outside an import is operator-mediated.

Each field carries one of three visibility levels · Maturity: Active. Public — the field appears on published pages. This is the default for every field, so published pages are unchanged until you restrict something. Workspace — the field stays inside your environment's workspace and never reaches published pages. Private — the field is visible to its owner only. You set visibility per field on the workspace Publish view, with a three-way control next to each field. The choice saves per field as you set it; publishing changes then rebuilds every entry in the table, applying the current visibility. Because the filter is applied when entries are built for publication, a newly restricted field disappears from already-published pages when those entries are next published. The researcher-tier walkthrough is The Publish view.

Per-field language settings control how searches match the field's text · Maturity: Active. Script — the field's dominant writing system (for example latin, greek, arabic), detected automatically from content. Empty until detection has run; you can override it per field. Accent folding — on by default: searches match the field accent-insensitively, on both the stored text and what is typed. Turn it off for fields where a diacritic is part of the letter's identity — Scandinavian å versus a, Vietnamese tone marks, Turkish dotted and dotless i, or a critical edition whose polytonic accents distinguish words. Applies to text fields, plain and rich. Once you set it, the choice is yours; no automatic process overwrites it. Language — the field's language code (for example el, grc, ar), detected automatically. You can override it; while it is empty, the script setting stands in for language-based defaults.

A text field can be set to hold more than one value per record — one for each language, register, script, edition, or calendar (or a custom kind of your own) · Maturity: Built. All the values land in one searchable entry, so a search matches the record no matter which value carries the match. Two parts of the field definition govern this, and they are independent: Field definition (the schema window) ├─ This column's language & script ← ONE language + script for the whole column │ Language code: [ grc ] (a single-value modifier on the column) │ Script: [ greek ] │ └─ Multiple values ← the column keeps a SEPARATE value per entry [✓] This column holds more than one value A separate value for each: [ Language ▾ ] (Language / Register / Script / Edition / Calendar / Custom) Allowed languages: [ GK ✕ ] [ LA ✕ ] [ AR ✕ ] ← chips: the allowed values Add a language: [________] (Add) ← type a new one; normalized to a chip There is one control for this. When you turn on This column holds more than one value, two settings appear: A separate value for each — what the values are distinguished by: Language, Register, Script, Edition, Calendar, or Custom. This choice drives the wording of the next setting and of the per-record editor (Allowed registers, + Add register, and so on). Allowed languages (the label follows the choice above) — the set of values the field accepts, shown as chips. This is a controlled, extensible picker, not a free-text list: type a value and it is added as a chip; the × on a chip removes it. Drift normalization — a typed value is normalized to a canonical short form before it joins the set, so variant spellings of the same value fold together: typing greek yields a GK chip, and GREEK and GK collapse to one entry rather than splitting the data across two headings. Researchers entering per-record values pick from this same normalized set, with a + new affordance for a value the set does not yet offer. Researchers fill the per-record values in the table cell or the record's form — see the researcher walkthrough Working in multiple scripts and languages. Right-to-left values (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu, Aramaic) render right-aligned in those editors. The researcher-facing wording avoids platform terms: the editor reads "Multiple values", "A separate value for each", and "Allowed languages", never "multikey", "key", or "kind". The kind labels (Language, Register, …) are the only domain terms shown.
documents.s: A field that holds several values

documents.t: Once a field holds more than one value per record, two more things follow from the kind you picked — where the allowed set of keys comes from, and which single value the grid and reader show for a record that has several · Maturity: Built. This active-variant rule does not reach the workspace's CSV export: exporting selected rows to CSV always writes every keyed value joined together, regardless of the column's configured strategy — a column showing one resolved variant in the grid exports all of them. (Exporting to JSON writes the row's raw stored value instead, not a rendered string at all.) Key source, by kind: Language and Script — keys are normalized against a known alias table (so equivalent forms collapse to one canonical entry — "greek", "GREEK", and "GK" all become the same key), and Script additionally checks a compact 4-letter code against the ISO 15924 script list. Beyond that, nothing is validated against a real language or script registry: an unrecognized code is trimmed and upper-cased, not rejected, and is accepted as a key like any other. Edition — when the column has no pinned allowed set (the default), keys come from the record's own linked-record connections to edition collections: the record's own edition is offered first, followed by every reference the linked collections' own rows carry, and a key added with + new outside those relations is accepted. Edition can still be given a pinned Allowed editions set in the field editor like any other kind, in which case the refusal below applies to it too. Register and Custom — keys come from your project's vocabulary, but that vocabulary is not reviewed in Vocabulary Review; see Managing the set below for where these two are actually governed. Calendar and Historical date (the temporal kind) — these two don't use the picker described in this section at all. A keyed cell for either opens a structured calendar/period editor instead, with two modes: declaring a value from scratch (start year, end year, precision, a period label), or resolving a value the platform read from free text but declined to guess at — what it detected, an optional AI suggestion, or your own entry. That second mode is the same dialog the standalone Vocabulary Review queue uses for its own per-row review, so a value can be resolved from either place. The calendar/period chooser this editor offers is seeded from the field editor's declared Allowed <kind>s list plus whatever calendar or period the record's own existing entries already carry — a calendar already present in the record's data stays selectable even when it was never declared, so declaring a set narrows what the chooser offers first without narrowing what it accepts. Allowed-set refusal: when a column has no pinned allowed set, any key is accepted — this is the default for every kind, and the normal case for Edition. Pin a specific set in the field editor's Allowed <kind>s, and typing a value outside it is refused in the per-record editor with an inline message naming the exact value and the field, for example "Slang is not one of this column's allowed registers." This refusal, and the picker that produces it, apply to Language, Script, Edition, Register, and Custom — Edition's un-pinned default reads keys from relations rather than from a declared set, but pinning still refuses like any of these. Calendar and Historical date are the exception: their structured editor never refuses an undeclared value (see above). Managing the set: while a column has no pinned allowed set, its per-record editor's picker shows a Manage <kind>s link for Register and Custom (Edition shows none either way — its default keys live in the linked collections themselves, which are already the management surface; Calendar and Historical date show no such link either, because neither uses this picker — see above). Register and Custom's link goes to the column's own field settings, because there is no review queue yet for those two categories (see Vocabulary Review's Current limits). Once a column is pinned, the Manage link disappears for every kind that has one — a pinned set is edited in the field definition itself (Allowed <kind>s), not from the per-record picker. Which value shows when a record has several: the column definition sets one active-value strategy that acts on the record's own stored variants — none of these invent a value the record doesn't already have: Show all variants joined — always joins every stored variant with a separator. Match another column in this record — reads a different, chosen column's value as the active key, and shows the one stored variant under that key. Exclude another column — reads a different, chosen column's value as the key to leave out, and shows every other stored variant, joined (for example, excluding the source-language column from a set of translations). If excluding it would leave nothing, the field renders empty rather than joining every variant, which would show the very one being excluded. Specific target <kind>s to display — filters the record's own stored variants down to an explicit picked set of keys, joined. A record with no variant in that set renders empty; it is a filter on what the record already has, not a source of values the record lacks. Fixed default <kind> — one key typed once in the field definition, applied to every record; a record with no variant under that key shows every variant joined instead. Auto-detect script from text content (Script columns only) — reads a different, chosen text column, detects the dominant Unicode script of its content, and shows the stored variant keyed to that detected script; a record with no variant under the detected key shows every variant joined instead. Match, Exclude, Target set, and Auto-detect each also offer an If nothing matches setting in the field editor (a fallback key, or "show all variants joined"). For Exclude and Target set specifically, choosing "show all variants joined" there has no effect — both always render empty on no match by design, for the reason given above, regardless of that setting. While editing this rule, the column editor previews the resolved value for the first loaded record (for example, a Greek headword resolving through its transliteration key to a Latin form) so you can see the effect before saving. Publication scope: a field that holds several values sets its Public / Workspace / Private scope the same way any field does (see Visibility above). Only a Workspace-scope field is eligible to be promoted to a public reader section when that section is first configured; a Private field is never offered for promotion, and the column editor states this plainly rather than silently leaving it out of the list.
documents.s: Where the allowed values come from, and which one the grid shows
