documents.t: Detail settings per kind · Maturity: Active: Number fields take a numeric format — integer, decimal, year, currency, percent, or duration — plus an optional decimal precision. The currency format requires an ISO currency code. Plain-text fields take a role: plain, URL, email, phone, or embed. Choice fields (single and multi select) carry their option list. Media fields declare which media kinds they accept: image, audio, video, file, or embed. Relation fields declare whether they hold one connection or many. Three field shapes derive their value rather than storing it directly: A link field (relation) holds live connections to records in other tables. The connections are stored as relationship records, not inside the record's own data. Its definition names which tables it may point to and which field of the connected record is shown as the link's display value. A lookup shows a value from the record on the other end of an existing link field. It is read-only: its definition names the link field it follows and which field on the connected record to show; nested paths and lists are supported. A lookup must always name its target field, and a field is either a link or a lookup, never both — both rules are enforced when the definition is saved. A formula field computes its value each time the record is read from a typed expression over fields, functions and bounded linked-record paths. Sentence mode can still build a composed phrase whose empty components are dropped. Computed values are not written back into source cells, and a formula field cannot also be a link or a lookup. Lookup and formula columns are read-only in the grid. To change what they show, edit the fields or linked records they derive from.
documents.s: Formats, roles, and the link / lookup / formula distinction

documents.t: Field definitions are edited in the workspace by people with field-edit permission. Administrators can also open Workspace account menu → Manage structure → Field settings to search every collection's fields from one page. Each Edit field name link opens the same field editor used by the collection table; the page does not create a second editor or a second way to save field definitions. A field that is not assigned to any collection remains discoverable through Browse all fields, including unassigned fields, which opens the retained advanced field list. Add a field: use the add-column control at the end of the table grid, or the table Details view's add-field action. The dialog asks for the field key (required, the stable identity), the kind, and the kind's detail settings. Edit a field: open the column header menu on the field's column, or use the Details view's edit action. Changing the kind of a column that already holds data is a deliberate act — review the field's values first. Require a value before activation: for a directly entered field, open Edit column, turn on Require a value before activation, and save. Drafts can still be saved while empty, but they cannot be activated until the field has a value. Formula, lookup, and linked-record fields derive their values, so the editor marks this setting as not applicable. Delete a field: from the same column header menu. Deleting removes the definition — the column and the form field — but not the stored values underneath. Re-adding a field with the same field key brings the values back. Set per-field visibility: open the Publish view, set each field's level (Public / Workspace / Private), then publish changes to rebuild the table's entries with the current visibility. Declare standards: a field definition can declare which standards its content conforms to, chosen from the platform's approved list — see Standards and Citations.

Self-serve for people with field-edit permission, in the workspace: Adding, editing, and deleting field definitions — kind, key, display name, field description, requiredness for directly entered fields, position, source path, language behavior, formats and roles, choice options, links, lookups, formulas, and standards declarations. Per-field visibility on the Publish view. Operator-mediated — contact your platform operator: Correcting a connection rule by hand outside an import. Changing a field's storage layer. The advanced administrator view also remains available for four settings that do not yet have safe self-service controls: source layer, resolver kind, arbitrary resolver details, and multiple relationship-target kinds. Field settings shows these remaining blockers rather than implying that the advanced view can already be retired. Existing field keys and collection identities are protected from raw renaming there.
documents.s: Which edits are self-serve, and which go through your operator

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix You edited a field's source path and a re-import reverted it The source path is refreshed from source on every re-import — the source is the truth for it Make the change in your source data or the import mapping; workspace edits to the source path do not survive re-import. A lookup or formula column cannot be edited row by row Lookup and formula values are derived, not stored Edit the linked record (for a lookup) or the fields the formula combines. You set a field to Workspace or Private, but it still shows on a published page Visibility is applied when entries are rebuilt for publication Open the Publish view and publish changes for the table; the rebuild applies the current visibility. You deleted a field and need its data back Deleting removes the definition only — the stored values remain in the record store Re-add a field with the same field key; the default source path matches and the values reappear. Searches ignore accent distinctions that matter in your material Accent folding is on by default Turn accent folding off for that field; its diacritics then count as letter identity in matching. A definition will not save A detail setting does not fit the field's kind — for example the currency format without a currency code, or a lookup without a target field Read the validation message; it names the setting to fix. A researcher's entered value is refused with "…is not one of this column's allowed <kind>s" The column pinned an allowed set and the value falls outside it Enter one of the allowed values, or edit the column's Allowed <kind>s in its field definition to add the new one — the picker's own Manage link does not render for a pinned column. An edition column's picker shows no Manage link and offers a key you don't recognize Edition's default keys come from the record's own linked editions, not a declared set, and edition columns show no Manage link even when pinned If the column is unpinned, check the record's edition relations; if it is pinned, edit Allowed editions in the field definition.

Researcher tier: The Publish view — field visibility and publishing changes as researchers experience them; Workspace walkthrough — the workspace these definitions shape. Companion pages: Making fields searchable — whether a field is searched, faceted, or suggested (this page covers how its text is matched); Data Import Wizard — where definitions are first created from your source; Standards and Citations — the standards declarations a field can carry; Voice and Vocabulary — environment-wide wording that composes with your field labels; Vocabulary Review — the review queue Calendar and Historical date columns share with their own inline cell editor (Register and Custom vocabulary is not reviewed there — see Managing the set above); Workspace configuration — the display field an edition column's keys can resolve a label through.

Your environment's public homepage is the first thing a reader sees. The homepage composer is where you decide what goes on it and in what order — a board of showcase blocks that draw on your own published content. You arrange the board here; readers see the result on the public homepage. The board is read live: when you save, the public homepage reflects your changes on its next load. There is no separate publish step for the board itself — the composer is the board. What a block can put in front of readers is still governed by the platform's publishing rules. A block only shows content that is published and current: an item you have not published, or a version that is no longer the current one, does not appear to readers even if it sits in the block. Arranging the board and publishing the underlying content are two separate decisions.

Compose the board — Maturity: Built. Add blocks with Add a widget, order them with Move up / Move down, and take one off the homepage with Remove widget. The board is a single ordered list — the order you set here is the order readers see. A block for each kind of content, at its own readiness — Maturity: Built (catalog); readiness varies per block. The Add a widget picker groups blocks into Suggested for you (ready to add), More blocks (coming soon), and Already on your homepage (already placed). Each block shows where it draws from (for example, From your Media, From your Place data) and its readiness: Building now — fully working: you can add it and choose exactly which items it shows. The 3D model showcase is at this stage — it draws on your 3D-model media and renders on the public homepage. Scaffolded — you can place it and it explains in the board what it will draw on, but it does not yet take a hand-picked item list. The Map, Timeline, and Relationship network blocks are at this stage. Design-ahead — shown in the picker so you can see what is coming, but not yet addable. The Image, Audio, and Video showcases are at this stage. Choose and order the items in a block — Maturity: Built. For a block that is Building now, open its item picker — Choose items on an empty block, Manage items once it has some — a single grid of your media, shown by thumbnail so you pick visual items by sight. Clicking a thumbnail selects it; each selected item shows a number marking its reading order, and Load more pages a long list. The picker does not filter by publication status — you can place any of your media — and whether a placed item actually reaches readers is decided after you save, by the published-and-current rule above (the reader preview flags the difference; see below). A block with nothing chosen shows No items chosen on the board rather than an empty frame to readers. Show or hide a block without removing it — Maturity: Built. Each block carries a Shown / Hidden switch. Hidden means declared but not shown to readers: the block stays on your board — with its chosen items and order intact — so you can bring it back with one click, but it is left off the public homepage entirely. This is separate from publishing individual items: hiding a block hides the whole block, while the publishing rule above governs each item within a shown block. Hiding takes effect on save, like any other board change — there is nothing to re-publish. Preview the reader's view — Maturity: Built. Preview reader view renders, read-only, what your saved board would look like to a reader — in board order, with hidden blocks left out. Within a shown block it marks any item a reader cannot yet see: Not published (the item's entry is not published) or Not saved (a change you have not saved yet); if every item in a section is marked, it says the section reads empty to readers. This is your one confirmation before you rely on the arrangement — the board is live-on-save, with no later checkpoint.

Feature your 3D models on the homepage. The 3D model showcase is the block that is fully working end to end: add it, then pick and order the models you want up front. They appear on the public homepage once their entries are published — the reader preview flags any that are not yet published. This is the recommended starting point for a live homepage. Lay out the rest of the board ahead of time. Place the Scaffolded blocks (Map, Timeline, Relationship network) where you want them; they hold their spot and describe what they will draw on, and begin showing content as each is completed — no rework to your layout when that happens. Stage a block privately. Add a block and choose its items while it is Hidden — it stays on your board, with its items visible to you there, but off the public homepage. Review it on the board itself while hidden; Preview reader view deliberately leaves hidden blocks out (it mirrors the public reader), so use it to confirm the block is not yet public, then switch it to Shown and preview again to see how it reads. Nothing you stage while hidden reaches the public homepage until you show it. Take something down instantly. Switch a block to Hidden and save; it leaves the public homepage on the next load, and its items and order are kept for whenever you want it back.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A block sits on your board but readers do not see it on the public homepage The block is set to Hidden Switch it to Shown and save. Check Preview reader view, which also leaves hidden blocks out, to confirm. A block is Shown but appears empty to readers, or is missing items you added Those items are not published, or the version you expected is no longer the current one The homepage only shows published, current content. Publish the items (or make the intended version current); arranging a block does not publish its items. In Preview reader view, an item carries a Not published or Not saved flag Not published — the item's entry is not yet published; Not saved — you have unsaved board changes For Not saved, save the board. For Not published, publish the item's entry (see Media Review Surface); until then a reader sees the block without that item. A block in the picker cannot be added It is at the Design-ahead stage — shown so you can see what is coming, but not yet addable Use a Building now or Scaffolded block for now; the design-ahead blocks become addable as they are completed. A block you placed offers no way to choose specific items It is a Scaffolded block, which does not yet take a hand-picked item list Use the 3D model showcase (Building now) when you need to choose and order specific items; scaffolded blocks explain in place what they will draw on. You removed a block by mistake Remove widget takes the block off the board Add it again from Add a widget and re-pick its items. To take a block off readers' view without losing its items, use Hidden instead of Remove widget.

Public Stream Profiles — how your environment's published content is exposed to readers, upstream of what you feature here. Media Review Surface — reviewing and publishing the media (including 3D models) that the showcase blocks draw on. Entry Surface Configuration — how individual published entries are presented to readers.

Reviewing a media artifact's attestations — confirming or correcting which part of the artifact maps to which term, adding bindings the automatic extractor missed, re-running the extractor, and pinning a working revision as a citable Edition — happens inside the workspace, on the media record's detail pane. Read this when reviewing a freshly ingested media artifact, when the extractor proposes bindings that look wrong, or when you are ready to pin a revision as an Edition. Two terms used throughout: an anchor is an addressable point inside the artifact (for a 3D model, a named node in the model file), and an attestation is the recorded link between an anchor and a term in your environment. The guarantees described in Citation Integrity rest on the review decisions you take here. The standalone admin review page (formerly at /admin/.../media-review/) has been retired — all of its review, re-extraction, and Edition-pinning actions now live on the workspace media detail pane described below. If you have an old bookmark to that page, open the record from the workspace Media view instead.

Open the Media view on a media table (it appears only on MEDIA tables), then open a record from the gallery. Its detail pane opens with the model rendered inline and a rail of tabs: Mesh→term — the review surface: each part of the model with the term it is matched to, a state chip, and per-part actions. Files — the artifact's stored files. Viewer (admins) — sets the model's opening camera framing as a live presentation default. Info — read-only record details. Version (admins) — pin a working revision as a citable, frozen Edition, or re-extract the mesh→term bindings. The researcher-facing walkthrough of the Mesh→term tab is in the See which mesh maps to which term help topic; tuning the camera is in Tune the 3D camera view.

Mesh→term review — the Mesh→term tab lists each part of the model with the term it is matched to and a state chip: auto (extracted, awaiting review), edited (you changed an existing binding), linked (you bound a previously-unmapped part), or unmapped — above counts of how many parts are mapped, edited, and auto. Selecting a part, in the list or in the model itself, highlights it on both sides and opens its card. Maturity: Active. Per-part Approve / Reassign / Strip — Approve confirms an auto binding as correct (shown only while the part is auto); Reassign / Assign term opens a picker to bind the part to a term (search the vocabulary by typing and choose a result by its display label, or paste a term record's id); Strip clears the term, leaving the part unmapped. Every action is recorded with your name and a timestamp. Maturity: Active. Strip is a recorded rejection, not a deletion: the decision is kept so a later re-extraction cannot silently re-propose the same binding. Manual attestation add — bind a part the extractor missed via the term picker: a typeahead searches the term records in your environment as you type, or paste a term record's id directly. Maturity: Active. The typeahead depends on search being activated for your environment; the paste path works regardless. Re-extraction dry run and apply — on the Version tab, re-run the extractor against the same artifact, first as a dry run that reports what would change without writing anything, then as an apply. The job runs in the background and the tab polls its status. Maturity: Active. The status is overall job status only — queued, running, succeeded, or failed — not step-by-step progress. Requires the Admin role. Re-extraction is refused once the version is a frozen Edition. Edition pinning — on the Version tab, pin a working revision as a citable Edition with an Edition label. Maturity: Active. Requires the Admin role. Once pinned, the Edition is frozen: the platform refuses any re-extraction against it. (Everyday citeability is automatic; pinning is the deliberate-permanence act.) Reviewer-decision preservation — approvals, reassignments, strips, and manual additions are all marked as reviewer decisions and survive re-extractions; the extractor never silently overwrites them. Maturity: Active.

Open the workspace, open a media table's Media view, and open a record from the gallery. Review actions and manual bindings require the Editor or Admin role in your environment; re-extraction and Edition pinning require Admin — the workspace hides the admin-only actions when your role cannot perform them, so you never dead-end on a permission error. The common review paths: Approve a correct binding: select the part, then Approve. The decision is recorded with your name and timestamp, and future re-extractions leave the binding alone. Reassign or bind a part: select the part, then Reassign / Assign term; search the term by typing and choose a match, or paste the term record's id. Strip a wrong binding: select the part, then Strip. Your rejection is recorded, and the extractor's next run will not re-propose the same binding. Re-extract: on the Version tab, dry run first — the job runs in the background and the tab polls its status until it succeeds or fails — compare the report against the current state, then apply (apply asks for confirmation, because it writes new anchors and attestations). Pin an Edition: on the Version tab, pin the working revision and enter the Edition label. After pinning the Edition is frozen — further extraction work requires a new working revision. The mesh→term counts refresh after each action, so the tiles always reflect the decisions you have taken so far.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The Media view does not appear on a table The table's records are not the MEDIA archetype The Media view appears only on MEDIA tables. Confirm the table holds media records. The model does not render in the detail pane The media record has no resolvable primary file The pane needs the artifact's stored primary file. Confirm the record was ingested completely; the rest of the pane still works for reviewing existing bindings. The re-extraction actions are disabled or refuse The current version is a frozen Edition, or the record has no resolvable source file Re-extraction is refused on a frozen Edition — start a new working revision by re-importing. If the record has no source file, add it. The term picker returns no matches for a term you know exists Search has not been activated for your environment, or the search found nothing for your query The picker shows a hint when this happens; paste the term record's id directly — the picker works regardless of search state. To get search activated for your environment, contact your platform operator. The Version tab's pin/re-extract actions are missing You do not have the Admin role Edition pinning and re-extraction require Admin. Review and binding actions are available to Editors. You stripped a binding but the next extraction proposed it again This should not happen — a strip is durable across re-extractions Contact your platform operator with the artifact id and the details of the stripped binding.

Citation Integrity — the structural guarantees behind Edition pinning. Permissions Panel — role assignment for Editor and Admin. Work with media in the workspace, See which mesh maps to which term, Tune the 3D camera view — the researcher-facing help topics for this surface.

The standard roles in your environment — and any custom role you compose — are built from one fixed set of permission building blocks. There are nine. Each block is a single capability: it is either granted or not. A role is a chosen combination of these blocks. This page names every block, says exactly what each one lets a contributor do, gives the default combination a new contributor starts from, and shows how the blocks combine into a reviewer, a supervisor, and an exporter. Read it when you are composing a custom role on the Permissions Panel and want to know precisely what each checkbox controls. The building blocks are fixed by the platform: you combine them, you cannot invent new ones. Composing roles and assigning them is yours to do as an administrator. Adding the contributor accounts those roles attach to is handled by your platform operator — see Onboarding a collaborator.

Each block below lists its name, what it gates, and its impact tier — low, medium, or high. The impact tier tells you how cautious to be when granting it; the three high-impact blocks are called out again in the next section.

Gates: reading and commenting on suggested changes before they are saved. A contributor with only this block can examine every proposed change and leave comments, but cannot save anything. Impact tier: medium.
Gates: saving additive changes — new records or new fields — that do not alter existing work. This is the lowest-impact save permission. Impact tier: low.
Gates: saving edits that change existing records. These are the everyday changes a working contributor makes, and they remain reviewable. Impact tier: medium.
Gates: running broad merges, deletes, and reorganizations — the changes that touch the most records at once. Impact tier: high.
Gates: reversing a just-saved change while the short undo window is still open. Without this block, a contributor can save but cannot self-reverse. Impact tier: low.
Gates: creating and updating the saved import setups the project reuses. Impact tier: medium.

Gates: changing the fields contributors use when they edit — which fields exist and how they behave. This reshapes the editing surface for everyone, which is why it sits in the high tier. Impact tier: high. See Field Configuration for what this controls.

Gates: inviting contributors into roles and deciding what each person can do — in other words, composing roles and assigning the other eight blocks. A contributor needs this block to open the role-management surfaces at all. Impact tier: high.
Gates: downloading aggregate metrics about suggestion quality and review patterns. The numbers are aggregate, never individual review text. Impact tier: medium.

When a contributor account first appears in your environment, it starts from a fixed default combination — the set the platform treats as a safe working baseline for a project team member. The five blocks below are on by default; the other four are off. Building block Default Review suggestions On Save additive changes On Save normal changes On Use the undo window On Manage import templates On Run high-impact changes Off Change field setup Off Manage roles Off Export suggestion metrics Off The default is a starting point, not a fixed role: from the Permissions Panel you assign a standard role or compose a custom one over it. The three high-impact blocks — run high-impact changes, change field setup, and manage roles — are off by default, and so is exporting metrics.

Three blocks are high-impact: run high-impact changes, change field setup, and manage roles. Granting one of these gives a contributor a capability that can affect a large share of the project's work, or affect what other contributors can do. These blocks decide who is allowed to make a high-impact change. They are separate from your environment's project rules, which decide how such a change is confirmed when it happens. The two work together: a block grants the capability; a project rule can require a second pair of hands before the change goes through. For example, your environment can require that a high-impact save is confirmed by a contributor who did not author it, and can require that destructive changes are confirmed either by two contributors or by a single contributor through an elevated confirmation step. So even a contributor who holds run high-impact changes is still subject to the project rules at the moment they apply a change. Granting the block does not bypass the rules; it only makes the contributor eligible to start the change. You set these rules on the Project rules tab — see the project rules described in the Permissions Panel. Manage roles is the one block that controls access to permission management itself. A contributor cannot open the role-management surfaces, or change anyone's permissions, without it.
documents.s: The high-impact blocks and the project rules

documents.t: These three shapes show how the blocks combine. They are illustrations, not extra preset roles — compose the equivalent as a custom role, or start from the matching standard role and adjust. A reviewer — someone who reads and comments but never saves. One block: Review suggestions Everything else is off. This shape can examine and annotate proposed changes and nothing more. A supervisor — a senior contributor who does the full editing job and can reorganize, but does not manage people or reshape the field setup. The save and undo blocks plus high-impact changes: Review suggestions Save additive changes Save normal changes Run high-impact changes Use the undo window Manage import templates Change field setup, manage roles, and export metrics stay off. This contributor can do every kind of save — including high-impact reorganizations — but reshaping the editing surface and managing other people's access remain with an administrator. An exporter — someone whose job is to pull aggregate metrics, with read access to the review stream but no save authority. Two blocks: Review suggestions Export suggestion metrics All save and management blocks stay off. This shape can read suggestions and download the aggregate quality and review-pattern metrics, without the ability to save changes or alter anyone's access.

Action Who Compose a custom role from the building blocks Administrator (self-serve, on the Permissions Panel) Assign a standard or custom role to a contributor Administrator (self-serve) Adjust a single contributor's blocks Administrator (self-serve) Add a new contributor account for a role to attach to Platform operator Add new building blocks beyond the nine Not available — the set is fixed by the platform

Permissions Panel — where you compose roles, assign them, and set the project rules these blocks work alongside. User and Access Management — the standard role set and how the four pre-loaded roles map onto these blocks. Field Configuration — what the change field setup block controls. Onboarding a collaborator — how a new contributor account is created before you assign a role to it.

The Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/ is the single surface for who-can-do-what in your environment. Contributor roles, custom role composition, project safety rules, wording overrides, ownership hand-off, and the project-history lookup all live here. Read this when changing a contributor's role, composing a custom role, handing off project ownership, or answering "who reviewed that import, and when?".

Contributors tab — every contributor in your environment, with their assigned role and last activity. Change a contributor's role, adjust individual permissions, or narrow the scope of their assignment. Maturity: Active. Limit: the panel manages roles, permissions, and membership state for existing contributors; contributor accounts are created by your platform operator — see User and Access Management. Member lifecycle menu (per contributor row) — each row carries a menu with Suspend / Reactivate, Change role (Admin, Editor, Viewer), and Remove (behind a confirmation). Suspension takes effect immediately — the person can no longer sign in, and a session that was already open stops working; a suspended contributor stays visible in the list with a "Suspended" marker rather than disappearing. Reactivation restores sign-in and re-derives the role's access. Removal is a soft retirement: access ends, but the membership record is kept for the project's audit history. Maturity: Active. Limit: the project-owner row's lifecycle actions are shown but disabled until ownership is transferred — the visible note on the menu says so; permission edits are unavailable on any suspended row (reactivate first). Roles tab with custom role composition — the standard roles come preloaded; custom roles are composed from a fixed set of permission building blocks. A standard role can be renamed inline; the new name is a display label only. Maturity: Active. Limit: the building blocks themselves are fixed by the platform. Role scoping — a role assignment (or a custom role) can be limited to specific record types or fields. Maturity: Active. Limit: a scope only narrows where the role applies; it cannot add permissions the role does not grant. Project rules tab — set your environment-wide review policy: whether high-impact saves need a reviewer who did not author the change, and how destructive changes are confirmed — by two contributors, or by a single contributor through an elevated confirmation step. Maturity: Active. Limit: the panel saves and displays these choices as your environment's declared policy; how each applied change was actually confirmed, and by whom, is shown on the Project history tab. Review learning setting — on the Project rules tab: opt in to record privacy-safe signals from your team's review decisions so future suggestions improve. Maturity: Active. Limit: off by default; switching it on requires acknowledging the privacy notice, and the change is recorded along with which admin made it. Wording tab — rename the permission-related labels shown in your environment, starting with role names. Maturity: Active. Limit: changes compose with your environment's voice and vocabulary settings; there is no separate translation table to maintain. Vocabulary review prompt — when the panel loads, it checks permission-related wording and flags entries that need review, with the reason and a link to edit each one. Maturity: Active. Limit: the check is read-only — it never changes anything; you act on a finding or dismiss it. Project history tab — look up the recorded history of an applied import proposal: its status, how it was confirmed, who reviewed it and when, the recorded reason, and the permissions that were in force at the moment it was applied. A record carries an "Edited after apply" marker when the applied content was changed afterwards. Maturity: Active. Limit: lookup is per proposal — you supply the proposal's ID from the import screens; records are read-only. Ownership hand-off — the current project owner can hand ownership to another contributor. The hand-off asks for explicit confirmation for both sides, completes as a single change, and is recorded. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the current owner can start a hand-off, and the new owner must be an active contributor holding the administrator role with permission management. Display density control — switch the panel between compact, cozy, and comfortable layouts. Maturity: Active. Limit: cosmetic only — it affects rendering, not permissions; the choice is remembered in the browser where you set it.

The panel's address is /admin/permissions/. It opens on the Contributors tab; the other tabs are Roles, Project rules, Wording, and Project history. The active tab is kept in the page address, so a bookmark or a shared link opens the panel on that tab. Change a contributor's role: Contributors tab, open the contributor's row, pick the role. To limit where the role applies, set a scope on the same row. Compose a custom role: Roles tab, combine the permission building blocks, name the role. Rename any role's display label inline with the edit control; the underlying building blocks stay fixed. Set project rules: Project rules tab. Switch the separate-reviewer requirement on or off, choose the destructive-change policy, and save. Enable review learning: Project rules tab. Switch the setting on, acknowledge the privacy notice, and save. The decision is recorded along with who made it. Hand off ownership: as the current project owner, use the "Hand off ownership" control, choose the new owner, and confirm for both sides. Look up an import's history: Project history tab, enter the proposal's ID, and load the history. The record shows the review decision and the permission snapshot from the moment of apply. Review flagged wording: when the vocabulary check finds entries needing review, a notice appears. Open the Wording tab, follow each flagged entry's edit link, or dismiss the finding.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A notice says permission wording needs review The load-time vocabulary check flagged entries Open the Wording tab. The check is read-only; follow the edit link on each flagged entry, or dismiss the finding. See Voice and Vocabulary. Renaming a standard role did not change what it allows A rename sets a display label only; the role's permission building blocks are fixed This is the intended behavior. Compose a custom role if you need a different set of building blocks. A contributor cannot act on content their role should allow Their role assignment carries a scope that excludes that content Open the contributor's row and check the scope. Widen it or remove it. The ownership hand-off will not complete Only the current owner can hand off, and the new owner must be an active contributor holding the administrator role with permission management Give the intended new owner the administrator role with permission management first, then run the hand-off again. Review learning is on, but suggestions do not seem to improve Signals accumulate gradually and stay within your environment This is expected early on. The setting records your team's review decisions over time; it does not change behavior immediately.

Companion pages: Voice and Vocabulary — the wording system the panel's overrides plug into; User and Access Management — the standard role set and how contributor accounts are created; Telemetry — what the review-learning setting records. Platform-level operations — cross-environment concerns such as incident response and platform-wide data-protection records are handled outside this panel. Contact your platform operator.

Every field in your environment carries its own search settings: whether the field's text is matched by search, whether the field can become a filter ("facet") control, and whether its values feed suggest-as-you-type. The settings live on each field's configuration record, are filled automatically when the field is created, and are exactly the configuration the Entry Surface readiness review reads. Read this page when a field matches (or fails to match) in search unexpectedly, when you are deciding which fields should become public filter controls, or when preparing your environment for a public launch.

Per-field search settings — each field carries three eligibility settings: searchable (text matching), filter ("facet") eligibility, and autocomplete eligibility. Maturity: Active. Limit: the admin screens do not currently include a control for editing a stored value — changing one is done with your platform operator. Automatic defaults from the field's type — when a field is created during an import, the platform fills the three settings from a fixed per-type table, the same for every environment. The platform never infers them from the content of your data. Maturity: Active. Limit: the automatic value fills a blank only; an explicitly chosen value is never overwritten, including by re-imports. Searchable fields define the search index — when a record is written to your environment's search index, only its searchable-marked fields contribute text. The search your team uses inside the environment reads this index. Maturity: Active. Limit: fields created before automatic defaults existed fall back to built-in platform rules until explicit values are stored for them. Filter ("facet") eligibility — a facet-eligible field can produce filter buckets, and the readiness review lists it as a reviewed filter field. Maturity: Active. Limit: a public filter control additionally requires a simple single-value field, your review, and promotion into the public configuration — eligibility alone does not create a public control. Autocomplete eligibility — an autocomplete-eligible field feeds suggest-as-you-type. Maturity: Active. Limit: a public suggestion source has the same additional requirements as a public filter: a simple single-value field and review. Search boost (reserved) — a field's configuration can record a weighting value for ranking its matches. Maturity: Built. Limit: the value is stored and preserved as yours, but no search engine consults it — it has no effect on results today. Leave it unset.

The settings sit on the field's configuration record, next to its label, type, and ordering. You do not set them by hand at creation time: the moment a field is created, the platform writes all three eligibility values from the field's type. Field type Searchable Filter-eligible Suggestions Short text Yes No Yes Long-form (rich) text Yes No No Single-choice list Yes Yes Yes Multiple-choice list Yes Yes No Link to another record Yes Yes No Looked-up value Yes No No Number, date, yes/no No No No Media No No No Three rows deserve a note. A link field is matched through the linked record's display text, which is why it is searchable even though it stores no text of its own. Number, date, and yes/no fields start with everything off — an opt-in you record explicitly is preserved and never reverted by the platform. A media field itself carries no searchable text; the descriptive fields on a media record (title, creator, and so on) are ordinary text and choice fields and follow their own rows in this table.
documents.s: Where the settings live, and what fills them

documents.t: You decide, your operator records: read each field's stored eligibility values and sampled evidence in the Entry Surface readiness report your operator shares, and send your review decisions — including deferring a filter or suggestion candidate with a reason — to your operator, who records them (the self-service review page returns with the admin tier). A recorded deferral is read by the public surface: the deferred control is reported unavailable, with a reason citing your review. Performed with your platform operator: editing a stored searchable, filter, or autocomplete value on a field (the admin screens have no control for this today); refreshing the search index after a change so existing records reflect it; promoting reviewed fields into the public Entry configuration; and enabling your environment's search engine in the first place. Whichever path sets a value, the same protection applies: an explicit value is yours. Re-importing your source data fills blanks with automatic defaults but never overwrites a value that was chosen deliberately.
documents.s: Changing a setting — what is self-serve and what runs through your operator

documents.t: Hiding works the same way in reverse. A field whose searchable setting is off contributes no text to the search index, so its values stop matching once the index is refreshed. A field explicitly marked not filter-eligible also leaves the readiness review's candidate list — the review stops proposing it.

The readiness report classifies every field of the public role's record type by its stored settings: A field marked filter-eligible appears as a reviewed filter field — listed with the reviewed single-value filter fields when its values are simple single values, or flagged separately when its shape is complex (multi-value, linked, looked-up, media). A field marked autocomplete-eligible with simple single values appears as a reviewed autocomplete field. A simple single-value field with no explicit eligibility appears as a candidate, with the review actions valid for it (review before promotion, choose a shorter label, defer with reason). Each row carries evidence sampled from your records: how many records carry a value, how many distinct values exist, and warnings where values are too long for a compact public control. The report is the place to confirm a setting change landed — see Entry Surface Readiness for the review workflow itself.
documents.s: How the settings feed the readiness review

documents.t: Inside your environment, the workspace search matches against the search index, so only searchable-marked fields produce hits. If your environment's search engine has not yet been enabled, a search request is refused with a plain message that search is not enabled for the workspace yet — enablement is an operator step. On the public Entry surface, a filter or suggestion control reaches readers only when the field is explicitly eligible, holds simple single values, has passed your review, and was promoted into the public configuration. A control that does not meet all of these is reported with an unavailable status and a short reason, one of four kinds: the field is not part of that public role's configuration; the control was deferred by a review decision you recorded; the field has not yet been reviewed and promoted; the field's value shape (multi-value, linked, looked-up, or media) has no public control of this kind. An automatic default alone never creates a public control: a field the platform seeded but nobody reviewed stays review evidence, not a public promise.
documents.s: What researchers and public readers see

documents.t: Request a fresh readiness report from your platform operator (the review runs operator-mediated until the admin-tier review page ships). Find the field's row and confirm its stored eligibility values and classification moved as expected — into the reviewed lists, into the candidates, or out of the candidates entirely. For a searchable change, ask your operator to confirm the index refresh ran, then search for a value that occurs only in that field and confirm it now matches (or no longer matches).

Symptom Likely cause Fix A field's text never matches in search The field is not marked searchable, or the index has not been refreshed since the setting changed Check the field's evidence in the readiness report. Have your platform operator set the field searchable and refresh the search index. Search reports it is not enabled for the workspace Your environment's search engine has not been enabled and confirmed Engine enablement is performed with your platform operator. A field you expect as a public filter is reported unavailable Not yet reviewed and promoted; deferred by a recorded review decision; or a multi-value, linked, or media field, which has no public filter control Open the readiness report and read the field's row. Record or revise the decision; promotion into the public configuration is performed with your platform operator. Suggestions never include a field's values The field is not autocomplete-eligible — long-form text, multiple-choice, and link fields do not feed suggestions by default If the field is short text or a single-choice list and should suggest, have your operator mark it autocomplete-eligible and refresh the index. You recorded a search boost and rankings did not change The boost value is stored but not consulted by any search engine This is current behavior, not an error. Leave the value unset. A re-import changed a search setting you chose It does not: automatic values fill blanks only If a value looks wrong, check the field's evidence in the readiness report — an explicitly stored value survives re-imports; only fields that never had one receive the per-type default.

Entry Surface Readiness — the operator-mediated review that reads these settings and records your decisions. Data Import Wizard — where fields enter your environment; their search settings are filled at that moment. Searching as a public reader — the reader-side companion to this page. Public reader — what external readers see once your public Entry surface launches.

This page is the environment administrator's working view of the platform's standards support. It tells you which standards-backed capabilities your environment inherits without configuring anything, what you can configure on top, what published entries expose to the outside world, and what stays your environment's own interpretation. Read this when an institutional reviewer asks "what standards does our knowledge environment comply with?", when a federation partner asks whether a specific export format is supported, or when you are deciding which standards a field in your environment should declare conformance with. The cross-audience overview is the Standards & Compliance Overview; this page is for someone running an environment.

These capabilities ship with every environment. None of them require per-environment engineering, custom code, or a separate contract. Each carries a maturity tag; the standards overview records the audited maturity of every standard the platform engages with. Stable, citable identity for published artifacts — a published artifact carries a stable public identity that an external identifier service (your library's DOI minter, for example) can target. The platform does not mint DOIs itself, and data cited against a frozen Edition cannot silently change · Maturity: Active · See Citation Integrity for the guarantees in detail. Citation framework built on Citation Style Language (CSL) — citations render through CSL styles, the same open format reference managers and journals use. A catalog of more than seventy standard styles ships with the platform (Chicago and APA among them), and each environment holds its own active styles · Maturity: Built · Limit: a style that is not in the catalog can be installed on request — contact your platform operator. Per-entry citation export in CSL JSON — every published entry's citation is available in CSL JSON, the interchange format reference managers read · Maturity: Built. Media locators that follow IIIF and W3C Web Annotation conventions — a cited region of an image, audio/video segment, or 3D model is addressed by the artifact's own natural self-description (an image region selector, a 3D-model node name, a text passage identifier), never a platform-invented code · Maturity: Built · Limit: locator support ships today; dedicated standard viewers are not yet integrated. See Citation Integrity. Vocabulary review backed by shared authorities — vocabulary values first seen in your imported data queue for review rather than being guessed at, and AI suggestions (when enabled) can reference public authority records: Wikidata for entities and concepts, PeriodO for historical periods. Suggestions are advisory only — a reviewer declares or rejects every value · Maturity: Active (the review queue); the authority-backed AI suggestions are Built · See Vocabulary Grounding. Typed, self-describing API — integrations read published data through a documented GraphQL API: a typed contract a partner can inspect, not an undocumented internal surface · Maturity: Built. Privacy-aware telemetry — activity records are redacted before they are stored and kept in a tamper-evident chain, supporting a defensible data-protection posture under GDPR · Maturity: Active · See Telemetry. Accessibility controls in the reading interface — readers can adjust font size, line height, color presets, and font family. The platform targets WCAG 2.2 AA; a full audit against that target has not yet been recorded · Maturity: Active. Capability-to-standard quick reference: Capability Backing standard(s) Stable citable identity for published artifacts DOI (minted externally against platform-held identity) Deep-linkable image / AV / 3D regions IIIF, W3C Web Annotation Citations consumed by reference managers CSL Vocabulary review informed by shared authorities Wikidata, PeriodO Typed API for integrations GraphQL Accessible reading interface WCAG 2.2 AA (target) Defensible data-protection posture GDPR

Citation style — one active venue style per environment. Adopt a style from the shipped catalog, or refine one through the review workflow described below. Applying a style requires the administrator role; styles are versioned, and the platform refreshes published citations after a style is applied · Maturity: Active. Vocabulary grounding — declare or reject queued vocabulary values through the Vocabulary Grounding workflow, with a display label of your choosing and optional links to standards from the platform's recognized list · Maturity: Active. Field standards declarations — a field definition in your environment can declare which standards its content conforms to, chosen from the platform's approved standards list. Declarations are validated when you save the field definition — a standard outside the list is rejected with a validation message — and the declarations are visible through the API · Maturity: Active. Voice and vocabulary substitution — independent of standards but composes with them: your wording is yours, the structural conformance underneath is the platform's. See Voice and Vocabulary · Maturity: Active. Reference evidence and citation rules — declared once per published entry type; described in the next section · Maturity: Active. How often you touch each of these: Citation style — once at environment setup; revisit when you adopt a new venue's or institution's style guide. Vocabulary grounding — during onboarding, and after any import that brings in vocabulary values your environment has not seen before. Field standards declarations — when designing or revising a field definition. They are part of the field's definition, not a day-to-day switch. Voice substitution — whenever the platform's default wording feels foreign to your researchers. Reference evidence and citation rules — once per published entry type, when deciding how its References section should read.
documents.s: What you can configure on top

documents.t: When a published entry shows a References section — one row per piece of evidence, each with a scholarly citation — two declarations on the entry type produce it. Both are configuration, not code: the platform supplies the machinery, your environment supplies the meaning. The evidence declaration — where your evidence lives and how it joins. You declare which record type holds the occurrences of an entry (the passages, witnesses, specimens, or find records), which link connects them to the entry, and which of your columns carry the locators (page, chapter, line, quote) and the source details (author, work, editor). Every column name in the declaration is your environment's vocabulary; the platform never assumes any of it. Citation rules — how citations are built and styled. You declare which of your columns map to the standard citation fields (author, title, editor, date, page), and which CSL style renders them. The result is a formatted citation per evidence row, plus standalone source citations beneath the evidence list. Two behaviors worth knowing when designing the declarations: Editions are optional. An occurrence with no published edition — a researcher's own catalogued manuscript or fragment — still appears as a full evidence row. Evidence is never gated on the existence of a published edition. Paired-edition bridging. When an occurrence is catalogued against more than one edition — say a modern critical edition and an early printed one — the row bridges them in the classics convention: the modern citation first, then = volume.page (abbreviated editor) for the paired edition. The abbreviations and locators are your data; the bridge composition is the platform's. Citation appearance (punctuation, abbreviated author forms, locale) is managed through CSL styles, not by editing rendered text. If a citation looks rough, the fix is a style refinement — see the review workflow below and the troubleshooting table.
documents.s: Reference evidence and citations on published entries

documents.t: Two different things govern how citations read on a published page, and they deliberately do not share a control: The venue style governs how the page itself is cited. It is the one active style for your environment — adopted, proposed, and applied in the citation console. A reader visiting from another discipline can re-render that one citation into a standard format with the citation format selector on the published page (described below); your style stays the default every reader sees first. Your reference conventions govern how rows of evidence and media figures read. Each shape of object carries its own declared style, and that rendering is part of your published content: it reads identically for every reader, and the citation format selector never touches it. The split reflects what each citation is for. The page citation serves the venue a reader is writing for, so the reader gets flexibility there. The evidence rows carry your discipline's own scholarly conventions, so they stay under your environment's authority.
documents.s: One venue style, many reference conventions

documents.t: A reference walk reads locators and source details out of your data, and your data can hold them in more than one shape. All of these shapes are available today and are picked directly in the citation binding section described in the worked example below — a keyed shape (like the per-edition locus) offers a key selector alongside the column picker. Linked relation columns. An occurrence row reaches its source and edition records through link columns, and the reference walk follows those links to gather the author, work, and editor details. This is the usual shape when your sources and editions are tables of their own. A per-edition locus field. One field on the occurrence holds a keyed locator per edition — the page in a modern critical edition alongside the locus in an early printed one — so a single passage carries its position in every edition it is catalogued against. This is the shape behind paired-edition bridging. Composed fields. A field assembled from several other fields on the record into one printable value, which then feeds the citation as a single locator or label. A formula column. A column computed from the row's other values. Useful when the printable locus is a transformation of stored parts rather than any one column as entered. Anchored locators on 3D models. For a media figure, a citation locator can be bound to a named part of a 3D model by clicking that part in the viewer. The rendered reference then shows the resolved term's label — the name your environment gave that part — never an internal identifier.
documents.s: Ways to shape a reference path

documents.t: When your environment publishes entries, the outside world can rely on: A rendered citation on each published entry, produced against your active CSL style · Maturity: Built. A citation format selector on each published entry — alongside your environment's own style (the default, shown as the project style), a reader can re-render the entry's citation as APA, MLA, Chicago author-date, Chicago notes & bibliography, or Harvard. The switch re-renders one copyable citation line in the reader's own browser from the citation's CSL JSON; it never changes your evidence rows, your active style, or what other readers see · Maturity: Built. The same citation in CSL JSON at a stable address per entry, ready for import into reference managers · Maturity: Built. Typed API access through which an integration partner reads published data under the same visibility rules as the reading interface · Maturity: Built. Machine-readable semantic export formats — JSON-LD representations of published entries and research-object packaging for archival hand-off — are committed in the platform's architecture but not yet available. The standards overview records the current maturity of each format; point a federation partner there rather than promising a format ahead of its maturity tag. Exports are produced by the platform; your environment does not build or maintain a custom export pipeline. What is yours is the data, the wording, and the entry-type design — not the export machinery.

The day-to-day operator paths: Pick a citation style at environment setup: the citation console at /admin/citations/ lets you browse the shipped catalog and adopt a style; adopting makes it the single active style for the environment. A style that is not in the catalog can be installed on request. Declare a field's standards conformance: edit the field definition and choose from the platform's approved standards list. A declaration outside the list is rejected with a validation message when you save. Review new vocabulary values: work the review queue through the Vocabulary Grounding workflow. When AI suggestions are enabled, a suggestion can reference a matching Wikidata or PeriodO record to inform your decision. Answer "what standards does our knowledge environment comply with?": point the asker to the standards overview. It is written for exactly that conversation, and its maturity tags distinguish what ships today from what is committed but still on the way.

When the active style renders roughly for your material, a style is refined through a three-step review path, so no one person silently changes how every citation reads: Propose. A proposed style (or a refinement of the active one) is generated from sample citations you want to match. The proposal is measured against your environment's pinned citation test cases and assigned a risk class (low / medium / high) based on how many existing citations it would change. Review and apply. An administrator reads the proposal's risk report — the changed cases, the blast-radius percentage, the risk class — and applies it, recording review notes. The style is stored in your environment — no code change is involved — and the platform refreshes published citations after the style is applied. Styles are versioned and never auto-applied by the platform; AI assistance never changes a published citation directly. Both steps run in the citation console at /admin/citations/: paste sample citations to propose, review the measured risk, then apply with notes. See Citation Style Administration for what each step reports back.
documents.s: Refining a citation style (the review workflow)

documents.t: Everything above comes together in one path: your tables in, a rendered reference out. This example follows a classics environment — ancient authors cited by conventional abbreviation, passages catalogued with loci, modern critical editions paired with early printed ones — but the path is the same for any discipline; only the table shapes are yours. Start from your tables. The environment holds three tables that matter here: a passages table (one row per passage, with its locus columns — book, chapter, page — and links to the work and the edition it is catalogued in), an editions bibliography (editor, title, year, covering both modern critical editions and early printed ones), and a small supporting table of abbreviations — a few dozen rows mapping authors to their conventional short forms and treatises to their short titles. The tables can arrive through import or be built from scratch in the workspace; from here the path is identical either way. Promote the abbreviations table to a vocabulary. Through the vocabulary promote flow, the supporting table becomes a vocabulary — a controlled list that other configuration can consume by name. The abbreviation list stays your data, editable like any of your tables; the platform ships no abbreviation list of its own. Declare the reference walk and its bindings. In the workspace surface where you shape how a collection appears publicly, a "How this is cited" section carries the citation bindings, declared per edition role. Bindings read as plain-language rows — which of your columns supplies the page, which vocabulary column supplies the short author form — and a binding can carry a fallback chain: use one column, and if it is empty, use another. A value assembled from several fields is authored as a composed field, with the same formula idiom used elsewhere in the workspace. As you bind, the section shows a live preview of a handful of real citations rendered from your own rows, and the underlying raw configuration stays available as a read-only advanced view. Every name in the bindings is your environment's own vocabulary; the platform assumes none of it. For the parts you haven't bound yet, Suggest bindings asks the platform's AI to look at your own columns — their names and a few real values — and propose which column could fill each empty part. Suggestions appear as tinted rows on the matching source tab with a one-line reason each; nothing is applied until you choose Use, and an accepted suggestion becomes an ordinary binding that saves, validates, and previews exactly like a hand-picked one. The AI can only propose columns your data actually carries — a proposal outside them is refused, never silently rendered — and when every part is already bound it says so instead of inventing work. Pin sample citations. Pin the previewed citations into the regression baseline with one click as you bind, or pin a representative sample from your published entries later. Every later style proposal is measured against this baseline; Citation Style Administration explains the numbers it produces. Adopt or refine the venue style. In the citation console, adopt a style from the shipped catalog if one fits your venue. If not, propose a refinement by pasting sample citations you want the output to match, read the returned risk class, blast-radius percentage, and changed cases, then apply with your review notes. Publish. After configuration changes, entries are republished — and occurrence references update across the corpus. A corrected abbreviation or a changed binding shows up on every published page that renders it, not only on new ones. What the reader sees. Two things on the published page: Evidence rows in your own convention, each one a link to the published edition page. In this classics environment a row reads: Hipp., Morb. Sacr. 3.4 = 6 Jones (11,21 Jouanna = VI.366 L.): Arist., HA III, 4, p. 138 Balme (515a3): The anatomy: the abbreviated author and treatise from your abbreviations vocabulary (resolved through the linked abbreviation rows); chapter and section; an equals-bridge to the modern edition's page and editor; and, in parentheses, the equivalent loci in the paired early editions — comma'd page,line with the editor's abbreviation where your data names one, a bare classical locus (a Bekker number) where it doesn't. Every piece is your data rendered through your declared conventions; the same declared bindings produce both shapes with no per-author rules anywhere. Hovering (or keyboard-focusing) an occurrence reference reveals its full details — author, work, and locus — with the author and work linking to their published entry pages when those exist. The page's own citation, with a citation format selector: your environment's style — the default, shown as the project style — plus APA, MLA, Chicago author-date, Chicago notes & bibliography, and Harvard. Switching re-renders the one copyable citation line in the reader's browser from the citation's structured data. Your style stays the default for every new reader, and the switch never changes your evidence rows.
documents.s: From your tables to a rendered reference — a worked example

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A published entry shows no References section The entry type has no evidence declaration — the platform does not guess where evidence lives Declare it on the entry type: the occurrence record type, the connecting link, and the locator and source columns. Evidence rows appear but without formatted citations No citation rules declared for the entry type, or the chosen citation style was not found Add citation rules mapping your columns to the standard citation fields, and confirm the style name matches an installed style exactly. Citations render with awkward punctuation or separators The active CSL style has not been refined for your material Refine the style through the review workflow (propose, review the risk report, apply). Do not hand-edit rendered text — the next refresh would overwrite it. An internal reference code appears inside a rendered row A locator or source-detail declaration points at a linking column rather than a plain-text column Re-point the declaration at the human-readable column; linking columns belong only in the join declaration. A style your researchers need is not pre-loaded CSL is an open standard; the style file is portable XML Contact your platform operator to install it. Provide the CSL file or a published style URL. A standards declaration is rejected when you save a field definition The declared standard is not on the platform's approved list Choose a standard from the list, or ask your platform operator to evaluate adding the one you need. The list is deliberately narrow: every entry on it is one the platform can stand behind. A vocabulary value cannot be declared or rejected from the review queue The acting account lacks the review permission for grounding decisions Ask an environment administrator to take the decision, or to grant your role the review permission — see Permissions Panel. A federation partner needs a machine-readable export format Semantic export formats are committed but not yet available Point the partner at the maturity tags in the standards overview, and raise the need with your platform operator. Neither you nor the partner should have to take a conformance claim on faith.

Cross-audience parent: Standards & Compliance Overview. Tenant admin companions: Citation Integrity — the published-citation guarantees in detail; Vocabulary Grounding — the Wikidata / PeriodO workflow; Voice and Vocabulary — your wording on platform surfaces; Telemetry — what the platform records and how it is protected.

The platform collects a deliberately small set of operational signals about how it runs — never a copy of your research content. This page tells you what those signals are, where they live, how long they are kept, what you control, and what to tell an institutional DPO or IRB. Read it when onboarding under a Data Processing Agreement, when an institution's information-security team asks the standard onboarding questions, or before enabling any optional capture. The default posture is capture-off: AI-call, import-run, and review-decision capture record nothing until switched on for your environment. The one exception is tip-activity capture, which starts on — with its own off switch — so that unhelpful tip categories can pause automatically.

AI-call records — for each AI call the platform makes on your environment's behalf, a structured record: the task, the model and its version, token counts, latency, a refusal or escalation flag, and the verdict of a prompt-injection screening check. The record carries one-way hashes of the prompt and response — never the raw text. A call whose prompt matches a high-risk personal-data pattern (such as an identification number) is dropped entirely: no record, no hash, no count. Maturity: Active. Import-run records — for each import run: the source format, entity counts before and after, error categories (never error values), and duration. By construction these records contain no personal data: raw source rows, filenames, staged file paths, document and table names, and credential references are deliberately not recorded. Maturity: Active. Review-decision records — structured signals from suggestion review: reject, undo, edit-after-apply, and feedback-button events, each with a structured reason code. The record carries a keyed fingerprint of the suggestion's shape, not its content, and never records free-form reviewer comments. Maturity: Active. Tip-activity records — which efficiency tips surfaced and whether they were accepted, aggregated into acceptance ratios that drive the automatic pausing of unhelpful tip categories. Tip records carry no researcher identity at all — which tip appeared and what happened to it, never who. Automatic pausing acts on a tip category only once it has at least five recorded responses (the default minimum sample), so it never reacts to a single researcher's actions. Supports the Efficiency Tips surface. Maturity: Active. Search-quality records — planned aggregate measures of search health (zero-result rates, hashed query patterns with small-count suppression). This signal class is not capturing yet: today the platform stores no search-query telemetry at all, raw or hashed. Maturity: Deferred. Per-environment capture switches — capture is controlled per signal class for each environment, and every switch starts off except the tip-activity pair, which starts on. Enabling review-decision capture additionally requires a recorded privacy acknowledgment (who acknowledged, when, and which version of the privacy notice) before the switch will take effect. Maturity: Active. Environment telemetry panel — a dashboard showing your environment's own signals: counts per signal class, a suggestion-quality summary, and any automatically paused suggestion categories. It reads only your environment's records and never displays raw source rows, filenames, file paths, credentials, or tokens. Maturity: Active. Telemetry export for access requests — a self-service, audit-grade export of your environment's telemetry is planned but not yet available. Today, your platform operator produces the export for you on request. Maturity: Deferred.

Read what is happening in your environment: open Workspace → Manage → Telemetry at /app/workspace/manage/telemetry. The panel shows your environment's signal counts by class, the suggestion-quality summary, and any paused automatic-suggestion categories. It is scoped to your environment only; cross-environment comparisons exist only on the platform operator's side. Existing bookmarks to /admin/monitoring/telemetry/ redirect here after the same administrator check. Turn capture on or off: capture switches live on your environment's platform record and are changed through the platform's administrative console — contact your platform operator to change your capture posture. Each signal class is switched independently; everything except tip-activity capture starts off. Enable review-decision capture: this switch requires a privacy acknowledgment to be recorded first. The acknowledgment (person, timestamp, notice version) is stored with your environment's record and is enforced — the switch cannot be turned on without it. Control efficiency-tip capture: tip surfacing and tip-event capture each have their own switch on your environment's record. Both are currently on by default. Tip-event capture continues while both switches are on, even where other capture classes are off — this keeps the automatic pausing of unhelpful tips working. See Efficiency Tips. Honor a data-access request (GDPR Article 15): contact your platform operator, who produces a telemetry export scoped to your environment. Honor an erasure request (GDPR Article 17): see the right-by-right table below; route the request through your platform operator. The configurable settings, summarized: Setting What it does Default Per-signal capture switches Turn each telemetry class (AI calls, import runs, review decisions) on or off for your environment. Changed by your platform operator. Off Review-decision privacy acknowledgment Required before review-decision capture can be enabled; records who acknowledged, when, and which notice version. Not acknowledged Tip surfacing Whether efficiency tips appear at all in your environment. On Tip-event capture Whether tip surface/acceptance events are recorded, independently of other capture classes. On Minimum sample for automatic tip pausing The number of recorded tip responses a category needs before automatic pausing will act on it, so the mechanism never reacts to a single researcher's actions. Changing it is a platform-level change — ask your platform operator. 5

Each environment's data lives in its own separate compartment of the database — its own database schema. The database itself enforces that isolation, and telemetry honors it: telemetry tables refuse to be read from outside an environment's schema. Data Where it lives Who can read it AI-call records (structure and hashes) Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only, for support) Import-run records Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only) Review-decision records Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only) Tip-activity records Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only) Cross-environment operational metrics (cost, latency, model name) Platform-level storage; never your content Platform team only Cross-environment metric rows identify an environment by an internal identifier and carry model name, token counts, cost, and latency — never content.

The platform's default retention policy per data class: Data Default retention AI-call records (structured shape) 30 days verbatim, then 12 months as hashed aggregate Import-run records 12 months Validation and abuse audit records (security-relevant) 2 years (GDPR Art. 17(3)(e) — defence of legal claims) Confirmed prompt-injection material (quarantined) 90 days; extendable under legal hold for specific incidents These defaults are calibrated against ICO and EDPB operational-log guidance, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 control A.8.15, and EU AI Act logging requirements. For retention questions beyond this table — including shorter environment-specific retention — contact your platform operator.

Right How the platform handles it Access (Art. 15) Your platform operator produces a telemetry export scoped to your environment, with an accompanying manifest. Rectification (Art. 16) Not applicable to operational telemetry. For environment content, rectification flows through the standard editing surfaces. Erasure (Art. 17) User-identifying telemetry rows are pseudonymized in place. Small-count-suppressed aggregates are retained as anonymous data (Art. 17(3)(d)). Restriction (Art. 18) Verbatim capture for a specific person can be suppressed on request while anonymous aggregates continue. Portability (Art. 20) Same export format as Article 15. Object (Art. 21) Per-person suppression on request; an environment-level objection turns the signal class off entirely. Automated decision-making (Art. 22) The platform does not make automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects on data subjects. AI output is advisory; researcher review gates any change to your data. Lawful basis is Legitimate Interest (Art. 6(1)(f)), with a documented assessment per signal class available from your platform operator. A data-protection impact assessment precedes production capture and is refreshed annually; environment-specific documentation is available on request.

Third party What they see AI model vendor Under the platform's standard routing, AI calls run inside a cloud provider's hosted model service, and the model vendor does not receive your data. Confirm the routing in force for your environment with your platform operator. Cloud provider hosting the model service Runs the model on each call; provider-side invocation logging is kept off, so the provider retains only the call envelope (model, role, timing) — not prompts or responses. Platform team Read-only access to your environment's schema for support; access to platform-level operational metrics (cost, latency — never your content). Anyone else Nothing. No third-party analytics, advertising, or telemetry services.

When an environment offboards, its database schema is dropped — all telemetry payload in it is deleted, including every aggregate stored there. Cross-environment operational metrics (cost and latency at the platform level) are retained for cost-history continuity; they identify the environment only by an internal identifier and contain no content. On request, that metric trail can be deleted too; the trade-off is the loss of platform-level cost-trend history for the periods your environment participated in.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The telemetry panel shows no signals Capture may be off, or no eligible activity has occurred. Search-quality telemetry is not capturing yet for anyone. Ask your platform operator to confirm the signal classes you need. Review-decision capture also requires the privacy acknowledgment to be recorded first. An import run reports that a stored service credential could not be retrieved The stored credential for that import source is missing, expired, or unreachable Check the import source's connection settings, or contact your platform operator. The telemetry row records the outcome only — no credential material is ever in a telemetry record. A DPO asks for the legitimate-interest assessment per signal class The assessment is maintained per signal class as platform documentation Contact your platform operator, who supplies the documented assessment for the signal classes in question.
