A researcher exercises the right to be forgotten Handling depends on the data class User-identifying telemetry rows are pseudonymized in place; anonymous aggregates are retained as anonymous data. Route the request through your platform operator. You want to verify no raw search queries are stored Raw query text is not captured at all in the current platform — the search-quality signal class is not yet capturing in any form Nothing to configure. When search-quality telemetry ships, it will store hashed, small-count-suppressed aggregates, not raw queries.

For researchers: Privacy and safety. Environment admin companions: Permissions Panel — the Project history tab records who reviewed what, and when; Efficiency Tips — the tip-capture switches. For platform-level monitoring, data-protection impact assessment records, or residency requirements, contact your platform operator.

Vocabulary Review is where a researcher decides how the project should treat date wording that the platform deliberately did not guess at. The queue keeps the value exactly as written, shows any deterministic reading beside it, and offers a direct choice: save that reading, ask for an advisory AI reading, enter the dates yourself, or keep the value as written. There is no proposal-and-approval step inside this page. A saved choice is the review decision. Closing the dialog with its close control or Escape cancels without changing the row.

Open the workspace account menu, then choose Schema & definitions → Vocabulary review. The page opens inside the shared workspace at /app/workspace/manage/vocabulary. Access follows the project-wide Review suggestions permission, not the name of a person's role. An active viewer, editor, or administrator can use the page when that permission applies across the whole project. A role whose permission is limited to particular record types or fields does not gain access to this tenant-wide queue. If the menu item is absent, ask a project administrator to check both the permission and its scope in the Permissions Panel. Old bookmarks under /admin/vocabulary/ and /temporal-review/ redirect to the workspace page while preserving their filters. Use the workspace address for new bookmarks.

One row per distinct value — repeated occurrences are reviewed once; the row shows how many records contain the value. What the platform read — recognized bounds, machine-readable EDTF, and a plain status are shown without rewriting the source wording. Near-duplicate groups — readings within one year of each other are shown together for comparison, but remain separate decisions. Only work still awaiting a decision — after a successful decision, the row leaves the queue and the live counts update. Explicit failure and partial-result messages — a failed save keeps the dialog open. If a saved decision reaches only some occurrences, the page reports what still needs attention.

Choose Review on the row. The dialog opens on the original value, which remains read-only and is labelled “as written — kept exactly.” Choose one of the three paths: What we read shows the deterministic parser's result. If its dates are correct, choose Save this match. AI suggestion requests one advisory reading for this value. Nothing is saved automatically. Choose Accept, Edit first, or Reject after checking the result and any linked authority. Enter it yourself lets you state a start year, optional end year, BCE/CE, precision, date kind, and period label, then choose Save these dates. Confirm the timeline used for comparison when the dialog asks for it. A calendar label describes the source; it never silently converts the years onto another timeline. To keep the wording without an operable date, choose Leave as written. This is a recorded decision and removes the row from the active queue. To make no decision, close the dialog instead. The original wording is preserved on every path. Accepting a reading creates a tenant-owned vocabulary declaration and fans that decision out to matching live occurrences where the platform can do so without inventing missing date semantics.

The AI tab is advisory and loads only when opened. AI suggestions are off by default for each project and are bounded by the project's token budget. If AI is off, the budget is exhausted, the field is restricted, validation fails, or an authority cannot be reached, the dialog says so and manual review remains available. External authority lookup is fail-closed. Values that do not pass the privacy and vocabulary checks are not sent outside the project. A linked authority is evidence to review, not an automatic decision.

The shared page currently presents a date-shaped review experience. The backend also tracks other vocabulary categories, but an in-page category switcher and category-specific review forms are follow-up work. Register and Custom values on a keyed column are not reviewed here yet — their "Manage" link in the column's per-record editor goes to the column's own field settings instead. See Field configuration. The queue itself shows values still awaiting review; it is not a history browser for completed decisions. A column-context link can offer Match these dates to run a complete census for that declared column. The general workspace menu opens the project-wide queue and does not show that column action. A column that behaves like unbounded free text is refused as a bulk vocabulary census. Deterministically readable dates remain usable; the page explains that nothing was queued from the open-ended tail.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Vocabulary review is missing from the workspace menu Your active membership does not have project-wide Review suggestions permission Ask a project administrator to check the permission and remove any record-type or field scope from that capability. The page says it could not load the queue Your session expired, access was revoked, or the request failed Refresh once. If it persists, sign in again or ask an administrator to confirm your access. Saving fails and the dialog stays open The decision was refused, access changed, or the server could not save it Keep the dialog open, read the error, correct the entry if needed, and retry. No change was applied. AI says it is unavailable AI is off, its budget is exhausted, the field is restricted, or a provider failed Use What we read or Enter it yourself. An administrator can review project AI settings separately. A saved match reports that some occurrences still need attention Some occurrences lacked a safe comparison timeline or had an extent the writeback could not apply Review the reported remainder; the platform kept those occurrences unchanged rather than guessing. A column census says the column reads as free text The distinct-value tail is not bounded enough to treat as a controlled vocabulary Review deterministically recognized dates and configure a narrower vocabulary-bearing column instead of forcing the free-text tail into the queue.

Permissions Panel — grant the project-wide review permission used by this page. Voice and Vocabulary — configure researcher-facing project wording. Field configuration — where a keyed column's Register, Custom, Calendar, and Historical date values come from; the pinned allowed-set refusal message that applies to every keyed kind except Calendar and Historical date's own structured editor, which never refuses. AI-Assisted Bootstrap — review structural suggestions during project setup. Standards overview — the scholarly and data standards used by authority-backed readings.

The platform talks to your researchers constantly — page headers, button labels, confirmation phrases, tips, chat copy. Voice and vocabulary is how you make that text speak your environment's language instead of generic platform English. Read this when onboarding a new environment, when a researcher asks "why does it say X?", or when a platform phrase needs to use your wording. Wording configuration is an environment-admin concern; researchers see the result but do not edit it. It applies only to text the platform itself emits — researcher-authored content is never reworded.

Per-environment wording entries — every platform-emitted phrase resolves through a wording table scoped to your environment, one entry per phrase. Surface families displayed today: import wizard pages, workspace headers and toolbar labels, assistant chat copy, permission and role wording, and telemetry panel labels. Maturity: Active. Limit: an entry only takes effect where the platform actually asks for that phrase. Built-in baseline with your labels substituted — every environment starts with a complete neutral-English baseline, and the platform automatically substitutes the names you gave your concept families (the categories your records belong to — "Person", "Place", "Text") into those phrases. A fresh environment already speaks in its own category names before anyone writes a wording entry. Maturity: Active. Layered resolution — for each phrase, the platform uses the most specific wording available: an explicit override set for your environment, then an AI suggestion you accepted during onboarding, then wording seeded during setup, then the baseline. Maturity: Active. Visible failure instead of blank text — if a phrase has no entry and no baseline, the platform renders the phrase's internal dotted key (for example wizard.stage3.match_card.header) rather than showing nothing. A raw key on screen is a signal, not your configuration error. Maturity: Active. Permission wording overrides — role names and permission labels can be renamed from the Permissions Panel. Renaming changes the displayed wording only, never what the role can do. Maturity: Active. AI suggestion provenance — a wording entry that came from an accepted AI suggestion carries a tamper-evident reference to the suggestion it came from. Maturity: Active. Limit: tamper-evident, not hidden — it proves origin, it does not encrypt anything. Two further families prepared, not yet displayed — the wording table also holds confirmation phrases for high-impact actions and review-history labels. Both are seeded with baseline wording, but no screen displays either family yet, so entries for them have no visible effect today. Having or lacking your own phrasing for these never blocks an action or locks any part of onboarding. Maturity: Built.

The highest-leverage move is naming your concept families well. Most of what researchers read is the baseline with those names substituted in, so a good set of category labels improves hundreds of phrases at once. Name your concept families: set the display label for each category of record your environment manages. This normally happens while you confirm an import; the labels can also be edited afterwards in your environment's admin area. Every platform phrase that mentions the category updates. Rename roles and permission wording: open the Permissions Panel and edit the role's displayed name inline. The underlying permissions are unchanged. Accept AI wording suggestions at onboarding: see AI-Assisted Bootstrap for the assisted onboarding path that proposes environment-specific phrasings for you to accept or reject. Act on the wording review notice: the Permissions Panel shows a read-only review notice when concept-family labels are missing or look machine-generated. Fix the flagged labels; the notice can also be dismissed, but it returns if your labels change again. Override a specific phrase: there is currently no self-service screen for editing an individual wording entry. If a specific platform phrase needs different wording and the paths above do not cover it, contact your platform operator.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A platform phrase shows generic wording in your environment No environment-specific wording exists for that phrase, so the baseline is rendering Check that the concept family the phrase mentions has a display label — that fixes most generic-sounding phrases. For a specific phrase that still needs different wording, contact your platform operator. A page shows a raw dotted key like wizard.stage3.match_card.header instead of readable text The phrase has no wording entry and no baseline — the platform deliberately shows the key so the gap is visible This indicates a platform-side gap, not an error in your configuration. Contact your platform operator. The wording review notice in the Permissions Panel returns after you dismissed it Dismissal applies to the labels as they were; the notice reappears when your labels change Fix the flagged labels rather than re-dismissing. The notice is read-only and never changes anything itself. You renamed a role but its permissions did not change Renaming a role changes its displayed wording only This is the intended behaviour. To change what a role can do, compose a custom role in the Permissions Panel.

Researcher tier: Workspace walkthrough — what researchers see (your wording in action). Tenant admin companions: AI-Assisted Bootstrap — assisted onboarding wording suggestions; Vocabulary Grounding — a different surface: grounding the research vocabulary in your data against external authorities; Permissions Panel — role renaming and the wording review notice.

This page is the reference for the collection settings that shape what researchers see in the workspace: the name, icon and order behind every sidebar entry; the field that names each record; the default field set; and the identity that keeps one collection distinct from its siblings. Administrators manage these settings on the workspace's Tables & visibility page. This reference also explains the related ontology entries and environment-wide saved views. Read it after an import has landed a new collection, when labels or ordering look wrong, or when curating the defaults your whole team shares.

Admin-self-serve. Renaming a collection, changing its icon, hiding it from the workspace, reordering the sidebar, choosing its row-title field, and choosing its default fields are all available from Tables & visibility. Saved views remain curated in the workspace itself. Re-importing source data never reverts a collection's label, icon, or order once you have edited them. Import-maintained. Workspace table records and ontology entries are created automatically when imported data is applied — you do not create them by hand for imported sources. The import also maintains a read-only record of which display column the source itself declared, and refreshes the ontology entries (including the anchor) each time an import is applied. Operator-mediated. Environments configured from a declaration file rather than through the import wizard receive their initial tables, labels, and anchor from a seeding run performed by your platform operator. Re-running that seeding converges on the declared file — if you change those values by hand, tell your operator so the declaration is updated to match.
documents.s: What you change yourself, and what the platform maintains

documents.t: Workspace collection records — one record per collection in the researcher workspace. Each record carries the collection's label, an icon name from the Material icon set, an active flag, and a sidebar position (lower numbers appear first). Switching Shown in workspace off hides the collection from the workspace without deleting anything or changing its public publication state. Maturity: Active. Limit: unregistering a collection deletes its saved views with it — hide rather than remove unless you mean to discard those views too. Record labels from the display field — the display field is the data column shown as each record's name in Details, Relations, Publish, search results, linked-record chips, and an Edition-kind keyed column's key picker (which offers each linked edition record labelled by its own collection's display field). It is written as a data path to one of the table's columns, in the form data.<column name>. It is set from the source's declared display column at import and refreshed on re-import only while you have not edited it — your edit always wins. A second, read-only field records what the source declared at the most recent import, so the platform can tell your edit apart from an import-written value. When the display field is blank or a row has no value there, records show a visible unnamed placeholder rather than a generic record type or a guessed column; in the edition key picker specifically, that same blank-value case falls back to the collection's own generic name instead (so several such rows can appear to share one key) — the platform never borrows a different column to fill the gap. Maturity: Active. Default visible columns — an optional list of field names that render as the table's columns by default; leaving it empty shows all fields. This is the environment's default for the table; researchers' own column arrangements and saved views sit on top of it. A re-import can add newly declared source fields to an explicit default list, but it does not remove the administrator's existing selections. Maturity: Active. Limit: the underlying field definitions can still be shared across a concept family, so two source tables that share one concept family may expose a broader shared field set until their views hide irrelevant columns. Table scoping — each table shows the records of one concept family (the configuration forms call this an archetype), optionally narrowed to a single record type and a single source table. Two source tables that share a record type stay two distinct tables rather than merging. When a source renames a table while keeping its stable identity, the platform reuses the existing record so saved views survive, leaves your label untouched, and adds a warning suggesting you review it. Maturity: Active. Limit: table records are scoped per source table, but field-definition scoping is not yet as narrow as table identity in every import shape; curate the default view after large cold imports. Advanced filter setting — a reserved setting on each table record for filtering a table beyond its record type. The workspace does not yet apply it to the rows researchers see; the import writes its own source-table scope into it, and that is the only shape in use. Maturity: Deferred. Limit: entering a custom value today makes the table's scope ambiguous, which switches off in-table record creation, relation editing, and table publishing for that table — leave it as the import wrote it. Ontology entries and collection relationships — each ontology entry pairs a platform concept family with the label your environment uses for it, an optional record type that narrows it, and an anchor flag. The anchor marks the concept family your environment is organized around; the platform allows at most one. The same read-only page lists the collection-to-collection relationships available in the environment's schema view and opens the full Schema Visualizer when you need a map. Maturity: Active. Limit: ontology entries are import-maintained — applying an import refreshes the labels and recomputes the anchor from the approved import decisions, so treat this list as something you read and verify; raise a lasting change with your platform operator. Environment-wide saved views — named views attached to a table, each storing filter conditions, sort order, column arrangement (order, visibility, pinning, sizing), row density (compact, cozy, or comfortable), and row color rules, plus the view mode it opens: Table, Details, Relations, or Publish. A view can be pinned to the primary tab row, and one view per table can be the default. Every saved view is shared with everyone working in the environment. Maturity: Active. Limit: the database allows at most one default view per table.

Open the workspace account menu and choose Workspace settings → Tables & visibility. The page shows one card for each registered collection, with its record count and a direct Open in workspace link. Create collection opens the workspace's existing creation flow, and Bring in data opens the import wizard; the page does not create a second lifecycle path. A data-derived collection that has not been registered stays read-only here and points you back to the workspace to register it first. Rename a collection, change its icon, or reorder the sidebar. Edit Collection label, Icon, or Default order, then choose Save name and order. Researchers see the saved label and order in their workspace sidebar. A later re-import does not undo these edits. Hide a collection without deleting it. Switch Shown in workspace off and save the collection settings. The collection, its records, configuration, and saved views remain, and it returns intact when you switch the setting back on. This switch does not publish or unpublish anything. Set which field names each record. Choose Row title field and save. The choice is shared by Details, Relations, Publish, search results, and linked-record chips. Source-declared label field shows what the latest import declared and is read-only; it remains visible as provenance rather than becoming another editable label. Clearing the row-title choice makes records show a placeholder instead of a name. Use in this view is different: it changes only a saved view's identifying column. Choose the default workspace fields. Select Show all configured fields, or Choose workspace fields and tick at least one field, then save. Researchers can still arrange their own columns, and saved views carry their own column arrangement. When a later import declares new source fields, the platform can add them to this default set without removing your existing choices. Curate first views after import. After a cold import with several source tables under one concept family, open each workspace table before researchers begin using it. If a table shows fields that belong to a neighboring source table, hide those fields in the default saved view and keep the table label source-specific so researchers can tell the tables apart. Review identity and filtering cautiously. Advanced identity and filter exposes the collection's canonical structure, canonical type, source table, and advanced filter. These values determine which records belong to the collection. Changing canonical structure resets the row-title field and default workspace fields because the old field names belong to the previous structure; choose the new presentation fields before saving if the defaults are not suitable. A save is refused while a public view or relationship depends on the identity being changed; do not treat that refusal as a reason to recreate the collection. Read the ontology and relationship map. Choose Schema & definitions → Relationships & ontology from the workspace account menu. The page shows each concept family's label, its optional record type, and whether it is the anchor or a supporting concept. Below it, the collection-relationships list names the source collection, relationship, and target collection; choose Open schema visualizer for the full interactive map. This page has no create, rename, retire, or delete controls. Verify it after an import; a label that needs to change durably should go through your import decisions or your platform operator, because the next import apply refreshes this list. Curate saved views. Saved views and the views researchers create in the workspace are the same records — there is no separate admin-only kind, and every view is visible to the whole environment. Shape a view in the workspace itself, where its filters, sort, column arrangement, color rules, density, pinning, and default status are stored as you work. Set the default view. Mark one view per table as the default; it is what the table opens with, for everyone. The database enforces at most one default per table, so clear the current default before assigning a new one.

Symptom Likely cause Fix An import created two similar-looking tables Two source tables share one record type; each source table becomes its own workspace table by design Rename the labels so researchers can tell them apart, or hide the one not in use. A table shows columns from a related source table The table record is scoped per source table, but the field definitions can still be shared at the concept-family level Hide the irrelevant columns in the table's default saved view. Escalate if the field set itself must be separated by source table. Records show a placeholder instead of a name The table's display field is blank — the source declared no display column — or it points at a column many records leave empty Set the display field to a data.<column name> path for a column every record fills. A re-import did not pick up the source's new display column You edited the display field, and your edit always wins over the import Compare with the read-only companion field showing what the source declared, and copy that value in if you want the source's choice. Creating records or editing relations is unavailable in one table, or the table cannot be published The table record carries a custom advanced-filter value, which makes its scope ambiguous Remove the custom additions from the advanced filter, keeping only what the import wrote. Marking a second view as the default fails A table can have at most one default view; the database enforces it Clear the default flag on the current default and save, then mark the new view. Saved views disappeared after a table was removed Deleting a table record deletes its saved views with it Restore from your environment's backup if available. Going forward, hide tables with the active flag instead of deleting them. Your ontology label edits were reverted Applying an import refreshes ontology entries, including labels and the anchor Make the label change part of your import decisions, or ask your platform operator to update the environment's declaration.

Same tree: Data Import Wizard — the import flow that creates these table records and maintains the source-declared display column. Companion page: Field configuration — the Edition-kind keyed column that reads this display field for its key picker. Researcher tier: Save your table arrangement as a view — how researchers create, duplicate, and share the same saved views you curate here; Workspace Walkthrough — what researchers see once these records are in place.

A new person is joining your environment mid-project — a research assistant, a co-investigator, a visiting scholar, or a short-term contributor who needs access for a few weeks. This page is the start-to-finish sequence for getting them from "no account" to "working in the right tables with the right role." It also marks clearly which steps are yours to do and which only your platform operator can do, so you know where to wait and where to act. Read this when someone new is arriving. For the new collaborator's own first session, hand them the researcher tutorial — Getting started — once their access is ready.

Onboarding has two owners. The account itself is created by your platform operator; everything about what the collaborator can do inside your environment is yours to configure on the Permissions Panel. Step Who does it Where 1. Decide the role and scope You Plan ahead — no UI yet 2. Request the account You ask; operator creates Outside your environment 3. Assign the role You Permissions Panel → Contributors 4. Prepare the workspace You Workspace views and sidebar 5. Brief the collaborator You Point them at the researcher tutorial 6. Verify their access You and the collaborator Permissions Panel + a check from their side You can do steps 1, 3, and 4 yourself. Step 2 depends on your platform operator. Steps 5 and 6 involve the collaborator directly.

Decide what the person should be able to do before the account exists, so you can assign a role the moment they appear in your Contributors list. Every environment ships with a standard role catalog: Reviewer, External collaborator, Researcher contributor, and Project admin. Match the person to the closest standard role: A reviewing scholar who reads and comments but should not save changes → Reviewer. A guest from outside the project making small additive changes in one area → External collaborator. A team researcher doing routine editing → Researcher contributor. A co-director who needs configuration and role-management authority → Project admin. If no standard role fits, compose a custom one from the platform's fixed set of permission building blocks on the Permissions Panel's Roles tab, and name it. You combine existing permissions; you cannot define new ones. See User and Access Management for the standard catalog and Permissions Panel for composition. A new contributor starts with a baseline set of permissions: they can review suggestions, save routine (low- and medium-impact) changes, undo recent changes, and manage saved import setups. They do not start with the ability to apply high-impact changes, configure fields, or manage permissions — those are granted deliberately, by assigning a role that includes them. Keep this in mind when matching a visiting or temporary collaborator to a role: the safe default already withholds the high-authority actions. You can also narrow where a role applies. A role assignment — or a custom role — can be scoped to specific record types or fields, so a collaborator working on one collection does not gain reach across the whole environment. This is the right tool for a visiting scholar who should touch one area only.
documents.s: 1. Choose or compose the role before they arrive

documents.t: Contributor accounts are created by your platform operator, not from inside your environment. Send the operator the person's details and ask them to create the account. This is the one step you cannot complete yourself; until the operator finishes, the person will not appear in your Contributors list.

Once the operator confirms the account exists, the person appears in the Contributors tab of the Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/. Open their row, pick the standard or custom role you decided on in step 1, and — if appropriate — set a scope on the same row to limit the role to specific record types or fields. If your environment has a project rule requiring a second contributor to confirm high-impact changes, that rule already applies to the new collaborator; you do not configure it per person. Project rules are environment-wide and sit on top of every role.

Make the collaborator's first session land them somewhere useful rather than on a raw table. Shared default view. Each table has one default view — the view that opens when anyone first visits that table. If your team has agreed on a working view (its filters, sort, and columns), set it as the default so the new person sees the same starting point as everyone else. The default is shared across the team, so this one action prepares the workspace for the collaborator without any per-person setup. See Save a view. Sidebar organization. The sidebar lists your environment's tables. If your environment groups or orders tables for clarity, that organization is already in place for the new collaborator; there is nothing per-person to configure.

Tell the collaborator three things and then let the product teach the rest: Their work is safe to explore — drafts do not publish by accident, and recent changes can be undone. Reading comes before writing — they can search and read existing records before editing anything. Help is built in — the contextual help is available without leaving the workspace. For everything beyond that, point them at the researcher tutorial: Getting started. It walks a new researcher through their first week — signing in, finding the team's default view, reading, and making safe first edits — so you do not have to write your own orientation.
documents.s: 5. Brief the collaborator on day one

documents.t: Confirm two things before you consider onboarding done. From your side: on the Permissions Panel's Contributors tab, the collaborator shows the role you assigned, with the scope you intended. From their side: ask the collaborator to open the search and reading area and look for a note about hidden collections. The platform shows a banner — "N collections are hidden — they require a review capability you don't hold" — whenever a person's role does not include the review capability some collections require. If the collaborator sees that banner and you intended them to have full access, their role is too narrow; widen it on the Contributors tab. If you intended to restrict them, the banner confirms the restriction is working. This from-their-side check catches scope mismatches that the Contributors tab alone can hide.
documents.s: 6. Verify their access — including a check from their side

documents.t: A visiting or short-term collaborator is onboarded the same way, with two adjustments: Prefer a scoped role. Limit the role to the record types or fields they need rather than granting environment-wide reach. The baseline new-contributor permissions already withhold high-impact actions; a scope narrows reach further. Plan the wind-down. When the visit ends, change or remove their role on the Contributors tab. Removing the account itself is a platform-operator action, like creating it — ask the operator to deactivate or remove the account when access should end entirely.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The new person does not appear in the Contributors tab The account has not been created yet Contributor accounts are created by your platform operator. Confirm the operator has created the account; until then there is no row to assign a role to. You assigned a role but the collaborator cannot act on content they should Their role assignment carries a scope that excludes that content Open their row on the Contributors tab and check the scope. Widen it or remove it. The collaborator sees a "collections are hidden" note Their role does not include the review capability some collections require If they should have access, assign or compose a role that includes that capability. If the restriction is intended, this is working as configured. See Permissions Panel. No standard role matches what the collaborator needs The standard catalog is fixed Compose a custom role from the available permission building blocks on the Roles tab. If the permission you need does not exist in the platform's set at all, contact your platform operator. You need to remove a departing collaborator's account entirely Account removal is a platform-operator action Change or remove their role on the Contributors tab to cut access immediately, and ask your platform operator to deactivate or remove the account itself.

Where you do the work: Permissions Panel — assigning roles, composing custom roles, and scoping assignments. The role model in one page: User and Access Management — the standard role catalog and how contributor accounts are created. For the collaborator: Getting started — the researcher tutorial to hand off on day one. Preparing the workspace: Save a view — setting the shared default view a new collaborator lands on.

A re-import brings a refreshed copy of source data you have imported before into your environment. Most re-imports are routine: the source gained a few rows, corrected some values, or grew a new column, and you want the environment to reflect that. This page is for the planning that happens before you press start — checking what would change, choosing how records are refreshed, and reading the practice run — so a refresh updates your data without quietly overwriting work your researchers have done. Read this before re-running a source you have imported once already, especially if researchers have been editing those records in the workspace since the first import. This page covers the planning and the choices. For the wizard's screens, size limits, and step-by-step controls, see Data Import Wizard. For what your researchers see afterwards, see the cross-links at the end.

A re-import is routine when: The source gained rows, or corrected values in fields the source manages. The source grew a new column you want as a new field. Nobody has hand-edited the affected records inside the workspace, so there are no researcher edits to protect. A re-import deserves a careful plan when: Researchers have edited records in the workspace since the last import — added notes, set field labels, marked fields required, or filled in fields the source does not manage. The source dropped or renamed columns that your researchers rely on. You are not certain which refresh behaviour a planned run will use. The wizard itself never publishes anything and writes nothing to your environment until you press Start import in the final step. The risk is not in opening the wizard. It is in choosing the wrong refresh behaviour for a source whose records carry researcher edits.
documents.s: When a re-import is routine, and when it is risky

documents.t: Researcher edits are the thing a re-import can put at risk, so locate them before you plan the run. Open the affected tables in the workspace and look for records that have been worked on since the last import — filled-in fields the source does not provide, renamed field labels, required flags, or notes. Field configuration you set — labels, required flags, field-level settings — is preserved across a re-import regardless of refresh behaviour. It is the record values that researchers entered into fields the source does not manage that depend on which behaviour you choose. If researchers have been working in these tables and you cannot tell what they changed, treat the run as risky and plan for the edit-preserving behaviour described below.
documents.s: Before you run: check for researcher edits

documents.t: The platform supports two behaviours for refreshing the records themselves. The difference is what happens to anything a researcher added that the source does not manage. Behaviour What it keeps What it replaces When to use Edit-preserving refresh Researcher edits to fields the source does not manage, on records it can match Only the values the source manages, refreshed from the new data The right default for routine re-runs Full refresh Nothing from the prior records Everything — the existing rows are removed and reloaded from scratch Only a genuine "start over", when you intend to discard prior records and their researcher edits Edit-preserving refresh matches each incoming row to an existing record by the record's source identity — the stable identifier carried from the first import — then refreshes the source-managed values and leaves everything else alone. Where there is no match, it creates a new record. Full refresh does not match at all: it removes the existing rows and reloads, which discards any researcher edit those rows held. This choice is made by your platform operator, not in the wizard. Edit-preserving refresh and full refresh are run as platform commands, not as buttons inside the wizard. If you are unsure which behaviour a planned re-import will use, confirm it with your platform operator before the run — this is the single most important step in planning a safe re-import. State plainly which one you want and why.

When you re-import a source you have brought in before, the wizard works for you rather than starting over: It recognizes the saved setup from the earlier import. It carries your unchanged decisions forward instead of re-asking them, so you review only what is new, changed, or ambiguous. Anything new, changed, or genuinely uncertain goes back to review. Uncertainty always routes to review — it is never carried forward silently. This carry-forward is about the structural decisions you made (how a table is read, what a column becomes). It is separate from the record-refresh behaviour above, which governs the record values themselves.
documents.s: What the wizard does on a re-import

documents.t: The wizard's practice run is a full dry run that happens before anything is written. It is your last and best check on a re-import plan. It reports how many records will be created, updated, or skipped, and how many are blocked by unresolved review items. Issues are grouped by cause rather than scattered by row, with a good / warning / error breakdown, and each group links back to the review queue. For a re-import of mostly unchanged data, the practice run should show nearly all records ready rather than blocked, because carried-forward decisions are already accounted for. Read the practice run as a forecast of the real run. If the numbers do not match what you expect — far more records updated than rows changed, or a table predicted to create nothing — stop and find out why before pressing start. The practice run is also where the wizard predicts each table's outcome, so the final receipt should confirm what the practice run forecast.
documents.s: Reading the practice run before you commit

documents.t: A re-import surfaces to researchers as a delta — a summary of only what is new, changed, carried forward, removed, or restored since their last import. It does not ask them to re-review decisions already made. Point researchers at these entries so they can read their side of a re-import: Understand what changed after a re-import — how the delta reads, and the reassurance that their own edits and labels are not overwritten by an edit-preserving refresh. What happens to saved views after a re-import — how a saved view adapts when a field it referenced is removed in the new source, and how it is restored if that field returns.

The safe direction is to plan so that nothing needs undoing. But if a re-import has already written records you wish it had not: Records written by an import cannot be undone from inside the wizard. The wizard's undo applies to review decisions before the final run; it does not reverse records written when you press start. The verified recovery path is to restore the affected records from your environment's backup, then re-run as an edit-preserving refresh. If your platform operator runs imports for you, ask them to restore from backup and use the edit-preserving behaviour. This is operator-mediated work, not something you reverse yourself. A re-import that was interrupted mid-run — rather than completed wrongly — is a different case: the setup, approvals, and practice run are kept, and starting again resumes from the stopped table without writing completed tables twice. A run that did not finish cleanly is reconciled by your platform operator before the next attempt; it is not something to force past. The honest statement is that a full refresh over records with researcher edits is destructive and the records themselves are recovered only from backup, not from within the platform. Plan the behaviour choice carefully and you avoid needing recovery at all.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A re-import replaced researcher edits with source values The run used a full refresh, which removes and reloads rows, instead of an edit-preserving refresh Restore the affected records from your environment's backup, then re-run as an edit-preserving refresh. If your platform operator runs imports for you, ask them to use the edit-preserving behaviour. The wizard re-asked every decision as if this were a first import The earlier import was never completed through the final step, so there is no carried-forward baseline Check that the previous import finished through the wizard's last step. Only completed imports produce a baseline for carry-forward. The practice run shows far more records updated than rows actually changed in the source The run may be matching on an identity that shifts between imports, so records are not recognized as the same record Stop before pressing start. Confirm with your platform operator that the source identity used to match records is stable across imports. You are unsure which refresh behaviour a planned run will use The behaviour is chosen at run time by your platform operator, not in the wizard Ask your platform operator which behaviour the run will use, and state which one you want and why, before the run. A new re-import is blocked, citing a previous run that did not finish A prior run was interrupted and left in an unfinished state Do not force the run. Your platform operator reconciles the unfinished run first, then a new run can proceed.

The wizard itself: Data Import Wizard — the screens, size limits, six-step flow, and the autonomy setting. Who reviews and who applies: Permissions Panel — the two-step approval a re-import's suggestions pass through. For researchers: Understand what changed after a re-import and What happens to saved views after a re-import — the researcher's side of a re-import.

This tutorial walks a new environment from empty to its first published records. It sequences the work — what to do first, what can wait, and which steps your platform operator performs for you — and hands you off to the feature page for each task when you are ready to act. Follow it once, in order, when you are standing up a fresh environment. Each later visit, you will go straight to the feature page you need. The platform ships generic. Setup is how you make one environment speak your domain's language, decide who can do what, bring in your data under review, and put your first records in front of readers.

You need an environment that already exists and an account in it that holds the administrator role with permission management. Creating the environment and your first administrator account is platform-operator work, not something you do from inside the environment. If you are reading this without an environment to sign in to, that is the step to request first. Two divisions of labor recur throughout this tutorial, so it helps to name them now: Admin self-serve — you do it yourself from your environment's admin area. Operator-mediated — you prepare and review the work, but your platform operator runs the step that takes effect. This is true for creating contributor accounts, applying a citation style, and launching the public surface. The tutorial flags which kind each step is as you reach it.

Stage What you do Self-serve or operator-mediated 1. Voice and vocabulary Name your concept families; review the vocabulary arriving in your data Self-serve 2. Roles and contributors Compose the roles your team needs; invite the people You compose roles; the operator creates the accounts 3. First import Practice-run a source, choose an autonomy level, review proposals Self-serve 4. First published records Run the entry-surface readiness review, then launch You review; the operator launches Stages 1 and 2 can overlap — you can name concept families and compose roles in either order. Stage 3 depends on having concept families named, because the import wizard works in your category names. Stage 4 depends on having records to publish, so it comes last.

The single highest-leverage move in setup is naming your concept families — the categories your records belong to, such as Person, Place, or Text. Most of what a researcher reads is the platform's standard wording with those category names substituted into it, so a good set of labels improves hundreds of phrases at once before you write a single custom phrase. A fresh environment already speaks in neutral English and substitutes your category names into its phrases automatically. You do not start from blank screens; you start from a working baseline and shape it. Name your concept families. This normally happens while you confirm your first import (Stage 3), and the labels can also be edited afterwards in your environment's admin area. If you are setting up before you have data to import, you can still set the labels directly. Watch for the wording review notice. When concept-family labels are missing or look machine-generated, the Permissions Panel shows a read-only notice with the flagged labels. Fix them; the notice returns if your labels change again, so treat it as a running check rather than a one-time gate. Full detail on how wording resolves, role renaming, and the one phrase you cannot edit yourself (an individual platform phrase, which is operator-mediated today): Voice and Vocabulary.

Separate from the platform's own wording, your records bring in vocabulary the platform does not recognize — today, calendar names appearing in your data and standard identifiers declared on your field definitions. The platform collects each new value in a review queue rather than guessing. Grounding is where you decide, value by value, whether each becomes a recognized part of your environment's vocabulary, with a label you choose and optional links to recognized scholarly and data standards. You do not need to ground anything to keep working — the queue is there when you are ready, usually after your first import. AI grounding suggestions, which can propose a label and a match against public reference sources, are switched off by default and turned on per environment; only the tenant administrator role can confirm a grounding. When to come back to this: after Stage 3, once an import has populated the queue. Full detail: Vocabulary Grounding.

Decide who can do what before people arrive, so a new contributor lands in a role that already fits. Every environment ships with four standard roles — Reviewer, External collaborator, Researcher contributor, and Project admin — and you compose custom roles from a fixed set of permission building blocks when the standard roles do not fit. Renaming a standard role changes its displayed label only, never what it allows. Open the Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/. It opens on the Contributors tab; the other tabs are Roles, Project rules, Wording, and Project history. Compose the roles your team needs. On the Roles tab, combine the permission building blocks and name the role. A role assignment can be narrowed to specific record types or fields, so a guest collaborator can be scoped to one part of your project. Set your project rules. On the Project rules tab, decide whether high-impact saves need a reviewer who did not author the change, and how destructive changes are confirmed. These rules tighten what a role allows; they never grant more. Invite your contributors — operator-mediated. Contributor accounts are created by your platform operator. Once a person appears in the Contributors section, you assign their role there. So the sequence is: prepare the role, ask the operator to create the account, then assign the role when the person shows up in the panel. A new contributor's account starts able to review proposals, apply low- and medium-risk changes, undo recent changes, and manage saved import setups — but not apply high-risk changes, configure fields, or manage permissions. Adjust from there with a role or a scoped assignment. Full detail: Permissions Panel for composing and assigning; User and Access Management for the standard role catalog and how accounts are created.

The Data Import Wizard is the supported path for getting data into an environment. It reads your source, proposes how each table and column should land, routes every proposal through a two-step approval, and writes records only when you press Start import in the final step. Nothing reaches your environment before that. Treat the first run as a practice run. The wizard's fifth step is a full dry run that writes nothing, so you can see exactly what would happen before committing. Start in the sidebar at Imports & AI → Imports. The wizard accepts an Excel workbook, a MySQL dump or live connection, a set of CSV files, or a Coda document. Start from an upload route — the plain admin "Add" form does not read a source. Choose how involved you want to be. Step 3 asks the autonomy question — Hands off, Stay informed, Ask if unsure, or Confirm everything — saved per import. For a first import you do not yet know well, a more involved setting holds more suggestions for your decision. High-risk and restructure suggestions wait for explicit review whatever the setting, and every automatic decision comes with an undo window. Read the practice run (Step 5). Issues are grouped by cause rather than by row, with a good/warning/error breakdown. This is where a misread table or a field you did not expect surfaces — before any record is written. Approve in two steps. A reviewer approves each suggestion, then an administrator applies it. If a suggestion's risk level shifted while it waited for review, the apply step blocks until you acknowledge the new level. Start the import (Step 6) once every suggestion is approved or rejected. Watch the per-table progress, read the completion receipt, and use Open your workspace to see the results. Naming your concept families (Stage 1) happens naturally here: confirming an import is the usual moment you give each category its display label. Full detail, including the four source types, background imports for large files, and re-import behavior: Data Import Wizard.

Once your data is in and your researchers have a working set of records, the last setup stage prepares the public surface external readers will see. Before your environment exposes a public Entry surface, the readiness review lets you review the filter and autocomplete controls that would become public, record a decision about each one, and confirm or defer each candidate. It is a review, not an apply step: recording decisions stores your review state and never changes the public surface by itself. The standalone review panel was retired with the transitional /app/admin/ shell; until its replacement ships in the admin tier, the review runs through your platform operator. Request the readiness report. Your platform operator runs the readiness audit for your environment and shares the report with you. The report is read-only — producing it never changes your environment's configuration. Work through each role's checklist. The report lists blockers, reviewed fields, candidate fields, and compact-control warnings — fields whose values are too long to show well in a compact public filter. Decide per field, with a reason for each decision, and send your decisions to your operator, who records them; each stored decision is durable and appears in the next report. Hand off for launch — operator-mediated. When the report reads clean, your platform operator performs the public launch. The report's "ratification unchanged" line confirms that review work never alters your environment's search configuration as a side effect; confirming that configuration and launching the surface are separate, explicit steps run with your operator. Full detail: Entry Surface Readiness, and Public reader for what readers see once the surface launches.
documents.s: Stage 4 — First published records and the readiness review

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A researcher-facing phrase still shows generic platform wording The concept family the phrase mentions has no display label, or no entry exists for that phrase Set the concept-family label first — it fixes most generic-sounding phrases. For a specific phrase that still needs different wording, contact your platform operator. See Voice and Vocabulary. A new contributor cannot be assigned a role Their account has not been created yet Contributor accounts are operator-mediated. Ask your platform operator to create the account; assign the role once the person appears in the Contributors tab. The "Add" form in the import area opened a bare form that does nothing The plain admin "Add" form does not read a source Close it and start from an upload route at Imports & AI → Imports. A re-import overwrote a researcher's manual edits The run replaced the rows instead of doing an edit-preserving refresh Restore from your environment's backup and re-run as an edit-preserving refresh. If your operator runs imports for you, ask them to use the edit-preserving mode. See Data Import Wizard. The readiness report reads clean but the public surface has not appeared Recording decisions does not launch the surface The launch is a separate step. Confirm with your platform operator that it was run. See Entry Surface Readiness. A vocabulary value you reviewed shows as unreviewed after a re-import A re-import should never reset a review decision This should not happen — contact your platform operator with the affected value and the import date.

Stage 1 — Voice and vocabulary (self-serve): name your concept families; act on the wording review notice; plan to work the grounding queue after your first import. → Voice and Vocabulary, Vocabulary Grounding Stage 2 — Roles and contributors (roles self-serve; accounts operator-mediated): compose the roles your team needs, set project rules, then have accounts created and assign roles. → Permissions Panel, User and Access Management Stage 3 — First import (self-serve): start from an upload route, choose an autonomy level, read the practice run, approve in two steps, then start the import. → Data Import Wizard Stage 4 — First published records (review and launch operator-mediated until the admin-tier review UI ships): work the readiness review per role through your operator, then the operator performs the launch. → Entry Surface Readiness

Environment administration home: Environment Administration — the reference index for every configuration surface this tutorial touches. Assisted wording onboarding: AI-Assisted Bootstrap — a one-pass path that proposes domain-specific wording; note its review screen is not yet available, so concept-family naming is the live wording path today. Researcher tier: Researcher guide — what your contributors see in the workspace and public reader once setup is done.

This page covers team membership and the standard role set. It is the lightweight overview; the live source of truth for contributors, roles, project rules, ownership transfers, and project history is the Permissions Panel. Read this if you want a one-page summary of the role model; go to the Permissions Panel page when you are about to make a change.

Standard role catalog — four pre-loaded roles every environment ships with: Reviewer, External collaborator, Researcher contributor, and Project admin. Maturity: Built. Limit: the permissions behind a standard role are fixed by the platform; renaming a standard role changes its label only. Custom role composition — build a role by combining permissions from the platform's fixed permission set. Maturity: Active. Limit: you combine existing permissions; you cannot define new ones. Project rules — environment-wide safety rules that sit on top of roles, such as requiring a second contributor to confirm high-impact changes. Maturity: Active. Limit: rules tighten what a role allows; they never grant more. Ownership transfer — moves ownership of the environment from the current owner to another contributor. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the current owner can start a transfer; both the owner and the receiving contributor must confirm; every transfer is recorded.

The Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/ is where you do this day-to-day. The panel has five sections: Contributors, Roles, Project rules, Wording, and Project history. Role names follow your environment's wording settings, so the role names you see may differ from the standard names used on this page. Assign or change a role: Contributors section. Pick the contributor and choose a standard or custom role. A role assignment can also be limited to specific record types or fields. Compose a custom role: Roles section. Combine permissions from the platform's set and name the role. Roles can be renamed at any time; a rename changes the label your team sees, never the permissions. Set project rules: Project rules section — for example, require that high-impact changes are confirmed by a second contributor. Transfer ownership: available to the current owner only. The owner starts the transfer, both sides confirm, and the transfer is recorded. Add a new contributor: contributor accounts are created by your platform operator. Once the person appears in the Contributors section, you assign their role there. Suspend, reactivate, or remove a contributor: each contributor row's menu, self-serve. Suspension is immediate — the person can no longer sign in, and an already-open session stops working; the row stays visible with a "Suspended" marker, and reactivating restores access. Removing a contributor ends their access while keeping the membership record for your project's audit history. The project owner's row shows these actions disabled until ownership is transferred. Where contributors sign in: at your project's /login/ page — an ordinary account with no operations access. Only contributors holding the admin role can open the /admin/ operations area; everyone works in the workspace. Standard role summary: Role What it allows Typical contributor Reviewer Read and review suggested changes; cannot save changes. External reviewers, students. External collaborator Review and save small additive changes in a focused area, without broader project authority. Guest collaborators from outside the project. Researcher contributor Review suggestions, save routine changes, undo recent changes, and manage saved import setups. Project team researchers. Project admin Everything, including high-impact changes, field setup, role management, and review metrics. Project directors, principal investigators.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A contributor cannot open the Permissions Panel Their account does not have administrator access Ask a contributor with the Project admin role to check their role in the Contributors section. If no one in your environment can resolve it, contact your platform operator. You need a permission shape no standard role provides The standard catalog is fixed Compose a custom role from the available permissions. If the permission you need does not exist in the platform's set at all, contact your platform operator. Renaming a standard role did not change what it allows Renaming changes the label only This is the intended behavior. Compose a custom role if you need a different set of permissions. A contributor can review changes but cannot save them Their role does not include saving (for example, Reviewer), or a project rule requires a second contributor for that kind of change Check the contributor's role in the Contributors section and the rules in the Project rules section. An ownership transfer will not complete Transfers must be started by the current owner; both sides must confirm; and the receiving contributor must be an active contributor holding the Project admin role with role management Confirm on both sides, and check the receiving contributor's role in the Contributors section. If the transfer was not started by the current owner, ask the owner to start it.
Live source of truth: Permissions Panel.

You are a scholar, student, archivist, or editor working in a knowledge environment built on this platform. You sign in, read, search, edit records, and cite them. You do not run the system; you use it. This guide is the entry point for everything researcher-facing. Read it when you join a new environment, when a control is not behaving as you expect, or when you want to know what the platform will and will not do for you. If you configure the environment — turning columns on or off, choosing which fields are searchable, managing other researchers' permissions — see the environment administration guide instead.

The researcher surface gives you nine capabilities, ordered by how often you will reach for them. Workspace table view — the main table of records for each record type, with a toolbar, a Manage columns panel, filters, a row-density toggle, cell ranges and targeted-cell copy, selected-row CSV/JSON export, paste-as-new-row targets on editable tables, and a Details panel for reading a full record. Maturity: Active. Limit: which controls appear for each record type is configured per environment; if a control you need is missing, your environment administrator can expose it. Inline editing — edit a field directly in the table: double-click a cell to open it and press Enter to save, while longer and multilingual fields open an editor with its own Save and Cancel buttons. Date fields use a date picker; text fields that merely look like timestamps stay text until their type is changed or converted. + New row adds a row to the table and opens it for editing, saved as you work. Maturity: Active. Structured scholarly writing — formatted-text fields share one popup/fullscreen editor for Text, headings, marks and links, lists, tables, callouts, mentions, footnotes, equations, accessible figures, block reordering, and document-local Undo/Redo. Maturity: Active. Limit: a figure chooses image media already available in the workspace; the editor does not upload a new file. Search across scripts — a quick search finds records across the collections you can access, a full Search & Read page filters and reads results in place, and the toolbar box narrows the rows already in front of you. Search matches the scripts your records carry — original script, transliteration, and translation — for fields marked searchable. Maturity: Active. Limit: only fields your environment marks searchable are covered. Media and citations — records can carry images, audio, video, and 3D models, and each media item carries a citation in your project's citation style, ready to copy. Maturity: Active. Limit: which media a record carries depends on what your project attached. Public reader and draft preview — a stable read-only view of published records, with an in-workspace preview that shows a record as a reader outside the project would see it. Maturity: Active. Limit: which records reach the reader depends on your project's review and publish workflow. Tips and guidance — small suggestions that appear in the workspace and in multi-step wizards. You can dismiss a single tip or mute a whole family of tips. A tip only suggests; acting on it is always your choice. Maturity: Active. Accessibility — keyboard navigation, visible focus indicators, the row-density toggle, and controls for font size, line height, font family, and color presets. Maturity: Active. Limit: screen-reader announcement coverage continues to improve. Privacy — the platform records usage as aggregate counts and timings, not transcripts of what you typed, and masks sensitive text before anything is stored. Privacy and safety explains exactly what is recorded and what is not. Maturity: Active.

Start with whichever matches what you want to do. New to the workspace, or unsure where a control lives → Workspace walkthrough. Creating a record, editing one, or deleting one → Adding and editing rows. Writing headings, lists, tables, mentions, footnotes, equations, links, or figures in a formatted-text field → Write formatted text. Turning messy dates — ranges, circa, named periods — into years you can sort and place on a timeline → Dating temporal values. Hunting for a record across scripts, opening media, or reading citations → Searching and reading. Curious about the small suggestions appearing beside the form or the table → Tips and guidance. Driving the platform from the keyboard, or adjusting display settings → Accessibility. Wondering what the platform records about you and what it does not → Privacy and safety. Wanting to know what a reader outside the project sees, and how to preview it → Public reader. Wanting to know how external tools, libraries, and AI agents read your published records → Your published data as an API. Stuck on one specific task, or after a quick answer in the moment → the in-product Help page (/app/workspace/help) groups short task-shaped guides by topic, and a ? beside a control opens the matching guide in a drawer. Browse the same guides in the help topics (see find help on a topic). A few conventions across all walkthroughs: Bold marks an on-screen control name — for example, + New row, Add filter, Delete row. A code-style font marks a path, URL fragment, or literal value. Examples use abstract content ("historical figures", "manuscript editions") rather than your specific project's records. The mechanics are the same regardless.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Where to escalate A column you expected is missing from the table. Either hidden in the current view, or not exposed in your environment's configuration. Open Manage columns in the toolbar; if the column is not listed there, ask your environment administrator to expose it. Your environment administrator. A field is read-only when you expected to edit it. Permissions on your account, or a workflow rule for that record type. Confirm your role with your environment administrator; if the restriction is intended, request edit permission for that record type. Your environment administrator. A record will not publish. A required field is still empty. Fill the required fields the message names, then publish again. See Adding and editing rows. Your environment administrator, if the message is unclear. Search returns nothing for a record you know exists. The relevant field is not marked searchable in your environment's configuration. Open the record directly through its Details panel; ask your environment administrator to mark the field searchable. Your environment administrator.
Environment administration guide — the companion guide for the person who configures your environment. Help topics — the same short, task-shaped guides that the in-product Help page shows.

Your knowledge environment is built to work with keyboard navigation, screen readers, and adjustable display settings. This page walks through what is available, where to find it, and what is still on the way. Read it when you want to drive the workspace without a mouse, when you need to adjust how text is displayed, or when a control is not reachable or readable the way you expected.

Workspace keyboard navigation — Tab / Shift+Tab, Enter, Escape, arrow keys, and Space cover the workspace's interactive controls. The combinations follow common conventions. Active. Visible focus rings (keyboard-only) — a clear outline on the focused element, drawn when you navigate with the keyboard and suppressed for mouse clicks, so the screen stays quiet for mouse users. Active. Inline editing with the keyboard — Tab into a field, type, Tab out; your change is saved when the field loses focus. Enter saves it too. Dropdown fields respond to arrow keys and Enter. Active. Formatted-text authoring with the keyboard — popup and fullscreen editing expose named toolbar controls, searchable / and @ menus, editor-local Undo/Redo, structural list and table navigation, and keyboard block-move actions. Active. Hints on fields that are not editable yet — a field whose editing surface has not shipped shows a hint in place of an editor. The hint is part of the keyboard tab order and is announced as disabled to screen readers, so you know the field exists and is intentionally not interactive yet. Active. Named workspace form controls — toolbar filters, column-header menus, Details fields, and New-row fields expose stable labels and form identities to browsers and assistive technology. Active. Row density control — three row heights (Compact, Cozy, Comfortable); your choice is saved with the view you are working in. Active. Accessibility control panel — font size, line height, font family, and a small set of background color presets, remembered by your browser. Available on your environment's reading and browsing pages; the workspace does not include it yet. Active. Finer-grained color customization is Deferred. Accessible inline tips — the tip panel that appears alongside your work is screen-reader-friendly and keeps focus stable when its content updates. Active.

Tab / Shift+Tab moves through interactive controls — toolbar buttons, filter controls, the search box, table cells, drawer fields. Arrow keys move within the table grid, the saved-views menu, and the row density control. In the column manager, the arrow keys on a column's reorder handle move that column up or down the list. Space selects the focused row. Hold Ctrl (Cmd on Mac) with Space to add a row to the selection or remove it. Shift + Up/Down arrow extends the selection across a range of rows. Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on Mac) opens the focused row's details. Enter activates the focused button or saves an edit in a focused field. Escape closes the active drawer, panel, or dialog. Focused elements show a visible focus ring — a clear outline marking where you are. The ring is keyboard-only by default; clicking a control with the mouse does not draw it.
documents.s: Driving the workspace from the keyboard

documents.t: Tab into a field, type, then Tab out — your change is saved as soon as the field loses focus. Pressing Enter saves it too. For dropdown fields, arrow keys move through the options and Enter selects one. For related-record lookups, type to search, then Tab to a result and press Enter to link it. Escape closes the panel when you are done.

Open a formatted-text field and use these editor-local controls: Type / to open the command list. Continue typing to filter it, use the Up and Down arrows to choose a command, and press Enter. Escape closes the list before it closes or restores the editor. Type @ and part of a record name to open the mention picker. Choose the record with the arrow keys and Enter. Press Enter after a heading or the last paragraph in a callout to continue in ordinary Text. Shift+Enter adds a soft line break inside the current block. In a list, Tab nests the current item and Shift+Tab lifts it. Enter continues the list; Enter on an empty item returns to Text. In a table, Tab and Shift+Tab move between cells. The named Table actions menu exposes row, column, header, merge, and split operations. Tab to a block's Block controls menu and use Move block up or Move block down when dragging is not suitable. Ctrl+Z or Cmd+Z undoes an editor change. Redo uses Ctrl+Y, Cmd+Y, or Shift+Cmd+Z. Ctrl+S or Cmd+S saves from inside the editor. The Viewing mode removes document mutation controls and makes the body read-only in popup and fullscreen. See Write formatted text for the complete structure workflow. An open insertion or existing link, equation, or figure editor is announced as a separate contextual form. The document Save and presentation switch remain disabled until that form is applied or cancelled; Viewing cancels it without applying the draft.
documents.s: Writing formatted text from the keyboard

documents.t: Some fields show a "not editable yet" hint instead of an editor. These hints are deliberately part of the keyboard tab order and are announced as disabled to your screen reader, so it is clear the field exists and is intentionally not yet interactive. They are not skipped, not invisible, and they do not pretend to be editable.
documents.s: Fields that are not editable yet

documents.t: The table toolbar has a row density control with three settings — Compact, Cozy, and Comfortable. Pick whichever works for your eyes and workflow; your choice is saved with the view you are working in, so it is there when you come back. On your environment's reading and browsing pages, the accessibility control panel adjusts how text is displayed. Open it from the accessibility button in the page header — announced to screen readers as "Open accessibility settings" — or press Alt+A. The panel is not available inside the workspace yet. It lets you adjust: Font size — make all text larger or smaller as a percentage of the base size. Line height — increase line spacing for easier reading; particularly helpful for dyslexia and low vision. Font family — switch between the default font and alternatives. Background color — a small set of page background presets, useful for contrast and reducing glare. A Reset to defaults button restores the standard settings. These settings are remembered by your browser on the device where you set them. If you sign in from a different device or browser, set them again there.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A control is not reachable with Tab. A gap in the focus order. Try Shift+Tab from a nearby control that is reachable. If the control still cannot be reached, contact your environment administrator — an unreachable control is a bug, not a setting. Your screen reader skips a "not editable yet" field. Your screen reader is set to skip disabled controls, or the hint did not load. Turn on your screen reader's setting for reading disabled controls. If the field is still skipped, contact your environment administrator. No focus ring appears after pressing Tab. You last interacted with the mouse — the ring is keyboard-only — or the page styling is interfering. Press Tab once more. If the ring still does not appear, contact your environment administrator. Font size resets after you sign out. Display settings are stored in your browser; the browser's stored data was cleared, or you are in a different browser or a private window. Re-apply the setting in the accessibility control panel. These settings do not follow your account across devices. You cannot find the accessibility control panel in the workspace. The panel lives on the reading and browsing pages; the workspace does not include it yet. Open a reading page and use the accessibility button in the page header, or press Alt+A there. Inside the workspace, use the row density control and your browser's own zoom. Your row density choice does not stick. The choice saves to the view you have open; the save may not have completed. Set the density again with the view open. If it still resets, contact your environment administrator. The highest-contrast preset is still not enough for your needs. The preset set is deliberately small for now; finer color customization is deferred. Use the preset closest to your needs and tell your environment administrator about the gap — reports shape what gets built next. An inline edit does not save when you Tab out. The field is read-only for your role, or the value failed validation (look for an inline error). Correct the value if there is an error shown. For a permissions question, contact your environment administrator.

Workspace keyboard navigation: Active. Visible focus rings: Active. Row density control: Active. Accessibility control panel on the reading and browsing pages (font size, line height, font family, background color presets): Active. Inline editing with the keyboard: Active. Formatted-text authoring with the keyboard: Active. Discoverable hints on fields that are not editable yet: Active. Accessible inline tips: Active. Screen-reader announcement coverage — for example, a spoken confirmation when an edit saves — is still expanding.
documents.s: What is there, what is still arriving

documents.t: Accessibility problems are bugs, not configuration questions. If a control cannot be reached from the keyboard, a screen reader misreads a field, or poor contrast makes text unreadable, contact your environment administrator so the problem reaches the people who can fix it.
documents.s: If something is not working for you

documents.t: Workspace walkthrough — the controls keyboard navigation moves through. Adding and editing rows — creating, editing and deleting records, and their keyboard behavior. Tips and guidance — how the inline tip panel behaves.

This page covers creating new records, editing existing ones, and deleting one you did not mean to make. The model is: a row exists the moment you ask for one, every edit saves as you finish each field, and nothing reaches public readers until you publish it. There is no Save button to forget.
