Read this when you create your first record, or when an edit is not behaving as you expect.

Create a row from the toolbar — one click adds a row to the current table and opens it for editing. Active. Insert and duplicate — insert a row directly below an existing one, or duplicate a row to start a new one from its values. Active. Autosave editing — every change saves when you finish the field. There is no Save button. Active. Undo and redo saved edits — value edits, pastes into existing rows, manual row order, field-definition changes, and relationship edits share one table history across Table, Details, and Relations. Active. Delete a row — right-click it and choose Delete row, or use Delete row in the record panel. Active. Editing in two places — the table cells and the Details panel edit the same record; a change made in one shows in the other. Active. Linked-record fields — search the related record type and pick a match, directly inside the field. Active.

Open the table you want to add to. New rows always belong to the table you are looking at. Click + New row in the toolbar. Your environment may label this button differently. The row is created right away, joins your table, and opens for editing. Fill in the fields. Each field saves when you finish it — click out of a text field or press Enter, and the value is stored. Choices and checkboxes save the moment you pick them. Leave and return whenever you like. Close the panel, navigate away, come back another day — your values are saved. Click the row to continue where you left off. Required fields can stay empty while you work. They must be filled before the record can be published. Two more ways to start a row: Insert row below — right-click an existing row and choose Insert row below. In views you order by hand, the new row lands directly below that one; in sorted or filtered views, the active sort and filters decide where it appears. Duplicate row — right-click a row and choose Duplicate row. This creates a new row with that row's directly editable values copied in; derived and linked fields are skipped. If + New row is unavailable, the button itself tells you why. Some views cannot accept new rows — for example, a view that combines or filters records rather than showing a single stored table.

Right-click the row and choose Delete row, or open it and use Delete row in the record panel. You are asked to confirm, and the deletion cannot be undone. Anyone who can edit the table can delete a row in it, including one a colleague created. Three kinds of row are not deleted here, and the message names which case applies: A row that has been published. Its address stays answerable so anyone who cited it is told it was withdrawn, rather than being left at a dead link. Withdraw it from the public site instead. A row that came from an import. It belongs to its source, and a later import would bring it back. A row that is linked to other records. Remove its links first, then delete it.
Nothing you add reaches the public reading site until you publish it. Until then the row is part of your team's shared workspace: colleagues with access to the table see it and can edit it.

You can edit in two places, and they stay in step: In the table — edit a cell directly. The change saves when you confirm it or move on to another cell. In the Details panel — click a row to open its Details panel. Click into a field, change the value, then leave the field or press Enter. The panel header shows Saving… and then Saved. A value you did not change is not re-saved. Date fields use your browser's date picker in table cells, new-row fields, and the Details panel. Choosing a date stores the date itself, such as 2025-10-19; the workspace does not add a time or timezone. A field that only looks like a timestamp but is configured as Text remains a text field until its type is changed. Changing the type reports how many compatible stored values were converted and how many need correction. Not every field takes typed input: Fields marked with a Read badge are not editable in place. These are derived fields (computed from other fields), media fields, and field types that do not have an in-place editor yet. To change a derived value, edit the fields it is computed from. Relation fields show the linked-records editor instead: existing links appear as removable chips, and a search box lets you type part of a related record's name and pick a match to add a link. Click the × on a chip to remove a link. If a save is refused, an error message tells you what went wrong and your value stays in the editor. In Details, use Retry save after resolving the conflict, or Discard retained edit to return to the stored value. The editor stays attached to the row and field where you made the change, so moving between records cannot carry a retained edit into another row. Saved value edits and pastes into existing rows enter the active table's workspace history. Use Undo in Table, Details, or Relations, or press Ctrl/Cmd+Z outside an editor. Redo accepts Ctrl/Cmd+Y or Shift+Ctrl/Cmd+Z. Creating, duplicating, and deleting a row are not undoable, and extra clipboard lines never create rows automatically. See What the workspace remembers — and what you can undo.

Symptom Likely cause Fix + New row is unavailable. No table is selected, or the current view cannot accept new rows. Hover over the button to see the reason, or switch to a regular table view. Creating or editing a row fails with a permission message. Your role includes read access but not edit access. Contact your environment administrator. A field will not accept your edit and shows a Read badge. The field is derived from other fields, holds media, or has no in-place editor yet. Edit the fields it is computed from. If you believe the field should be directly editable, contact your environment administrator. A link is declined. One of the two records is a proposal nobody has accepted yet. Read the message near the field — it names the record holding the link up. A change did not save. The value failed a check, the field never lost focus, or a newer edit made this save stale. Look for the error near the field or panel. Confirm the edit; if it is refused, use Retry save after checking the latest value, or Discard retained edit. Deleting a row is declined. The row has been published, came from an import, or is linked to other records. Read the message — it names which case applies, and what to do instead. A field you expected is missing from the form. The field is hidden in the current view, or it is not configured for this record type. Check the view's hidden fields first. Otherwise, ask your environment administrator to add the field.

What you can do in the workspace reflects your role in the project. Members with read access browse, search, and view Details; adding and editing rows requires edit access. If your role does not include editing, the platform declines the change with a permission message. Roles are assigned by your environment administrator; the permissions panel page describes what each role covers.

Workspace walkthrough — the table and Details panel. Searching and reading — how records surface in search. Public reader — how completed and published records reach public readers. Make a field required — controlling which fields must be filled before a row is complete. Accessibility — keyboard-first editing and screen-reader support.

You are about to cite something from your knowledge environment in a paper — a published record, a passage, a region of an image, a named part of a 3D model. This page explains what the platform guarantees about that citation: what stays fixed once you have cited it, what an Edition is and why it matters before anything goes to a peer-reviewed venue, and what a citation style is — including how a style gets changed when the active one does not suit your venue. Read it before a platform citation goes into print, or when you want to understand why a citation reads the way it does. For the steps of actually copying a citation, see Copy a citation for a record or media item.

Stable web addresses for published records — every published record keeps a stable address that stays valid even if your project later reorganizes its pages. Maturity: Active. Limit: stability is per record; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort. Frozen, citable Editions for media items — a media item's version is either a working copy that can still change, or an Edition: frozen and safe to cite in print. Maturity: Active. Limit: freezing a version as an Edition is a deliberate administrator action, never automatic. Refusal of re-processing against an Edition — an automatic re-processing run that would change an Edition's data is refused outright; it stops before anything is touched. Maturity: Active. Rejections that stay rejected — when a reviewer in your project rejects a wrong label that automatic processing proposed, the rejection is recorded permanently; later re-processing does not bring the label back. Maturity: Active. Citations rendered in your project's citation style — published entries carry citations rendered in the style your project has adopted, ready to select and copy. Maturity: Active. Limit: how complete a citation reads depends on the fields your project has filled in. A shipped catalog of standard styles — more than seventy standard citation styles ship with the platform, Chicago and APA among them. A project adopts one active style for how its pages are cited, readers can re-render a page's citation into standard formats right on the page, and the project's own reference conventions (how rows of evidence read) carry their own declared styles. Maturity: Built. Limit: a style outside the catalog can be installed on request through your environment administrator. Reviewed style changes — a style change passes through a proposal built from sample citations, a measured risk report, and a deliberate apply by an environment administrator. No proposal takes effect without that review of its measured reach. Maturity: Active. Citations readable by reference managers — every published entry's citation is also available in Citation Style Language JSON, the format reference managers such as Zotero read. Maturity: Built.

Nothing changes underneath your citation by accident. The address you cite keeps resolving, and a published record's content changes only when someone in your project changes the record — no background run rewrites published content on its own. For media items, the guarantee is stronger still: data frozen as an Edition cannot change at all, and the platform enforces that refusal itself rather than relying on anyone's caution.

A published record's stable web address is one half of citable identity. The other half matters when you cite a media item — a 3D model, an image, an audio or video segment. The platform can propose labels connecting your project's terms to regions of a media item — a named part of a 3D model, a region of an image. Reviewers in your project approve, amend, or reject each one. That reviewed state lives on a version of the media item, and a version is one of two things: A working copy — annotation on it can still change as your project reviews and refines. An Edition — frozen. Once an environment administrator promotes a version to an Edition, its data is protected: the platform refuses any re-processing run that would alter it. Before a media citation goes to a peer-reviewed venue, the version you cite should be an Edition. If your venue or repository needs a DOI, that DOI is minted by your institution's library or repository service against the Edition's stable identity — the platform itself does not mint DOIs, it provides the stable target. A citation never exposes the platform's internal identifiers; locations are described in the item's own terms, such as the name of a model part or a region of an image. In the references rows of a published entry, "edition" usually means a published edition of a source text — a different thing. The Edition on this page is a frozen, citable version of a media item held on the platform.
documents.s: What "Edition" and stable identity mean before you cite

documents.t: Three things hold after you cite: File updates do not touch your citation. When the underlying model or image file is updated, the new file comes in as a new working copy under its own version label. The Edition you cited — and any DOI adopted for it — keeps its data intact. The new version earns its own review and can become its own Edition later. Automatic re-processing cannot alter an Edition. A re-processing run against an Edition is refused before any data changes. This is not a warning someone could click past; the platform stops the run. Review decisions survive re-processing. A rejection a reviewer made is recorded permanently and is not re-proposed by later runs. Labels a reviewer has approved or amended are likewise preserved — even while the version is still a working copy. Every review action keeps a record of who acted and when, stored with the data.
documents.s: What stays fixed across model updates and re-processing

documents.t: A citation style is the set of rules for how a citation reads: the order of author, title, and date; the punctuation; the abbreviations. The platform defines styles in Citation Style Language — an open format used by reference managers such as Zotero and by thousands of journals — so a style is data your environment holds, not something hand-edited into each record. A catalog of more than seventy standard styles ships with the platform; your project adopts one active style for its pages, and its own reference conventions carry their declared styles. To tell whether the active style suits your venue, read a rendered citation against the venue's style guide or a recent issue: open a published entry, or its draft preview, and compare. The preview shows the same rendering before anything goes public — if a citation will read roughly in print, it reads roughly in the preview. If you are unsure which style is active, ask your environment administrator; the active style and its version are recorded in your environment.

Style changes run on the administrative side — there is no self-service style control in your workspace. Your part is the request and the evidence: Collect sample citations formatted the way your venue requires — real examples covering the kinds of material you typically cite. Send them to your environment administrator with the request. For a standard venue, the administrator may adopt a matching style straight from the shipped catalog. A proposal is drafted from your samples and measured against your environment's pinned example citations. The proposal carries a count of existing citations it would change and a risk level, so reviewers see the consequences before anything is decided. A proposal may be drafted with machine assistance, but no proposal — machine-drafted or not — takes effect on its own. A scholar reviews the proposal. The platform refuses to apply a proposal that has not passed this review. An environment administrator applies the reviewed style. Styles are versioned, the record of who applied which version is kept, and published citations render in the applied style — you do not edit any record to pick up the change.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A citation reads wrong for your venue — punctuation, ordering, or abbreviations are off. The active style does not match the venue, or no style has been adopted yet for that collection. Collect sample citations in the form the venue requires and send them to your environment administrator with a request to adopt or refine the style. A citation shows placeholder text or is missing pieces. The fields the citation draws on are incomplete on that record or media item. Complete those fields on the record — see Copy a citation for a record or media item for the details. You want to cite a 3D model or image in print and worry a later update will change it. The version you are citing may still be a working copy. Ask your environment administrator to confirm the version is an Edition — or to freeze one — before the citation goes to press. A wrong label your project rejected has reappeared after re-processing. This should not happen — a recorded rejection is permanent across re-processing. Report it to your environment administrator, naming the media item and the label. A recurrence is a platform defect, not something you mis-clicked. Your venue or repository asks for a DOI. The platform does not mint DOIs itself. Ask your environment administrator — DOI minting is handled by your institution's library or repository service against the frozen Edition's identity.

Copy a citation for a record or media item — the short task-shaped steps. Read the references section on a published entry — what each evidence row in the References area means. Public reader — stable addresses, the draft preview, and what readers see. Citation integrity (for environment admins) — the same guarantees in administrative detail, including Editions and DOI safety. Standards and citations (for environment admins) — the style catalog and the review workflow from the administrator's side. Standards overview — the platform's standards posture for institutional readers.

A collection is one of the kinds of things you keep track of in your workspace — people, manuscripts, terms, events, and so on. You can create a new collection, rename one, and remove one, all from the workspace sidebar, without leaving for an administration screen. This page covers those three actions and what each one does to your records. Your records are never deleted by anything on this page. Removing a collection only removes it from your sidebar — the records underneath stay.

Open the workspace. In the sidebar, select Add table. Give the collection a name in Table name — for example, "Glossary", "Sources", or "People". Choose a Table meaning — what each row in this collection represents. The choices are: Terms & concepts — a glossary or controlled vocabulary. Documents & texts — works or sources you cite or read as a whole. Named things — people, places, organizations, or other named things. Events — things that happened in time. Passages — excerpts or quoted spans drawn from documents. Annotations & notes — notes or comments attached to other records. Media — images, audio, video, or 3D models. Optionally pick a Sidebar icon. Select Create table. The collection meaning sets how the platform stores and connects the records, so choose the one that best fits what you are recording. A new collection starts empty and with no project-specific fields; you add fields and rows next (see Build a knowledge environment from scratch without importing). "3D" is a property of an individual media item, not a separate kind of collection. Choose Media for images, audio, video, and 3D models alike.

When you import data, the platform shows your records grouped into collections automatically. A collection that came from your data this way can be registered — turned into a collection you can rename, configure, and delete — while keeping all of its records exactly as they are. In the sidebar, open the actions menu for the collection (right-click it, or use its actions control). Select Register this table…. Confirm the name, adjust the icon if you wish, and create it. Registering does not change or move your records; it gives the collection a permanent home in your sidebar so its name, icon, and settings are yours to manage. A collection that holds no records yet cannot be registered — start one from scratch with Add table instead.
documents.s: Register a collection the platform built for you

documents.t: In the sidebar, open the actions menu for the collection. Select Rename table…. Change the Table name or the Sidebar icon. Select Save changes. Renaming changes only how the collection appears in your sidebar. It does not touch the records inside it.

In the sidebar, open the actions menu for the collection. Select Delete table…. Read the confirmation, then select Delete table. Removing a collection unregisters it — it takes the collection out of your sidebar but never deletes the records underneath. If the collection still holds records, it remains browsable as an automatic collection built from your data. If the collection has published entries, its curated publish settings are reset, and the next time you publish it falls back to defaults. Pages and citations you already published stay exactly as they are.

Creating, renaming, and removing collections is available to editors and administrators. If these actions appear dimmed in your sidebar, your role does not include them — the sidebar shows the reason in place. Ask your environment administrator if you need access.

Build a knowledge environment from scratch without importing — adding fields and relations to a new collection. Table layout: sorting, column controls, and the column manager — arranging the columns once a collection has fields. The workspace walkthrough — the whole workspace in one tour.

Dates in real sources are rarely tidy. A column of dates might hold 384 BCE – 322 BCE, c. 80–150, mid-4th c. BCE, a century, a dynasty, or a named period. This page explains how the workspace turns those into operable dates — years you can sort, filter, and place on a timeline — without ever rewriting what you wrote, and without converting one calendar into another. Read it when a date column has messy values, when you want your dates to line up on a timeline, or when you are deciding whether to date a value by hand.

Two things live side by side on a dated value, and the workspace never lets one overwrite the other: What the source says — the date exactly as written. This is always kept, character for character. It is the record of what you found. Years the workspace can work with — an optional, separate reading that turns the words into start and end years the platform can order and place on a timeline. Adding the second never changes the first. You are annotating the value with dates, not editing its text. And nothing here converts calendars: if a value is written in one calendar, its years are placed on the timeline you choose, as you entered them — the platform does not silently restate a date in a different calendar.
documents.s: The idea: keep the words, add the years

documents.t: Which editor a date cell opens depends on the column and the value, but they all follow the same rule — keep the words, add the years — and differ only in how much structure they offer.
Most date cells open Date this entry as a manual form: you keep your value as written and enter its years — and, for a named period, a label — directly, rather than being offered readings to accept.
documents.s: Date this entry — the manual form

documents.t: When a value has been flagged for grounding through the vocabulary review, the same Date this entry editor opens a guided version that shows your value at the top, kept exactly as written, and offers three ways to turn it into dates: What we read — a deterministic parser's reading of your text: the years it resolves to, and the precision (for example circa). Same input, same result, no AI involved. If the text cannot be read into years — a named period, a non-Gregorian calendar — nothing is guessed; it stays as written and you use one of the other paths. AI suggestion — an advisory reading, offered only when you open it. It never writes anything on its own: it proposes a label and dates for you to Accept, Edit first, or Reject. Enter it yourself — type a start year (and optional end year) with BCE/CE, a precision, and a calendar. Your original text stays above the fields, read-only. Each tab records the dates its own way: Save this match on What we read, Accept (or Edit first) on AI suggestion, and Save these dates on Enter it yourself. Leave as written is always there to close without adding any.
documents.s: Date this entry — the guided version

documents.t: The Edit time range editor keeps the same two-part shape explicit. As written is the reading exactly as your source gives it, and is required. Below it, an optional Make it comparable section lets you add: a From year and optional To year (a plain number; negative for BCE, and a blank To year dates the start year on its own — that one year, decade, or century at the chosen precision, not a span), a Precision — instant, day, month, year, decade, or century, and a Comparison axis — which timeline the years sit on. It is required once you enter years; — not comparable — is only for keeping the value as written, with no years to place. Give it no years and the value is saved as written only; a value that already has years keeps them if you save without changing them. Fill in a year, a precision, and a comparison axis together and it also becomes comparable. Enter a year but leave the axis on — not comparable — and the editor keeps Save blocked until you either complete the three or clear the years to save as written. Here too, the calendar is a label on the value while the comparison axis is what lets it be ordered against others — choosing one never converts the other.

"Comparable" means the value carries real years placed on a stated timeline, so it can be sorted, filtered, and shown on a timeline beside other values. A value that is only kept as written is still a first-class record — it simply is not placed on a timeline until someone gives it years. The comparison axis is the deliberate part of this: it names which timeline the years belong to, rather than assuming one. That is what keeps dates from different calendars from being quietly mixed together as though they shared a single line.

There are two ways your date work is saved, and they differ in reach: Editing a cell — typing years into a single time-range cell, or dating a single entry — changes that one value. Grounding a value — accepting a reading for a value through the vocabulary review, where the same value occurs across many records — applies that reading across its occurrences in a single action, so you never redo the same reading record by record. Where an occurrence can't take the reading — a legacy record a structured date can't be fitted onto, for instance — it is reported back to you rather than dated; the occurrences that can take it are still dated, and nothing is placed on a timeline by guesswork. Grounding is the path to reach for when a value repeats across your data; editing a cell is for a one-off.
documents.s: Grounding a value reaches its occurrences in one action

documents.t: Adding and editing rows — creating records and editing fields, of which dating a value is one. Keep non-standard values as is — when a value should stay exactly as written. Quick help: Date a value and Edit a time range — the short, in-product guides for each editor.

Some environments pair their records with interactive 3D models — an anatomical structure, a scanned artifact, a molecular form. The model viewer lets you and your readers turn a model, name its parts, and open the scholarly entry behind each part. This page walks through opening a model, reading what a part means, shaping the view so you see what matters, working through a model group by group, and what to expect from attachments that have no built-in viewer.

When a table holds media, a Media view joins Table / Details / Relations / Publish in the view bar. It appears only on media tables. The Media view shows your media records as a gallery of cards — each card carries the record's title and a media-type badge (for example 3D model). Opening a 3D-model card renders the model right there in a detail pane, where you can orbit and zoom to inspect it, alongside a rail of tabs for the model's parts, files, viewer framing, info, and versions. Maturity: Active. From the Mesh→term tab you review which part of the model is matched to which term and approve, reassign, or strip those matches; environment admins use the Viewer tab to set the framing the model opens at. Two researcher how-to guides cover this in the workspace: See which mesh maps to which term and Tune the 3D camera view. When a record has no file yet, its detail pane shows Attach a file first; editors and admins use Attach media there to reference a URL or upload a file — see Work with media in the workspace. The reader experience below — the public viewer your readers see — is described separately in this page.
documents.s: In your workspace — the Media view

documents.t: Click a part, read its entry — hovering over the model names the part under your pointer; clicking it opens a panel with the entry's headword, translations, transliteration, description, and a link to the full entry. Maturity: Active. Limit: a part shows entry details only where your project has linked that part to an entry. View shaping, part by part — fade, hide, isolate, or zoom to any part. Every shaping action raises an on-screen bar with its own undo, and one control resets the whole view. Maturity: Active. Group-by-group exploration — a strip labeled LAYERS lists the model's groups; each group opens a list of its parts with individual show/hide toggles. Maturity: Active. View controls — on-screen orbit, zoom, and pan controls plus a reset; scroll-wheel zoom and middle-button pan with the mouse; touch gestures on phones and tablets. Maturity: Active. Built-in walkthrough — a short guided tour starts on its own the first time you open a model in a browser, and can be rerun from the Help button. Maturity: Active. Typed attachment cards — a record page lists its attachments as labeled cards (3D model, Image, Audio, Video, Molecular). A 3D model card opens this viewer; cards of other types open only when the attachment carries its own viewing address. Maturity: Active. Limit: the built-in viewer exists for 3D models today; other media types display as cards and rely on the address the attachment provides.

Open a record that has a 3D model attached. Its attachments appear as a strip of cards, each labeled with its type. Select the card labeled 3D model. The viewer opens with the model's name in the top bar. To leave, use the back arrow beside the model's name — it returns you to the page you came from, or to the reading site's opening page if you arrived by direct link. Your environment's reading site may also feature its models directly — for example on its opening page — and selecting a model there opens the same viewer. Beside the model's name sits Model Info. If the model carries an overview, it unfolds in place, with a Read Full Model Info link to the model's full information page; if there is no overview, the button takes you straight to that page. The overview folds away when you select a part. If the model includes an animation, a play/pause control appears near the top of the view.

Hover over the model (on a computer): the part under your pointer is highlighted and its name appears beside it. Click a part: a detail panel opens. The heading is the entry's headword, with its translations in parentheses; the transliteration sits underneath; below come the description and the part's place in the model's structure, from the largest group down to the part itself. Full Details, at the bottom of the panel, opens the part's full entry page in a new tab. Click empty space to close the panel and clear the selection, or use the panel's close control. When a part has not been linked to an entry, the panel falls back to the part's name as written in the model, and a notice reports that no entry details were found for it. Linking parts to entries is part of how your project prepares its models — if a part you need is unlinked, tell your environment administrator.

Right-click a part (on a computer) to open a circular menu around your pointer. On a touch screen, tap the part: a small card names it, offers See Details, and unfolds the same actions from its menu control. The menu offers four ways to shape the view, each marked with its keyboard letter: Fade (F) — the part turns translucent, so you can see past it while keeping it in place. Hide (H) — the part is removed from view. Isolate (I) — the part is shown on its own. Zoom (Z) — the camera moves in on the part. Each state raises a bar at the edge of the model area naming the affected part: A faded part's bar reads Part Faded, with Invert — the faded part returns to full strength and everything else fades instead — and Reset. With several parts faded, the bar shows their count and their names, with Invert All and Reset All. A hidden part's bar reads Part Hidden, with Unhide. With several hidden, the bar shows the count and a list; picking a part from the list brings it back, and Unhide All brings back everything. An isolated part's bar reads Isolated, with Exit. A zoomed part's bar reads Zoom, with Exit. To start over entirely, use the round Reset the view control among the view controls, or press Alt+R. The circular menu also carries the part's name — selecting it opens the detail panel — and Cite, which opens the page's citation form.
documents.s: Shaping the view: fade, hide, isolate, zoom

documents.t: On a computer, the pointer is reserved for parts — hovering names them, clicking selects them — so moving the view goes through dedicated controls: The round controls at the edge of the model area: Orbit the view (two turn buttons; press and hold to keep turning), Zoom in/out in the view (press and hold to keep zooming), Pan the view (four direction arrows), and Reset the view. The mouse: scroll to zoom; drag with the middle button to pan. On a touch screen, drag with one finger to turn the model, pinch with two fingers to zoom, and drag with two fingers to pan.

The strip along the bottom of the screen, labeled LAYERS, lists the model's groups. Select a group: its parts light up and a list opens showing every part in the group, each with an eye toggle. Toggle a part's eye to show or hide that part. Hide all / Show all at the top of the list switches the whole group at once. Moving the pointer away from the strip clears the group highlight. This is the steady way through a dense model: open a group, hide what is in the way, study what remains, then move to the next group.
documents.s: Working through the model in groups

documents.t: The first time you open a model in a given browser, a short walkthrough starts on its own once the model has loaded. It tours navigation, part selection, the view-shaping menu, the groups strip, the model information, and the page's cite, help, and feedback buttons. To run it again, use the round Help button at the edge of the page. The walkthrough is remembered per browser, not per account — on a new device or browser it introduces itself again. The neighboring round buttons offer Cite — a citation for the page, formatted in common styles (APA, MLA, Chicago) and ready to copy — and Feedback, which opens a form for sending your impressions to the team behind the site.

With a part selected, four shortcuts act on it: F fades, H hides, I isolates, Z zooms. Alt+R resets the view at any time. Two honest limits: Selecting a part requires a pointer — a mouse click or a tap. There is no keyboard-only way to move through the model's parts, so the shortcuts extend pointer work rather than replace it. The model area itself is not part of the keyboard tab order. If a keyboard-only path matters to your work, tell your environment administrator — an accessibility gap is a bug to report, not a setting to find. The model view follows the background color chosen in the accessibility settings on your environment's reading pages: a dark background there gives the model a dark backdrop here.

A record's attachments appear as cards in a strip, each labeled with its type — 3D model, Image, Audio, Video, Molecular, or the type name your project recorded. A card shows the attachment's image where one is catalogued (a type placeholder otherwise), its title, and its creator where catalogued. A 3D model card opens this viewer. A card of any other type opens only when the attachment carries its own viewing address; selecting it then leads to that address. A card with no viewing address is a labeled reference: it tells you the attachment exists and what it is, without leading anywhere.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Clicking a part shows its name, but a notice says no entry details were found. The part is not yet linked to an entry. The rest of the model still works. Ask your environment administrator to link the part if you need its entry. Parts of the model seem to be missing. Parts are hidden, or one part is isolated. Check the bars at the edge of the model area — Unhide All or Exit — or reset the view with the Reset the view control or Alt+R. Dragging with the mouse does not turn the model. On a computer, the pointer selects parts; turning the model goes through the view controls. Use the Orbit the view control; scroll to zoom; drag with the middle button to pan. On a touch screen, a one-finger drag turns the model. The keyboard shortcuts (F, H, I, Z) do nothing. No part is selected — the shortcuts act on the selected part. Click a part first, then press the shortcut. The walkthrough did not appear. It starts on its own only on your first visit in a given browser, and only once the model has loaded. Use the Help button at the edge of the page after the model finishes loading. An Image, Audio, or Video card on a record page does not open anything. The attachment carries no viewing address of its own; only 3D model cards have a built-in viewer. The card still documents the attachment. If it should open somewhere, ask your environment administrator to add a viewing address to the attachment. The model never finishes loading. A large model file, or a connection problem. Wait — larger models take longer — then reload the page. If the problem persists, contact your environment administrator.

Public reader — the reading layer where published records and their models live. Accessibility — display settings and keyboard behavior across your environment. Searching and reading — finding the records a model is attached to.

The task guides answer "how do I do this one thing." This page answers the questions that cross several of them — the ones that come up when something behaves in a way no single step explains. Each answer is short, and points you to the guide with the full steps.

The sign-in page uses one message for every refusal, on purpose: it never confirms whether an account exists. Besides a typo (both fields are case-sensitive), the most common cause is that your membership in the project was suspended or ended — suspension takes effect immediately, even for a browser where you were already signed in. Your project administrator can restore access; nothing is deleted when access is suspended. See Sign in and manage your password.
documents.s: Sign-in says my username and password are wrong, but I am sure they are right — what happened?

documents.t: The operations area is for project administrators — it asks for the admin role, not just a signed-in account. Researcher work happens in the workspace, and a researcher account deliberately carries no operations access. If you believe you should have the admin role, ask your project administrator to change it in the Permissions Panel.
documents.s: Why can't my account open the /admin/ area?

documents.t: That address belonged to an early operations page that has been retired; its tasks moved into the /admin/ area. Old bookmarks are redirected to your workspace rather than left pointing at a page that no longer exists. Nothing about your data changed.
documents.s: My old bookmark to /app/admin/… now opens my workspace — why?

documents.t: A record you create is part of the shared workspace straight away, so a colleague with access to that table sees it. If they are looking at the public reader instead, that is a separate step: publishing is what makes a record visible to the world. See Publish a record. If they still cannot see it, check that they have access to that table, and that no filter on their view is hiding the row.
documents.s: Why can't my colleague see the record I created?

documents.t: The public page keeps the version it was last published with — your edits sit in the workspace until the next publish, they do not flow out automatically. The same is true for a field's visibility setting or a renamed label: the public page catches up only when you publish again. Open the Publish view and select Publish changes to push the current version live. To see the steps, see The Publish view.
documents.s: I edited a published record, so why does the public page still show the old version?

documents.t: Publishing is controlled by your role, not by the record's stage — anyone whose role includes publish access can publish any record, reviewed or not. The platform has no separate sign-off gate that holds a record back until a reviewer approves it. If your team needs review to come before publishing, ask your environment administrator to arrange roles so that only reviewers hold publish access. For how reviewing works today, see Reviewing your team's work.
documents.s: Who can publish in my project, and why can a colleague publish work I have not finished reviewing?

documents.t: Saved views are shared. When you change the filters, columns, or sort on a view, everyone working in that collection sees the change immediately, and deleting a view removes it for everyone. If you want to experiment without disturbing your team, Duplicate the view first and work in the copy. For the full behavior, see Save your table arrangement as a view.
documents.s: Are my saved views private, or does the whole team see them?

documents.t: A shared search link reproduces your exact search, filters, and result page, but results always respect the person opening them — they see only the collections and records their own access allows. So fewer results for your colleague usually means they lack access to a collection you can see, not that the link is broken. If they need that collection, ask your environment administrator. To copy a link that reproduces your search, see Share a search.
documents.s: I sent a colleague a search link, so why do they see fewer results than I do?

documents.t: They are still there if the run used an edit-preserving refresh: the platform matches incoming source rows to existing records, refreshes source-managed values, and keeps the fields your team owns. Field labels and field settings you changed are also yours and are not reset by the re-import. A full refresh is different: it reloads rows from scratch and is destructive to researcher edits, so it should be planned with your environment administrator before it runs. A re-import shows you a delta: only what is new, changed, or removed since your last import, so you are not asked to re-decide settled structure. To read the delta, see Understand what changed after a re-import.
documents.s: Where did my changes go after I re-imported my source?

documents.t: Your label is yours, and a re-import is not supposed to bring the source name back. One case looks like that but is not: in the delta view, changed items are listed under their source-side names until you confirm them, after which your label reappears in the workspace. That label guarantee is separate from record value refresh behavior: edit-preserving refresh protects researcher-owned values, while full refresh is destructive. If your label is genuinely overwritten in the workspace itself after a re-import, that is a defect worth reporting. See Rename a field label and Understand what changed after a re-import.
documents.s: A field I renamed is showing its old source name again after a re-import — is that a bug?

documents.t: The most common cause is a renamed column in your source. When a column's name changes, the platform sees the old name disappear and a new name arrive, so the delta lists one removed field and one new field for what is really the same column. Approve the new one and your label carries over to it. Your saved views adapt to a removed field rather than breaking — see What happens to saved views after a re-import.
documents.s: A field I know is in my source shows as "removed" after a re-import — why?

documents.t: When two columns in your source would map to one field, the import stops before writing anything and lists every collision at once, so you can fix them together rather than one error at a time. Give the clashing columns distinct names in your source and re-import. For the full walkthrough, see Fix colliding column names during import.
documents.s: My import stopped with a message that two columns would become the same field — what do I do?

documents.t: No. AI assistance can add proposals during an import, but it does not replace the parser or the review flow. If AI assistance is unavailable or a call fails, the import keeps parser-only proposals for you to review; it does not discard your source, your saved import decisions, or your workspace edits. Review the same import decisions before starting the import. See See what you decided in an import, table by table.
documents.s: My import continued without AI suggestions — did it lose my data?

documents.t: Search and the table look at different things. The toolbar filter box answers only for the collection in the active table, while search looks across collections — but only at the fields your environment has marked searchable. So a record can sit in your table yet stay out of search because the word you typed lives in a field that search does not cover. Try a word from a different field, or use full search across collections. See Find a record when search returns nothing and Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read.
documents.s: Why can search find a record I can see right in front of me in the table?

documents.t: Searching across a collection requires a review capability for that kind of record, and the note counts the collections your access does not cover. The records are not gone — they are held back from your search until your access includes the capability that covers them. Ask your environment administrator for the capability you need. See See why some collections are hidden in Search & Read.
documents.s: Why does the search results panel say some collections are hidden?

documents.t: A collection needs a display field — the field that names each record — for results to read as names. When no display field is set, the result falls back to an internal identifier, which is the string of letters and numbers you are seeing. This is set per collection by your environment administrator; ask them to set a display field for that collection. For how search reads across your data, see Searching and reading.
documents.s: Why do some search results show strings of letters and numbers instead of a name?

documents.t: Two different reasons. For Greek, breathings are set aside in matching but the acute accent still counts — a term typed without its acute accent can miss a record whose stored form carries it. For transliteration, the match works only if the transliteration field actually holds a value and is marked searchable; if it is empty on that record, the native-script form will still find it. See Working in multiple scripts and languages and Find a record when search returns nothing.
documents.s: Why does my search miss a Greek term, or a transliteration that I know is there?

documents.t: Formatted-text fields support Text, headings, callouts, quotes, code, marks and links, typed lists, editable tables, workspace mentions, document footnotes, TeX equations, and accessible figures chosen from workspace media. Press Enter at the end of a heading or callout to continue in Text, or choose Text from the block menu at any time. Mentions, footnotes, and equations use their scholarly reader forms when the field is included in a published entry. A figure appears only when its selected image media is also admitted to publication and has a frozen primary image; otherwise the reader omits it. See Write formatted text for the complete keyboard and editing workflow.
documents.s: What can I put in a formatted-text field, and how do I get back to ordinary text?

documents.t: Some fields are not edited directly. A field that is computed from other fields, holds media, or links to other records shows as read-only; you change it by editing the fields it is built from, or by adding links and media after the record exists. A field can also be read-only because your role has read access but not edit access. To tell the cases apart and act on each, see Adding and editing rows.
documents.s: Why can't I edit this field — it has no editor or shows a "Read" badge?

documents.t: You can link a record you have just created, and link to it, straight away — there is no stage to clear first. A link is declined in one case: a record the platform proposed that nobody has accepted yet cannot be either end of a link. The message near the field says when that is what happened. To add the link, see The Relations view.
documents.s: Why can't I link my new record to another record yet?

documents.t: Your table layout — column order, sort, filters — is stored on the active view, and views are shared, so a layout can change because a collaborator adjusted the same view, or because you are looking at a different view tab than before. The sidebar is the exception: its width and collapsed state are remembered per browser, while your pins and groups follow your sign-in. For what is remembered where, see What the workspace remembers, and how undo works.
documents.s: My column arrangement reverted, or a colleague's looks different from mine — why?

documents.t: The workspace keeps up to 50 edits for each table while this browser tab keeps the workspace page open. Table, Details, and Relations share that chronology for value, paste, manual row-order, field-definition, and relationship edits. A reload, closed tab, or new browser tab starts fresh. Saved-view presentation has a separate history of up to 20 changes. Workspace Undo never publishes or unpublishes, changes field visibility, privacy, citation rules, Appearance, or media files. Its shortcuts are inactive on those surfaces. See What the workspace remembers, and how undo works for conflict refusals and relationship restore limits.
documents.s: How far does Undo go, and can it change publishing or privacy?

documents.t: The column's field type decides how the workspace treats the value. A Date field shows a readable date in the table and uses a date picker when you edit it. A Text field that happens to contain a timestamp stays text, so it still shows the full stored string until someone changes or converts the field type. See Adding and editing rows and Table layout: sorting, column controls, and the column manager.
documents.s: Why does one date look friendly while another still shows the full timestamp?

documents.t: Copying a focused cell copies one field value. A cell range copies only the rectangular cells you selected by dragging, Shift-clicking, extending with Shift and the arrow keys, using the row-gutter Select visible cells in row action, or using the column menu Select visible column cells action, without row headers. When you need cells that are not next to each other, Target cells lets you click individual cells, press Enter or Space on the focused data cell, or add visible row/column groups with the same row-gutter and column-menu commands; the status line shows Sparse cells: N, and copy/paste then uses only those targeted cells. When you paste one copied value while several rows are selected, the workspace can fill that same column for the selected rows on editable tables; when a cell range is active, paste targets that rectangle. Pasting extra rows into existing rows does not create records automatically; create those rows with New row, Insert row below, or Duplicate row, then paste values into them. For the full distinction, see Copy and paste table values.
documents.s: Why are there several copy actions in the table?

documents.t: They start a managed collection from two different places. Add table creates a brand-new, empty collection — you give it a name and choose what its rows represent, and then add fields and records yourself. Register this table is for a collection the platform already built from your imported data: it gives that existing collection a permanent home in your sidebar so you can rename and configure it, without changing any of its records. Use Add table when you are starting from nothing; use Register when the records already exist. See Create, rename, and delete a collection.
documents.s: What is the difference between Add table and Register this table?

documents.t: No. Removing a collection only unregisters it — it takes the collection out of your sidebar but never deletes the records underneath. A collection that still holds records stays browsable as an automatic collection built from your data. The one consequence to know about: if the collection had published entries, its curated publish settings reset and the next publish falls back to defaults, while pages and citations you already published stay live. See Remove a collection without deleting its records.
documents.s: If I delete a collection, do I lose my records?

documents.t: Open the record in the Media view. A record with no file yet shows Attach a file first; editors and environment admins get an Attach media button there. It opens a sheet with two choices: Reference a URL points the record at media already hosted at a web address, and Upload a file stores a file with the record. Once the file is attached the record fills in — a 3D model opens in its viewer. Referencing a URL is offered only on a record that has no version yet; to add a file to a record that already has one, upload it. The record's name and description are separate fields, edited in the collection's Details view. See Work with media in the workspace.
documents.s: How do I add a 3D model or image to a media record that has none?

documents.t: A table-wide publish includes every ready record, and a withdrawn record is still a record in your table — so publishing the whole table can put it back. Withdrawal is held by your environment's administrators, not by the workspace publishing controls. If a record must stay out of public view, agree with whoever publishes that it stays out of table-wide publishes. See Withdrawing a published record.
documents.s: I withdrew a published record, so why is it back on the public site?

documents.t: It depends on which it is. Placeholder text means the fields the citation draws on are incomplete on that record, and completing those fields fixes it on the next publish. Rough punctuation or ordering means the collection's citation style is not the right one yet, or is still being refined — that is set by your environment administrator, not on the record. See Copy a citation for a record or media item and Citations you can trust.
documents.s: A citation looks rough or shows placeholder text — is that mine to fix?

documents.t: Yes. Every published entry shows its citation with a citation format selector: your project's own style — the default every reader sees first — plus standard formats: APA, MLA, Chicago author-date, Chicago notes & bibliography, and Harvard. Switching re-renders the citation in the reader's own browser from the citation's underlying data. Nothing changes for other readers, and your project's style stays the default. See Citations you can trust.
documents.s: Can readers cite my pages in their own format?

documents.t: No. The rows of evidence on a published entry render through your project's own conventions — your abbreviations, your loci, your bridges between paired editions — and they read the same for every reader. The citation format selector applies only to the citation of the page itself; a reader switching it never changes how your evidence reads. How those conventions are set up is described in Standards and citations (for environment admins).
documents.s: Do my reference conventions have to follow a standard format like APA?

documents.t: In your own data. The abbreviated author and treatise forms in your references come from a small supporting table your project keeps — promoted to a vocabulary so the citation rules can read from it. No abbreviation list is built into the platform. Because it is your table, correcting an abbreviation is a data edit: change the row and republish — references that draw on it update across your published pages. See Standards and citations (for environment admins).
documents.s: Where do the abbreviations in my references live?

documents.t: No — the refusal is deliberate. Between drafting the proposal and applying it, another administrator changed the project's active style, so the proposal's measurements no longer describe what applying it would actually do. Rather than silently rebasing onto a style nobody reviewed, the platform asks for a fresh proposal against the current style. Propose again and review the new numbers. The workflow is described in Citation style administration.
documents.s: Our style proposal was refused because "the active style moved" — is something broken?

documents.t: You have just joined a knowledge environment. This page is a guided first week — a sequence to follow, not a reference to memorize. By the end you will have signed in, found your bearings, read a few records, made a safe first edit, previewed it as a reader would see it, and learned where to turn next. Every step links to the page that covers it in full; this tutorial puts those pages in order so nothing surprises you. Work through it once, in order. After that, the Researcher Guide is your map back to any single piece.

When your environment administrator gives you access, you sign in at your project's /login/ page — a simple username-and-password page in your project's colors — and land in your workspace. You do not need any special account type; researcher accounts are ordinary accounts, and the operations area at /admin/ is a separate, admin-only place you will not need. Your password is yours to change from the workspace account menu; details in Sign in and manage your password. The screen has a stable shape you will see everywhere: a left sidebar listing the tables you can work with — figures, terms, manuscript editions, whatever your project tracks; a top bar with a search control and a command palette; a toolbar of table controls; and view tabs that switch between Table, Details, Relations, and Publish. Media tables also show a Media view. Click a table in the sidebar. You land in that table's workspace at an address like /app/workspace/<record-type>/, and you can bookmark or share that address. If your project has several record types, each has its own workspace. Do not try to set anything up yet. Just open two or three tables and notice that they all open into the same shell. The full tour of every control is in the Workspace walkthrough — read it when you are ready, but you do not need it to keep going here. What you are looking at is your team's shared workspace. Other researchers see the same tables; you are not alone in here.
documents.s: Day 1: sign in and look around

documents.t: Above the table sit view tabs. A view is a saved arrangement — which filters are on, how the rows are sorted, which columns show, how tall the rows are, and which view kind opens first. Your environment may have set one view as the default: the shared view and view kind the table opens with when you do not follow a link to another view. For now, stay on whichever view opens first. Look at the columns and ask yourself what each record represents. You are reading the shape of your team's data — what a "record" is here, and what fields describe it. You will arrange your own views later; Workspace walkthrough covers saving and switching them when you get there.
documents.s: Find the view your team starts from

documents.t: The instinct on a new project is to start adding records. Resist it for a day. Reading first tells you the conventions your team already follows. You have two ways to find records: Quick search, for jumping to one record. Click Search database… in the top bar (or press Ctrl+Shift+F, ⌘⇧F on Mac), type a term, and pick a result. Results group by collection and show which field matched. This is the right tool for "find this person, source, or term, wherever it lives." Search & Read, for dwelling among many records. From the quick search panel, choose Open full Search & Read — your typed term carries over — or pick Search & Read from the command palette (Ctrl+K / ⌘K). The full page lets you filter, page through results, and open a record in a reading pane beside the list. Its address encodes your whole search, so you can bookmark or share it. Search matches across the scripts your records carry — original script, transliteration, and translation — for the fields your environment marks searchable. The full behavior, including how diacritics are handled, is in Searching and reading. For now, search for something you expect to exist, open it, and read its fields.

You do not have to come back to these pages to get help. The platform carries the same guidance inside the workspace, in two places. A small ? sits beside many controls. Click it and a help drawer opens beside your work, showing the guide for that exact control — so you can read it without losing your place. Inside the drawer, Related guides are one click away, and a breadcrumb with a Back button lets you return to where you started. Press Escape to close it. The Help page at /app/workspace/help lists every guide grouped by topic. Open one to read it in place. When a guide is tied to a control that is always on screen, its Show me where button jumps you to the workspace and highlights the matching ? spot. When you are stuck mid-task, reach for the nearest ? first; when you want to browse, open the Help page. Find help on a topic covers both.
documents.s: Find help without leaving your work

documents.t: Editing here is built so you cannot lose work or publish by accident. Three things are true before you touch anything: A new row is real the moment you create it. Click + New row in the toolbar and the row joins your table immediately. Your project sees it; public readers never do until you publish. Every change saves as you finish each field. There is no Save button to forget. Click out of a text field or press Enter, and the value is stored; choices and checkboxes save the moment you pick them. You can leave and come back another day — the row waits in the table. Undo exists in two clear histories. Table, Details, and Relations share workspace Undo for saved values, paste, manual row order, field definitions, and relationships. Saved-view filters, sort, columns, and density keep their separate Undo view change and Redo view change actions. Required fields can stay empty while you work; they only need filling before the record can be published. Nothing reaches the public reading site until a record is published, and that is a deliberate step you take, never an accident. Creating, editing, linking and deleting records are covered in Adding and editing rows. Make one small edit to a row you create yourself and watch it save. Practice workspace Undo with Ctrl/Cmd+Z outside the editor, then redo with Ctrl/Cmd+Y or Shift+Ctrl/Cmd+Z. To practice the separate view history, hide a column, change density, or add a harmless filter, then choose Undo view change. Neither history publishes anything; Appearance, Publish, and Media do not intercept workspace-history shortcuts.

Now string the pieces together into one loop you will repeat for the rest of the project: Search for the area you are working in — a person, a source, a term. Read a few neighbouring records to learn the conventions. Edit or add a row, letting each field save as you finish it. Preview the record. Open its Details panel: alongside the fields, a reader-preview pane renders the record exactly as a reader outside your project would see it — same layout, same fonts, same citations — without publishing anything. Read it, spot anything wrong, and fix it in the fields beside it. That loop — search, read, edit, preview — is the daily rhythm of the workspace. Searching and reading covers the search and preview ends of it; Adding and editing rows covers the editing end.
documents.s: A first full session, end to end

documents.t: You now have the loop. Here is the map for everything around it. The whole workspace, control by control → Workspace walkthrough. Creating, editing and deleting records in full → Adding and editing rows. Search behaviour, media, and citations → Searching and reading. Working across scripts and languages → Working in multiple scripts and languages. What a reader outside the project sees, and how to preview it → Public reader. Driving the platform by keyboard, and display settings → Accessibility. What the platform records about you → Privacy and safety. The small suggestions beside the form and the table → Tips and guidance. One specific task, right now → the in-product Help page (/app/workspace/help), or browse the help topics — start with find help on a topic. If a control is missing, grayed out, or behaving unexpectedly, that almost always traces back to how your environment is configured, and your environment administrator is the person to ask. The Researcher Guide troubleshooting table lists the common cases.

Researcher Guide — the entry point and map for everything researcher-facing. Workspace walkthrough — the full tour this tutorial sequences. Adding and editing rows — how records are created, edited and deleted. Searching and reading — search, reading, and the reader preview. Find help on a topic — the in-product help page and the contextual ? buttons.

These pages give short answers to everyday questions about doing your work in your knowledge environment — finding and sharing material, shaping your fields and records, bringing in your source data, and publishing your entries. Each page covers one task, so you can read what you need and get back to your research.

When you add a row to a table, the platform creates it right away — no Save button needed. Every field you fill in saves the moment you leave it. The new row is a real row in your table from the start: you can close the panel and come back to it another day. Nothing you add is public until you publish it. See Preview an entry before publishing.

Open the table you want to add to. Click + New row in the toolbar. Your environment may label this button differently. The row is created and opens for editing. Fill in the fields. Each value saves when you click out of the field, press Enter, or make a choice. There is no Save button to forget. Leave and return whenever you like. Your values are stored. Click the row in the table to pick up where you left off. Required fields can stay empty while you work. They must be filled before the record can be published. Two more ways to start a row: Insert row below — right-click an existing row and choose Insert row below. Duplicate row — right-click a row and choose Duplicate row. The new row starts with that row's editable values already filled in — a useful way to create a second entry that shares most of the same details. If + New row is unavailable, hover over it to see why. Some views cannot accept new rows — for example, a view that combines or filters records rather than showing a single stored table.

Right-click the row and choose Delete row, or open it and use Delete row in the record panel. You are asked to confirm, and the deletion cannot be undone. Some rows cannot be deleted here, and the message says which case applies: A row that has been published. Its address stays answerable so that anyone who cited it is told it was withdrawn, rather than being left at a dead link. Withdraw it from the public site instead — that hides it from readers and keeps the citation honest. A row that came from an import. It belongs to the source it was imported from, so removing it here would not be the real fix, and a later import would bring it back. A row that is linked to other records. Remove its links first, then delete it. Anyone who can edit the table can delete a row in it, including a row a colleague created.

Symptom Likely cause Fix + New row is unavailable or greyed out. The current view cannot accept new rows. Hover over the button to see the reason, or switch to a regular table view. Creating a row fails with a permission message. Your role includes read access but not edit access. Contact your environment administrator. A field did not save after you typed a value. The field may not have lost focus, the value failed a check, or a newer edit made the save stale. Click outside the field or press Enter. Look for the message near the field. If the editor retains your value, retry after checking the latest saved record or discard the retained edit. Delete row is unavailable. The view is not a stored table, so there is no row for it to act on. Switch to a regular table view. Deleting a row is declined. The row has been published, came from an import, or is linked to other records. Read the message — it names which case applies, and what to do instead. The row you added has disappeared from the table. It may have been filtered out of the current view. Remove or adjust any active filters, or switch to a view that shows all rows. Creating, duplicating, and deleting a row are not part of workspace Undo. If you only need to update existing records from a spreadsheet, paste into an editable table cell; extra clipboard lines are reported rather than turned into new rows.

Make a field required — controlling which fields must be filled before a record can be published. Preview an entry before publishing — checking how a record will look to public readers before you publish it. Build a knowledge environment from scratch without importing — creating the collections and fields that hold your records.

When a column is set up to hold several values — one for each language, register, script, edition, or calendar — you fill those values in per record, in the table cell or in the record's form. Every value here is one you enter. The platform never translates a value into another language or fills one in from another field.
documents.s: Add a value in another language

documents.t: Open the record, either by editing the cell in the table or by opening the record's form. You see one row per value the record already has — each row pairs the value with the language (or register, script, edition, or calendar) it belongs to. To add a value, click + Add language (the wording follows the column's setup — + Add register, + Add script, and so on). A new row appears. Choose the language for the new row from the dropdown. It lists the values the column allows; if the one you need is not there, click + new and type it. When the column is set up with a fixed list, a value outside that list is refused with a note — pick from the list, or ask whoever set up the column to allow the one you need. A column with no fixed list accepts any value you type. Type the value beside it. Keep the changes: in the table cell, click Save; in the record's form, your edits save on their own. Either way, a row left blank is dropped.
When a row's language is Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu, or Aramaic, its value box writes from right to left, so the text reads correctly as you type. Other languages write from left to right.

The language for each row is a dropdown of the values the column allows — not a box you type into freely. This keeps every record's values lining up under the same set of languages. When you genuinely need a value the list does not offer, + new lets you add one, and it is tidied into the same standard short form the rest of the column uses. Which languages a column allows is set on the column itself — see Let a column hold several values.
documents.s: Choosing the language is a pick, not free typing

documents.t: When the column has no fixed list, the dropdown fills itself from the right place for what the column holds: language and script columns offer the standard code lists; an edition column offers the editions linked to the record first, then the rest of your edition collections — those keys ARE your edition records, so you manage them by editing the edition collections themselves; register, custom, and calendar columns offer the values your project has used before. A Manage link beside the add button takes you where those offered values are governed: a calendar column's link opens the review page for that set, and a register or custom column's link opens the column's own field settings, where its allowed list is kept.
documents.s: Where the dropdown's values come from

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Arabic or Hebrew text writes left to right. The row's language is not set to a right-to-left language. Pick the right-to-left language from the dropdown; the value box switches direction. The language you need is not in the dropdown. It is not yet in the column's allowed list. Click + new and type it; if the column has a fixed list it is refused, so ask whoever set up the column to add it (see Let a column hold several values). A row's value no longer shows in the table cell. The value is empty, or its language is not the one the column shows. Open the cell to see every row; the cell shows the column's chosen language and skips empty values. A blank row disappeared. Empty rows are dropped when your changes are kept. Fill in both the language and the value.
Let a column hold several values — setting up the column and its allowed languages. Add a new record — creating a record and filling its fields.
Alongside search, a published environment offers an index — a browsable, alphabetised list of every entry. It is the way to explore the whole corpus when you are not looking for one specific item.

A project can publish more than one index, and you switch between them from the controls at the top of the list. For a multilingual corpus that often means browsing the same entries by transliteration or by original script — the same entries, ordered and bucketed by whichever index you pick. The available indexes are chosen by your project; you see only the ones it publishes.
Each row in the index can show more than a bare headword — typically the transliterated form, the original-script form, and a short gloss together — so you can recognise an entry without opening it.

A character rail runs alongside the index. Click a letter to jump straight to that bucket; the list pages as you scroll, so even a very large corpus stays responsive. Which index is the default, and what each row shows, are set by your project when the environment is published — different projects will offer different index choices.

You do not need a spreadsheet or data file to start. You can create collections, define their fields, and wire up relations between them directly in the workspace — no import wizard required. An empty workspace opens on a front door offering two ways in: Create your first collection and Import a spreadsheet. Each is offered only to a role that can carry it out — creating a collection and running an import are both admin actions today. When your role cannot do one of them, the control stays visible and tells you why rather than sending you to a page that would turn you away; ask a project admin to run it, or to widen your role.
documents.s: Build a knowledge environment from scratch without importing

documents.t: A knowledge environment is made of: Collections — the types of things you are keeping track of (people, manuscripts, events, places — whatever is relevant to your project). Fields — the pieces of information you record for each item in a collection (a person's name, a manuscript's date, a place's region). Relations — links between collections that let you say "this person wrote this manuscript" or "this event happened in this place." All three are created the same way whether you are starting from scratch or refining a set that an import created.

Open the workspace. In the sidebar, select Add table. Give the collection a name in Table name — for example, "People" or "Manuscripts". Choose a Table meaning — what each row represents (terms, documents, named things, events, passages, annotations, or media). This helps the platform apply sensible defaults for search and display. Select Create table. The new collection appears in your sidebar. It has no project-specific fields yet; you add them next. For renaming and removing collections, see Create, rename, and delete a collection.

Open the collection. Use the Add column header at the end of the table, or choose Insert column... from an existing column's header menu. Pick a field type from the compact list. The shared field editor opens with that type already selected. Give the field a label — the name as you want it to appear in the table (for example, "Full name", "Date of composition", "Language"). Finish any settings the type needs, then save. A Select list or Multi select starts with editable Option 1; Checkbox has no option list. URL link accepts safe http:// and https:// addresses. Repeat for as many fields as the collection needs. You can always add more fields later. To change an existing field, open its header menu and choose Column type. A self-contained type applies immediately. A type that needs a target or other required settings opens the same field editor with your choice selected. When you create a field this way, the label you type is the only name it ever has. There is no source column name to fall back on — what you typed is exactly what appears everywhere.

A relation lets a record in one collection point to a record in another. For example, a field on "Manuscripts" that points to a "People" record for the author. Open the collection where the relation field will live (e.g., "Manuscripts"). Use Add column or Insert column... from a column header menu. Give it a label (e.g., "Author"). Choose the field type Linked record. Select the collection this field points to (e.g., "People"). Save. When you open a Manuscripts record, the "Author" field shows a picker that lets you search and select a People record. The link is live — clicking the linked record opens that person.
documents.s: Creating a relation between two collections

documents.t: You can mix import and manual. Start with a skeleton you build by hand, then import data later. Or import first and add extra fields by hand. The rules are the same either way. Relations you create manually are immediately active. Unlike some imported relations that go through a review queue, manually created relations are ready to use as soon as you save. AI can advise, but a person approves imported relationship structure. AI may originate or refine a relationship proposal during import; it cannot write arbitrary links directly. Approved proposals create the relationship field and approved imported links. Your labels are your labels. Every field you create from scratch is researcher-owned from birth — no import will ever overwrite the label you gave it (see Rename a field label). Removing a field. If you later decide a field is not needed, use the column header menu and choose Delete column.
