Deleting removes the field definition from the table and form, but it does not erase the stored values underneath; re-adding a field with the same field key restores them.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Add table is dimmed in the sidebar. Your role may not have permission to create collections. The sidebar shows the reason in place; ask a project administrator if you need access. The collection meaning I need is not in the list. The list offers a fixed set of meanings (terms, documents, named things, events, passages, annotations, media). Pick the closest meaning; you can always add your own fields afterward. A relation field I created is not showing the picker when I open a record. The relation may need a moment to become active, or the target collection has no records yet. Refresh the record; if the target collection is empty, add a record there first. I created a field but it does not appear in the table columns. New fields may not be visible in all views by default. Open Manage columns (from the toolbar) and enable the field.

Make a field required — requiring a value for any field. Rename a field label — how labels work and what you own. What changed after re-import — if you later import source data into a hand-built collection.

A column's kind decides how its values are shown, sorted, filtered and edited. You can change it after the column exists, and the workspace shows you what the change would do before you agree to it. The preview counts how many loaded values would not fit, which is the number worth reading. It reads each value by the rules the conversion itself uses, so the count tells you what to expect; the conversion is the one that decides, and an unusual value can still come out marked. The preview's wording for the two formatted-text directions is a summary rather than a full account — converting into formatted text can empty a value that carries nothing a reader could see, and converting out of it writes the formatting down as Markdown rather than discarding it. Both are described below.
documents.s: Change what kind of value a column holds

documents.t: Open the column's menu — Column actions on the column header, or right-click the header. Choose Column type. The list of kinds opens beside the menu. Point at a kind without clicking. Until you do, the panel says "Point at a type to see what the change would do to this column's values." Resting on a kind replaces that line with a plain summary of the change. Click the kind to make the change, or move away to leave the column alone. Pointing at Number from a text column reads: Text → Number Values that read as number are kept as number; the rest stay as typed and are marked in the column until corrected. 100 of 100 loaded values would be marked "needs correction" and kept as typed. The count covers the rows currently loaded in your table, not the whole table — load more rows first if you want a wider check.
documents.s: See what a change would do, before making it

documents.t: A value the new kind cannot read is kept and marked needs correction in its cell, so you can find and fix it in your own time. Values that do read as the new kind are converted. For a plain-text column, what is kept is exactly what you typed. For a formatted-text column it is the Markdown form of the value: the cell is read as text before the new kind tries it, so a bold word that cannot be read as a number is kept as **word** — the formatting written down rather than dropped, which is the same text a change back would read as bold again. One case does lose content, and it is worth knowing before you convert into formatted text: text that carries nothing a reader could see — an HTML comment, or markup the platform strips as unsafe — has nothing left once it is read as formatted text, so the cell ends up empty rather than marked. If a column holds raw markup rather than prose, check a value before converting the rest. That holds even where the new kind has less room than the old one. A cell holding several values, in a column changed to a single-choice list, keeps all of them and is marked "several values in a single-choice column" — the cell cannot show them as a choice until you pick one, but none of them is lost in the meantime. You do not have to act on the mark. A marked value keeps its mark until you edit that cell to something the column's kind can read. What "left as it is" means depends on where the value came from. From a plain-text column it is exactly what you typed. From a formatted-text column the value was read as text before the new kind tried it, so what stays is that text — a bold word arrives as **word** — and it is that form the cell keeps and that you edit.
documents.s: What happens to values that do not fit

documents.t: If a change converts even one stored value, it is final: the receipt after the change says so, and the table's undo history is cleared at that point. There is nothing left to undo — not the rewritten values, and not the kind either. To go back you change the kind again yourself, and the values convert a second time. This is why the preview is worth using before you commit to a change rather than after. One change is worth understanding before you make it: formatted text to plain text. The formatting is not thrown away — it is written down in Markdown, so emphasis becomes *emphasis*, strong becomes **strong**, and a list becomes lines beginning with -. That is the same form the reader already renders for plain text, so the words read correctly either way, and changing the column back reads that Markdown as formatting again. What you see in the cell changes, though: a formatted paragraph becomes text with Markdown marks visible in it. If your fields carry richer structure than emphasis, lists and links, check one converted value before converting the rest. More generally, a value the new kind can read is rewritten into that kind's own form — a date becomes a standard date, several values becoming plain text join into one line — and it is that rewritten form the column keeps afterwards. Only values the new kind cannot read are left untouched and marked. A column that was created as a formula has no stored values of its own, so it cannot become an ordinary column. See Build a formula column. Choosing a kind for a computed column does something different from the rest of this page: it stops the column computing. The formula is removed, and the values the column held before the formula was added come back — exactly as they were, because a computed column's cells are never rewritten. Ones that do not read as the new kind are marked until corrected. The panel says this instead of offering a count, since the values on screen are the computed ones and not the ones you will be left with.

The full column editor has the same choice with more room: open Edit column from the column's menu, then Change type…. That view groups the kinds — Words and text, Numbers and amounts, Dates and time, Choices, Connections and links, Pictures, sound, and files, and Built from other fields — and shows a small sample of how each one reads. Its footer note says what this page says: "Stored values stay; switching changes how this field is read and edited."
documents.s: Where else the kind can be changed

documents.t: The structure of a linked-record column comes from the source it was linked from, so it cannot be converted into an ordinary column, and an ordinary column cannot become one. Add a new linked-record column instead.
Build a formula column — a column computed from other columns rather than typed into. Rename a field label — changing what a column is called, which is separate from what it holds.

A row color rule belongs to one column. You pick a value and a color, and every row whose field holds exactly that value shows a stripe of that color at the left edge of the row, next to the row number. The row itself is unchanged — the stripe lets your eye pick out the matching rows while every column stays readable. You can give several values of the same field their own colors — "Reviewed" in moss green, "Needs attention" in rose — and set rules on more than one column at the same time.

Click the ⋯ (Column actions) button on the column's header. Right-clicking the header opens the same menu. Select Conditional format. Under Color rows where value is, pick the value you want to highlight. For a choice field, the list offers the field's options; for other fields, it offers values found in the rows already loaded in the table. Select a color: Rose, Amber, Moss, Steel, Violet, or Graphite. The stripes appear on the matching rows, and Saved with view shows next to the panel title. To color another value of the same field, pick it in the same list and choose its color.

The stripes themselves: a colored edge on a row means at least one rule matches it. In a column's menu, the Conditional format entry reads Saved when that column has a rule. Inside the Conditional format panel, the color marked with a check is the one assigned to the value shown in the list. Rules are kept per column, so to review them, open each column's menu. A row shows one stripe color even when it matches rules on more than one column.

Open Conditional format on the column: Clear value removes the color from the value currently shown in the list. Clear this column's rules removes every value and color on that column. The button is there only while the column has a rule. Changing or clearing color rules is a view change like any other: the Undo view change arrow in the toolbar restores what you cleared, and Redo view change re-applies it.

Color rules are part of the view, alongside filters, sort order, and column layout. They are stored on whichever view is active as you work, and they are waiting for you when you return. Duplicating a view copies its color rules; each view keeps its own set. See Save your table arrangement as a view. Views are shared with everyone working in your environment. A color rule you add or clear on a view reaches your collaborators too — to highlight rows for your own work without changing what your team sees, duplicate the view first and set the rules in the copy.
documents.s: Rules are remembered by your views

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix The value I want to color is not in the list. The list offers a choice field's options plus values found in rows already loaded in this table. A value no loaded row holds does not appear, and when a column holds many distinct values, the list offers only the first ones found. Check that at least one row in the table holds the value, then reopen the column menu. The panel says no values are loaded yet. The column has no data in the rows loaded for this table. The value list appears once the column has data in the active table. A row I expect to be colored shows no stripe. The rule matches the value exactly as it is displayed. The row's value may differ — a different option, extra wording, or another spelling. Compare the row's value with the value named in the rule, and add a rule for the variant if both forms are in use. I colored a value, but a row shows a different color. The row also matches a rule on another column — a row shows one stripe color even when several rules match. Open the other columns' menus and clear the rule you no longer want. My rules disappeared after switching view tabs. Each view keeps its own color rules. Switch back to the view where you set them, or set rules on the view that is now active. My rule changes are not kept when I come back. Changes are stored on the active view — if your role is read-only on this table, the view cannot be changed. Ask your environment administrator for editing access.

Save your table arrangement as a view — views remember your color rules along with filters, sort, and columns. Narrow the current table with filters — hide the rows you don't need instead of coloring the ones you do.

When you open a published entry — or its draft preview — the reading view shows the entry's citations rendered in your project's citation style. Select and copy the text to paste it into a bibliography, footnote, or document. Citations sit in the entry's References area. Rows of evidence carry their citations, and when your project has set up a citation for the record itself, it appears as its own row there too. Read the references section on a published entry explains what each row means.
documents.s: Copy a citation for a record or media item

documents.t: A media item attached to a record can carry its own citation details — separate from the record's citation. When your project has given a media item full citation details, its citation appears among the entry's references, rendered in your project's style and ready to copy.

Your project's citation style is set by your environment administrator. It is defined in Citation Style Language — the same format reference managers such as Zotero use. Your project has one citation style, applied across all of its collections.
documents.s: What citation style your project uses

documents.t: The draft preview shows an entry exactly as a reader will see it, references and citations included, so you can copy a citation before anything goes live — see Preview an entry before publishing.
documents.s: Copying before an entry is public

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A citation shows placeholder text or looks incomplete. The fields the citation draws on are missing or only partly filled in on that record or media item. Open the record in your workspace and complete those fields. The citation updates on the next publish; the draft preview shows the result first. If the needed fields are not clear, ask your environment administrator. The citation style looks wrong for your field. Your project has not yet adopted a citation style, or the style is still being refined. Contact your environment administrator. One style applies across the project; the citations update once it is applied. A citation renders roughly — punctuation or ordering looks off. Your project's citation style is a proposed draft that has not yet been reviewed and applied. Raise it with your environment administrator. A reviewed and applied style replaces the rough rendering on the next publish. No citation appears for a media item. The media item's citation details are missing, or your project has not set up citations for media items in that collection. Complete the citation fields on the media item's record, or ask your environment administrator whether media citations are set up for that collection.
The workspace table has separate clipboard paths for cells, cell ranges, and targeted cells. Use the one that matches what you want to paste next.

Focus the cell whose value you want. Press Ctrl+C on Windows or Linux, or Cmd+C on Mac. Move to the cell where the value should go and paste with Ctrl/Cmd+V. When several rows are selected and the focused column is editable, pasting one copied value fills that same column for each selected row. Read-only fields, derived fields, and fields your role cannot edit are skipped rather than silently changed.

Use a cell range when you want a rectangle of cells, not entire records. Click the first cell in the rectangle. Drag to the opposite corner, Shift-click the opposite corner, or hold Shift and use the arrow keys to extend the range. To target a whole displayed row, use the row-gutter action Select visible cells in row. To target a whole displayed column, open Column actions and choose Select visible column cells. The status line shows the range shape, such as Cell range: 3 x 3, Row range: 1 x 22, or Column range: 100 x 1. Press Ctrl/Cmd+C to copy the range as tab-separated values, without row headers. Paste while the range is active to target that rectangle. A single copied value fills the editable cells in the rectangle. Tabular data follows the visible row and column order; cells that cannot be written are skipped and reported. Press Escape to clear the cell range. Clearing a cell range does not clear selected rows.
documents.s: Copy or fill a cell range

documents.t: Use Target cells when the cells you want are not next to each other. Select Target cells in the table status line. Click each cell you want to include. Click a targeted cell again to remove it. To add a displayed row to the targeted cells, use the row-gutter action Select visible cells in row while Target cells is on. To add a displayed column, open Column actions and choose Select visible column cells while Target cells is on. Using either command again removes that visible group from the targets. When a data cell has focus, press Enter or Space to add or remove that cell. The status line shows Sparse cells: N. Targeted cells do not select whole rows. Press Ctrl/Cmd+C to copy only those targeted cells as tab-separated values, in visible row order. Paste while targeted cells are active to use those cells as the paste target. A one-cell paste can fill the editable targeted cells. Tabular paste is conservative: the clipboard must contain exactly the same number of values as the targeted cells, or the table rejects the paste and reports the mismatch. Read-only targeted fields are skipped and reported. Press Escape to clear targeted cells and leave Target cells mode.

When you need selected rows outside the workspace, focus a row and press Space. Use Ctrl/Cmd+Space to add or remove another focused row, or Shift with the arrow keys to extend the selection. Then choose Export in the table toolbar and select Download CSV or Download raw JSON. See Export selected rows for the complete steps.

If you copied rows from a spreadsheet or from another workspace view, focus the top-left editable target cell and paste. The table lines up pasted columns by header label when the copied data includes headers, otherwise it starts at the focused column. Pasted rows update rows already visible in the table; extra rows are reported as skipped instead of being created by accident. A saved paste becomes one reversible workspace operation, even when it updates many cells. Use Undo in Table, Details, or Relations, or press Ctrl/Cmd+Z outside an editor, to restore the prior values. If a paste review is still waiting for confirmation, Undo cancels that pending paste first.
documents.s: Paste tabular data into existing rows

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Pasting one copied value changed only the last focused cell. No cell range was active, the destination rows were not selected in the table grid, or focus was not in the editable column to fill. Use a cell range for a rectangle of cells, or select the target rows and focus the column to update. A paste into targeted cells was rejected with a value-count message. The targeted cells were sparse, and the pasted table had more than one value but not exactly the same number of values as the targets. Paste one value to fill all editable targets, or copy exactly one value per targeted cell. A copied range pasted with some cells skipped. Some target fields were read-only, derived, hidden, unknown, or not editable by your role. Check the paste summary, then edit those fields manually if the table offers an editor. A browser permission prompt or copy failure appears. The browser blocked clipboard access for this site. Allow clipboard access for your environment and retry. Some pasted fields were skipped. The pasted columns include read-only, derived, hidden, unknown, or not-yet-editable fields. Check the paste summary, then edit those fields manually if the table offers an editor. The table did not create new rows from extra pasted lines. Paste updates existing rows only; overflow rows are skipped deliberately. Create new rows with New row, Insert row below, or Duplicate row, then paste values into them.

Some columns hold dates that people wrote in many shapes — 384 BCE – 322 BCE, c. 80–150, a century, a named period, a dynasty. The workspace can turn those into operable dates (years you can sort, filter, and place on a timeline) without ever rewriting what you wrote. Your original text is kept exactly as written, always. Open a cell in a date column and you get the Date this entry editor. It shows your value at the top with as written — kept exactly, and offers three ways to date it.

What we read — a deterministic parser's reading of your text: the years it resolves to, the precision (for example circa), and why. Same input, same result, no AI involved. If the text can't be read into years (a named period, a non-Gregorian calendar), nothing is guessed — it stays as written and you use one of the other two paths. AI suggestion — an advisory reading from the assistant, offered only when you open this tab. It never writes anything on its own: it proposes a label and dates for you to Accept, Edit first, or Reject. If AI suggestions are turned off or unavailable, you'll see a short note and can still date the value by hand. Enter it yourself — type the start year (and optional end year) with BCE/CE, a precision, and a calendar. Your original text is shown read-only above the fields; you're adding the dates, not changing the words.
documents.s: Three ways to date a value

documents.t: The footer always shows the value's current standing — Not yet dated, Dated here, or Kept as written — and a Leave as written button that closes the editor and writes nothing. How you record the dates depends on the tab you are on: On What we read, Save this match grounds the reading you are looking at. On AI suggestion, Accept records the suggested reading — or Edit first to adjust it, Reject to dismiss it. On Enter it yourself, Save these dates records what you typed. Whichever you use, the original text stays exactly as written.

The What we read panel may show an EDTF line (for example 0080~/0150~). EDTF is a machine-readable date standard; a trailing ~ marks an approximate date. It's there for reference — you never have to type it.

An import you are still setting up can be thrown away. Open it and choose Discard import in the bar at the top of the import screens. This works up until a start actually goes through. Pressing Start import is not the boundary on its own: if the start is refused before it begins — an import that is not ready to run, or a source that could not be reached to check it — nothing is queued and the import can still be thrown away. Once a start does go through, the import is kept — not only while it is adding records, but from the moment it is queued to do so, which is before anything of it has run. (Arriving from a failed run's own link, the same button reads Start again; reached any other way — from your history, or by navigating back to the import — it still reads Start import.) An import is kept once it has been started even if it added nothing at all: a run that stops early, or one that finds no rows to bring in, may still have applied part of your setup, and the import is the only record of what it changed. A dialog asks you to confirm. It names the import, warns that "Everything it proposed goes with it" and that "This can't be undone.", and offers two choices: Keep it, which closes the dialog and changes nothing, and Discard import, which throws the import away. The import's name in the dialog is whatever it is called at that moment. If you rename the import and then discard it without reloading the page, the dialog uses the new name.
documents.s: Discard an import you no longer want

documents.t: Once an import has added records to your workspace, it is no longer yours to throw away — the records it created point back to it as their record of origin, so removing it would leave them with no account of where they came from. This is one of the reasons an import is kept; the others are below. In that case the dialog stays open after you confirm, and the reason appears inside it: This import already added records to the workspace, so it is kept as their record of origin. Re-run it to finish what it started. Nothing is deleted — the import and everything it set up are still there, and so is anything it added to your workspace. Ignore the second sentence if your import finished normally. When this is the reason you are shown — that is, when the import is neither queued nor running — the wording appears whether or not it completed, so an import that ran all the way through shows it too. If yours finished, it has nothing left to finish and does not need running again. Re-run it only if you know it stopped part-way. An import is also kept in the situations below, each with a message of its own. While a run is queued or under way — the same message covers both, because from here the two are not told apart: This import is queued to add records, or is adding them now. Wait for it to finish before discarding it. Waiting will not let you discard it. Once the run ends, one of the reasons below applies instead — records written, or a run having been attempted, or the import marked as finished — so a start that goes through makes the import permanent whatever the run does next. The message asks you to wait because the screen cannot say more while a run is in flight, not because waiting changes the answer. And when a run was started before and wrote no records — whether it stopped part-way or ran all the way through — since your setup may have been partly applied even though nothing was added: This import has already been run once. Some of your setup may have been applied before it stopped, and discarding it would remove the record of what it changed. And an import already marked as finished, with no records pointing at it, says neither of those — it does not mention records, because at that point there are none: This import is marked as finished, so it is kept as the record of what it did. You find out by pressing the button. The confirmation dialog looks the same whether an import can be thrown away or will be kept — same title, same warning, same two choices. The reason only appears after you confirm. Pressing Discard import on an import that is kept is safe: nothing is removed.
documents.s: When an import is kept instead

documents.t: An import can meet more than one of these conditions at once — it can both have added records and have been run before. Only one reason is shown, and it is the first one that applies, in this order: an import that is queued or adding records, then one that has already added records, then one that has been run before, then one marked as having finished. So an import that both added records and was run before tells you about the records.

Setting up and discarding imports is an administrator task. If your account is not an administrator of the workspace, the import screens do not open for you, and there is nothing on the page to discard. Ask an administrator of your project to do it. Opening the screens is not by itself permission to discard: the two are granted separately, so an account can reach an import, see Discard import, and still be refused on permission. If that happens, ask an administrator who has permission to delete imports.
documents.s: If you cannot open the import at all

documents.t: The Edit time range editor keeps two things separate: what the source says, and years the workspace can work with. You always record the first; the second is optional.

As written is the date exactly as it appears in your source — reign of Augustus, circa 1200, mid-4th c. BCE. A reading is required; this is it. Once a value has been saved, As written is shown read-only: what you wrote is kept as written and cannot be changed here. A new value lets you type it freely.

If you give it no years, the value is saved as written only — a perfectly good record of what the source says. Add years when you also want the value to sort, filter, and sit on a timeline alongside others. A value that already has years keeps them: opening it and saving without changing the years leaves its timeline placement intact — nothing is stripped unless you clear the years yourself. From year — the start year, as a plain number. Use a negative number for BCE (for example -383 for 384 BCE). To year — the end year. Leave it blank to date the start year on its own: the value covers that one year — or decade, or century — at the precision you choose, not a span between two years. (A zero-width instant needs the instant precision.) Precision — how exact the years are: instant, day, month, year, decade, or century. Comparison axis — which timeline the years sit on. It is required once you enter years; leave it on — not comparable — only when you are keeping the value as written, with no years to place. There are two ways to save. To keep the value as written only, leave the years blank (or clear them) — nothing is placed on a timeline. To save a comparable value, provide a From year, a precision, and a comparison axis together. These go as a set: enter a year but leave the axis on — not comparable — and the editor shows a note and keeps Save disabled until you either complete the three or clear the years to save as written.

The calendar is a label on your value — it says which calendar the reading belongs to. The comparison axis is what lets the value be ordered against others. Choosing one never changes the other, and nothing here ever converts your dates from one calendar into another. Your years are placed on the axis you pick, exactly as you entered them.
documents.s: The calendar and the axis are different things

documents.t: Save records the value — the reading, and the years if you added them. Cancel closes the editor and writes nothing. If the column holds a reading per calendar, the editor shows a tab for each; fill in the calendars you have and leave the rest blank.

The Schema Visualizer draws your whole environment as one picture: every collection, and every relation between collections, laid out so you can see how the pieces fit together. Open it from the Visualizer section of your environment's management area, or go straight to /app/workspace/visualize/schema. Any active viewer, editor, or administrator can open it. The management navigation can be narrower than the route itself, so a missing link does not mean that the visualizer is administrator-only. It reads your live schema — the structure exactly as it stands right now. The header tells you how many collections and relations it found, and Sync schema re-reads them if you have just changed something in the workspace.
documents.s: See the shape of your environment in the Schema Visualizer

documents.t: The same map is drawn four ways. Switch between them with the buttons at the top — Schema, Constellation, Metro Map, Estate. Each is the same collections and the same relations; only the drawing changes, so pick whichever one makes your structure easiest to read. Schema — each collection is a card that lists its fields, with labelled arrows for the relations between them. The most literal view. Focus a collection name and use the arrow keys to move its card; hold Shift for a larger step. Constellation — each collection is a glowing orb; related orbs are joined by lines. The most-connected collection anchors the centre and glows brightest; the others gather around it by how closely they relate to that anchor, and a larger orb means a collection with more fields. Metro Map — collections are stations on lines, one line per kind of collection. Where two collections relate, their lines meet at an interchange. Estate — each collection is a room whose size grows with how many fields it holds; a relation is a doorway between rooms.

Once you know what maps to what, any view reads the same way: In your environment Schema Constellation Metro Map Estate A collection a card an orb a station a room A relation between two collections a labelled arrow a line between orbs an interchange a doorway A field a row on the card — the field count under a station a shelf The kind of collection (term, document, passage…) a tag on the card the orb's colour which line it sits on the room's tag Each view carries a small key on screen naming its own symbols, so you do not have to remember this table.
documents.s: The same things, named differently in each view

documents.t: Click any collection — an orb, a station, a room, a card — and a detail panel opens beside the map, showing its Structure: the collection's fields, in order. The panel stays open when you switch views, so you can select a collection in one view and keep reading it while you flip to another.

The visualizer is a read-only survey. Nothing you do here — dragging a card, zooming, opening the detail panel — changes your structure or your data. To actually add a collection, a field, or a relation, go to the workspace; see Build a knowledge environment from scratch and Link one record to another. Come back and use Sync schema to see your changes on the map.
documents.s: It only shows — it does not change

documents.t: The workspace now marks a few structural milestones with a brief animation — for example when you first draw a relation from one collection to another, or when a new collection is created. In the Constellation view, the Moments toggle plays a short guided tour of your environment, one collection at a time. These are a visual touch on top of the structure; they add nothing you cannot already see and do in the workspace and the other views.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A collection I just created is not on the map. The map is showing the schema from before your change. Select Sync schema in the header to re-read the live structure. The map looks empty or nearly empty. A brand-new environment has few collections and no relations yet. Add collections and relations in the workspace; see Build a knowledge environment from scratch. I clicked a collection but nothing changed. The detail panel may have opened off to the side, or you clicked empty space. Click directly on the orb, station, room, or card; the panel opens beside the map. I cannot edit anything here. The visualizer is read-only by design. Make structural changes in the workspace, then use Sync schema. The schema could not be loaded. The live structure request failed. Select Retry. The message deliberately does not show server or database details.

Build a knowledge environment from scratch — creating the collections, fields, and relations this map draws. Link one record to another — the relations that show up here as arrows, lines, interchanges, and doorways. Register a collection the platform built from your data — bringing an imported collection into your environment so it appears on the map.
Select one or more rows, then use Export in the table toolbar to download them as a file. The Export menu is unavailable until you select a row.

One row: focus the row in the table grid and press Space. Add rows one at a time: hold Ctrl (Windows / Linux) or Cmd (Mac) and press Space on another focused row. Select a range: select the first row, then hold Shift while moving with the arrow keys. Every row between them is selected.

Select the rows you want to download. In the table toolbar, select Export. Select Download CSV for a spreadsheet-friendly file, or Download raw JSON when you need the structured row data for a technical workflow. Your browser saves the downloaded file to its usual downloads location. The CSV contains the visible columns and a header row. JSON preserves the raw row data. Selecting rows in one view does not carry over to another view or to another table. Switching views or tables clears the selection.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Clicking a row opens the record instead of selecting it. Click opens record details on some workspace routes. Use keyboard selection: focus the row and press Space. Export is unavailable. No row is selected. Focus a row and press Space, then choose Export in the table toolbar. The selection is cleared when I switch to another view. Selections are per-view and per-session — they are not saved. Re-select your rows after switching views.
The toolbar above your table has two filtering tools. They work together and are both only about this collection — they do not search the rest of your workspace.
documents.s: Narrow the current table with filters

documents.t: The Filter rows… box in the toolbar answers for every row in this collection, not only the rows the table happens to have scrolled into view. Type a term and the table shows the matching rows from the whole collection; clear the box and every row comes back. A row matches when its value contains what you typed, ignoring letter case. Accent marks are set aside the same way quick search sets them aside (see Working in multiple scripts and languages): breathings, iota subscripts, circumflex and grave accents, and Arabic and Hebrew vowel marks do not count, so a term typed without them reaches both the marked and the unmarked forms of a record, and a term typed with one of them is more exact — it reaches only rows carrying the same marks. The acute accent and the diaeresis still count on both sides: cafe does not find café, and café does not find cafe. The filter box answers for this collection. If the record you want lives in a different collection, it will not appear here — use the Search database… control at the top of the workspace instead. This text is not saved with the view. When you navigate away and return, the filter box is empty. For a filter you want to keep, use the filter builder below and save the arrangement as a view.
documents.s: The filter box — narrowing as you type

documents.t: Click Filter in the toolbar to open the filter builder. Each filter condition targets one field. Pick the field, then set a value with a control suited to that field's kind: Field kind What you set Text A word or phrase, typed in a text box Number A number, typed in a number box Date A date, picked with a date control Boolean Yes, No, or Any value, chosen from the state list Choice (single or multiple) One of the field's option values, picked from a list Any other field kind takes a word or phrase, matched against the value as it is displayed in the table. A row stays visible when the field's value contains what you set, with the same accent-mark folding the filter box uses: a term typed without the marks that are set aside reaches both the marked and unmarked forms, a term typed with one reaches only the marked ones, and the acute accent and the diaeresis count on both sides. Matching ignores letter case. Comparisons such as greater-than, before and after, or ranges are not available in the filter builder. One exception to the folding: a Date, Number or Boolean field, and a field marked private or not searchable, is matched on its stored text exactly as written — letter case is still ignored, but accent marks are not set aside. Those fields are not part of the search index the folding comes from. A rich-text, time-range or media field outside the index cannot be filtered at all — its stored form is not the text its cell shows — and the filter says so. A Date field's control still picks a calendar date, but the table now matches it the same "contains" way as every other field: the picked date is sent as plain digits (YYYY-MM-DD) and a row matches when its stored value contains that text. The earlier rule — reading both sides as dates and comparing calendar days, so a stored value with a time and timezone could match a date it did not literally contain — is removed. A field that only looks like a date but is configured as Text keeps text matching until its field type is changed. Changing the type reports any stored values it converts or leaves for correction. The table narrows as soon as you set a value, and the condition appears as a chip in the toolbar, shown after "filtering by". The chip names the field and the value, with a count of the rows that currently match, so you can see at a glance what is active.
documents.s: The filter builder — conditions by column

documents.t: Add more than one condition by picking another field in the filter builder. All active conditions must match a row for it to stay visible — the conditions work together. Each field carries one condition: setting a new value for a field replaces that field's earlier value. The filter box and the filter builder also compose: you can apply column conditions and then type in the filter box to narrow further.
Click the × on any chip to remove that condition. The table widens to include rows that now match. Click Clear — visible when at least one chip is active — to remove every condition at once.

You do not need a search term to use filters. If you want to survey a slice of your corpus — all records with a particular choice value, all rows that mention a particular place — open the filter builder, set your conditions, and browse the matching rows directly. No typing in the search box required.

Filters set while a saved view is active are remembered on that view. Open or create a view, set your conditions, and the next time you open that view your filters are already applied. See What happens to saved views after a re-import for how saved filters behave when a field changes.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The filter box does not find a record you expect. The filter box answers for this collection only; the record may be in a different collection. Use the Search database… control at the top of the workspace to search across all collections you can access. A filter condition I set is gone when I come back to the table. You set the condition using the quick filter box, which is not stored. Conditions from the filter builder chips persist only when a saved view is active. Set the condition in the filter builder, then save the view. The grid shows "Filter unavailable — search is not enabled for this workspace" instead of rows. This workspace's search engine is not enabled, so the filter box and filter builder have nothing to select matches from. Contact your environment administrator to enable search for this workspace. I cannot find the Filter button. In a narrow window the toolbar lays its controls out on more than one line. Widen the window, or look for the button on the toolbar's following line. After I clear all chips, rows I expected do not reappear. The quick filter box may also have a term in it. Check the filter box in the toolbar and clear it. The filter builder does not show the field I want to filter on. The filter builder lists the fields configured for your collection. Contact your environment administrator if a field you need is missing from the filter builder. The foot says index updates are "pending" while a filter is active. A recent edit has not finished being written to the collection's search index yet. Wait for reindexing to finish, then check the filter result again.

Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — when to use search rather than filtering. What happens to saved views after a re-import — how your saved filters survive source updates. Share a search — copy a URL that includes your filters so a colleague sees the same rows.

A field definition and the collections that display it are kept separately. A collection lists the fields it shows; the definitions themselves — the label, the type, the settings — live on the record kind. So a definition can outlive every collection that listed it. Whether it then disappears depends on what is left: a collection of that record kind set to show every field displays it anyway, and a record kind whose collections are all removed can be given one that lists every configured field. It stops appearing only where no remaining collection shows it — and in that case nothing was deleted. Having such a field and being shown the section below are separate questions, though: a workspace can hold one and still not see the section, for the reasons set out there. The structure page gathers these together, at /app/workspace/manage/structure/fields. That page is open to workspace administrators only, so if you do not administer this workspace, ask someone who does to look — the rest of this entry describes what they will see and do. If any such fields exist, a section appears for that record kind, headed with that kind's own name and then "— fields in no collection" — for a record kind named Terms, "Terms — fields in no collection". It explains: These field definitions exist but no collection of this record kind lists them, so they appear in no section above and in no workspace table. Add one to a collection's fields to edit it. Each row shows the field's name, its key, its type and where its data comes from, with the action Choose which collection shows it. The heading appearing tells you something; its absence does not. It shows only when there is a stranded field to list — but it is also absent while the page is still loading a record kind, when loading that record kind failed, when Find a field has text in it that the stranded field's name does not match, and when any collection of that record kind is set to show every field rather than a chosen list. That last one is the case to know about: such a collection shows this field too, so the field is not stranded and the section is right not to appear — even though you never put the field on a list yourself. So treat the section as a way of finding stranded fields, not as a way of confirming there are none: to check that, look at a fully loaded page with the search box empty, and at whether the record kind has a collection showing everything.
documents.s: Find fields that no collection shows

documents.t: Choose Choose which collection shows it on the row. That opens the workspace's Collections page — every collection in it, not that record kind's — and it does not pick one or change anything on its own, so the field is still stranded until you finish these steps: Find the collection you want it to appear in, and check it is one of the same record kind as your field. The page is not filtered — it lists every collection in the workspace, in no particular relation to the field you came from — and a collection of another kind only ever offers that kind's fields, so yours will not be among them. A card of another kind set to show all its fields can look as though nothing needs doing. In that collection's settings, select Choose workspace fields. A list of the record kind's fields appears with a checkbox each. If the collection is set to Show all configured fields instead, it already shows this field and there is nothing to do here. Tick your field. Press Save collection settings. It then reappears in that collection's tables with its label, type and settings intact — they were never removed. One case where it will not: if you had hidden that column in the collection's saved view before it was removed, the view still hides it. Collection membership and which columns a view shows are separate settings, and this only restores the first. Show the column from the table's own column controls if it stays missing. One thing to check while you are choosing which collection: under Workspace presentation, a collection can be set Shown in workspace or not. Saving your field into a hidden collection does take it out of the stranded list, but the collection is left out of workspace navigation — so you will not come across the field by browsing, even though it is there. The collection keeps an Open in workspace link on its own card, and following that shows it with your field in place. If you want it found rather than only reachable, either pick a collection that is shown, or tick Shown in workspace on the one you chose. If the record kind has no collection at all, there is no list to add it to and the page offers Create collection instead. Make one and choose the meaning that matches; a new collection starts out showing every field the record kind has, so the field appears there without being added to anything.
Help is available without leaving the workspace, in two places.

The Help page (/app/workspace/help) lists the available guides grouped by topic — working with your data, finding and sharing, and importing. Open a guide to read it in place; each one answers a single task-shaped question in plain language. A direct link to one guide looks like /app/workspace/help/<guide-name>, so you can share a specific guide with a colleague.
Many controls have a small ? affordance beside them. Clicking it opens the matching guide in a drawer, right where you are working — so you can read the relevant help without losing your place.
If a guide does not cover your question, or a control is not behaving as you expect, that is worth reporting to your project's administrator — the help set grows as new behaviour ships.
documents.s: When help does not answer it

documents.t: When your source has two columns whose names are so similar that the platform cannot tell them apart as separate fields, the import stops before writing anything and shows you every problem at once. The report names each set of colliding columns so you know exactly what to fix.
documents.s: Fix colliding column names during import

documents.t: Each column in your source becomes a field with an internal identifier built from its name. Spaces, punctuation, and capitalisation differences are smoothed out so the identifier works consistently across languages and formats. When two differently named columns produce the same identifier after that smoothing — for example, "Author Name" and "Author-Name" both become the same field — the platform cannot accept both without overwriting one with the other. Rather than silently discard data, the import stops and reports every such collision in one message.

For each collision, the report names the identifier the columns would share and lists every source column that produces it — including which table each column comes from when your source has more than one table. If there are several collisions, they all appear together — the import never stops at the first one and leaves the rest hidden.

You have two options. Option 1 — Rename one of the columns in your source. Open your spreadsheet or data source, give the conflicting column a name that is meaningfully different from its counterpart, then run the import again. A small change like adding a word or removing an ambiguous character is enough. Option 2 — Leave one of the colliding columns out during the import review. In the review step, reject the proposed field for one of the colliding columns so only one of them becomes a field. The other column is not deleted from your source — if you need both, rename one there and bring it in with a later import. Your data is never changed or written while a collision is unresolved. The import stops entirely and waits for you to fix the source or adjust your review decisions before it touches anything.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The same column keeps appearing in the collision report after renaming. The new name still smooths out to the same identifier as the other column. Make the names more distinct — change more than capitalisation or a single punctuation mark. The collision report shows columns from different tables in my source. Two differently named columns in different tables feed the same collection and produce the same identifier. Rename the column in one of the tables, or leave one of them out during the import review. The import worked before but now shows a collision after I added a column. A new column you added has a name too similar to an existing one. Rename the new column to something clearly distinct before re-importing.

Rename a field label — giving a field a friendlier name after a successful import without changing your source. Understand what changed after a re-import — what the platform carries forward when the import completes successfully.

A formula column is computed from the row's other columns. You write the rule once; every row shows its own result, and the result follows the columns it reads — change a value in one of them and the formula's value changes with it. The column is read-only in the table: you edit the columns it reads, not the result.

A formula is something a column has, not a separate kind of column. You can give one to a column you already have, or start a new column with one. Give a formula to a column you already have Open the column's menu — Column actions on the column header, or right-click the header. Choose Add formula…. The column editor opens with the formula editor already showing. Build the formula (below). The preview under With your rows shows the result on five of the rows already loaded in your table, updating as you type. Click Save changes. The column becomes read-only in the table and shows a computed value in every row. The column keeps the formatting it already had wherever the result can still use it — a money column whose formula returns a number is still shown as money, and a web-address column whose formula returns text is still shown as a link. Start a new column with a formula Click + at the right end of the column headers (or Insert column… in a column's menu). Give the column a label, then open Change type… and pick Formula under Built from other fields. The card shows a sample formula and an Open the formula editor… button that takes you straight there. Build the formula and click Add column. A linked-record column cannot take a formula. Its structure comes from the source it was linked from, so the menu shows Add formula… greyed out with the reason. Add a separate column for the formula instead.

Sentence mode is for joining columns with text between them — a full name, a citation line, a label with a dash in it. Type { where the column should go and pick it from the list that opens; the letters you type after { narrow the list. Or press Insert column at the end of the sentence to pick one for the caret. Chips move as one piece; a focused chip is removed with Backspace or Delete. Type the text you want between chips straight into the sentence box. When a column is empty, skip it — and the text glued to it (checked by default) drops the text next to a column when that column is empty in a row, so you do not get a stray dash after a missing translation. Under Result the editor names what kind of value the formula produces — a sentence produces text.

Switch the toggle to Expression to see the same formula written out — a sentence appears as Template("{column_key} — {other_key}", true) — and to go beyond what a sentence can say. A column in the formula shows as a pill with the column's label (its key on hover). Typing { opens the list of columns to pick from, and the letters after it narrow the list. A pill is one piece: Delete or Backspace on a selected pill removes it whole. To swap a pill for another column, press Enter on it, double-click it, or press Backspace right after it — it reopens as text with the column list filtered to its label; Escape puts it back. Text goes in double quotes; & joins pieces of text. As you type a name, a list of matching columns and functions opens (columns first). Arrow keys move, Tab or Enter accepts, Escape closes; a function is inserted as Name( with the caret inside the parentheses, a column as a pill. After Link( the list offers your relation columns, after .Field( the linked table's columns, and after . the functions that apply to the value on the left. Inside a function call a hint above the caret shows its signature with the argument you are on highlighted, plus a one-line description and an example. Functions below the box lists the whole catalogue with a search box. The editor checks the expression as you type. The piece with a problem is underlined and the problem is explained under the box in words — "‘translatoin’ is not a column — did you mean Translation?" with a button that makes the replacement, or "Expected a comma or a closing parenthesis after Length(…)". While the expression has a problem the preview is empty, and the column cannot be saved until it is fixed. Resting the caret on a piece of the formula (or hovering a pill) shows its value on the first preview row — a pill shows that row's cell, any other piece shows the whole formula's result for that row. A formula that uses functions or operators the sentence cannot show stays in expression mode; the note "This formula uses functions the sentence cannot show" explains why the Sentence button is greyed out. Some formulas produce a number, a date, or a yes/no value rather than text. Result names which, and the column is shown accordingly. Tick Store as text to keep the result as plain text instead.

If your project has drafting turned on and you are allowed to change columns, the editor offers Describe it — say what the column should show in your own words and get a formula back to check. Type the description under In your words, naming your own columns — for example "the title in capitals, then a dash, then the short summary". Click Draft it. The draft appears marked Proposed. Nothing is saved yet. Choose Use this to put the formula in the editor, Adjust by hand to edit it there, or Discard to drop it. Sometimes there is no formula to choose between: if what you wrote left the platform with a question it cannot answer — a column it could not place, a rule it could not read — it comes back with the questions and no formula at all. Use this and Adjust by hand are not offered then, because there is nothing yet to use or edit. Answer what it asked by rewriting the description, and draft again. A draft shows you four things: the formula itself, not only a description of it — shown as column chips and the text between them when the draft is simple enough for the sentence view, and as the expression written out when it is not, a sentence restating what it understood, in words, how many of your columns it used and whether it found them all, the result on your first rows. Your column is not changed until you accept the draft and then save the column, so discarding one leaves the column exactly as it was. Each request does use part of the session's drafting allowance, and that is spent whether or not you keep the result — so a draft you discard is free of consequence for your data, not free of allowance. A drafted formula is shown to you, not applied, and that matters when it names something your table does not have. The draft is returned as written — the unknown name still in it — with the problem stated as a question beside it, rather than quietly swapped for a guess. So a draft can carry a name that will not resolve until you change it. That case also has no row results: the preview needs a formula the platform can read, so a draft naming something unresolved shows its questions and leaves the rows blank. Read the questions and the restating sentence, and where there are rows, read those too — a formula can be valid and still not be the one you meant. If you do not see Describe it, either your account cannot change columns — which a project administrator can grant — or drafting is not turned on for your environment, which is set by the platform operator rather than from any project setting.
documents.s: Describe it instead of writing it

documents.t: Formula comparisons are exact by default. That is useful when a spelling difference is part of the evidence, but it also means two visually similar forms can compare as different text. Use Fold() on both sides when you want the comparison to behave like search: Fold({Word}) = Fold({Variant}) Contains(Fold({Title}), Fold("βίος")) Fold() follows the column's comparison setting. A column configured for exact comparison keeps its marks, so use an ordinary comparison there. Use Fold() inside a comparison rather than as the whole column value: it produces a search key, not display text. When an empty preview would gain answers from this change, the editor shows a notice with the number of affected rows.
documents.s: Comparing different spellings of the same word

documents.t: Three functions, RegexMatch, RegexExtract and RegexReplace, take a pattern: a description of a shape of text rather than the exact text. RegexExtract({Citation}, "\d+") pulls the first run of digits out of a citation; RegexReplace({Note}, "\s+", " ") squeezes every run of spaces down to one. Patterns here are written the way they are almost everywhere else, with these things worth knowing. \w, \d and \s read whatever alphabet your text is written in. \w is a letter, digit or underscore in any script, so \w+ matches λόγος and café whole; \d is a digit in any numbering system, including ٤٢ and ४२; \s is any space, including the no-break space you get from pasted documents. \W, \D and \S are their opposites. \p{Greek} names a script, and so do \p{Hebrew}, \p{Cyrillic}, \p{Han} and \p{Latin}; \p{L} is a letter in any of them. This is the dependable way to say "Greek letters"; a hand-written range like [Α-Ωα-ω] leaves out every accented form. There is no \b. A word edge is refused rather than accepted, because the only kind available recognises A-Z, 0-9 and _ and nothing else: it would step straight over a word in Greek, Hebrew, Cyrillic or accented Latin and report that nothing was found. Write the edge as characters instead. To find or take out the word, (?:^|[^\w])(κόσμος)(?:[^\w]|$) hands back the word itself. To replace it, (^|[^\w])κόσμος([^\w]|$) with $1 and $2 in the new text, because the characters either side are part of what matched and would otherwise be replaced along with the word. Replacing a word takes two passes when it can occur twice in a row. The character between two occurrences belongs to the first match, so a single replace resumes past the second and leaves it alone: RegexReplace("κόσμος κόσμος", "(^|[^\w])κόσμος([^\w]|$)", "$1λόγος$2") gives λόγος κόσμος. Feed that call into a second one with the same pattern and new text and every occurrence is replaced, however long the run. The RegexReplace entry in the function list shows the nested form to copy. $ means the end of the value, not the end of a line. If a value ends in a line break, "ology$" will not match it; write "ology\n?$", or put (?m) at the front to make ^ and $ mean the start and end of each line. The value is searched exactly as it is stored, line breaks and all, so RegexReplace({Note}, "\s+$", "") takes a trailing line break off. The flags you can set are (?i) to ignore case, (?m) for ^ and $ per line, and (?s) to let . match a line break. (?i) reads the dotted and dotless I as one letter. I, i, İ and ı all match each other, so (?i)istanbul finds İstanbul and ıstanbul as well. Every other letter ignores case the way you would expect; this is the one pair where two scripts disagree about which capital belongs to which small letter, and ignoring case here joins all four. To keep them apart, leave (?i) off and write the letters you mean. Write the pattern out in quotes. A pattern is part of the formula, not something read from a column, so RegexExtract({Citation}, {Pattern}) is refused as you type. A pattern taken from a column would be a different pattern in every row, which is both unknowable before you save and slow: on a preview of several rows it is seconds of preparing patterns before any searching starts. A few things a pattern can do elsewhere are unavailable, so that no pattern can ever be slow on a large table: looking ahead or behind ((?=…), (?<=…)) and referring back to a group (\1). A pattern that uses one is refused as you type, in words, with what to write in its place. A pattern may be 500 characters long, searches at most 10,000 characters of a value, and a part in {} may repeat at most 1,000 times. Those limits are not the only thing that can make a pattern too big. A part such as \w or \p{L} stands for every letter in every alphabet, so repeating one builds far more than its two characters suggest. A repeated \w reaches a few hundred rather than the full thousand, and a long run of such parts inside something that itself repeats can be refused as too large to build well before either published limit. The message says so, and the fix is smaller counts in {} or fewer parts. Nothing about \w+ or an unrepeated part is affected.

Open the column's menu and choose Edit formula… — the same editor opens on the formula the column already has. To remove the formula, clear the expression in the editor and save. The column stops being computed and becomes editable again, keeping the kind of value it was producing: a formula that returned a number leaves a number column behind. Nothing is lost by removing it, because a formula's values were never stored — they were worked out each time the column was read. A column that was created as a formula has no data path to fall back on, so clearing it cannot turn it into an ordinary column. The editor says so and asks you to add a new column instead. Columns that already held values before you gave them a formula are not affected.

Cells of a formula column are read-only. To change a value, edit the columns the formula reads. The column header names the kind of value it produces: Formula → text, Formula → number, and so on. The same line appears under Field key in the column's menu.

A formula column is published like any other column, with the value it holds at the time of publishing. Use Check before publishing (the Publish preflight experiment in Labs) to review what will be published before you do. A published formula is only as open as the columns it reads. A formula carries the values of the columns it draws on, so publishing it would publish those values too — even where those columns are not public themselves. So the publish refuses instead. If you publish a table whose public formula reads a workspace-only or private column, the receipt reads Published 0 · skipped … and every affected row is listed under … entries skipped — why. The entry for the formula names three things — the formula column, the visibility of the column it reads, and that column's name — with two buttons: Make field public — raises the read column's visibility, resolving the block where you stand. Remove from label — opens the Appearance settings, where what the published row is built from is declared. It moves you to the setting rather than changing it, so make the edit there and publish again. The wording of these two buttons is written for a row's title rather than for a column. On a formula column they do what is described above, whichever noun they use. Fixing the cause and publishing again is the whole remedy — nothing is partly published in the meantime, because a row that cannot publish cleanly is skipped whole. The same refusal applies when the platform cannot work out what a formula reads: a formula it cannot analyse cannot be checked, so it does not publish until the formula is fixed.

Symptom Likely cause Fix I want a formula on a column I already have. The formula lives on the column, so you do not need a new one. Open the column's menu and choose Add formula…. Add formula… is greyed out. The column is a linked-record column, whose structure comes from the source it was linked from. Add a separate column for the formula. I cleared the formula but it will not save. The column was created as a formula, so it has no data path to become an ordinary column with. Add a new column of the kind you want, and delete this one. The preview is empty. The expression has a problem (underlined, and explained under the box), or no rows are loaded in the table yet. Fix the problem named under the box; or load some rows and reopen the editor. A column I typed as {key} did not become a pill. The caret is still inside the braces, or the braces are inside quotes — text in quotes is text. Move the caret past the closing brace; take the reference out of the quotes. A dash or comma appears in a row where one of the columns is empty. The formula uses & in expression mode, which joins pieces as written. Use sentence mode with the skip-when-empty box checked, or write the formula so the empty case is handled. The Sentence button is greyed out. The formula uses functions or operators the sentence cannot show. Keep editing in expression mode, or simplify the formula to columns and text only. I cannot type in the column. Formula columns are computed, not entered. Edit the columns the formula reads; the result updates. The editor says the formula is too long to read. A formula may be up to 10,000 characters. That is far more than any formula that can run: one is limited to 2,000 steps, and 2,000 steps written out is under 4,000 characters. Shorten the formula, or build the value across several columns and read one from the other. A date formula says the pattern is too long. DateFormat and DateParse read a pattern of up to 200 characters, whether you write it out or read it from a column. Write the layout of a single date, such as DD/MM/YYYY. A pattern longer than this is not a date layout. A number column shows blank and says the number is too large to record. Multiplying or adding two very large values makes a number past what the platform can store. Divide before you multiply, or scale the values down first, so the working numbers stay in range. My pattern with \b in it is refused. The only word edge available recognises A-Z, 0-9 and _, so it would miss words in every other alphabet. Write the edge as characters instead. The form differs by function, so take it from the examples on RegexMatch, RegexExtract and RegexReplace in the function list, where each one is shown working. My pattern is refused as too large to build, and it is well under 500 characters. A part such as \w, \d or \p{L} stands for every letter or digit in every alphabet, so repeating one many times builds far more than its length suggests. Use smaller counts in {}, or fewer repeated parts. A formula is refused for a pattern that is in another column, not in what I wrote. A formula prepares the patterns of every column it reads as well as its own, and there is one allowance for all of them together. Several columns that each hold a large pattern are each fine on their own and too much to prepare at once. The message names the column whose pattern would not fit and the columns that used the allowance before it. Make one of those patterns smaller, or read fewer of those columns from one formula. I put a column reference where the pattern goes and it was refused. A pattern is part of the formula. Read from a column it would differ in every row, so nothing about it could be checked before saving. Write the pattern out in quotes. If different rows need different handling, use one formula column per pattern, or use If on the result rather than on the pattern. A pattern ending in $ matches nothing, on values that look right. The values end in a line break, and $ is the end of the value. Write \n?$ instead of $, or put (?m) at the front of the pattern.
Rename a field label — the label is separate from the column key the formula uses. Publish a record — what publishing does with a column's values.

Sometimes the import's checks flag a column not because anything is broken, but because its values don't match the type or script the platform expected — and that mismatch is intentional. Approximate dates like "c. 350 BCE", a column that mixes scripts, or free-form notes in a field the platform read as numeric are all normal in scholarly data. When the only objections are advisory like this, you can bring the column in as-is: its values are stored as text, exactly as they appear, with nothing converted or dropped.
documents.s: Keep non-standard values as-is during import

documents.t: If your approved choices would bring in zero rows, the practice run stops and says "Nothing will import yet" rather than completing with nothing. For a column that was flagged only for advisory reasons (a type or script mismatch that may be deliberate), one of the offered actions is Import these as-is (keep non-standard values). This is offered only for advisory flags — a structural problem, such as a duplicate identifier or a missing column, must be corrected and is never offered as keep-as-is.

The flagged column is brought in as a plain text field, and each value is kept exactly as written in your source. The platform does not try to reinterpret the values as numbers or dates, and it does not drop the ones that didn't fit — the point is to preserve what you have rather than force it into a shape it wasn't meant for.

Before anything is written, a DRY RUN card previews the decision: The flagged column moves from skipped to kept, with a note that its values are kept as text. A few example values from your source are shown for context. A Won't touch list bounds what stays exactly as it is — every other approved choice is left alone. A seal states that no source rows are written until you run the import. Nothing is saved from this preview; it is a dry run of the one decision.

Keeping a column as-is is reversible. If you undo the decision, it is fully reversed — a later normal approval will not silently bring the column back in as text. And because the values are stored exactly as written, you can revisit the column in your workspace after the import. A flagged column is a suggestion, not a verdict. The import never forces your data to conform — keeping non-standard values is a supported choice, because what counts as "standard" depends on your material.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The "Import these as-is" action isn't offered for my column The column was flagged for a structural reason (a duplicate identifier or a missing column), not an advisory one Structural problems must be corrected — use the offered fix action or adjust the column in your source, then run the practice run again. I kept a column as-is but want it typed as a date or number instead Keep-as-is stores the column as text by design Go back to the review step and change how that column is mapped, rather than using keep-as-is. The practice run still says "Nothing will import yet" after I kept a column Other approved choices still bring in zero rows Resolve the remaining cause the stop names — fix conflicting columns, return to review, or align the other flagged columns.

Fix colliding column names during import — the other kind of import stop, where two columns would become the same field. Understand what changed after a re-import — what the platform carries forward when you bring the same source in again.

Relation fields connect a record in one collection to one or more records in another. For example, a "Text" record might have an "Author" field that points to a "People" record. Once a link is in place, it appears as a small labelled chip in the field. Linking happens in the Details view or directly in the table cell in the Table view — whichever you find easier to work with.

Open the record you want to edit, or click its cell in the table. Find the relation field (it shows existing links as chips, or says there are no linked records yet). Click into the field. A search box appears. Type part of the name of the record you want to connect to. Matching records appear as you type. Click the record you want. It appears as a chip in the field. The link saves immediately — there is no separate save step. In the table cell, the field also lists records from the target collection for you to browse before you type anything. You can add more than one link to the same field by repeating the search and pick steps. A record that is already linked is not offered again.

Open the record or click its cell. Find the chip for the link you want to remove. Click the × on the chip. The link is removed and the change saves straight away. The link change joins the active table's workspace history. Use Undo in Table, Details, or Relations, or press Ctrl/Cmd+Z outside an editor, to reverse the most recent link change. Redo accepts Ctrl/Cmd+Y or Shift+Ctrl/Cmd+Z. Undoing an unlink restores the same recorded connection, including its status, provenance, detail, anchor, and attribution. The restore works only for the same signed-in person and environment, within 90 days, and while the current relation field still permits the link. If any of those checks fail, the workspace refuses the restore rather than creating a different connection.

The Relations view shows every link for a selected record — both the links it makes and the links other records make to it. Select a link there to see its details, or to remove it. Link changes from Relations share the same table history as changes from Table and Details.

A row you have just created can be linked straight away, and can be chosen as a link target, the same as any other row in the table. There is no stage to clear first. Links are still declined in one case: a record that is not approved — one the platform proposed and nobody has accepted yet — cannot be either end of a link. The message says so when it happens.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The search box shows no results when I type. The target collection has no records yet, or your search term does not match any. Add a record to the target collection first, or try a shorter or different search term. The record I want to link to does not appear in the results. It may be a proposed record nobody has accepted yet, or it may not match the field's record type. Check the record's own page, or widen your search. The relation field is not visible in the Details view. The field may be hidden in the current view. Open Manage columns from the Table view toolbar and make sure the field is shown. I cannot add a link to my row from the table. One of the two records has not been approved yet. Check the message near the field — it names the record that is holding the link up. The × to remove a link is not showing. Your role may not include edit access for this collection. Contact your environment administrator. Undoing a removed link is refused. The restore is stale, already used, belongs to another person or environment, would duplicate a current link, or the relation field changed. Refresh the record and review its current links. Add the link again only if the current field permits it.

Build a knowledge environment from scratch without importing — how to create the relation field itself between two collections. Add a new record — creating a row, and deleting one you did not mean to make. Make a field required — controlling which fields must be filled before a record can be published.

When a field is required, a record cannot be published while that field is empty. You can still save the row and come back to it — the requirement is checked at publication, and the refusal names the fields that are still empty. People with field-edit permission can change this setting in the same column editor used for labels and types. If Edit column is not available to you, ask an environment administrator to make the change. This setting applies to fields where people enter a value directly. Formula, lookup, and linked-record fields derive their values elsewhere, so their editor says the requirement does not apply instead of showing the toggle.

Open the collection whose field should become required. Open the field's column header menu and select Edit column. Turn on Require a value. Select Save changes. Create a row and confirm that it cannot be published while the field is empty. From then on every record in that collection needs a value in this field before it can be published — an existing record with the field empty included. Nothing changes in the table itself, and no existing record is altered; the requirement is met or refused at publication, and the refusal names the field.
