When you leave a required field empty, the form surfaces a hint beneath it. The row still saves — autosave keeps your progress — but publishing it is refused until the field has a value, and the refusal names the field.
documents.s: What "required" means at the record level

documents.t: Required is checked when a record is published, so turning it on reaches records that already exist. It changes nothing in the table and alters no stored value — a record you never publish is never refused. Your import does not decide this for you. Requiredness is configuration your team controls. To make the field optional again, return to Edit column, turn off Require a value, and save.

Symptom Likely cause Fix You cannot find Edit column. Your role does not include field-edit permission. Ask an environment administrator to change the field configuration. Edit column does not show the required toggle. The field is a formula, lookup, or linked-record field. Set the requirement on a directly entered source field instead. You opened Edit column but cannot save. Another workspace change may still be in progress, or the field changed after the dialog opened. Wait for the other change to finish. If the field is stale, close the dialog, refresh the workspace, and try again. An existing record shows no required-field hint even though the field is empty. The table does not mark existing records when the setting changes. The check happens at publication — publish it and the refusal names the field. Publishing is still refused after filling in the required field. Another required field may also be empty. The refusal names every field that is still empty — check each one.
Rename a field label — how to change what a field is called, without losing your data. Build from empty — creating tables and fields without importing a spreadsheet.

A public view gives one collection a stable reader-facing identity. Project administrators can manage these identities and review readiness evidence at Public views & readiness (/app/workspace/manage/structure/public-views). Creating a public view does not publish any records. Publishing remains a separate, deliberate action in the collection's Publish view.

Under Create a public view, choose the collection. Enter a short, stable role key, such as people_public. Select Create public view. Open Appearance to set the reader-facing name, web address source, sections, and other presentation choices. Preview and publish from the collection when the records are ready. Role keys become part of public identity and are reserved permanently. Choose a key that describes the view rather than a temporary campaign or date.

Each active public view shows its current readiness status, the number of records sampled, and any blockers or warnings. If the platform offers a resolution action: Read the finding and the action label. Enter a reason that will still make sense to a later administrator. Select the action to record the decision. The page shows all reviewed controls and up to 50 candidate controls for each public view. When a view has more candidates, the card states the displayed and total counts instead of silently hiding the remainder. Select Refresh evidence after the underlying data changes. A prior decision can reopen when the evidence it reviewed is no longer current. An all-view refresh distributes a 2,000-record sample budget across the active public views, so adding views does not multiply the amount of record data loaded without bound. If the number of views leaves no sample for a role, that role is marked Sample budget exhausted instead of showing incomplete totals as if they were complete. The refresh reads the persisted freshness state for existing decisions instead of reopening their original sample windows. Recording a decision and rebuilding a view perform the targeted freshness maintenance for that view. Readiness decisions do not approve or change the project's search engine. Search ratification remains a separate platform decision.

Enter the replacement under New role key. Select Rename and preserve old links. The new key becomes the current identity. Previously advertised links remain connected to the same records, and the old key stays reserved rather than becoming available to another view.

Enter a clear Retirement reason. Confirm Reserve this key permanently and withdraw this view. Select Retire permanently. This withdraws the view immediately and queues published-search cleanup in the background. The removed-view card retains the latest cleanup state after reload, including a failure that needs operator attention; search results can remain briefly while work is pending or running. The key cannot be reused, and old links are not reassigned to unrelated records. This is intentionally different from pausing an active configuration.

Some columns are most useful when one record carries several values at once — a term in each of its languages, a title in each script, a date on each calendar. You set this up once, on the column, and from then on every record can keep a separate value for each. You choose what kind of values the column separates by, and which ones are allowed. The platform never adds or translates a value for you — every value is one you entered.
documents.s: Let a column hold several values

documents.t: Add or edit a column. In the schema window, find the Multiple values section near the bottom. Turn on This column holds more than one value. Two more controls appear. Under A separate value for each, choose what the column separates by: Language, Register, Script, Edition, Calendar, or Custom. In Allowed languages (the label follows your choice — Allowed registers, Allowed scripts, and so on), build the list of values the column accepts. Type a value into Add a language and press Enter. Each entry shows as a chip; the × on a chip removes it. Under Active variant in cards & public reader, choose how summary cards and the public reader select which value to display by default: Show all variants joined: Displays all entered values separated by a dot (·). Match another column: Reads the active key from another field in the same record (for instance, showing the transliteration matching the record's Source Language), with an optional fallback key. Exclude another column: Displays all translations in languages other than the record's source language (for instance, showing non-source translations for a Greek lemma), joined by a dot. Specific target languages: Filters variants to an explicit subset of languages or registers (e.g., only English and Arabic translations). Fixed default key: Always selects a specific language, register, or edition (e.g., EN or GRC). Auto-detect from text: For script columns, automatically detects the writing system from the text of another field using Unicode script blocks. For Match another column, Exclude another column, Specific target languages, or Auto-detect from text, choose what happens when the rule finds no matching value: use a default value you enter, or show all entered values joined by a dot (·). The preview below the controls uses the first loaded record so you can check the pending choice before saving. Under Where it shows, choose the visibility for an existing column: Public: Its values reach readers at the next publish. Workspace: A reader index can promote it to public when an entry-surface configuration is seeded. Private: It is never promoted; change its visibility intentionally before publishing it. Save the column. From now on, each record can hold one value for every allowed entry. To fill them in, right-click the cell in the workspace table and choose Edit values..., or see Add a value in another language.

The platform maintains a built-in standards authority registry conforming to international standards: Languages: ISO 639-1 (2-letter), ISO 639-2/3 (3-letter), and BCP 47 composite tags (e.g., grc, el, ar, la, syc, cop, arc, sa, zh, ja, ru, grc-Latn). Scripts: ISO 15924 4-letter titlecase codes (Grek, Arab, Hebr, Latn, Syrc, Copt, Armn, Geor, Deva, Ethi, Hani, Hira, Kana, Hang). Standard Abbreviations: Informal scholarly abbreviations (such as GK for Ancient Greek, LAT for Latin, ARA for Arabic) automatically resolve to their canonical standard forms. When you type a new entry, the platform normalizes it into its canonical standard form before adding it to the allowed list — so typing "GK" or "ancient greek" gives you a standard GRC chip (while typing "greek" gives you an EL chip for modern Greek), and typing "grc-Latn" yields canonical grc-Latn BCP 47 formatting. If collaborators enter variant spellings, they fold into a single canonical heading.

Higher in the same window, This column's language & script sets one language and script for the whole column at once — useful when every value in the column is in the same language. Multiple values is the opposite case: the column keeps a separate value for each entry you allow. The two sections are independent; set whichever fits the column.
documents.s: The column's own language is separate

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix The Multiple values controls are greyed out. The column has a fixed text role (such as a URL or email column), which holds a single value by design. Multiple values are not available for those columns; use a plain text column instead. A value you typed turned into a different short form. New entries are tidied into a standard short form so records line up. This is expected — after you add it, the value appears as a chip in its standard short form. Two spellings of the same value collapsed into one chip. The platform folds variant spellings of the same value together. This is intended — it keeps every record under the same headings. The column shows in the table but not in the public reader. The column's visibility is Workspace or Private. Open Edit column, select Public, and save. Its values will reach readers at the next publish.
Add a value in another language — filling in the per-record values once the column is set up. Rename a field label — changing what a column is called without losing its data.

The left sidebar lists every table in your knowledge environment. When your environment has many tables, you can pin the ones you use most, gather them into named groups, and collapse or hide everything else — so the tables you need are always at the top, not buried in a long list.
documents.s: Pin and group tables in the sidebar

documents.t: Pinning adds a table to a Favorites group at the top of your sidebar. The table also stays in its regular group. Click the star next to the table's name in the sidebar — or open the table and press Shift+S. The table appears under Favorites at the top of the sidebar. To unpin it, click the star again, or press Shift+S while the table is open. Pinning is yours — it does not change what your colleagues see in their sidebar.

Named groups let you gather related tables under a heading you choose, so the sidebar reflects how you think about your work rather than the order the tables happen to arrive in. Press Ctrl+Shift+G (Cmd+Shift+G on Mac), click Add group at the bottom of the table list, or open the command palette with Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac), type "sidebar", and choose Create sidebar group. The new group appears at the bottom of the table list with its name ready to edit — type a name and press Enter. Drag tables into the group, or drag them between groups to reorganize. Collapse a group by clicking its heading — only that group folds away, and the others stay open. Expand it again the same way.
Recent appears near the top of the sidebar and lists the five tables you opened last. Use it when you remember working in a table but cannot remember where it sits in your groups.

When you want more room for your table, press Ctrl+B (Cmd+B on Mac) to collapse the sidebar to a narrow icon rail. Each table is still reachable as an icon. Press Ctrl+B again to expand the sidebar back to full width.
documents.s: Collapse the sidebar to an icon rail

documents.t: If you want to undo all your pinning and grouping and start from scratch: Open the command palette with Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac). Type "reset sidebar" and select Reset sidebar to default groups. This puts the sidebar back to its original layout. Your records and views are not affected — only the sidebar arrangement resets.
documents.s: Reset the sidebar to its defaults

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Shift+S does nothing. Your cursor is in a text box, or no table is open — the shortcut pins the table you currently have open. Click the table in the sidebar to open it, then press Shift+S — or click the star next to its name instead. I cannot find the group I created. New groups are added at the bottom of the table list, and sidebar changes are saved only when you are signed in. Scroll the sidebar down. If the message near the bottom of the sidebar asks you to sign in, sign in and create the group again. Dragging a table into a group does not work. Tables listed under Favorites or Recent cannot be dragged — dragging works from a table's row in its regular groups. Drag the table's row from its own group. Or click the table once, press Space to pick it up, move it with the arrow keys, and press Space again to drop it. The sidebar looks different on another device. Your pins and groups follow your sign-in, but the sidebar's width and its collapsed or expanded state are remembered by the browser you used. Press Ctrl+B (Cmd+B on Mac) or drag the sidebar's edge to set the size you want on each device.
Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — finding records when the sidebar is not the right tool. Find help on a topic — more ways to get answers while you work.
Before an entry is visible to the public, you can see it exactly as a reader will — the same page, the same layout, the same references — so nothing about the published result is a surprise.

In the workspace Publish view. Pick a record from the row list and the public reader rendering appears beside it. The list shows a sample of the table's records for previewing; publishing always covers the whole table. While editing a record. The record drawer shows the reader view next to the editing form. After you save a change, the preview refreshes to the saved version. During an import. The import wizard includes a draft reader preview step, so you can check how approved rows will read on a public page. Previewing publishes nothing — no page goes live until you publish.

The preview is produced by the same renderer as the public entry page, so what you see is what a reader gets: the entry's sections, the field labels in your project's own wording, the references section, and any media. Published pages include only the fields whose visibility is set to Public; fields kept private or workspace-only do not appear on them. The preview reflects your entry as currently saved, not edits still in progress. A change to field visibility reaches the published page when you next publish — after adjusting visibility, labels, or citation rules, publish and preview again to confirm the result.

Saving and publishing are two separate steps. Everything you write is saved as you go and is immediately part of your team's shared workspace; none of it reaches a public reader until someone publishes it.
documents.s: Publish a record — and why saving is not publishing

documents.t: Where What it means What to do In your workspace The record exists the moment you create it. Colleagues with access to the table can see, edit, link and cite it. No public reader can. Fill it in; every value saves as you leave the field. Published The record has a public page that anyone with the address can read. Publish from the workspace Publish view (publish access required). A record can stay in the workspace for as long as your project needs. Internal review, peer checking, or waiting for a companion record to be ready — all of that happens before you publish.
documents.s: The two places a record lives

documents.t: Publishing happens in the workspace Publish view and covers a whole table at a time — every ready record in the table gets its public page built in one pass: Open your collection's table in the workspace. Select the Publish view from the view tabs. (If it is not listed, add it with + Add view.) Select Publish changes. The platform queues the work and shows you progress as it runs. When the job finishes, the receipt tells you how many records were published and whether any were skipped. Records that are already published are refreshed with your latest saved version, so the same action serves a first publication, a single new record, and a table-wide update after a period of internal review. If Publish changes is unavailable to you, your role may not include publish access. See "Who can publish" below.

The public page shows the record as it was last published. When you change a published record — a text correction, a new media item, a citation update — the change reaches the public page the next time you publish. Edit, review, then select Publish changes again.

Publishing requires publish access, which belongs to your environment's administrators. Researchers whose roles include only edit access can add and edit records but cannot publish them. If you are ready to publish but do not have access, contact the administrator of your environment. They can either publish on your behalf or adjust your access.

Publishing is a deliberate, additional act because research is often collaborative and time-sensitive: a project may want to hold records until a companion table is complete, until a review is signed off, or until a specific date. Keeping the two steps separate means your team controls the moment of public release, independently of when individual records are finished internally.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A record is in the workspace but does not appear in the reader. Saving and publishing are separate steps; the record has not been published yet. Publish from the workspace Publish view, or ask a colleague with publish access to do so. Publish changes is unavailable, or publishing stops with a permission message. Your role does not include publish access. Contact your environment administrator to publish the records or to adjust your access. You changed a published record but the public page still shows the old version. The public page shows the record as it was last published; edits wait for the next publish. Open the Publish view and select Publish changes again. The publish receipt shows some records skipped. A skipped record is not ready for a public page — most often a required field is still empty, or something it reads is not public. The receipt names the reason per record. Fill what it names and publish again.

Your workspace has two search tools. They are intentionally separate — the right one depends on whether you want to jump straight to a record you already know, or browse, filter, and read across many records in one place.
documents.s: Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read

documents.t: Open quick search from the Search database… control at the top of the workspace, or press Ctrl+Shift+F (⌘⇧F on Mac). A search panel opens over whatever you are doing. Type a word. Results appear grouped by collection, each one showing the record's label and the fields where your term matched. Select a result and the platform opens that record directly — whichever collection it lives in. The panel also controls the scope: search everything you have access to, search only the current table, or narrow the search to a single collection. Use quick search when: You want to land on one specific record and open it. You know roughly what you are looking for. You are in the middle of editing and need to jump to a related record fast.
documents.s: Quick search — for jumping to a known record

documents.t: Search & Read is a full search page you can dwell in. Open it from the quick search panel — the Open full Search & Read button at the bottom carries your typed term over — or from the command palette (Ctrl+K / ⌘K), where it appears as Search & Read. The result list is built for reading. For any result you can expand its content inline, open a preview panel beside the list, or click through to the record itself. You can page through the results and sort them by relevance, by recently modified, or by label. Filtering goes further than quick search. Switch to Advanced mode to: Scope the search to one collection, or leave it across everything you can access. Each collection carries a type badge, so you can see at a glance what kind of records it holds. Add conditions on field values. Each condition names a field, a match type (contains, equals, or starts with), and a value; a condition can also be negated. Conditions combine with Match all or with any. The page address encodes your query, filters, page, and sort order — paste the address to a colleague and they see the same results. See Share a search. Use Search & Read when: You want to look at several records, not only one. You want to apply filters — by collection, by a field value, by any combination — and see everything that matches. You want to share the search with a colleague. You want to read records without navigating away from the results.
documents.s: Search & Read — for browsing, comparing, and reading in place

documents.t: Quick search Search & Read What it does Jump to one record Browse and read many records in place Filters Scope only — current table or one collection Collection scope, field-value conditions, Match all / any Shareable address No Yes How to open Search control at the top of the workspace, or Ctrl+Shift+F (⌘⇧F on Mac) Open full Search & Read in the quick search panel, or the command palette (Ctrl+K / ⌘K) Best for "Find this record" "Show me everything that matches…"

If quick search finds results but you want to explore the full set, or you want to narrow it with filters: select Open full Search & Read at the bottom of the quick search panel. Your search term carries over. Switch to Advanced mode to add field-level conditions.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Quick search returns no results even though you know the record exists. Search matches against the fields your environment includes in its search configuration; your term may appear only in a field that is not covered. Try a word from a different field of the record. If it still does not appear, contact your environment administrator to review which fields are searchable. You cannot find Search & Read. It opens from the quick search panel or the command palette — there is no permanent menu entry. Your role may also not include access to workspace search. Open quick search and select Open full Search & Read. If the page reports an error or shows no collections, contact your environment administrator. Results show strings of letters and numbers instead of names. The collection has no display field configured, so results fall back to an internal identifier. Contact your environment administrator and ask them to set a display field for that collection.
Share a search — copy an address that reproduces your exact search and filters. What changed after re-import — using Search & Read to verify changes after an import update.

When you import data, the platform groups your records into collections for you. A collection created this way is browsable straight away, but it does not yet have a permanent home in your sidebar — so you cannot rename, configure, or remove it until you register it. Registering keeps every record exactly as it is and gives you control over the collection's name, icon, and settings.
documents.s: Register a collection the platform built from your data

documents.t: In the sidebar, open the actions menu for the collection (right-click it, or use its actions control). Select Register this table…. Confirm the name and, if you wish, choose a sidebar icon. Create it. The collection is now yours to manage — you can rename it, change its icon, and remove it, and its records are untouched throughout. Registering never changes, moves, or re-imports your records. It only gives the collection a permanent entry in your sidebar.

A collection that holds no records yet cannot be registered. Start an empty collection from scratch with Add table instead — see Create, rename, and delete a collection. If Register this table… is dimmed, your role may not include creating collections; the sidebar shows the reason in place.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Register this table… is dimmed and says the collection has no records. Empty collections cannot be registered. Use Add table to start a new collection from scratch. Register this table… is dimmed for a role reason. Your role does not include creating or registering collections. Ask your environment administrator about your role. I do not see Register this table… at all. The collection may already be registered. A registered collection shows Rename table… and Delete table… instead.

Build a knowledge environment from scratch without importing — starting a brand-new collection and adding fields. Understand what changed after a re-import — how re-imports refresh the records inside your collections.

Removing a collection takes it out of your sidebar without deleting any of the records inside it. The platform calls this unregistering: the collection's name, icon, and settings go away, but the records stay.
documents.s: Remove a collection without deleting its records

documents.t: In the sidebar, open the actions menu for the collection (right-click it, or use its actions control). Select Delete table…. Read the confirmation, then select Delete table. Your records are never deleted by this action. If the collection still holds records, it stays browsable as an automatic collection built from your data — only its custom name and settings are removed.

A collection you have published can still be removed, with one consequence: its curated publish settings — the display column and publish configuration — are reset, so the next time you publish it falls back to defaults. Pages and citations you already published are not affected and stay live exactly as they are.
documents.s: If the collection has published entries

documents.t: Removing a collection is available to editors and administrators. If Delete table… is dimmed, your role does not include it; the sidebar shows the reason in place. Ask your environment administrator if you need access.

Symptom Likely cause Fix I removed a collection but its records are still searchable. Removing only unregisters the collection; records are kept and a populated collection remains browsable. This is expected. To take records off the public site, withdraw or re-publish them — see Publish a record. Delete table… is dimmed. Your role does not include removing collections. Ask your environment administrator about your role. I see Register this table… instead of Delete table…. The collection is not registered yet, so there is nothing to unregister. An automatic collection has nothing to remove; register it first if you want to manage it.
Register a collection the platform built from your data — the opposite action: giving a collection a managed home. Publish a record — how publishing and the public site work.

You can give any field in your collection a name that makes sense in your project's language — regardless of what the original source data called it. Your label is yours. Re-importing your source data never overwrites it.

Open the collection whose field you want to rename. Open the column's header menu with the Column actions button or by right-clicking the column header. Edit the Column label field in the menu and select Rename. If you need to change more than the label, choose Edit column from the same menu. The edit dialog contains the label and the column's other settings. The new label appears immediately in the table columns, in the record detail view, in filters, in the column menu, and in CSV headers when you export selected rows.

When you first import a spreadsheet or data source, each field gets a label from your source — the exact column heading as it appears in the original file. For example, if your spreadsheet has a column called "Author full name", the label starts as "Author full name." From that moment on, the label is yours: What the import controls What you control The underlying field identity (which column this is) The label — what it is called in the workspace The raw data values Whether the field is required The field type detection (text, number, date…) Any notes or help text on the field Re-importing the same source updates the data but does not touch your label. Even if the column heading changed in the source, your label is preserved. The import may tell you a column was renamed in the source (it will show as "new" + "removed" in the delta), but it will never silently overwrite what you typed.
documents.s: What the import sets and what you own

documents.t: Your label has no length limit, but short and clear works best in table column headers. Renaming a label does not change any data. Records are not affected. Two fields in the same collection can share a label — the platform does not enforce uniqueness on labels. Unique field identities are managed internally.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The Label field is not editable. Your role may not have permission to change field configuration. Ask a project administrator. After renaming, the old name still appears in a filter chip. Filter chips may cache the name briefly. Refresh the page if the old name persists after a few seconds. Hard-refresh the browser (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+R). A re-import brought back the original source name. This should not happen: label is researcher-owned and never overwritten. If it did happen, it is a bug — please report it with the import project ID.

What changed after re-import — what the platform carries forward versus what it updates. Make a field required — other field settings you own that survive re-imports. Build from empty — creating fields from scratch where your label is the only name the field ever has.

A view is a named tab above the table that remembers exactly how you left it — which mode it opens in, which columns are visible, their order and widths, any pinned columns, active filters, sort order, row density, and row color rules. Open the view and everything is waiting for you. Views belong to the table and are visible to everyone working in your environment. When you create a view, your collaborators see it too.
documents.s: Save your table arrangement as a view

documents.t: A saved view stores: Which columns are visible, and in what order. Column widths, pinning (left or right), and sort order. Filter conditions and their values. The view kind it opens in: Table, Details, Relations, Publish, or Media on media tables. Row density (compact, cozy, or comfortable). Row color rules. One thing it does not remember: the quick-filter text in the toolbar. That bar is a temporary per-session search — it is not saved with the view, so you always land on the full filtered result rather than yesterday's text.

Open the table you want to organize. Set up filters, columns, and sort the way you want this view to look. Click + Add view in the view tabs above the table. Type a name — something descriptive like "18th-century records with manuscript citations" — and select Create. The new tab appears. From this point on, any change you make while this view is active — adjusting columns, adding a filter, changing the sort — is stored on the view as you go. Changes are saved to whichever view is active — including the table's default view. If you want to experiment without changing what your collaborators see, duplicate the view first and work in the copy.

The default view is what opens when you first visit the table without following a link to another view. It is shared backend state, and includes the view kind: if the default view is a Details view, the table opens in Details for everyone who starts from the default. Open the ⋯ menu on the view tab. Select Set as default. The default is shared: a table has one default view, and it applies to everyone in your environment, not only to you. Your browser may remember a concrete non-default view you opened, but it does not replace the table's default.
documents.s: Set a view as the default

documents.t: Because views are shared, editing one changes it for all your collaborators. Duplicating creates a separate copy you can adjust without touching the original. Like any view, the copy is visible to your collaborators — but your changes no longer affect the view your team relies on. Open the ⋯ menu on the view tab. Select Duplicate. The copy appears as a new tab named after the original, with "copy" added. Rename the copy so it is clear which one is the original. Work in the duplicate. When you are happy with the result, you can either keep both views or delete the duplicate once its changes have been folded back into the original.

Open the ⋯ menu on the view tab. Select Delete view and confirm. The view is removed for everyone in your environment. Talk with your collaborators before deleting a shared view — there is no undo. The table's default view cannot be deleted. To remove it, set another view as the default first.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Columns I arranged look different the next time I open the table. Views are shared — a collaborator may have adjusted the same view since your last visit. Or your changes were made on a different view tab. Check which view tab is active. For an arrangement collaborators will not change, duplicate the view and work in the copy. I changed a filter and now my collaborators see the change too. Views are shared — any change to a view reaches everyone immediately. Use Duplicate to make a copy before experimenting. I deleted a view and a colleague lost their work. Deleting removes the view for everyone. Check whether the view can be rebuilt from the column and filter arrangement. Going forward, agree with your team before deleting a shared view. The Set as default option is grayed out. The view may already be the default, or your role is read-only on this table. Look for a Default badge on the tab. If your role is read-only, ask your environment administrator. The Delete view option is grayed out. It is the table's default view — the default cannot be deleted. Set another view as the default first, then delete this one. Creating or changing a view fails. Your role is read-only on this table — creating and changing views needs editing access. Ask your environment administrator.
Saved views and re-imports — what happens to your views when you re-import your source data. Share a search — copy a link that reproduces a view or search for a colleague.

Saved views belong to the table and are shared with everyone in your environment. A re-import does not reset or overwrite a saved view. What your team named it, which columns it includes, which mode it opens in, how it is sorted and filtered — all of that survives. There is one exception: if a field that a view referenced is removed in the re-import (because it no longer exists in your source), the view adapts gracefully.
documents.s: What happens to saved views after a re-import

documents.t: A saved view stores: Which columns are visible and in what order. Column widths, pinning, and sort order. Filter conditions and their values. The view kind: Table, Details, Relations, Publish, or Media on media tables. Row density setting. The view's name. All of this is preserved across re-imports. Data values may update (a field's value in a record changes to match the new source), but the view's layout and filters are not touched.

If your source data no longer includes a field that your saved view referenced — for example, you removed a column from your spreadsheet before re-importing — the platform handles it gracefully: The view keeps working. The removed column is dropped from the display, but the rest of the view (its other columns, filters, sort) is unaffected. The import delta tells you. The re-import summary names the removed field and lists which saved views were affected. You do not have to discover this by accident. If the field comes back, a later re-import that includes the column again will restore it — and the view will include it again automatically.

If a saved view has a column that was removed: The view opens normally. The removed column is absent from the table. A notice at the top of the view (or in the views menu) indicates that one or more columns in this view are no longer available. Filters that reference the removed field are also suspended — the view does not try to filter on a field that no longer exists. You can update the view (remove the reference to the missing column and save again) or leave it as-is and wait for the field to be restored.

Sharing a saved view copies its URL. The recipient opens that saved view, subject to their own permissions. The URL names the view; the live saved-view record supplies the current layout, filters, and view kind. If a collaborator changes the shared view later, the same link opens the updated arrangement.
documents.s: Sharing a saved view with a colleague

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A column I pinned is gone from my view after a re-import. The field was removed in the re-import. Check the import delta summary for "removed" fields. Restore the field in your source and re-import, or update the saved view. Filters in my saved view stopped returning results after a re-import. The field being filtered on was removed, or the value that was filtered on no longer exists in the updated data. Open the filter chips and verify each one; delete and re-create any that reference removed fields. I see no notice about a degraded view but know a column is missing. The notice appears in the views panel; you may have dismissed it. Open the Saved views menu and look for any view marked with a warning indicator.

What changed after re-import — the full delta: new, changed, carried forward, removed, restored. Rename a field label — how your field configuration is preserved across re-imports. Share a search — copying a URL that reproduces a search or view for a colleague.
When you search for a record you know is there and nothing comes back, one of four things is usually happening. Each has a different fix.
documents.s: Find a record when search returns nothing

documents.t: Search matches against the fields your environment includes in its search configuration. If the word you typed appears only in a field that is outside that set, the record will not surface — even though it exists and you can see it by scrolling the table. What to try: type a word from a different field of the record — the label, a short description, or a name you know it carries. If that finds it, the original field is not in the search configuration. If no combination of words finds the record, contact your environment administrator and ask which fields are included in search.
documents.s: 1. The record's field is not included in search

documents.t: Search is forgiving about some diacritics and strict about others. Ignored (you can leave these off when searching): Breathings in polytonic Greek (smooth and rough) Iota subscripts Circumflex and grave accents Arabic vowel marks (short vowels / harakat) Not ignored (these still count): The acute accent — in Greek and in any Latin-script language The diaeresis (umlaut) This means: typing a word with no accent at all can miss a record whose stored form carries an acute accent. If you are searching a polytonic-Greek collection and your term has an acute accent, include it. If you are not sure of the accent, try a word from another field of the same record instead. Diacritic handling is part of your environment's search configuration, and individual fields can be set to match every mark exactly. If you have confirmed the accent is correct and search still misses the record, contact your environment administrator.
documents.s: 2. Accents and diacritics — what the search ignores and what it does not

documents.t: If your environment stores records with a native-script field, a transliteration, and a translation side by side, a search term in any of those fields can find the record — but only if those fields are searchable and have values. If you search with a transliterated form and nothing comes back: Open the record directly from the table. Check whether the transliteration field has a value. If the field is empty, add the transliteration — or ask your environment administrator whether the transliteration field is included in search. If the transliteration field has a value but search still misses the record, the field may not be in the search configuration. Contact your environment administrator.
documents.s: 3. The transliteration field is empty or not searchable

documents.t: When a collection has no display field configured, search results for that collection cannot show a record name. Each result shows a placeholder instead — "(unlabeled …)", or the collection's name with a "no display field" notice. The records are there and your search did find them; the problem is that you cannot recognize them. If you see this: Look for the type badge beside each result — it names the collection the result belongs to. Contact your environment administrator and ask them to set a display field for that collection. Once set, search results for that collection will show the record's name as the label.
documents.s: 4. Results show a placeholder instead of the record's name

documents.t: Symptom Most likely cause First thing to try No results at all for a term you know is in the record The field is not in the search configuration Try a word from a different field of the record Found nothing with a transliterated term but the record is visible in the table Transliteration field is empty, or not searchable Open the record; check whether the transliteration field has a value Term in native script finds the record but transliterated term does not Transliteration field not in search configuration Contact your environment administrator Search matches most Greek terms but misses a specific word Stored form carries an acute accent your search omitted Retype the term with its acute accent Results appear but show "(unlabeled …)" or a "no display field" notice instead of names No display field set for that collection Contact your environment administrator to set a display field Search panel reports "Search isn't enabled for this workspace yet" Search has not been switched on for this environment Use the table's filter box for the current table; contact your environment administrator for the workspace-wide fix

Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — which search tool to use and how to escalate from a quick search to a full filtered search. Share a search — copy a link that reproduces your exact search for a colleague.
A cell that links to records in another table shows each related record as its own labelled chip, laid out on a single line so every row in the table keeps the same height.
documents.s: See related records in a cell

documents.t: The cell shows as many whole chips as the column's width allows, then a +N button, where N is the number of chips not shown. Nothing is dropped or hidden silently — the count is exact. Choosing +N opens a panel listing every related record for that cell, not only the ones that did not fit. The panel opens over the table, so it is never cut off by the edge of the grid, and closing it returns you to where you were.
documents.s: When there are more related records than fit

documents.t: With a linked-record cell selected: Enter moves into the cell's controls and lands on the first one. Enter or Space on the +N button opens the panel. Escape closes the panel and returns to the +N button; Escape again returns to the cell, and the table's arrow-key navigation carries on from there.
Widening a linked-record column shows more chips before the +N button appears; the row height does not change either way.

After a review session of approvals, set-asides, and reopened reviews, the Ready page (step 6) answers one question in one place: what did I finally decide, per table and column? Open the fold named "What you decided, table by table" near the bottom of the page.
documents.s: See what you decided in an import, table by table

documents.t: Each of your source tables gets its own section, with a count line naming how many of its items you have decided and how many are still open — "19 decided · 53 still open". Once everything in a table is decided the second half drops away and the line is just the count, "74 decided". Under it, every decided item appears with its kind (column match, table meaning, connection, shape change, display label) and its outcome in plain words. Most outcomes that are not a plain Approved name which decision or check produced them, so a set-aside is usually more than a set-aside: Approved — the decision is applied and the item imports as decided. Set aside — your chosen outcome. followed by what that means for this kind of item, in the same words the review card showed you. Set aside. with the same consequence sentence, where the set-aside carries no recorded reason. Superseded — this value imports through an approved shape change instead. Nothing is missing: a shape change you approved carries this item, so it does not import separately as well. It appears on a column, and also on a Table meaning row when the approved shape change covers the whole table. Auto-dropped as source bookkeeping — working columns are not imported as fields. A column the platform excluded on its own; these are not your decisions. The receipt and import report name each affected column. Those are the outcomes seen most often, not the whole list. A column can also be rejected by the import's own checks rather than by you, and decisions made elsewhere in the review — on connections, or under strict transcription — write their own lines here in the same shape. Read the line rather than assuming a set-aside: where it names what produced the outcome, that is the answer.

An undecided column keeps the final import from starting; it is not silently skipped. The import refuses to begin and names what still needs your decision, so a column you have not reviewed is never imported one way or the other. That is different from a column listed as Auto-dropped as source bookkeeping. The platform records those fields as source bookkeeping. The import report and receipt list every affected column by name.

If a column you expected is missing after the import, type its name into "Find a table or column". The list narrows to that column and shows the recorded decision that explains it. If the column's decision was reopened and not yet re-decided, the search answers "Still open — not decided yet." instead of leaving you guessing. Read the outcome before concluding the value was lost. Superseded means a shape change you approved carries it, which is why there is no separate field — for a column, and for a whole table where the shape change covered one. Nothing is dropped. The summary appears on the Ready page before you start the import, so it is first a statement of what your decisions will do; the same summary stays there afterwards as the receipt for what they did.

A 3D model in the workspace has a Mesh→term tab beside its viewer — the first tab in the rail. Each binding links one mesh — one named part of the 3D model — to a term in your vocabulary, so you can see which part of the model carries which term, and review or change that match. Open a 3D model from the Media gallery and select the Mesh→term tab. (For opening media, see Work with media in the workspace.)
documents.s: See which mesh maps to which term

documents.t: The tab opens with three counts — how many parts are mapped, how many are edited, and how many are auto — above a list with one row per binding. Each row shows the model part's raw name as written in the model file, the term it is matched to, and a state chip. The state chip tells you where a binding came from and how settled it is: auto — the platform extracted this binding from the part's name. It is awaiting your review. edited — you (or a colleague) changed an existing binding on this part. linked — you bound a previously-unmapped part to a term by hand. unmapped — the part has no term matched to it yet. The header count of mapped parts covers every part that has a term matched to it — that is, the edited and linked parts together with the auto parts still awaiting review.

The list and the model are linked, so you can move between them either way: Select a row, and that part of the model is highlighted in the viewer and the row stays selected. Click a part in the model, and its row is selected in the list. This lets you check, part by part, that each mesh is matched to the term you expect.

Select a row — or click a part in the model — to open its card above the list. The card shows the part's raw name, the term it is bound to, and where the binding came from, followed by the actions for that part: Approve — confirm an auto binding as correct. Approving settles the binding so a later re-run leaves it alone. (Approve appears only while the part is still auto.) Reassign (or Assign term, when the part has no term yet) — open a picker to bind the part to a different term. Search your vocabulary by typing and choose from the results, each shown by its display label. Searching a word in one language can surface a term that carries that word in another language. You can also paste a term record's id directly to bind it. This writes the link between the part and the term. Strip — remove the term from the part, leaving it unmapped.

Symptom Likely cause Fix There is no Mesh→term tab. The tab appears only on 3D models. Open a media record whose type is a 3D model. The tab shows no bindings. No parts of this model are matched to a term. Open a 3D model whose parts are already matched to terms, or bind a part with Assign term. Clicking a row does not highlight anything in the model. The row's part may not be present in the model that is loaded. Compare the part name in the row with the model, and try a row whose part you can see. There is no Approve button on a part. Approve appears only for auto parts awaiting review; a part you already changed shows as edited or linked. Use Reassign to change the term, or Strip to clear it. The term picker finds nothing when you type. Search may not be activated for your environment, or there is no match for your query. Paste the term record's id into the picker instead — that path works regardless of search.
Work with media in the workspace — open a 3D model from the Media gallery. Tune the 3D camera view — set how a 3D model is framed when it opens.

You do not get a password from anyone. Nobody — not an administrator, not the person who invited you — chooses, sees, or sends your password. You choose it yourself, once, from the link in your invitation.
documents.s: Set up your account from an invitation

documents.t: An email titled "You have been invited to join …" naming the environment you were invited to. It contains a link, and one line you should read before you click it: Your username is (the address the invitation arrived at). That address is your username. Keep the email, or write the address down — the page where you choose your password does not ask for a username, so this is the only place you are told it. The link is unique to you and expires in 14 days.

Open the link. You land on a page headed Set your password, with the note "Your password is known only to you." Type your password in Password, and again in Confirm password. Choose Continue. If the password is rejected, the page comes back with the reason on the field — for example "This password is too short. It must contain at least 8 characters." or "This password is too common." Nothing has been created yet; try another password on the same page. When it is accepted you go straight to your workspace. You are signed in already — there is no separate sign-in step the first time.

From then on, sign in at /login/ on the same address, with the username from your invitation and the password you chose. See Sign in and manage your password. Each environment has its own sign-in. If you already work in another environment on this platform, that password does not carry over — set a new one here.

The link works once. After you have used it, opening it again shows: This invitation is no longer valid — contact your KE admin. What you see Why What to do "This invitation is no longer valid" right after you set your password. The link is spent — your account already exists. Sign in at /login/ with your username and the password you just chose. "This invitation is no longer valid" before you ever used it. The invitation expired (14 days), or an administrator withdrew it. Ask the person who invited you to send a new one. A new invitation replaces the old link. You have the email but the link goes to a page that will not load. You may be on a different address from the one in the invitation. Use the link exactly as it appears in the email — each environment has its own address. The page deliberately gives the same answer in every one of those cases, so it never reveals whether an invitation exists for a particular address. Treat the link like a password: anyone who opens it can set the password for your account. Do not forward the invitation email.
documents.s: When the link does not work

documents.t: When you run a search in the Search & Read section, the link in your browser carries the whole search — the words you searched, the filters, the sort, and the page you are on. Copy that link and send it; whoever opens it lands on the same search, with results filtered by their own access.
documents.s: Share a search so a colleague sees the same results

documents.t: Open Search & Read in the workspace and run your search — type your words and press Enter, or build filters in Advanced and select Search. Select Copy link, directly below the search box. The button confirms with Copied. Paste the link into an email, chat message, or document and send it. You can also copy the link from your browser's address bar — once the search has run, the address bar carries the same link. When your colleague opens the link: They see the same search words, the same filter conditions, the same sort, and the same page. They must be signed in to the same knowledge environment. They see only results their own access allows. If a collection is outside their access, its results are absent — sharing a link does not extend anyone's access.

A saved view (a named combination of filters, columns, and sort) has its own link: Open the view in your workspace. Select Copy current view link in the toolbar, or Copy view link in the saved view's menu. Paste and send. Saved views are shared across your knowledge environment, so a colleague with access to that workspace opens the same view — the same columns, filters, and sort. The link points to the view itself: if someone later edits the view, the link opens the edited version.

The search words (if any). Every active filter condition — the field, the match type, the value, and the Match all / any choice. The collection the search is scoped to, if you narrowed it. The sort order and the page you are on. It does not carry the records themselves. The results are live: whoever opens the link runs a fresh search against the knowledge environment as it is at that moment. A link shared today may return different results next month if records were added, edited, or removed. The link reproduces your search faithfully, not a snapshot of your data.
The same link works as a personal bookmark. Add it to your browser bookmarks, and you can return to the same search at any time without rebuilding the filters.

Symptom Likely cause Fix My colleague opens the link but sees fewer results than I did. Their access excludes some collections or records. This is expected — results respect each person's access. If they need access to a collection, contact your environment administrator. The link I copied is missing my newest filter changes. Search words and filters enter the link when the search runs, not while you type. Run the search — press Enter, or select Search in Advanced — and then copy. The link opens but the filters look different from what I sent. The link may have been truncated by a messaging app. Send it as a raw link rather than wrapped display text. A saved-view link shows a different layout than when I sent it. Someone edited the saved view since — views are shared, and the link opens the view as it is now. To keep a layout fixed, duplicate the view under a new name and share the copy's link.
Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — which search tool gives you a shareable link. Saved views and re-imports — what a saved view remembers and how it survives a re-import.

Your project has one sign-in page: /login/ on your project's address. It carries your project's colors and asks only for your username and password. After signing in you land in your workspace — the same place the sidebar's tables live. Any page that needs an account sends you to this sign-in page first and returns you to where you were headed afterwards. You do not need any special account type to work in the workspace. Signing in as a researcher never opens the operations area at /admin/ — that area asks for a project-admin role, and the two are separate on purpose.
documents.s: Sign in and manage your password

documents.t: Open the account menu in the workspace and choose Change password. The change takes effect immediately, and the confirmation returns you to your workspace.

The sign-in page has a Forgot your password? link below the form. It opens Reset password, which asks for your email address and sends a reset link to it. Use the address you sign in with — each environment has its own sign-in, so ask for the reset on the same address you were trying to sign in to. If no link arrives, or you no longer have access to that address, ask your project administrator; they can send you a new one.
documents.s: If you have forgotten your password

documents.t: The account menu's Sign out ends your session on this browser.

The sign-in page shows one message for every refusal: "Please enter a correct username and password." It deliberately does not say which part was wrong, or whether an account exists. The common causes, in order: A typo — both fields are case-sensitive. Your membership in this project was suspended or ended. Suspension takes effect immediately, including for sessions that were already open. Your project administrator can restore access; nothing about your account is deleted when access is suspended. You are on the wrong project address — an account belongs to one project. If none of these fit, contact your project administrator.
You do not need a password to start — you need an invitation. See Set up your account from an invitation, which also tells you where to find your username.
documents.s: If you have never signed in here

documents.t: A 3D model can open at a chosen angle and zoom, so everyone who views it starts from the same framing. This framing is a live presentation default — the view a reader lands on. It stays navigable, and it is not frozen into the record's citation; what a citation points to is fixed separately when the record is published. Setting the framing is an environment-admin task: the Viewer tab appears beside a 3D model only for environment admins. Open a 3D model from the Media gallery and select the Viewer tab. (For opening media, see Work with media in the workspace.)

In the viewer, drag to orbit and scroll to zoom until the model is framed the way you want it to open. Select Set as presentation default to read that framing into the tab's controls. Fine-tune if you want: the controls hold the camera target offset and the framing — radius, minimum and maximum distance, and field of view. To start over, select Reset to auto-fit to return to the framing the platform fits to the model automatically. Select Save viewer settings to store the framing on this record. From then on, the model opens with the framing you saved. The Viewer tab is available only to environment admins. If you do not see it on a 3D model, ask your environment administrator to set the framing.

Symptom Likely cause Fix There is no Viewer tab on the 3D model. The Viewer tab is shown only to environment admins. Ask your environment administrator to set the framing, or sign in with an account that has admin access. The model still opens at a different angle after I captured it. The captured framing is not stored until it is saved. After Set as presentation default, select Save viewer settings. I want to undo my framing. The model has an auto-fit framing to fall back to. Select Reset to auto-fit, then Save viewer settings to store it.
Work with media in the workspace — open a 3D model from the Media gallery. See which mesh maps to which term — the Mesh→term tab on a 3D model.
When a reader opens one of your published entries, the References section lists the evidence behind it — one row for each place the entry is attested.
documents.s: Read the references section on a published entry

documents.t: One row per occurrence. If a term is attested in twelve passages, the references section has twelve rows. Each row is independent. Your project's citation style. When you have declared citation rules for a collection, each row is rendered in your own scholarly format — author, work, locator (page, chapter, line), and any abbreviations exactly as your field uses them. The format is yours to control, not a fixed platform style. Paired editions. When an occurrence cites both a modern edition and an earlier one, the row bridges them — the primary citation followed by the paired locator, so a reader sees the equivalence at a glance. A quote, when the occurrence carries one, sits with its row.

Each row's text is chosen in order: your declared citation style first; if a collection has no citation rules, a plainer structural composition of the edition's locator fields; and the occurrence's own label as a last resort. A row always renders something — a missing edition never blanks the row. If the citations read roughly, the citation style for that collection has not been refined yet. Citation styles are tuned per collection (a scholar reviews a proposed style; an administrator applies it); the rows update on the next publish.
Use the draft preview to see the references section exactly as a reader will, before the entry is public — see Preview an entry before publishing.

When you import your source data a second time (a re-import), the platform shows you a delta — only what is new, changed, or different from your last import. It does not ask you to re-review decisions you already made.
documents.s: Understand what changed after a re-import

documents.t: At the top of the import review the platform shows a summary line like: Since your last import: 3 new · 1 changed · 147 carried forward Term What it means New A field or table that did not exist in the previous import. You need to review and approve it. Changed Something that existed before but is now different — a field type changed, a collection was restructured, or the source renamed something. You need to confirm the change. Carried forward A decision you made in a previous import that the platform has automatically recognized and kept. You do not need to act on these.

"Carried forward" means the platform compared your source to the last import and found no difference on a given field or collection — the same data, the same structure, the same decisions you already made. The platform keeps those decisions automatically and does not show them as review cards. You can expand the "Carried forward (K)" disclosure to see the full list if you want to verify what was carried.

A field or collection shows as removed when it existed in your previous import but is no longer present in the new source data. The field is not permanently deleted. Any notes, labels, or settings you made on it are preserved. If you bring the field back in a later import, it is restored — you get your previous settings back. The delta view names every removed field so you know exactly what changed. If a saved view referenced a removed field, the view keeps working but drops that column from its display (see Saved views and re-imports). The platform uses the words "removed" and "restored" — plain language that describes what happened. You will not see the word "inactive" or other system terms. Removed is removed; you can bring it back.
A field shows as restored when it was removed in a previous import and has come back in this one. Your previous settings — any label you gave it, any notes, your required flag — all return with it.

Your configuration edits — labels you renamed, field settings you changed, required flags you turned on — are yours and are not reset by a re-import. Record values depend on the refresh behaviour your administrator or platform operator chose: Edit-preserving refresh matches incoming source rows to existing records, refreshes source-managed values, and keeps researcher-owned values. Full refresh reloads rows from scratch. It is destructive to researcher edits and should be used only for a deliberate start-over. If you are unsure which behaviour a planned re-import will use, ask your environment administrator before it runs. See Rename a field label for the full list of what survives a re-import.

Before the import writes anything, the wizard runs a practice run (sometimes called a dry run). It tells you how many records will be created, updated, or skipped — including how many are blocked by unresolved review items. With carried-forward decisions accounted for, a re-import of mostly unchanged data should show nearly all records ready, not blocked.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The import still shows a full review list as if it were the first time. The platform did not recognize this as a re-import of the same source, or an earlier import was never completed. Check whether the previous import was completed through Stage 6 of the wizard. Only completed imports produce a carried-forward baseline. A field I labelled is showing its original source name in the delta. The delta view shows source-side names for changed items; your label is preserved and will appear in the workspace once you confirm the change. Confirm or carry forward the item in the review. A field I know exists in my source is showing as "removed." The source column may have been renamed in the source system. A renamed column appears as a new column plus a removed column in the delta. Review the "new" items — one of them is likely the renamed version. Approve it, and your label will be carried to the new identity.
Rename a field label — which of your settings survive a re-import. Saved views and re-imports — what happens to your saved views when fields change.

When you run a search in Search & Read, a note may appear above your results saying that a number of collections are hidden. It reads: 2 collections are hidden — they require a review capability you don't hold. This is not an error, and your search worked. It tells you that your environment holds more collections than your current access lets you search, and how many were held back.
documents.s: See why some collections are hidden in Search & Read

documents.t: Your search ran across every collection your access allows, and returned those results. Collections you are not permitted to search are withheld before the results reach you — the platform counts them and shows that count in the note, rather than letting them vanish silently. The number is the difference between all the collections in your environment and the ones your search could reach.

A review capability is one of the access permissions your environment administrator assigns. It governs whether you can search and review a particular kind of record across the whole environment. Some collections are open to anyone on the team; others are restricted to people who hold the review capability for that kind of record. The hidden-collections note appears when at least one collection in your environment falls into the restricted group and you do not hold its capability.

The note never blocks the collections you do have access to. Your results already include every collection your access allows; only the restricted ones are missing. You can keep searching, filtering, and reading those results normally — both in Search & Read and in the quick search panel. You can also still open any individual record you reach by a direct link, even one in a collection you cannot search across. If instead the page tells you that you have no search access at all, your role does not include a review capability on any collection. That is a different message — contact your environment administrator.

Access is assigned by your environment administrator, not changed from the search page. Note which kind of records you are missing — the type of collection you expected to find. Contact your environment administrator and ask for the review capability that covers it. Once they grant it, rerun your search. The hidden-collections note drops by the collections you can now reach, and their records appear in your results.
documents.s: How to get access to a hidden collection

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix The note says collections are hidden, but you expected to see them. Your access does not include the review capability for those collections. Contact your environment administrator and ask for the capability that covers the kind of records you need. The note's number does not drop after you were granted access. The new access has not yet taken effect in your session. Reload the page and rerun your search. If it still shows, confirm with your environment administrator that the capability was applied. You see "You don't have search access here" instead of the hidden note. Your role includes no review capability on any collection. This is a separate, full-page message. Contact your environment administrator — you can still open individual records by direct link.

Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — the two search tools and how to escalate from one to the other. Find a record when search returns nothing — other reasons a record you expected may not appear. Your environment administrator assigns the access that controls which collections you can search, from the permissions panel in the administrator documentation.

A collection that holds media records — images, 3D models, and other files — has a Media button alongside Table, Details, Relations, and Publish above the table. Other collections do not show it. Select Media to browse those records as a gallery instead of as table rows.
documents.s: Work with media in the workspace

documents.t: The gallery opens with a count of how many media records the collection holds and one card per record. Each card shows a media-type badge (for example, 3D MODEL), the record's title, and its index status. When a record has a thumbnail, the card shows that image; otherwise it shows a generic media icon. Use the Grid / List toggle to switch between a card grid and a compact list. Select a card to open that record on its own.

Selecting a card opens a detail pane with a Back button to return to the gallery, the record's title, and — for a 3D model — the model itself rendered right there, with the model filling the pane and a rail of tabs beside it. Drag to orbit the model and scroll to zoom. Above the model, a Heatmap chip tints its parts by binding state and a Rotate chip auto-rotates it. Beside the viewer is a row of tabs: Mesh→term — for a 3D model, the parts of the model and the terms they are matched to; see See which mesh maps to which term. Files — the files attached to the record, with the count in the tab label. Viewer — for environment admins, the camera framing the model opens at; see Tune the 3D camera view. Info — the record's descriptive text. Version — the record's version and edition history, with the count in the tab label. For environment admins this tab also holds two actions — pinning a citeable edition and re-extracting — described below. Which tabs appear depends on the record's type and your role: the Mesh→term tab is shown for 3D models, and the Viewer tab only for environment admins.

A media record with no file yet opens to Attach a file first — the viewer, configuration, and mesh mapping stay locked until the record has a primary file. Editors and environment admins see an Attach media button there; other roles see the message without the button. Selecting Attach media opens the Attach media sheet, with two ways to add the file: Reference a URL — point the record at media that already lives at a web address. Enter the Media URL (an absolute https:// address) and select Attach reference. The file stays at its own address; the record just points to it. Upload a file — choose a file from your computer to store with the record. The record's name, author, and description are not set here — those are fields edited in the Details view of the collection, and the sheet says so; it only attaches the file. Once the file is attached, the sheet closes and the record fills in: a 3D model opens in the viewer, and other media show their files and versions. If you attach media that is already on the record, the sheet stays open and reports that the media is already attached and nothing new was created. If an attach is refused — for example, the file is protected — the sheet shows the reason. Referencing a URL is offered only on a record that has no version yet. Once a record already has a version, the Reference a URL tab explains that URL references are unavailable for a record that already has one; add another file by uploading it instead — an upload is recorded as a new version.
documents.s: Attach a file to a media record (editors and admins)

documents.t: For environment admins, the Version tab adds two actions above the version list. Other roles see the version list read-only.
documents.s: Pin a citeable edition or re-extract (environment admins)

documents.t: Everyday citation already works without pinning — a citation resolves to the current version on its own. Pin a revision as an edition only when you need a fixed, unchanging cut to cite: enter an edition label, then select Pin as citeable edition and confirm. The record's header then shows an EDITION state with a frozen marker, and the version is a permanent, citeable reference — a citation pointing at it stays stable, because the cited content is captured when the record is published, not read live. A frozen edition can no longer be re-extracted (the automatic re-reading of the model file). You can still amend individual Mesh→term bindings by hand: a binding change is a claim about the model — new information, a new term, a reviewer's amendment — not a change to the model file, so it needs no re-extraction and no new version, and it does not disturb a citation already made against the edition.

Re-extract re-reads the model file and refreshes the mesh→term bindings — which part of the model is matched to which term. It never creates a new version or file, and any bindings you set by hand are preserved. Dry run reports what would change without writing anything. Apply writes the refreshed bindings, then the Mesh→term tab and the coverage heatmap update to match. Re-extraction is refused on a frozen edition; to re-extract, re-import the file to start a new working revision.

The Info tab shows the record's title, author, and description, but it does not edit them. These are fields on the media record, edited in the Details view of the collection — not in the viewer. When a record has no descriptive fields yet, the Info tab says so.
documents.s: Where titles and descriptions are edited

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix There is no Media button above my table. The Media button appears only on collections that hold media records. Open a collection whose records are images, 3D models, or other files. The gallery says there is no media yet. The collection holds no media records. Add a media record, or open a collection that already has some. A card shows a generic media icon instead of a thumbnail. That record has no thumbnail set — thumbnails are optional and the icon is the normal fallback. This is expected; open the card to work with the record. An environment admin can add a thumbnail reference for the record if one is wanted. A record says Attach a file first and nothing renders. The record has no primary file yet, so the viewer stays locked. Editors and admins: select Attach media and either reference a URL or upload a file. Other roles: ask an editor or admin to attach one. I see Attach a file first but no Attach media button. Attaching a file is limited to editors and environment admins. Ask an editor or admin, or sign in with an editor or admin role. The Attach media sheet won't let me reference a URL. Referencing a URL is offered only on a record with no version yet; this record already has one. Use Upload a file instead — it adds the file as a new version. The sheet says the media is already attached and nothing was created. The URL or file you gave matches what the record already points to. Nothing to do — the record is unchanged. Give a different URL or file if you meant to change it. I changed the title in the Info tab but nothing happened. The Info tab shows the title and description; it does not edit them. Open the Details view of the collection and edit the record's fields there. The Version tab won't let me re-extract or pin an edition. Those two actions are shown only to environment admins; other roles see the version list read-only. Ask an environment admin, or sign in with an admin role. Re-extraction says it is refused on a frozen edition. The current version is a pinned, frozen edition, which never changes. Re-import the file to start a new working revision, then re-extract that.
See which mesh maps to which term — the Mesh→term tab on a 3D model. Tune the 3D camera view — set how a 3D model is framed when it opens.

Labs collects workspace features that are still being tried out. It sits at the bottom right of the table, showing how many are on — Labs 0/8 when none of the eight is on, which is how it starts. Your choices are saved in this browser only. They do not follow you to another computer, and they are never sent to your project — nobody signing in elsewhere sees them. The panel says so: "Experiments, this browser only." They are stored against the browser, not against you. If two people share one browser profile on a shared machine, they share these switches: what one turns on, the other opens the workspace and finds on. Signing out does not reset them.
documents.s: Turn workspace experiments on and off

documents.t: Click Labs at the bottom right of the table. Switch anything on or off. Most take effect immediately; Reading row is marked after reload and needs the page reloaded first. When you change it, a Reload page button appears in the panel. All on and All off switch every experiment at once.
