Switch What it changes Status line keyboard hints Adds keyboard shortcuts to the line under the table. Column quick menu Puts one-tap sort, filter, pin and hide at the top of each column's menu. Work queue Adds a way to work through the rows a filter matched, one at a time. Reading row Expands a long text into a full-width reading card inside the table. Needs a reload. Publish drift Marks records that changed since they were last published. Publish preflight Adds a check you can run on a table before publishing it. One search door Replaces the two search controls at the top with a single one. Refined Appearance and Publish The redesigned Appearance and Publish views. Infinite scroll used to be on this list and is not any more. Loading more rows as you scroll is simply how the table works now, so there is no switch for it and no Previous/Next buttons under the table. The line at the foot tells you how many rows are loaded out of how many exist, and when a filter matches rows that are not loaded yet, a Search all button beside that line takes the search to Search & Read.

The redesigned workspace used to be a switch here, and is not any more: it is simply how the workspace looks, and there is no way to go back to the previous look. A few things sit in different places than they once did, which is worth knowing if someone describes a control you cannot find: Clicking a column's name sorts by it. To select the column's cells instead, use Select visible column cells in the column's menu. The table's name and row counts are in the row of view tabs, not in a separate bar above them. Export appears in a strip above the table once you have selected rows, rather than sitting in the toolbar all the time. See Export selected rows. The line under the table now only speaks when there is something to say, instead of always showing status.
documents.s: The redesigned workspace is the normal one now

documents.t: Switch it off. Nothing in Labs changes your records — these switches affect how the workspace is shown to you, not what it holds. If a switch is marked after reload, reload the page after changing it.
Export selected rows — where export lives. Save a view — saving column choices and filters, which is shared with your project, unlike these switches.

Open a formatted-text field from a table cell or the record panel. The editor opens as a popup; select Maximize when you want the fullscreen writing view. Both views edit the same document and offer the same formatting controls. Use the toolbar for common actions. Type / in the document to search the insert and block command list, or select text to open the compact selection toolbar. Bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, inline code, highlight, and links keep the selected words in place. A link accepts http, https, or mailto addresses; choose Apply to add it, or Cancel to leave the text unchanged. Hover or focus an existing link to copy its address, change the address without changing its visible text, or remove the link formatting.

The block menu calls an ordinary paragraph Text. Choose Text whenever you want regular prose. At the end of a heading, press Enter to start a new Text block. At the end of a callout, press Enter to continue in a Text block after the callout. Press Shift+Enter for a soft line break inside the current block.

Type @ where the mention should appear. Type at least part of the record's name. Choose a result from the workspace picker. The saved document keeps the record's stable identity, not a copied label or URL. When you reopen it, the editor resolves the current label you are allowed to see. A published page shows the mention only when that record is available through the publication rules. Hover or focus a saved mention to see the record's current name and type. When that record is published, the card also offers Open to visit its reader page.

Put the caret where the reference should appear. Select Footnote in the toolbar. Open the numbered reference and write the note. The reference and its note belong to the same document. If you remove the last reference, the editor removes its unused note with it. Undo and Redo restore or remove the pair together.

Put the caret where the equation belongs. Choose Inline equation for math in the current line. For a separate display equation, type / and choose Block equation. Enter the TeX expression and confirm it. To revise it, select the rendered equation, change the TeX expression, then choose Apply. Choose Cancel or press Escape to leave it unchanged. Equation insertion and editing use the editor's Undo and Redo controls. Both forms remain editable after Save and reopen. Viewing shows the rendered equation without edit controls.

Choose Bulleted list or Numbered list for the current Text block. You can also type a marker followed by Space at the start of a Text block: - for bullets; 1. for decimal numbering; A. or a. for alphabetic numbering; and I. or i. for Roman numerals. Press Enter to continue with another item. Numbered items continue counting. Press Tab to nest an item below the preceding item. Press Shift+Tab, or choose Lift list item, to move it up one level. Press Enter again on an empty item to leave the list and continue in Text. Tab in ordinary Text moves focus to the next control. Inside a code block, Tab adds code indentation instead.

Choose Table to insert a table, then place the caret in a cell to enable Table actions. From that menu you can add rows or columns, change selected cells between header and body cells, and merge or split cells. Press Tab or Shift+Tab to move between cells. Table and list changes use the editor's Undo and Redo controls and survive Save and reopen in both popup and fullscreen editing.

Put the caret where the figure belongs and choose Figure. Choose an existing workspace image. Write alternative text that conveys the image's purpose or content. A caption is optional. Choose Insert figure. To change its alternative text or caption later, open the figure and choose Apply. The picker lists image media already available in the workspace; it does not upload a new file. If no image is available, close the picker. An editor or environment admin can open the collection's Media view and use Attach media on a media record, or the environment can import the media. See Work with media in the workspace. Figure insertion and edits participate in the editor's Undo and Redo history. A saved figure can show No image file attached when its media record has no usable image, or Preview unavailable when a preview cannot be resolved. Publication also requires that image media to be admitted with a frozen primary artifact; otherwise the public reader omits the figure.

Hover a top-level block to reveal its left gutter. Drag the grip to move the block within this editor, or open the block's three-dot menu and choose Move block up or Move block down. Content moves between separate editors with copy and paste, not drag and drop.

Select Save to persist the document. Cancel discards the current editor session. Viewing makes the document read-only: formatting, block controls, Save, and the save shortcut are unavailable until you return to Editing. The Editing/Viewing switch is available in both popup and fullscreen. When an insertion or an existing link, equation, or figure edit is open, the document's Save button and the popup/fullscreen switch stay unavailable. Choose Apply or Cancel first; switching to Viewing cancels the open contextual edit without applying it. In fullscreen, the Outline follows the document's headings. The width control switches between a reader-width writing column and a wide drafting column. Print preview in the overflow menu hides editing chrome for a clean review before printing. Within the editor, Ctrl+Z or Cmd+Z undoes a document change. Redo uses Ctrl+Y, Cmd+Y, or Shift+Cmd+Z. These are the editor's unsaved document history, not the workspace operation history outside the editor. Ctrl+S or Cmd+S saves the rich text document. If focus is in a link, equation, or figure form, the shortcut applies a valid form first and then saves; an invalid form stays open and the document is not saved. If focus has returned to the document while a form is still open, the save and presentation shortcuts wait for you to Apply or Cancel.

Symptom Likely cause Fix @ shows no useful result. The query is too short, the record is outside your permissions, or workspace search is unavailable. Type more of the record name. If search is unavailable, save without the mention and try again later. Footnote is unavailable. The caret is not at one collapsed text position, or it is inside a link, code block, or footnote definition. Place the caret in ordinary prose, then select Footnote again. Inline equation is unavailable. The caret is inside a link or code block, where the saved format permits text only. Move the caret to ordinary prose, then select Inline equation again. Figure says that no image media is available. The workspace has no selectable image media yet. If you are an editor or environment admin, open Media and use Attach media on a media record; otherwise ask one, or import an image. Then reopen the picker. A saved figure says No image file attached or Preview unavailable. The selected media has no usable image file, or its workspace preview could not be resolved. Open the record in Media, attach or repair its image if your role permits, and retry. A non-image media record cannot be used as a figure. A link will not apply. Its address is empty or uses a scheme outside the rich-text contract. Enter an http, https, or mailto address. A formatting action is disabled. The current block or saved rich-text format cannot represent that structure safely. Read the control's explanation and move the caret to a supported Text block. The editor does not save. The document failed validation or the save request failed. Keep the editor open, correct the reported issue, and retry. Your current editor session remains available.

This page walks through one full research loop without a mouse: reach a table, open a record, fill its fields, preview it, and move on. It collects the keyboard paths that other pages describe in passing and puts them in the order you would actually use them, with the exact keys for each step. Read it when you work by keyboard or screen reader and want a single route through a session, or when you want to know which parts of that route are solid today and which still need a hand from the mouse. Accessibility is the companion reference: it lists every keyboard control and the display settings. This page sequences those controls into a working session and does not repeat the full list. Some steps in this loop are not yet fully reachable by keyboard alone. Those gaps are listed up front, in Where the keyboard path is still incomplete, so you know before you start where you may need to reach for the mouse.

Two things shape what the keyboard does: Mac or Windows / Linux. Shortcuts that use Command (⌘) on a Mac use Control (Ctrl) elsewhere. Where a shortcut appears below, both forms are shown. Where focus is. Shortcuts that act on the whole workspace are ignored while you are typing in a text box, a text area, or a dropdown — so a stray keystroke never fires a command while you write. Step out of the field first (Tab or Escape), then use the shortcut.

When the workspace opens, focus starts in the page. Tab moves forward through the controls — the top bar, then the sidebar of tables, then the table toolbar, then the table itself. Shift+Tab moves back. A clear focus ring marks where you are; the ring is drawn when you navigate by keyboard and stays hidden for mouse clicks. Two faster ways to reach a table: Command palette — press ⌘K (Ctrl+K). A search box opens; type part of a table's name, use the Down and Up arrows to move through the matches, and press Enter to open the one you want. Escape closes the palette without choosing. Sidebar — Tab into the list of tables and press Enter on a table to open it. To give yourself more room, ⌘B (Ctrl+B) hides and shows the sidebar.

Reading before writing saves duplicate records. Two search routes, both keyboard-first: Quick search — press ⌘⇧F (Ctrl+Shift+F). The search panel opens with focus in its box. Type a term; results appear grouped by collection. Use the Down and Up arrows to move through results and Enter to open the highlighted one. Escape closes the panel. Search & Read — for browsing many records, open the command palette (⌘K / Ctrl+K) and choose Search & Read, or escalate to it from the bottom of the quick search panel. Your typed term carries over. Within that page, the typeahead and the results list respond to the Down and Up arrows and Enter. How search treats accents and scripts — and why a search matched or missed — is covered in Searching and reading.
documents.s: 2. Find a record before you create one

documents.t: Open the new-row drawer from the command palette: ⌘K (Ctrl+K), then choose New row. (The drawer is also reachable by tabbing to the toolbar's new-row button and pressing Enter.) The drawer opens as a dialog and focus moves into it. A status line at the top tells you where the record stands — "Saving…", "Saved", "Not saved", and so on — so you always know what a screen reader would otherwise have to infer.

Inside the drawer: Tab moves from one field to the next; Shift+Tab moves back. Type into a text field, then Tab out — your entry is held as you go. For a dropdown field, the Down and Up arrows move through the options and Enter selects one. For a field that links to another record, type to search, Tab to a result, and press Enter to link it. Required fields are marked, and a record cannot be published while a required field is empty. A line near the top names the next save step, so the path forward is always stated rather than implied. A field whose editor has not shipped yet shows a short hint in place of an editor. The hint stays in the Tab order and is announced as disabled, so you can tell the field exists and is intentionally not editable — it is not silently skipped. If the field is formatted text​ Press Enter on the field to open the shared editor. Its popup and fullscreen views use the same document and keyboard commands: / opens the searchable command list; @ opens record mentions. Enter continues headings, callouts, and lists according to their structure; Shift+Enter keeps a soft break inside the current block. Tab and Shift+Tab nest and lift list items, or move between table cells when the caret is in a table. Ctrl+Z or Cmd+Z and the redo shortcuts affect the unsaved editor document, not another workspace panel's history. Escape dismisses the active command or insertion form first. In fullscreen, the next Escape restores the popup; it does not silently save or discard the document. Ctrl+S or Cmd+S saves. A valid open link, equation, or figure form is applied first; an invalid form keeps focus and blocks the document save. While an insertion or existing link, equation, or figure edit is open, the footer Save and popup/fullscreen switch are unavailable. Apply or cancel it first. Viewing cancels the open contextual edit without applying it. Use the named block-controls menu for Move block up and Move block down. Choose Viewing to review without mutation controls, then Editing to resume. The complete guide is Write formatted text.

Press Escape to leave. If you have unsaved work, a confirmation appears first so a stray Escape does not discard it; confirm or cancel it from the keyboard. Everything you filled in is already saved, and the row stays in your table. To remove a row you did not mean to make, Tab to Delete row and press Enter. A confirmation follows, and the deletion cannot be undone.

Open a record's full view to read it and preview the public page: From the table, Tab to the row and press ⌘Enter (Ctrl+Enter) to open its details. The details view shows every field beside a reader preview rendered with the same engine as the public reader, so you can check how the record will read before anything is published. The path to a published page — who can publish, and the per-field visibility controls — is covered in Public reader.

Several view controls are keyboard-driven: Row density — Tab to the density control and use the Left and Right (or Up and Down) arrows to move between Compact, Cozy, and Comfortable. Your choice is saved with the view. Saved views — the view tabs respond to the Left and Right arrows; Enter or Space opens the focused view. Sidebar groups — ⌘⇧G (Ctrl+Shift+G) creates a group, ⌘⇧E (Ctrl+Shift+E) expands all groups, and ⌘⇧C (Ctrl+Shift+C) collapses them. ⇧S (Shift+S) pins or unpins the current table. Sidebar width — Tab to the resize handle between the sidebar and the table; the Left and Right arrows narrow and widen it, Home and End jump to the minimum and maximum, and Space collapses the sidebar.
documents.s: 7. Adjust the view as you work

documents.t: The platform is being made fully keyboard- and screen-reader-driven, and some of the loop above still has gaps. The honest state today: Some command shortcuts work only from the command palette, not as direct keystrokes. The palette lists hints next to several actions — filtering the current table, creating a new row, undoing and redoing a view change. Those actions are reliable when you select them inside the palette (⌘K / Ctrl+K). The single-key forms shown as hints (such as a lone slash, or a lone letter) are not all wired as global keystrokes yet, so reach these actions through the palette rather than relying on the bare key. Undo and redo by keyboard are scoped to editing views. In Table, Details, and Relations, ⌘Z / Ctrl+Z undoes the next labelled workspace operation. Redo accepts ⌘Y / Ctrl+Y or ⇧⌘Z / Shift+Ctrl+Z. The shortcuts are ignored while focus is in an editor or a dialog is open. Appearance, Publish, and Media do not intercept them, so an edit from another panel cannot be replayed accidentally there. Saved-view presentation remains available through the distinct command-palette actions Undo view change and Redo view change. The display-and-reading settings panel is not in the workspace. Font size, line height, font family, and background presets live on your environment's reading and browsing pages, opened with the accessibility button there or with Alt+A. Inside the workspace, use the row density control and your browser's own zoom. See Accessibility. If a control you expect to reach cannot be reached from the keyboard, that is a bug rather than a setting. Tell your environment administrator so it reaches the people who can fix it.
documents.s: Where the keyboard path is still incomplete

documents.t: The workspace exposes named roles and labels to screen readers: the new-row drawer is announced as a dialog with a title, fields that are not yet editable are announced as disabled, the focus ring follows keyboard navigation, and the inline tip panel keeps focus stable when its content updates. Spoken confirmations for every action — for example, a spoken note when an inline edit saves — are still expanding, so a screen reader may not yet announce every state change out loud. The on-screen state pill in the new-row drawer names the current state in text, which a screen reader can read on demand.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A workspace shortcut does nothing. Focus is inside a text box, a text area, or a dropdown, where workspace shortcuts are intentionally ignored. Press Escape or Tab to leave the field, then use the shortcut. A single-key shortcut shown in the command palette does not fire on its own. Not every palette hint is wired as a global keystroke yet. Open the command palette with ⌘K (Ctrl+K) and select the action there. The focus ring disappears. The ring is keyboard-only; a recent mouse click suppressed it. Press Tab once more to bring it back. Escape closes the new-row drawer but a dialog appears first. You had unsaved work, so a discard confirmation is shown before anything is lost. Confirm to discard, or cancel to keep editing. Either choice is reachable by keyboard. Delete row will not respond. The row has been published, came from an import, or is linked to other records. Read the message — it names which case applies. You cannot find the display-and-reading settings in the workspace. That panel lives on the reading and browsing pages, not the workspace. Open a reading page and use its accessibility button or Alt+A. In the workspace, use row density and browser zoom.

Accessibility — the full list of keyboard controls, display settings, and the broader accessibility status. Workspace walkthrough — the controls this session moves through. Searching and reading — how search behaves, including across scripts and accents. Adding and editing rows — creating, editing, and deleting records. Public reader — the path to a published page.

At some point your work leaves the knowledge environment: citations go into a paper, a set of records becomes a bibliography or an appendix, a slice of your corpus turns into a teaching handout, a colleague needs to see exactly what you found. This page sequences that workflow — narrow your records to a working set, download a file or share a link, and copy citations in your project's citation style. Read it when a deadline is close and your material needs to be somewhere else.

Selected-row export from the table toolbar — select one or more rows, then open Export in the table toolbar to choose a download. Maturity: Active. Export selected rows as a file — downloads the selected records as a CSV file for spreadsheets, with raw JSON available as an advanced option for tools and scripts. Maturity: Active. Limit: CSV carries only the columns visible in the current view. Citations in your project's citation style — a published entry, and its draft preview, render citations ready to copy into a bibliography or footnote. Maturity: Active. Limit: how complete a citation reads depends on the fields filled in on the record. Shareable search and view links — a search's address carries the whole search, and a saved view has its own link. Maturity: Active. Limit: whoever opens a link sees only what their own access allows. Stable web addresses for published records — every published record keeps a stable address you can put in a syllabus, a slide, or a footnote. Maturity: Active. Limit: stability is per record; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort.

Three common shapes, three routes: Citations for a paper or a bibliography — you need formatted citation text. Work record by record in the reading view; see Copy citations in your project's style below. A table of records for a handout, appendix, or analysis — you need rows and columns. Filter down to a working set, then export the selection. Something a colleague or a reader opens themselves — you need a link, not a copy; see Share by link instead of by copy. Most projects mix all three: a saved view holds the working set, citations come from the reading view, and the finished records are shared by their public addresses.

Use search and filters to get exactly the records you need in front of you: quick search to find records anywhere you can access, Search & Read for browsing with conditions on field values, and the table's filter builder for column conditions. Searching and reading covers each tool. When the working set is right, save it as a view so you can return to it for the life of the project — see Save your table arrangement as a view. A view remembers your filters, visible columns, order, and sort. Views are shared with everyone working in your environment, so name it descriptively; to refine it without changing what collaborators see, duplicate it first and work in the copy.
documents.s: Narrow to a working set — and save it as a view

documents.t: Focus a row and press Space to select it. Use Ctrl/Cmd+Space to add or remove another focused row, or Shift with the arrow keys to extend the selection. In the table toolbar, select Export. Select Download CSV to save a spreadsheet-friendly file, or Download raw JSON when a technical workflow needs the raw row payload. Two details are worth knowing before a deadline: CSV follows your view. The CSV download carries the columns visible in the current view, in their current order — arrange the view first and the file comes out right. JSON is for raw payloads. Use JSON only when a tool or script needs the stored row payload rather than the visible spreadsheet view. A selection lives in the view where you made it: switching to another view or table clears it. The full selection mechanics, including keyboard paths, are in Export selected rows.

Citations come from the reading view, not from the table: Open the published entry — or its draft preview, which shows the entry exactly as a reader will see it, references included, before anything goes live. Find the entry's References area. Rows of evidence carry their citations, and when your project has set up a citation for the record itself, it appears there as its own row. A media item with full citation details carries its own citation too. Select the citation text and copy it into your bibliography, footnote, or document. Each citation is rendered in the citation style your project has adopted — set per collection by your environment administrator and defined in Citation Style Language, the same format reference managers such as Zotero use. Before the citation goes to a venue, check that the active style suits it: compare a rendered citation against the venue's style guide, and if it does not match, collect sample citations and send them to your environment administrator with a request. Citations you can trust explains what the platform guarantees about a citation once it is in print — including why a media item you cite should be a frozen Edition first — and walks through the style-change request. The short copying steps live in Copy a citation for a record or media item.
documents.s: Copy citations in your project's style

documents.t: A link keeps the material live — whoever opens it sees the records as they are at that moment, filtered by their own access. A search, for a colleague in your environment — run the search in Search & Read, then select Copy link below the search box. The link carries your search words, every filter condition, the sort, and the page. See Share a search. A saved view, for your team — a saved view has its own link, from Copy current view link in the toolbar or Copy view link in the view's menu. The link points to the view itself: if the view is edited later, the link opens the edited version. A single record, for a colleague — right-click the row and select Copy row link. The link points to that record in the workspace; the colleague must be signed in to the same knowledge environment. A single record, for anyone — once the record is published, its public page has a stable web address that stays valid even if your project later reorganizes its pages. That address is the one for a syllabus, a slide, or a footnote — readers outside the project need no account. Public reader covers the path from workspace to published page.
documents.s: Share by link instead of by copy

documents.t: From a table, selected rows can be downloaded as CSV or raw JSON. There is no Excel workbook export. No workspace control assembles a single bibliography file from many records at once. Citation text is copied per entry from each record's reading view. For reference managers, a published entry's citation is also available in a machine-readable form — see Citations you can trust.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The exported file is missing hidden columns. CSV export follows the columns visible in the current table view. Show the columns you need, then download the CSV again. Your selection disappeared after switching views. Selections are per view and per session; switching views or tables clears them. Re-select your rows in the view you are working in. A citation shows placeholders or looks incomplete. The fields the citation draws on are missing or only partly filled in on that record or media item. Open the record and complete those fields; the draft preview shows the corrected citation before publishing. See Copy a citation for a record or media item. A colleague opens your search link and sees fewer results than you did. Results respect each person's access; collections outside their access are absent. This is expected. If they need access to a collection, contact your environment administrator.

Export selected rows — full selection mechanics and the toolbar in detail. Copy a citation for a record or media item — the short task-shaped citation steps. Citations you can trust — what stays fixed once you cite, Editions, and citation styles. Share a search — what a search link carries and how access applies. Save your table arrangement as a view — keeping a working set for the life of a project. Searching and reading — the search tools that build your working set. Public reader — stable addresses and what readers outside your project see.

This page explains what the platform records about you while you work, what it deliberately does not record, and the safety rules that occasionally hold content back. The bias throughout is to keep your project's content inside your project and to minimize what flows anywhere else. Read it when you want to know what the platform sees, when a feature seems to be holding a number back from you, or when a new chat panel appears and you want to understand what it is doing.

Your data stays inside your environment (Active) — your project's records, search queries, and edits live inside your environment's boundary. Researchers in other environments cannot see across it, and the boundary is enforced at the data layer, not by convention. Content-free activity records (Active) — when the platform records that an action happened (a search ran, an import finished, an assistant answered), it stores numbers and short labels — duration, row count, success flag — never the content itself. One-way redaction of sensitive text (Active) — where the platform must keep a record involving text you wrote, the text is replaced with a one-way fingerprint keyed to your environment; the original cannot be reconstructed from it. Text that looks like an email address, a phone number, or an identification number is dropped entirely — not even a fingerprint is kept. Small-sample protection on cross-environment statistics (Active) — a statistic computed across environments is published only when enough separate environments contributed to it that no single environment or small team could be identified from it. Below that threshold, the number is withheld. Tamper-evident activity records (Active) — the platform's activity records cannot be silently edited or deleted; the platform-level log links each entry cryptographically to the one before it, so any alteration becomes visible during routine verification by the platform operator. Chat conversations are not kept (Active) — a chat assistant keeps your conversation only for your current working session, or reads it once to extract the structured details you confirmed and then discards the raw text. No chat surface keeps conversations longer (see below). Data-protection assessment tracking (Active) — when deeper activity recording is switched on for an environment, the platform records that the environment's Data Protection Impact Assessment must be refreshed, and tracks that refresh to completion. Per-environment usage statistics (Active) — whether your environment records usage statistics about features such as in-form tips is a per-environment setting, not a platform-wide constant. Your environment administrator can tell you whether it is on.

If you have only a minute: Your project's data and the queries you type stay inside your project. They are not visible to researchers in other environments, and the platform operator sees only redacted aggregate numbers, never your content. Statistics computed across environments are published only when enough separate environments contributed that no single environment or small team of researchers could be identified from them. Chat panels keep your conversation only for your current session, or read it once to pull out the details you confirmed. No chat surface keeps conversations longer today. The record of who edited what stays inside your environment. It exists to give your editors and your administrator a clear history, not to surveil you.

Your researcher account. Sign-in identity, display name, role, permissions. Stays inside your project. Your edits. Rows you create, fields you change, rows you delete. Attributable to you within your project, so editors and reviewers can see who did what. Chat conversations, within limits. A chat assistant follows the retention behaviors described below; the default keeps nothing beyond your session.
documents.s: What is recorded about your activity

documents.t: Your search queries do not leave your environment. Searches are matched inside your project. The platform-wide measurement layer never receives the words you typed — by design, it can only hold counts, timings, and one-way fingerprints. No content leaves your workspace. Platform-level activity records hold numbers and short labels, not the content of searches, imports, or conversations. Small-sample statistics are withheld. A cross-environment number with too few contributing environments is not published at all. Sensitive strings are redacted before storage. One-way fingerprint, keyed to your environment; text matching high-risk patterns (email addresses, phone numbers, identification numbers) is dropped entirely. The platform's activity records are tamper-evident. A background guarantee; no action needed from you. Much of this measurement is also switched off unless the platform operator deliberately turns it on — the platform's default posture is not to collect.
documents.s: What is deliberately not recorded or transmitted

documents.t: Two situations: Publication readiness. A row missing a required field, or one in a review queue, is not eligible for the public reader. The publish view shows what a record still needs before it can go live — see Preview an entry before publishing. Small-sample statistics. Where a precise cross-environment number could identify the behavior of a small group, the platform withholds it. This rule applies to platform-published numbers; it never hides your own data from you inside your workspace.
documents.s: When the workspace holds content back

documents.t: A chat assistant on the platform follows one of these retention behaviors: Session only (the default). The conversation exists for your current working session and disappears when the session ends. Nothing goes into durable storage. Extract only. The conversation is read once by an extractor that pulls out structured details you confirmed (for example, a summary of what you said you were importing); the raw conversation is then discarded immediately. Nothing longer. No chat surface keeps your conversation beyond the two behaviors above. Longer retention is not available today. The chat panel itself tells you what it records: it carries a visible notice stating that questions may be included in usage records and that no workflow changes happen through chat. The assistant can answer questions and explain what it sees, but it cannot change your data at all — it cannot approve, apply, publish, or delete anything. Actions happen only through the regular controls you click. One practical note: records belong to the project, not to you personally. Removing a researcher account does not remove the project's published records. If you are leaving a project and want to know exactly what account removal covers, ask your environment administrator.

Which chat surfaces are enabled, and what each one retains. Whether usage statistics — such as tip acceptance numbers — are being collected in your environment (see Efficiency tips for environment administrators). Whether a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) has been completed for the project. A DPIA names who can see what, for how long, under what conditions. Your administrator can find out its status from the platform operator and tell you what it covers. A worked example: suppose you notice a chat panel today that was not there last week. The right question to your administrator is two-part — "What does this panel retain?" and "Is the DPIA updated to cover it?" If both have clean answers, the surface is operating inside the platform's normal posture. If either is open, the platform's default — nothing kept beyond the session — is what applies until the answers land.
documents.s: What to ask your environment administrator

documents.t: Your project's database records, search index, and change history all live in their own slice of the platform. Operations that touch your project read from your slice. Operations that produce platform-wide numbers read from a separate measurement layer that holds counts and timings, never content. When you type into search, the query is matched inside your slice; the platform-wide layer can learn at most that a search happened, how long it took, and how many results it returned. Multiply by every action on every surface and you get the platform operator's view: a picture of motion without content. Researchers in another environment see less — they cannot see across the boundary at all.
documents.s: What the environment boundary means in practice

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Where to escalate A statistic you expected shows no value, or is missing entirely. Small-sample protection withheld it: too few environments contributed for the number to be published safely. This is intentional. The number appears when more environments contribute. Your environment administrator; Tips and guidance. A new chat panel appeared and you do not know what it retains. The panel was enabled for your environment. Read the panel's own notice about what it records; if it is unclear, ask your administrator what the panel retains and whether the DPIA covers it. Your environment administrator. You cannot find what an administrator can see about your activity. The change history is the answer for "who changed what"; it stays inside your environment and is visible to editors and administrators. Ask your administrator to walk you through the change history for your account's actions. Your environment administrator. You want to verify that the platform's activity records have not been tampered with. The platform-level activity log is tamper-evident by design — verification is run by the platform operator, not the researcher. Ask your environment administrator to request a verification report from the platform operator. Your environment administrator.

Tips and guidance — the tip surface whose usage statistics are covered by small-sample protection. Efficiency tips for environment administrators — the tip surface from the administrator's side, including the per-environment setting for measuring tip activity. Activity measurement for environment administrators — what an administrator can configure about activity recording. Voice and vocabulary — how the wording you see is configured (not a privacy setting, but a related per-environment setting). Standards posture — the compliance framework that backs these privacy guarantees.

When somebody outside your project reads one of your records on the web, they are using the public reader — the reading-facing face of your knowledge environment, with stable URLs, scholarly citations, clean typography, and no editing controls. This page explains what the reader is, how a record reaches it, and how to preview a record before it is public. Read it when you want to know what a reader sees, when you are about to publish, or when you want to share a finished record with someone outside the project. The reader is configurable, so what your readers see depends on your project. The sections below describe how it works; your environment may use all of it or a subset.

Published reading layer — the reader reads from a separate, read-only snapshot of your data, rebuilt when your project chooses Publish changes. Readers never touch your working data. Maturity: Active. Stable, citable URLs — every published record has a stable web address that keeps citations valid even if the page is later reorganized. Maturity: Active. Limit: stability is per record; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort. Side table of contents — a navigation list down the side of the page that highlights where the reader is as they scroll. Maturity: Active. Limit: how fine-grained it is depends on how the record is sectioned. True-to-life preview — an in-workspace preview that renders a record exactly as a reader would see it, with no mockup substitution. Maturity: Active. Limit: the preview lives in your workspace; it is not a public address. Citations for media items — a media item can carry a structured citation in your project's citation style (defined in Citation Style Language, the same format reference managers use), rendered with the record's citations and ready to copy into a bibliography. Maturity: Active. Source-traced citations — citations on the record itself, built by tracing where each piece came from (source manuscript, prior publication, contributor) and rendering that chain. Maturity: Active. Limit: fidelity depends on the source links your project declared at import. References — one row per piece of evidence — every occurrence of the record in the sources gets its own row. Where the project has catalogued a modern and an early edition of the same source, the row bridges them into one scholarly reference (modern citation, then the early edition's locator and abbreviated editor); where the project has full citation styling configured, the row carries a formatted citation; and an occurrence with no published edition at all — a catalogued manuscript or fragment — still appears, shown by its own label. Quotes catalogued on an occurrence display beneath its row, and source citations the rows did not absorb appear once each, deduplicated, below the evidence list. Maturity: Active. Limit: how rich each row reads depends on what the project catalogued — locators, editions, quotes, and abbreviations are project data. Browsable indexes, switchable per project — beside search, readers can browse the whole corpus from an alphabetized index, and a project can publish more than one (for a multilingual corpus, for example by transliteration or by original script), switchable from the reader. Index rows are rich (transliteration, original-script form, and a short gloss together); a character rail jumps to a letter; large letter groups page smoothly. Maturity: Active. Limit: which indexes exist, the default, and what each row shows are configured by your project. Media on the record page — a published record lists its attached media — 2D images, audio, video, 3D models, and molecular visualizations — each item with its label and, where catalogued, a link to its source plus its identifier and version. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the media your project attached and published appears. Dark mode and reading-first layout — selectable text, a scholarly typeface, and a darker color scheme readers can switch to, remembered in their browser. Maturity: Active. Structured formatted text — published formatted-text fields keep semantic callouts, marks and links, lists, tables, code, record mentions, document footnotes, TeX equations, and admitted image figures instead of flattening them into plain text. Maturity: Active. Limit: a mention links only when its target has a public reader route, and a figure appears only when its image media has an admitted frozen primary artifact.

The reader is a separate layer from your workspace. The workspace is where you and your colleagues add, edit, review, and approve. The reader is where the world reads what your project has decided to publish. The platform builds the reader from a published snapshot — a separate, read-only copy of your data, refreshed when your project publishes something new. A reader visiting a page does not reach into your workspace; they read from the snapshot. Your editing speed is not affected by outside traffic, and a reader cannot accidentally see a draft.
documents.s: What the reader is, in one paragraph

documents.t: Readers do not have to search to explore. The reader offers a browsable index — an alphabetized list of every published entry — and a project can publish more than one. A multilingual environment commonly offers the same entries by transliteration and by original script; the reader switches between them from the controls at the top of the list. Each index row can show the transliterated form, the original-script form, and a short gloss together, so an entry is recognizable without opening it, and a character rail jumps straight to a letter. Which indexes exist and which is the default are set by your project when it publishes. See Browse entries by index.

In your workspace. You created it. It is in the table and in workspace search from that moment, and colleagues with access to the table can see, edit, link and cite it. No public reader can. Published. You — or a colleague with publish access — open the table's Publish view and select Publish changes. Publishing covers the whole table and applies its current field visibility. The platform builds the published snapshots, and the public pages go live. Publication is its own step, separate from saving. Saving an edit to a published record does not replace the public snapshot automatically. Return to the Publish view and choose Publish changes when the current workspace version is ready for readers.
documents.s: How a record reaches the reader

documents.t: Use the preview to see exactly what a reader will see, before committing: Open the record in your workspace — anything you are working on, published or not. Open its reader preview. The preview renders the record exactly as a reader would see it — same layout, same fonts, same citations, same media rendering. During an import, the wizard's final step offers the same preview for newly imported records. Read it. Spot anything awkward. Close the preview. The record has not moved; you have only looked at it. The preview is a real rendering, not a mockup. If a citation will look rough in the reader, it looks rough in the preview too — that is the point. See Preview an entry before publishing. The preview reflects the current draft. The published page updates on the next publish, not instantly.

A reader visiting a published page can: Read and select text — lines are individually selectable for quoting and note-taking. Link to a published record through its stable web address; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort. Copy citations formatted in your project's citation style. Follow media to its source — each attached media item appears with its label and, where catalogued, a link to its source. Switch to dark mode (remembered in their browser). A reader cannot edit, comment on, or add anything. The reader is read-only by design.
documents.s: What a reader can do, and what they cannot

documents.t: Draft preview Published Who can see it You and colleagues with workspace access Anyone with the public URL URL Not a public URL — preview-only Stable, citable URL Visible on the public web No Yes Reflects edits On re-opening the preview after a change Only after Publish changes rebuilds the snapshot In short: the preview lets you see the reader's view without committing to it. The published view is what the world actually sees.
documents.s: Differences between draft preview and published

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A record is in the workspace but does not appear in the reader. Saving and publishing are separate steps; the record has not been published yet. Publish the record, or ask a colleague with publish access to publish it. If you are unsure who publishes in your environment, contact your environment administrator. The preview shows different formatting than the table view. The reader renders from the published layout, not from the editing surface. Some fields render differently. This is intended — the preview is the truthful render. Adjust the record to match the reader layout you want. A citation for a media item shows placeholder or incomplete values. The media record's citation fields are missing or incomplete. Open the media record and complete its citation metadata. If the citation style itself looks wrong, contact your environment administrator. A media item attached in the workspace does not appear on the published page. The table has not been republished since the item was attached, or the item is not part of what your project publishes. Open the Publish view and choose Publish changes. If it is still missing, confirm that the media and its field are public. You changed a published record but the change has not surfaced in the reader. Workspace Save and publication are separate operations. Open the Publish view and choose Publish changes to rebuild the table's public snapshots. A reader reports a broken section link they previously cited. The record was restructured; the record's own URL stays stable, but links to individual sections are best-effort. Share the record's stable URL and advise the citer of the new section location. If section links break often, contact your environment administrator. The preview is blank or shows a loading state that never finishes. The preview has not yet been built for this record, or it is failing to load. Refresh and retry. If the problem persists, contact your environment administrator.

Searching and reading — how search and the reader work together inside the workspace. Adding and editing rows — creating, editing and deleting records in the workspace. Preview an entry before publishing — the short task-shaped version of the preview workflow. Browse entries by index — switching indexes and jumping by letter. Read the references section on a published entry — what each evidence row means. Citation integrity (for environment admins) — the companion surface controlling the citation styling the reader presents. Entry surface readiness (for environment admins) — the companion surface controlling what gets published to the reader.

The Publish view is the workspace tab where your table meets its public audience. Here you decide, field by field, which parts of your records appear on published pages, check the result in a reader preview, and then publish the whole table in one pass. Read this when you are preparing a collection for first publication, when you want to keep a working field off the public page, or when edits to published records are waiting to go live. Publishing here is a whole-table action: one run builds or refreshes the public page of every ready record in the table. There is no separate publish button per record — a single new record reaches the public the same way, through a table run that refreshes what is already published and picks up what is new. How a record becomes ready in the first place is covered in Publish a record — and why saving is not publishing.

Per-field visibility — every field in the table is set to Public, Workspace, or Private. The choice saves to the field's configuration the moment you make it and applies to every record in the table. Active. Public fields only on published pages — when a record is published, only its Public fields are included. Fields set to Workspace or Private are left out of the public page. Active. Reader preview with field highlighting — a sample of the table's records, each rendered exactly as a public reader would see it, with two-way highlighting between the field list and the preview. Active. Whole-table publishing with a progress report — one action publishes every ready record, shows progress as it runs, and ends with a receipt: how many records were published, skipped, or failed. Active. Whole-table visibility selector — the Whole table control at the top of the panel is a planning aid only; the control itself says the choice is not saved. Deferred. Preview visitor state — shown in the view but not yet available. Deferred.

Open your collection's table in the workspace and select Publish from the view tabs (alongside Table, Details, and Relations). You can also get here from a column's header menu — Open Publish view... — or by right-clicking a row and choosing Review publish field. The view has two halves: a panel on the left with the field visibility list, the preview row picker, and the publish action; and a reader preview on the right showing the selected record as a public reader would see it.

The Fields list shows every field in the table, in display order, with its label, its internal name, its field type, and a tag for the part of the published page where it appears (or not on reader if it does not render there). Each field has a three-way choice: Public — the field appears on the record's published page. Workspace — the field stays inside your project's workspace. Published pages never include it. Private — the field is marked for its owner only. Like Workspace fields, it never appears on a published page. Fields are Public unless someone restricts them, so a table publishes whole until you decide otherwise. Three things to know about changing a field's visibility: It saves immediately. There is no separate save step — pick a setting and it is stored in the field's configuration. The counts in the panel header (public, workspace, and private fields) update as you go. It is a table-wide decision. Visibility belongs to the field, not to a row. Setting a field to Workspace removes it from the published page of every record in the table. Published pages catch up at the next publish. The setting is saved at once, but a page that is already public keeps showing its last published version. Run Publish changes to apply the current visibility to every published page in the table. If a visibility change is declined — most often because your role does not include field configuration access — the control returns to its previous setting rather than showing a saved state that did not happen. The Whole table selector above the field list is a planning aid for thinking about the table's overall visibility. Its own label tells you the choice is not saved — field-level settings are the ones that count.

The row picker lists a sample of the table's records, in default record order, using the same collection-wide row title as Details and Relations. A row without a value in that configured title field is shown as unnamed rather than with a generic record-type label or a guessed field. A note under the list tells you exactly how many of the table's records you are looking at — open the Table view to browse all records. The sample only bounds the preview; publishing always covers the whole table. Publish does not bind the workspace-operation Undo/Redo shortcuts. A Ctrl/Cmd+Z pressed here cannot undo an edit from another panel or change field visibility, publication, privacy, or public scope. Return to Table, Details, or Relations to undo a record, field, paste, row-order, or relationship edit. Pick a record and the preview beside the panel shows it as a public reader would see it. The preview is produced by the same renderer as the public entry page, showing the record as currently saved. Two things connect the preview to the field list: Point at a field in the list and the part of the preview where it renders is highlighted and scrolled into view. Point at a part of the preview and the matching field row lights up — useful for answering "which field is this on the page?" before restricting it. Rest the pointer on the preview's content and a hint names the source column that filled that part of the page. If the preview area reports that no public reader rendering is available for a record yet, the record cannot render a public page in its current state — most often a required field is still empty.

Select Publish changes to queue the run. The button needs a workspace table selected, and it works at whole-record granularity: each ready record's public page is built or refreshed in full, applying the current field visibility. While the run is in progress, the view reports how many records have been published so far, and how many were skipped or failed. When it finishes, the receipt gives the final counts: Published — records whose public page was built or refreshed. Skipped — records not ready for a public page; the receipt names the reason per record. A skip is not an error. Failed — records whose page could not be built. A failure does not stop the run; the platform continues through the rest of the table, counts the failures, and shows the first error message in the receipt. The report belongs to the table you ran it on — switching to another table clears it, so a count never reads as the outcome of the wrong table. Publishing requires publish access. If Publish changes is unavailable to you, or the run is declined with a permission message, contact your environment administrator — the permissions panel page describes how access is assigned.

Both show the same saved reader rendering, so use whichever fits the task: Details panel — best while editing one record: the saved reader preview sits next to the record you are working on. See Preview an entry before publishing. Publish view — best for table-level decisions: checking how field visibility plays out across several records, spot-checking a sample, and then publishing.
documents.s: Publish view preview or Details panel preview?

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A field you set to Workspace or Private still shows on the public page. Published pages keep their last published version; visibility changes wait for the next publish. Select Publish changes, then check the page again. A visibility setting snaps back to its previous value. The save was declined — most often your role does not include field configuration access. Contact your environment administrator. Publish changes is unavailable. No workspace table is selected, or a publish run is already in progress. Select a table from the sidebar and wait for any running publish to finish. If the button stays unavailable, your role may not include publish access — contact your environment administrator. The receipt shows skipped records. A skipped record is not ready for a public page — most often a required field is empty, or something it reads is not public. The receipt names the reason per record. Fix what it names and publish again. See Publish a record. The run ends with a publish failed message. The publish job stopped before it finished, or some records could not be built — the receipt shows the first error. Run Publish changes again. If the same records keep failing, contact your environment administrator with the error message from the receipt. The record you want to preview is not in the row picker. The picker shows a sample of the table's records, not all of them. The sample is only for spot-checking — publishing covers the whole table regardless. To check a specific record, open it from the Table view and use the Details panel's saved reader preview.

Publish a record — and why saving is not publishing — what publishing does, and who can publish. Preview an entry before publishing — every place a reader preview appears, including the record drawer and the import wizard. Public reader — what published pages look like from the reader's side. Adding and editing rows — creating, editing and deleting records; what makes one ready to publish. Workspace walkthrough — the table, the Details panel, and the view tabs this page builds on.

Everything you publish to your public reader is also available as a machine-readable API — the same frozen records your reader pages serve, in JSON, for external tools, library systems, citation managers, and AI agents. You do not switch anything on: if a record is published, it is on the API; if you withdraw it, it leaves the API the same moment it leaves the reader. This page describes what an external consumer sees. It was written against the live behavior of a populated research environment (2026-07-02).

The API serves only published records — the same publish decision that governs your reader pages governs the API (one gate, not two). Drafts, working data, private fields, and records you have not published do not exist as far as the API is concerned. Each response is the frozen published copy: exactly what was captured when you (or a teammate) pressed publish, unchanged until the next publish. No system rewrites, summarizes, or "improves" it on the way out — that stability is deliberate, so that anything citing your record receives the version you approved.
documents.s: What is served — and what never is

documents.t: Records are served at stable addresses (the same identity your reader pages use): …/api/v2/entries/<slug> — by the record's public route (e.g. a transliterated headword like burhān; non-Latin slugs work directly or percent-encoded). …/api/v2/entries/<id> — by the record's permanent identifier (survives renames). …?role_key=<section> — when your environment publishes more than one reading surface, this picks the section; asking for a section a record is not published in answers "not found" — never a different section's record. …/api/v2/entries?archetype=<FAMILY> — lists published records of a family (paginated). …/api/v2/citations/<id>.csl.json — the record's citation data in CSL, for reference managers. The interactive contract (for developers) is published at …/api/v2/docs.

When you withdraw a published record, its address does not turn into a dead link: the API answers "410 — withdrawn", telling readers and citation tools the record existed and was deliberately removed — distinct from "never existed" (404). Slug renames follow your reader's redirects.

Anonymous access is rate-limited per visitor per environment — generous for reading and polite tools, a brake on bulk scraping. A consumer who exceeds it receives "429 — too many requests" with a standard retry signal, and the limit resets within a minute.

Not a way to read drafts or private data (there is none of it on this surface). Not a live view of your workspace — it is the published snapshot, by design. Not an upload/edit channel: the API is read-only.

This page is for reading a published knowledge environment from the outside — as someone who received a link, found a record through a search engine, or wants to browse a project's corpus without a workspace account. It walks through arriving at a page, reading a record, copying a citation, and moving between records. Read it if you are an external reader making sense of what you see, or if you are a researcher who wants to know exactly what a reader encounters once your project publishes. What you see depends on how the project configured its published pages. The sections below describe how the reading layer works; a given project may use all of it or a subset. For the publisher's side of this — how a record becomes a published page, and how to preview before publishing — see Public reader.

Stable, citable URLs — every published record has a stable web address, so a link shared today still resolves to the same record later. Maturity: Active. Limit: stability is per record; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort. Browsable indexes — beside searching, you can browse the whole corpus from an alphabetized index, and a project can publish more than one (for a multilingual corpus, often one by transliteration and one by original script). Maturity: Active. Limit: which indexes exist and what each row shows are set by the project. Record pages with a side contents list — a published record reads as titled sections with a navigation list down the side that highlights where you are as you scroll. Maturity: Active. Limit: how fine-grained the contents list is depends on how the record is sectioned. A references section — the evidence behind a record, one row per place the record is attested, rendered in the project's citation style. Maturity: Active. Limit: how rich each row reads depends on what the project catalogued. Copyable citations — citations are rendered in the project's citation style, defined in Citation Style Language — the same format reference managers such as Zotero understand — ready to select and paste into a bibliography. Maturity: Active. Attached media — a record lists its attached media, each item with its label and, where catalogued, a link to its source. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the media the project attached and published appears. Several values shown together — where a record keeps more than one value in a single field (several translations of a term, a transliteration beside its original-script form), the page shows them together on one line. Maturity: Active. Limit: a project can instead choose to show one value per record for such a field; showing them all is the default. Dark mode and reading-first layout — selectable text, a scholarly typeface, and a darker color scheme you can switch to, remembered in your browser. Maturity: Active. Scholarly formatted text — formatted fields retain callouts, marks and links, lists, tables, code, record mentions, numbered footnotes, rendered TeX equations, and admitted image figures with authored alternative text and optional captions. Maturity: Active. Limit: a mention is linked only when its target has a published reader route, and an image appears only when its media is admitted with a frozen primary artifact.

There are two common ways in: A shared link. Someone sent you the web address of a single record. Open it. The address is stable, so it keeps resolving to the same record even if the project later reorganizes its pages. The browsable index. When you want to explore rather than land on one record, open the project's index — an alphabetized list of every published record. A project can publish more than one index; for a multilingual corpus, that often means the same records listed by transliteration or by original script, switchable from the controls at the top of the list. Each index row can show the transliterated form, the original-script form, and a short gloss together, so you can recognize a record without opening it, and a character rail jumps straight to a letter. See Browse entries by index.

A published record reads as a sequence of titled sections, with a Contents list down the side that highlights the section you are currently reading and lets you jump to any section. Below the sections, a record can carry: Connections to other records, where the project published them. A References section — the evidence behind the record. Each place the record is attested gets its own row, rendered in the project's citation style: author, work, locator, and any abbreviations as the field uses them. Where an occurrence cites both a modern and an earlier edition, the row bridges the two; where it carries a quote, the quote sits with its row. See Read the references section on a published entry. A Media section listing each attached item with its label and, where the project catalogued it, a link to the item's source. Items such as 3D models open in their own viewer — see Exploring 3D models. Where a field on the record holds more than one value — a term given in several languages, or a transliteration alongside its original-script form — the page shows those values together on one line, separated by a comma or a middot. A project may instead set such a field to show a single value per record; when it does, you see only that one. Either way, what you see is what the project entered — nothing is translated for display.

Formatted text keeps its scholarly structure on the page. Inline and display equations are typeset while retaining an accessible TeX representation. Footnote references are numbered and link to a footnote list at the end of the field, with a return link back to the reference. A mention shows the record's published label and links to that record when the project has published a reader route for it. Links open only the address the author supplied; the reader never exposes a mention target's workspace identifier, a private label, or a media-storage location as a fallback. Published figure markup may carry the admitted media record's canonical identifier so the reader can request its public delivery; it does not carry a storage key or signed storage URL.

Citations appear in the record's References area, rendered in the project's citation style. Select the citation text and copy it to paste into a bibliography, footnote, or document. Because the style is defined in Citation Style Language — the same format reference managers understand — the copied citation is consistent with the conventions those tools use. A media item attached to a record can carry its own citation, separate from the record's, and it appears among the references the same way. See Copy a citation for a record or media item.

Follow connections. Where a record links to another, follow the link to that record's page; your browser's back button returns you. Return to the index to pick another record, or switch to a different index where the project publishes more than one. Switch to dark mode. A reading-first layout offers a darker color scheme, remembered in your browser for your next visit.
documents.s: Moving between records and switching the view

documents.t: A published page shows only what the project chose to publish. A record's working notes, draft fields, or unpublished records are not on the public web at all — they live in the project's workspace, which a reader does not reach. If a record you expected is missing, it has most likely not been published yet rather than hidden from you specifically.
documents.s: Why some content is not visible to you

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A link someone shared returns a "not found" page. The record was withdrawn after the link was shared, or the address was mistyped. Re-check the address. If a record was deliberately withdrawn, the project may show a short notice in its place rather than the record. Ask the person who shared the link, or browse the index for the current version. A citation reads roughly — punctuation or ordering looks off. The project's citation style for that collection is still being refined. Nothing to do as a reader; the citation is still usable. The rendering improves once the project applies a reviewed style. A record is in the index but its page shows a placeholder where a citation should be. The fields the citation draws on are incomplete on that record. Nothing to do as a reader. The project completes those fields and the citation fills in on the next publish. You browsed to a record you read last week and the contents list looks different. The project edited and republished the record. This is expected — published pages refresh when the project republishes. The record's web address stays stable across the change. The index switcher shows only one index. The project publishes a single index. Use it as the entry point; more than one index appears only where a project publishes more than one.

Public reader — the publisher's view of the same reading layer: how a draft becomes a published page, and how to preview before publishing. Browse entries by index — switching indexes and jumping by letter. Read the references section on a published entry — what each evidence row means. Copy a citation for a record or media item — getting a citation you can paste into a bibliography. Exploring 3D models — reading an attached 3D model in its own viewer. Searching as a public reader — finding records on a published environment when you do not have one in front of you.

Every relation field on a record creates a connection to a record in another collection — an author to a text, a passage to a term, a manuscript to an edition. The Relations view, one of the workspace's view tabs alongside Table, Details, and Publish, shows all of those connections for one record at once: the links it makes, the links other records make to it — including connections an import created that no relation field declares — and what the platform knows about each one: its status, its confidence, and where it came from. Read this page when you want to audit a record's connections, review links that arrived from an import or a reviewed process, or remove a link with its full context in front of you. For quick link editing while you work on a record's fields, the Table and Details views are usually faster — see Link one record to another.

Connections in both directions (Active) — for a focused record, the view lists its outgoing links per relation field and, in a separate Incoming section, every link other records make to it. Three layouts (Active) — Graph, Matrix, and Stream modes present the same links as a centered overview, a field-by-field grid, or a flat list with status, confidence, anchor, and provenance columns. Lifecycle and confidence filters (Active) — narrow the picture to one link status, or hide links below a confidence level you set. The filters apply to outgoing and incoming links alike; the Other linked records section is deliberately not filtered, so nothing it shows is ever hidden. Linked records without a relation field (Active) — connections that arrived from an import can exist even when no relation field declares them. They appear read-only in an Other linked records (from imported relationships) section, grouped by the relationship rule that created them — so the view shows the same connections a published entry shows its readers. Add a link by search-and-pick (Active) — search the relation field's target table and click a match to link it. Links you add are saved immediately and recorded under your name. Inspector with safe unlink (Active) — select any link to see its status, confidence, provenance, and anchor detail, and remove it behind a hold-to-confirm step. Undo and redo with exact relationship detail (Active) — link changes join the same table history as edits made in Table and Details. Undoing an unlink restores the connection's recorded status, provenance, detail, anchor, and attribution rather than creating a new generic link. Approve and Reject buttons — visible in the Inspector but not yet available; changing a link's status from this view is not possible.

Open a table and switch to the Relations tab. The left-hand Rows list shows the table's records; click one to focus it. A record you already opened in the Table or Details view stays focused when you switch to Relations, so the usual path is: find the record where you are, then switch tabs. For a large table the Rows list shows only the first stretch of records — focus the record first and bring it with you. When a collection declares a shared row-title field, the Rows list uses it, as do Details and the Publish row picker. If a row has no value in that configured field, it is shown as unnamed rather than being labelled with the collection's generic record type or another guessed field. A collection without a declared row-title field may use the platform's conventional label fallback. Beside the rows, the Predicate panel lists the table's relation fields — each with its label and the collection it points to. Pick a field to see the focused record's links through it. A table with no relation fields still shows its connections: instead of the Predicate panel, the view lists the focused record's linked records grouped by relationship rule — the connections an import created — with incoming links marked by a ← arrow and "links here". These are read-only here; to make links of your own from such a table, create a relation field first — see Build a knowledge environment from scratch. The message No relation fields declared and no linked records found for this row appears only when the focused record has neither.

The central panel counts the visible links — the view calls each connection an edge — and offers three modes: Graph places the focused record at the center and lists each link with the connected record's label, its status, its confidence, and an A marker when the link points at an anchor. Matrix crosses the linked records against the table's relation fields (the first five), a dot marking which field carries each link, with its confidence beside it. Stream is a flat list: one row per link, with Target, Status, Confidence, Anchor, and Provenance columns. When the focused record also has connections that no relation field declares — links created by an import under a rule of their own — they are listed beneath the modes in an Other linked records (from imported relationships) section, grouped by relationship rule, each with a → arrow and its status. These entries are read-only: there is no relation field behind them to edit through, and the lifecycle and confidence filters do not hide them. Below the modes, the Incoming section lists the links that point at the focused record from elsewhere. Each entry shows the other record, the relation field it used, and the link's status. These links belong to the other record's relation fields — Relations is the one place you can see them gathered on the receiving side.
documents.s: Reading the picture: outgoing and incoming

documents.t: Not every link is made by hand. Imports can create links between the records they bring in. AI can confirm or refine a parser-surfaced relationship during import, but a person approves that proposal before the platform creates the relationship field and its approved links; AI cannot write arbitrary links directly. The status tells you which links are settled: approved — a settled connection. Links you add by hand are approved immediately, under your name; links created by an import arrive approved. proposed — an unsettled lifecycle value the view can display when a process recorded it. The current AI-assisted import path does not directly create individual proposed links; approved import decisions materialize approved links. rejected — a connection that was rejected. It stays listed under its own status rather than disappearing, so the decision remains visible. To review what is unsettled, use the Lifecycle filter in the Predicate panel: each status shows a count of the chosen field's links in that state. The Confidence floor slider beneath it hides links below the level you set. Every link can carry a confidence score recorded by whatever created it; a link with no recorded score counts as full confidence when approved and zero otherwise. Confirming or rejecting a link from this view is not yet available — the Inspector's Approve and Reject buttons are visible but not yet active.
documents.s: What link statuses mean for your work

documents.t: Focus the record in the Rows list and pick the relation field in the Predicate panel. Under Add target, type part of the name of the record you want to connect. The search runs against the field's target table and shows the closest matches (up to five). Click a match. The link is created immediately — approved, under your name — with no separate save step. Choosing a record that is already linked does not create a second link. Both ends must be approved records: a proposal nobody has accepted yet cannot be either end of a link.
