The search box stays unavailable until a record is focused and the chosen relation field declares a target table.

Select any link — outgoing or incoming — and the Inspector on the right shows its relation field, status, the connected record on each side, confidence, and provenance (where the link came from: the source recorded by the process that created it, or the person's name). An Anchor card states whether the link points at a specific place inside the connected record or at the whole record. Below that, the Inspector shows the link's full recorded detail, useful when you need to check exactly what an import or an approved review process recorded.

Select the link in any mode, or in the Incoming section. In the Inspector, tick Hold-to-confirm unlink. Click Unlink edge. Only the connection is removed; both records stay exactly as they are. There is one connection between the two records, seen from two sides — so the link disappears from the other record's relation field at the same time, and an incoming link you unlink is removed from the record that made it. Adding and removing links requires edit access in your environment; if an attempt is declined, contact your environment administrator. The unlink joins the active table's workspace history. Select Undo in Relations, Table, or Details — or press Ctrl/Cmd+Z outside an editor — to restore the same recorded connection. Redo accepts Ctrl/Cmd+Y or Shift+Ctrl/Cmd+Z. Restore is allowed only for the same signed-in person and environment, within 90 days, while the current relationship field still permits the link. A stale, already-used, duplicated, or no-longer-valid restore is refused instead of widening the current relationship rule. An import run itself is not undoable here. If an import created an approved link through a declared relationship field and you later unlink it in the workspace, that later unlink can be undone. Connections in Other linked records have no editable field behind them and remain read-only.
documents.s: Removing a link — and what happens to the other record

documents.t: The Table and Details views edit links field by field, as chips on the record — the fastest way to add or remove a link while editing, covered in Link one record to another. Relations shows the whole connection picture for one record: both directions, statuses, confidence, provenance, and anchor detail — and it is the only view that shows incoming links. All three views contribute to one chronological edit history for the table. Use Table and Details to make links as you work; use Relations to audit them.
documents.s: How Relations differs from the Table and Details views

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix The view says no relation fields are declared and no linked records were found for this row. The table has no relation field and the focused record has no imported connections either. Create a relation field between the two collections — see Build a knowledge environment from scratch — or contact your environment administrator. Some linked records sit in an "Other linked records" section and cannot be edited or removed. Those connections came from an import under a rule no relation field declares, so the view can only show them. This is by design — they are the same connections a published entry shows. To manage links yourself, use a relation field. No links show, with a message about the predicate, lifecycle, and confidence filter. The filters are narrower than the data. Set the Lifecycle filter to All, slide the Confidence floor to 0%, and check that the right relation field is selected. The Add target search box cannot be typed in. No record is focused, or the chosen relation field does not declare a target table. Pick a record in the Rows list and a relation field that points at a collection. If the field should have one, contact your environment administrator. Adding a link is declined with a message about approval. One of the two records is a proposal nobody has accepted yet. Accept the proposal for that record, then add the link. The search shows no matching records. The target collection has no record matching your term. Try a shorter or different term, or add the record to the target collection first. Unlink edge stays gray. The hold-to-confirm box is not ticked. Tick Hold-to-confirm unlink, then click Unlink edge. A row or linked record shows as unnamed. Its collection has no row-title field, or that record has no value in the configured title field. The workspace does not guess another field. Contact your environment administrator and ask them to set a row-title field that the records fill. Undoing an unlink is refused. The restore belongs to another person or environment, was already used, is older than 90 days, would duplicate a current link, or the relationship field changed. Refresh the view and inspect the current relationship rule and links. Add the link again only if the current rule permits it. Adding or unlinking fails with a permissions message. Your role does not include edit access for this environment. Contact your environment administrator.

Link one record to another — adding and removing links from the Table and Details views while you edit. Workspace walkthrough — the view tabs, toolbar, and sidebar around the Relations view. Adding and editing rows — creating, editing, and deleting records. Searching and reading — finding the record you want to focus before switching to Relations. Build a knowledge environment from scratch — creating the relation field that connects two collections.

This page is for the researcher who oversees others — a project director, a senior scholar checking a junior colleague's entries, anyone who reads and signs off on work before it reaches the public. It walks the review loop the platform actually supports today: read what your colleagues have written, tell an unfinished record from a finished one, check the connections between records, and use publication as the deliberate checkpoint it was built to be. Read it when you take on a supervisory role, or when you want to know exactly which parts of review the platform handles for you and which stay a matter of talking to your team. A note before the steps: the platform gives you a workspace where every stage of a record is visible, and a publication gate that you control through who holds publish access. It does not give you a separate "submit for review" queue or an in-record comment thread. Where a mechanism exists, this page names it; where one does not, it says so plainly rather than implying a workflow that is not there.

Read everything in one place (Active) — unfinished records, finished ones, and published records all sit in the same workspace table. Nothing your team works on is hidden from a colleague with read access; review starts by reading what is already in front of you. Tell an unfinished record from a finished one (Active) — a record with a required field still empty cannot be published, and the publish receipt names it. That refusal is what tells you a record is not finished. Review the connections between records (Active) — the Relations view gathers every link a record makes and every link made to it, with each link's status, so you can audit how your team has connected the corpus. Publication as the review checkpoint (Active) — publishing is a separate, deliberate act, and publish access belongs to your environment's administrators. Composing roles so that only reviewers hold publish access turns "publish" into a real sign-off step. A separate review queue or in-record comments — not part of the platform. Feedback happens through the record stages, the link statuses, and conversation outside the platform, not through a built-in review inbox.
documents.s: What you can review, and how

documents.t: Work in progress is not hidden. A record joins the workspace table the moment a colleague creates it, alongside finished records. Any colleague with read access can open it, read its fields, and follow its connections. So the first move in reviewing work is to open the relevant collection's table and read. There is no separate filter that isolates "only unfinished" or "only finished records" in the table today. You tell them apart by behavior rather than by a status column — described next. To narrow a large table down to the records you care about while you review, use the ordinary filters and saved views covered in Searching and reading.
documents.s: Reading what your team has written

documents.t: Where a record stands is read from two things — whether it is finished, and whether it is public: In the workspace. Every record your project creates is here from the moment it is made. Colleagues with access to the table can read, edit and link it. No public reader can. Required fields may still be empty. Published. The record has a public page anyone with the address can read. Finished is not a stage the platform stores; it is something you check. A record with a required field still empty is refused at publication, and the receipt names the field. That refusal is the signal, and it is why publishing is where review bites. The lifecycle is described from the editor's side in Adding and editing rows and from the publisher's side in Public reader.
documents.s: Telling an unfinished, a finished, and a published record apart

documents.t: Connections are part of the work, and the Relations view is where you audit them for one record at a time. Open a collection, switch to the Relations tab, and focus the record you are checking. The view shows the links that record makes to others and — in a separate Incoming section — the links other records make to it. Each link carries a status: approved — a settled connection. A link a colleague adds by hand is approved immediately under their name; links that arrive from an import are approved. proposed — suggested by an automated step rather than by a person, and not yet settled. This is the status to watch when you want to know what a machine suggested and a person has not yet confirmed. rejected — a connection that was turned down. It stays listed under its own status so the decision remains visible. Use the Lifecycle filter in the Relations view to show only one status — setting it to proposed is the fastest way to see what automated analysis has suggested but no one has yet acted on. One caution on what you can do from there: the Inspector shows Approve and Reject buttons, but they are not yet available — confirming or rejecting a proposed link from this view is not possible today. What you can do is read the proposal, its confidence, and where it came from, and remove a link you judge wrong, behind a hold-to-confirm step. The full Relations workflow is covered in The Relations view.

Saving and publishing are deliberately separate steps, and that separation is what lets publication act as a review gate. A record can sit in the workspace for as long as your project needs — through internal checking, peer reading, or waiting on a companion record — and nothing reaches the public until someone publishes it. Publishing requires publish access, and publish access belongs to your environment's administrators. Researchers whose roles include only edit access can add and edit records but cannot publish them. This is the lever that makes review real: when roles are composed so that contributors can finish records but only reviewers hold publish access, publication becomes a sign-off that a reviewer performs after reading the work. Your environment administrator composes those roles; the permissions panel page describes what each role covers and how custom roles are built. Publishing itself — including what happens when you publish a whole table at once — is covered in Publish a record.

The platform does not carry a built-in review queue, an approval workflow you route a record through, or a comment thread attached to a record. Feedback in the platform happens through the things that are visible to the whole project: the stage a record sits at, the links and their statuses, and the values in the fields themselves. A reviewer reads the work, and the decision to publish (or not yet) is the recorded outcome. Conversation about the work — "this field needs a source", "hold this record until the companion table is ready" — happens between you and your colleagues outside the platform. Keep that in mind when you set up a review practice: the platform records the state of the work and who published it, not the discussion around it.

When your team re-imports its source data, the platform protects the edits your colleagues made and shows only what is new, changed, or different from the last import. As a reviewer this is the moment to check that an automated refresh did not undo deliberate work. Two pages cover what to look at: Understand what changed after a re-import explains the delta — the new, changed, removed, and carried-forward items — and confirms that labels, settings, and other edits your team made are never overwritten; Saved views and re-imports explains what happens to the views your team relies on when fields change.
documents.s: Watching what changed after a re-import

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix I cannot find a "review" or "submitted" filter to see only records awaiting sign-off. The platform has no separate review queue or record-state filter; unfinished and finished records share the table. Read the records directly. Use ordinary filters and a saved view to narrow the table — see Searching and reading. A record I want to check refuses to link to another record. One of the two records is a proposal nobody has accepted yet. The message near the field names the record holding the link up — see Adding and editing rows. The Approve and Reject buttons on a proposed link do nothing. Changing a link's status from the Relations view is not yet available. Read the proposal's status, confidence, and provenance to judge it. You can remove a link you decide is wrong; see The Relations view. A colleague published a record I had not finished reviewing. Their role includes publish access. Ask your environment administrator to compose roles so that only reviewers hold publish access — see the permissions panel. I want to leave a comment on a record for a colleague. There is no in-record comment or feedback thread. The platform records record state and who published; discuss the work with your colleague directly, and use the record's stage and links as the shared reference.

What you can see and do as a reviewer reflects your role. Read access lets you open and read every stage of your team's records and follow their links; edit access adds creating and linking; publish access — the gate that makes review a real checkpoint — belongs to your environment's administrators. Roles are composed and assigned by your environment administrator; the permissions panel page describes the building blocks each role is made from.

Adding and editing rows — creating, editing and publishing, from the editor's side. The Relations view — auditing a record's connections and reading link statuses in full. Publish a record — why saving is not publishing, and who can publish. Public reader — the full path from workspace to published page. Understand what changed after a re-import — the delta, and why your team's edits are safe. Saved views and re-imports — what happens to shared views when fields change.

This page covers two things that go together: how you find records in your knowledge environment, and how you read what you find — fields, related records, media, citations, and a preview of what a published record looks like to a reader outside your project. Read it when search is not finding what you expect, when you need a scholarly citation from a record, or when you want to check how a record will read before it is published. What is available depends on how your environment is configured. The sections below describe what the platform supports; your project may use all of it or a subset.

Quick search — a search panel that finds records across every collection you can access. Results are grouped by collection and show which fields matched; selecting a result opens the record. Scope it to the current table, to everything you can access, or to a single collection. Maturity: Active. Search & Read — a full search page for browsing, filtering, and reading results in place. Scope the search to a collection and add conditions on field values; the page address encodes your whole search, so it can be shared. Maturity: Active. Current-table filtering — a toolbar box that narrows the active table to the rows in the whole collection that contain a typed term, and a filter builder for column conditions. Maturity: Active. Details panel — every field of a record, including fields the table does not display as columns. A separate Relations view shows the record's connections. Maturity: Active. Reader preview — the Details panel includes a preview pane rendered with the same engine as the public reader, so what you see is what a reader would see. Maturity: Active. Media and citations — a record's reading view lists its attached media, and citations are rendered in your project's citation style (defined in Citation Style Language, the format reference managers like Zotero understand). Maturity: Active. Limit: which media appear depends on what your project attached.

Open quick search from the Search database… control at the top of the workspace, or press Ctrl+Shift+F (⌘⇧F on Mac). Type a term. Results appear grouped by collection, each showing the record's label and the fields where your term matched. Select a result to open that record. The panel starts scoped to Current table when a table is active. Switch to All workspace to search everything you can access, or narrow the search to a single collection. This is the right tool for "find this person, source, or term, wherever it lives." Quick search matches against the fields your environment includes in its search configuration — by default, the text fields of each record. Matching is forgiving about diacritics: in a polytonic-Greek project, a term typed in modern monotonic Greek finds its polytonic spellings — breathings, iota subscripts, and circumflex and grave accents are all ignored — and Arabic vowel marks are ignored the same way. The acute accent and the diaeresis still count, in Greek and in Latin script alike: a term typed with no accents at all can miss a record whose stored form carries one. If your project keeps a native-script field, a transliteration, and a translation side by side, a term in any of them finds the record, provided those fields are searchable. Which fields those are is set by your environment administrator.
documents.s: Quick search — find a record anywhere you can access

documents.t: When you want to look at many records rather than jump to one, open Search & Read: select Open full Search & Read at the bottom of the quick search panel — your typed term carries over — or choose Search & Read from the command palette (Ctrl+K / ⌘K). Search & Read is built for dwelling. Switch to Advanced mode to scope the search to one collection and add conditions on field values — each condition names a field, a match type (contains, equals, or starts with), and a value, and can be negated; conditions combine with Match all or with any. Sort results by relevance, by recently modified, or by label, and page through them. For any result you can expand its full fields inline, open it in a reading pane beside the list, or click through to the record itself. If a collection needs a review access you do not hold, the page tells you how many are hidden rather than failing silently. The page address encodes your query, filters, page, and sort order. Paste the address to a colleague and they see the same results — see Share a search. For a side-by-side comparison of the two search tools, see Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read.
documents.s: Search & Read — browse, filter, and read in place

documents.t: The table toolbar gives you two ways to narrow what is in front of you: Filter rows… — type a term and the table shows the rows from the whole collection that contain it, in whichever script the text is written, with the same forgiving matching as quick search: breathings, iota subscripts, circumflex and grave accents and vowel marks are set aside — a term typed without them also matches their marked forms, and a term typed with one matches only those — while the acute accent and the diaeresis still count on both sides. It narrows the collection in front of you and does not search the rest of the workspace. Filter — opens the filter builder for column conditions. Active filters appear as chips on the toolbar; remove one, or clear them all. You can combine the two — apply column filters, then type in the filter box — or use either alone. Filter-only browsing, with no typed term, is a good way to survey a slice of your corpus.

Click a row to open its Details panel. Every field of the record is shown, including fields the table does not display as columns. Relation fields are marked as such; the Relations view shows the record's connections in one place. Alongside the fields, a Saved reader preview pane renders the record as a reader outside your project would see it — same layout, same fonts, same citations, same media rendering — without making anything public. Read it, spot anything that looks wrong, and fix it in the fields beside it. Public reader covers the full path from draft to published page.

A record's reading view lists its attached media — images, audio, video, or 3D models, whichever your project attached. Each media item is itself a record, with its own description and its own citation. Where a dedicated viewer exists for a media type, the item opens in that viewer. Citations are rendered in your project's citation style and are ready to copy into a bibliography — the same structured form reference managers understand. The same applies to source records: opening one shows a citation you can reuse. How citations are composed and how they appear to outside readers is covered in Public reader.
documents.s: Media and citations on a record

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Quick search returns nothing for a record you know exists. Your term appears only in a field your environment does not include in its search configuration, or your term is missing an acute accent the stored form carries. Type the term with its accents, or try a word from a different field of the record. If it still does not appear, contact your environment administrator to review which fields are searchable. The search panel reports "Search isn't enabled for this workspace yet." Search has not been switched on for your environment. The toolbar filter box shares that switch and reports "Filter unavailable — search is not enabled for this workspace" until it is on. Contact your environment administrator. A transliterated search misses a record whose native-script form you know is there. The transliteration field is empty on that record, or it is not marked searchable. Try the native-script form. If that succeeds, contact your environment administrator so the transliteration field can be reviewed. The toolbar filter box does not find a record you expect. The box answers only for the collection in the active table, so the record may live in another collection; or your term omits an acute accent or diaeresis the stored form carries, or carries one the stored form lacks. Use quick search for other collections — it searches every collection you can access. Otherwise retype the term with the same acute accents and diaereses as the stored form. Search results show strings of letters and numbers instead of names. The collection has no display field configured, so results fall back to an internal identifier. Contact your environment administrator and ask them to set a display field for that collection. A citation under a media item looks incomplete or shows placeholders. The citation fields are missing on the media record itself. Open the media record's Details and complete the citation fields. If the field requirements look wrong for your project, contact your environment administrator.

Workspace walkthrough — search and the Details panel in the context of the whole workspace. Adding and editing rows — how drafts behave before they become records. Public reader — the full path from draft to published reader view, including citations as readers see them. Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — which search tool fits which task. Share a search — copy an address that reproduces your exact search. Citation integrity — for environment administrators: configuring the citation engine.

This page explains how search works on the public face of a knowledge environment — the published site that anyone can visit, with no account and no sign-in. Read it when you want to know what a visitor can find, when you are checking your own project's public face, or when search behaves differently in public than it does in your workspace. Searching inside the workspace is a different tool with different controls — that is covered in Searching and reading. The public site is configurable, so what a reader sees depends on your project. The sections below describe how the platform behaves; your environment may use all of it or a subset.

Public full-text search — a search box on the public site that searches the records your project has published. Available to anyone; no account needed. Maturity: Active. Limit: which fields are searched is set by your project's search configuration. Suggestions as you type — after a few characters, a list of matching records appears beneath the search box; selecting one goes straight to that record. Maturity: Active. Limit: a project decides whether suggestions are on; when they are not, the panel says so instead of staying empty. Result filters — menus on the results page that narrow results by values your project defined, drawn from the current result set. Maturity: Active. Limit: which filters exist — by author or by chronology, for example — is set by your project. Result groupings — tabs that reorganize the same results: a flat list of matching records, or grouped views under headings. Maturity: Active. Limit: which groupings appear and what they are called come from your project's configuration. Explained unavailability — a filter or suggestion source that is not available shows a reason rather than failing silently with empty results. Maturity: Active. Results-page guided tour — a short walkthrough of the results page, shown once automatically and replayable on demand. Maturity: Active.

The search box appears on the public site's front page and at the top of most other public pages. Nobody needs to sign in to use it. It searches what your project has published — the same read-only published layer the rest of the public site reads from — in the fields your project includes in its public search configuration. Unpublished drafts and workspace-only records are not in it. The box takes a single term or phrase. There are no operator or per-field controls on the public search bar; refinement happens on the results page, with the filter menus. How forgiving the match is — accents, alternate scripts — follows your project's search configuration. Type a term and press Enter, or select the Search button — it activates once you have typed something. The results page opens.

Once you have typed at least three characters and pause briefly, a suggestion panel can open beneath the box. Each suggestion shows the record's label, with a secondary line where the record has one. Selecting a suggestion opens that record's page directly, skipping the results page. The panel always tells you what it is doing: While it is looking, it shows Searching.... When nothing matches what you typed, it shows No suggestions. When your project has not switched suggestions on, it shows Suggestions unavailable with a short explanation. Suggestions never block the search itself. Whatever the panel shows, pressing Enter runs the full search.

The public site is built not to fail silently: A filter menu that is configured but currently unavailable appears disabled, reading unavailable or No … values in place of its choices, and carries the reason — shown as a tooltip, and read aloud by screen readers. If the address you arrive by carries a filter the public site does not offer — an old bookmark, for example — the page shows a Filter unavailable notice naming the filter, instead of a misleading empty result list. Remove that filter, or start a fresh search from the search bar.
documents.s: When a filter or control is unavailable, the page says so

documents.t: The results page shows how many records matched, ten results per page, with numbered page buttons at the bottom. The page address carries your search term, so a shared or bookmarked address repeats the search. When nothing matches, the page says No results found. Each result shows the record's title — a link to its page — a secondary line, a short excerpt ending in Read more, and a handful of labeled field values from the record. Records with attached media list them on the result. Beside the list, a summary panel previews the first result — its title, description, and key values — with a control in its corner that opens that record in a new browser tab. Above the results, a row labeled Filters: holds one menu per filter your project defined. Each menu starts at Any … and lists the values present in the current result set; choosing a value narrows the results immediately. When any filter is active, a RESET button appears and clears them all. Which menus exist — by author, by chronology, by some other field — is decided by your project; treat those as examples, not platform universals.

A row labeled Sort by: offers one tab per grouping your project configured. The first tab is a flat list of the matching records, named for what your project calls its entries. The other tabs reorganize the same results under headings — one heading per author, per period, or per whatever value the grouping uses. Different organizations suit different reading tasks: the flat list is best for scanning the strongest matches alongside the summary panel; a grouping by author surveys what each author contributes to the result set; a grouping by chronology reads the results period by period. A record with no value for the current grouping appears under Not Specified.

Selecting a result's title opens that record's page at its own stable address — the same address anyone can cite or share. The page you land on is the published record: what your project last published, not anyone's working copy. If you are a researcher checking your own project's public face and a recent edit is missing, that edit has not been published yet. To see unpublished work as a reader would, use the preview in your workspace — see Preview an entry before publishing — and Public reader for the full path from draft to published page.
documents.s: From a result to a record page

documents.t: The first time your browser lands on a results page with results, a short guided tour opens by itself and walks through the filter menus, the grouping tabs, and a result; where results carry related media, the tour points those out too. The browser remembers that you have seen it, so it does not repeat. To replay it, select the help button on the results page. The button is inactive when there are no results to tour.

Symptom Likely cause Fix No suggestion panel appears while typing. Fewer than three characters typed, or no pause yet — suggestions wait for both. Keep typing, or press Enter to run the full search without suggestions. The panel says "Suggestions unavailable." Your project has not switched suggestions on for the public site. The full search still works — press Enter or select Search. If suggestions should be on, contact your environment administrator. A search that should match a record returns nothing. The record is not published, or your term appears only in a field your project does not include in its public search. If it is your project, check the record's publication state in the workspace. Otherwise, try a term from a different part of the record, or contact the project's environment administrator. A filter menu is grayed out and cannot be opened. That filter is not currently available on the public site, or no values exist for this search. Hover over the menu to read the reason. Narrow the search with the other menus. If the filter should be available, contact your environment administrator. The page shows "Filter unavailable" instead of results. The address carries a filter the public site does not offer — often an outdated bookmark or shared link. Remove the unavailable filter, or start a fresh search from the search bar and reapply the filters the page offers. Records pile up under "Not Specified" in a grouped view. Those records have no value for the field the grouping uses. Switch to the flat list grouping. If it is your project's data, fill in the missing field in the workspace. The guided tour does not open. It opens by itself only on the first visit — your browser remembers it — and it needs at least one result. Run a search that returns results, then select the help button on the results page to replay the tour.

Public reader — what the public site is, and how a record reaches it. Searching and reading — searching inside your workspace, a different tool with different controls. Browse entries by index — the non-search way for readers to explore: an alphabetized index of everything published. Preview an entry before publishing — see unpublished work exactly as a reader would, from your workspace.

Every column in your table carries its own set of controls — sorting, a per-column filter, pinning, renaming, row colors — and the table as a whole has a column manager for visibility and order. This page describes each control, where to find it, and what the active view remembers about your arrangement. Read it when you want to know what a control does before you use it; for step-by-step tasks, the help entries linked throughout are shorter.

Each table shows its own columns (Active) — when several of your tables share the same record kind (for example, more than one Terms table), each table shows only the columns that belong to its own source, not the combined set of every same-kind table. So a lemma table shows its lemma columns and an abbreviations table shows its abbreviation columns, even though both are "Terms". Hiding columns for yourself (the column manager, below) is a separate, per-view layer on top of this. Sorting (Active) — sort by clicking a column's name, from the column's header menu, or from the toolbar Sort button. The sort is stored on the active view as you change it. Column header menu (Active) — every column header has a menu with the column's label, type, filter, sort, pinning, visibility, row-color rules, and field actions in one place. One field-type picker (Active) — the trailing Add column control, an existing column's Column type menu, and Edit column show the same types. Adding a field opens the editor with your type selected; self-contained changes to an existing field apply immediately. Per-column filter (Active) — a filter control in the header menu matched to the column's type: choice columns offer their options, checkbox columns offer checked or unchecked, dates open a date picker, numbers take a number, and text columns match as you type. Column manager (Active) — a dialog listing every column in the table: show or hide, reorder by dragging, search by name or type, and choose the view's display column. In the current workspace build, pinning remains in the column header menu and resizing happens in the table itself by dragging a column's edge. Pinning (Active) — pin a column to the left or right edge from its header menu so it stays visible while you scroll. Pinning is remembered on the active view. Not yet available — Duplicate column and Group by this column appear in the header menu but are grayed out; their tooltips state the reason.

From a column header​ Click a column's name to sort the table by that column. Clicking the name again reverses the direction, and a third click removes the sort. An arrow in the header shows the current direction. To sort by a second column without dropping the first, hold Shift while clicking the other column's name. The same controls live in the column's header menu under Sort: Sort ascending, Sort descending, and Clear sort. A sort applied from one column's header menu does not remove a sort already on another column. From the toolbar​ The toolbar Sort button opens the Sort rows dialog. Pick a field, choose Ascending or Descending, and select Apply. The dialog applies a single field: applying it replaces any sort already active in the table, including sorts on other columns. Clear sort removes the active sort; Cancel or Escape closes the dialog without changes. What sorting affects​ The sort is stored on the active view as you change it, alongside filters and column layout. See Save your table arrangement as a view. While a sort, filter, or search is active, rows follow that order — dragging rows into a hand-arranged order is paused until the table is back in its free order.

Open the menu with the ⋯ button at the right edge of a column header, or by right-clicking the header. With the header focused, Enter or Space opens it too. The menu is titled with the column's label, and the first editable control is Column label. Column type, filtering, sorting, pinning, wrapping, visibility, and display-column actions are grouped below it. The field key remains visible in record details and the column manager, where it helps administrators identify the underlying field without replacing the label researchers chose. Menu item What it does Column label Type a new label and select Rename. The new label appears immediately in the table, in record details, and in filters. See Rename a field label. Edit column Opens the column's editing dialog — label, type, the other field settings, and whether a value is required for directly entered fields. Formula, lookup, and linked-record fields mark that as not applicable. See Make a field required. Column type A searchable list of field types. Text, number, date, choices, checkbox, URL, and other self-contained changes apply immediately. A type that still needs a target, expression, range policy, or media setting opens Edit column with that type selected. Conditional format Adds a color stripe to rows by a choice column's value. Pick a value, pick one of six colors; rules are saved with the view. You can clear one value's color or all of the column's rules. The panel needs values loaded in the table before it offers choices. Filter A filter control matched to the column's type — described below. Sort Sort ascending, sort descending, or clear this column's sort. Insert column… Adds a new column after this one. Duplicate column Visible but not yet available. Pin left / Pin right / Unpin Keeps the column at the table's edge while you scroll. Unpin is available only while the column is pinned. Wrap text Lets long values take more vertical space instead of ending with an ellipsis. When wrap is off, truncation follows the column's width. Visibility A preview of where the field is expected to be visible (private, workspace, or public), plus Open Publish view… to review the field where visibility is decided. Hide column Hides the column in this view. Hiding never deletes the field or its values. Use in this view Makes this column the active saved view's first identifying field. This is a presentation choice for that view. Use as row title Makes a compatible Text or URL field the collection-wide title used for rows in Details, Relations, and Publish. This is shared field configuration, not a saved-view presentation choice. Manage columns… Opens the column manager dialog. Delete column… Opens a confirmation first. Deleting removes the field's definition and hides the column; stored values are not deleted, and re-adding a field with the same field key restores the column. A small dot appears in a column's header while that column has an active filter, and the table's display field carries a display tag. Adding or changing a field type​ The trailing Add column header and Insert column… open the same compact type list used by Column type. Pick the type first; the field editor then opens with that choice already selected so you can name the field and finish any settings. For an existing field, self-contained choices apply as soon as you pick them. Linked record, Lookup, Formula, Time range, and media types open the field editor instead because the workspace still needs a target or another required setting. Select list and Multi select start with an editable Option 1 when they do not already have choices. Checkbox is yes/no and has no option list. URL link remains a text field with URL behavior. A valid http:// or https:// value opens as an external link; malformed or unsupported addresses stay visible as text rather than becoming unsafe links. Changing a field type can normalize stored values that fit the new type. The workspace reports how many cells were converted and keeps incompatible values as they were, marked for correction. If at least one cell was rewritten, the receipt says the conversion cannot be undone and the table's local Undo/Redo history starts over; schema-only type changes remain undoable. Filtering from the header menu​ The Filter entry in the header menu shows a control suited to the column's type: Column type Filter control Choice (single or multiple) A list of the column's options, with Any value to clear the choice Checkbox Checked or Unchecked Number or year A number box Date A date picker Anything else A text box that matches as you type A row stays visible when the column's value matches what you set. Text-like columns match when the displayed value contains your text, ignoring letter case. Date columns use the date picker value as a date: a stored timestamp on the same calendar date still matches the date you picked. If a column is still configured as text even though its values look like timestamps, it keeps text-style matching until someone changes or converts the field type. The condition appears as a chip in the toolbar after "filtering by", with a count of matching rows — the same chips the toolbar Filter button produces, and the two compose. Clear filter in the panel removes this column's condition; the chip's × does the same from the toolbar. See Narrow the current table with filters.

Open it with the toolbar Columns button, or with Manage columns… in any column's header menu. The dialog is titled Manage columns with the table's name, and shows how many columns are visible out of the total. Visible / Hidden / All tabs group the list, each with a count. A search box narrows the list by field name, key, or type. Each row shows the column's label, its field key, a type tag, and four controls: a star (set as display column), an eye (show or hide in this view), and Move up / Move down. Rows can also be dragged into a new order by their drag handle. A checkbox on each row toggles the column's visibility; Show all restores every hidden column at once. Undo, Redo, and Reset step the reordering inside the dialog backward and forward, or return to the order you started from. A preview strip at the bottom shows the first visible columns in the order you are arranging, with the display column highlighted. Visibility changes apply to the table immediately. Order and display-column changes are held as a draft until you select Save presentation — the saved order applies to the table, the record details fields, and the reader preview sequence. Two things this dialog deliberately does not do — pinning lives in the column header menu, and column widths are set in the table itself by dragging a column's edge. Both are remembered on the active view. Row title versus view display column​ These two choices have different reach: Use as row title changes the collection's shared record name. Details, Relations, and Publish use that field's value for each row. If a row has no value there, the workspace shows an unnamed placeholder rather than guessing from another field. Use in this view changes only the active saved view's identifying column. Set it with the star in the column manager or from the column header. The column manager's Display column selector offers the same choice plus Use row display label, which returns to the collection's shared row title. Hiding either column from a saved view does not delete the field or its values.

Sort order, filter conditions, column order, widths, pinning, hidden columns, the view display column, row density, and row-color stripe rules are all stored on whichever view is active. The view-history Undo and Redo step those presentation changes backward and forward. Field types, values, pasted edits, row order, and relationship edits use the separate workspace-operation history described in What the workspace remembers — and what you can undo. Changing the shared row title is not in either short-lived history; choose the prior title field again if you need to reverse it. Views are shared with everyone working in your environment, so arrange a shared view deliberately or duplicate it first. See Save your table arrangement as a view.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Where to escalate Applying a sort from the Sort button removed the sort I had on another column. The Sort rows dialog applies a single field and replaces the active sort. Re-apply the other column's sort from its header menu, which leaves existing sorts in place. n/a My column arrangement reverted later. Layout is stored on the active view; you may have been on a different view tab, or a collaborator changed the shared view. Check which view tab is active; duplicate the view for an arrangement collaborators will not change. n/a I set a display column and the table looks unchanged. The display column identifies rows in compact previews; it does not restyle the table grid. Open a record preview or compact listing to see it in use. n/a A type opened the field editor instead of changing immediately. That type needs a target or another required setting. Finish the highlighted settings and save. n/a Undo refused a field-type change. The field definition changed after the history entry was recorded, so replay would overwrite newer work. Review the current definition. Reapply the intended change deliberately, or ask the colleague who changed it which version should win. Contact your environment administrator if the current definition looks wrong. I cannot find pinning in the column manager. Pinning is not in that dialog. Use Pin left or Pin right in the column's header menu. n/a Duplicate column or Group by this column is grayed out. These controls are visible but not yet available. Hover the control; its tooltip states the reason. n/a Conditional format says no values are loaded yet. The column has no data in the active table, so there are no values to color by. Add or load rows with values in that column first. n/a Renaming, editing, or deleting a column fails or is missing. Changing field definitions needs editing access on this table. Ask your environment administrator about your role. Contact your environment administrator.

Save your table arrangement as a view — naming an arrangement and sharing it with your team. Narrow the current table with filters — the toolbar filter box and filter builder. Rename a field label — relabeling a column without touching your data. Workspace walkthrough — the whole workspace in one tour.

While you work, the platform may show small tips beside the record or the import you are reviewing — short notes about a faster way to do what you are already doing, or about something a record might be missing. Tips are advice, not commands. They never change your data, never block you, and go away on their own once they no longer apply. Read this page if you are wondering why a tip appeared, what to do with it, or why one you expected did not.

Improvement tips in the workspace — when the record you have selected has noticeably fewer filled fields than similar records in your environment, a tip names a field you could add. The comparison needs at least three similar records, and the tip stays silent when there is nothing meaningful to suggest. Maturity: Active. Efficiency tips during import review — when you make the same correction three or more times while reviewing an import, a tip notes the pattern, so you can adjust the rule once instead of correcting every remaining row by hand. Maturity: Active. A panel that stays out of the way — tips appear in a panel beside your work. In the workspace, the most confident tips show directly and the rest wait under a collapsed "More suggestions" heading; during import review, only confident tips appear. When nothing clears the confidence bar, no panel appears at all. Maturity: Active. Environment-wide off switch — your environment administrator can turn tips off for the whole environment; when off, no tips appear anywhere. Maturity: Active. Standardization tips — a third kind, which recognizes when a value matches a term already in your environment's controlled vocabulary, is built but not yet shown anywhere in the product. Maturity: Built — not yet available. Quiet-down for unhelpful tips — the platform can pause a kind of tip that researchers in an environment consistently pass over, so persistent noise switches itself off. This automatic pause is built but not yet running. Maturity: Built — not yet active. Aggregate-only usage figures — tip measurement, once running, records tip activity without naming the researcher, and figures about whether tips help are reported only in aggregate, withheld until enough activity contributes. Measurement is built but not yet collecting. Maturity: Built — not yet active.

You are editing a record or reviewing an import. A short note appears beside your work: one sentence of advice, with a brief reason underneath. Decide: Act on it. Make the edit it points to, the way you normally would. A tip is text — it carries no button and runs nothing on your behalf. Every change remains an edit you make yourself. Pass. Keep working. Nothing counts against you, and the tip goes away once it no longer applies — when the field is filled, or the review session moves on. That is the rhythm: small notes beside your work, yours to act on or pass over, never blocking.

You are editing a person record for Galen. Similar person records in your environment carry more detail on average, and this one has an empty birth-place field. An improvement tip surfaces, pointing out that records like this one usually have more fields filled and naming the birth place as a place to start. If the omission is deliberate — the birth place is genuinely unknown, or out of scope for your work — keep going. The tip does not insist, and it disappears once the comparison no longer holds. Later, you are reviewing an import and correct the same field the same way on a third row. An efficiency tip appears, noting that you have made the same correction several times. That is your cue to consider fixing the underlying mapping rule for the remaining rows instead of repeating the correction one row at a time.

When the review step of the import wizard is open, the tip panel sits beside the correction cards. Tips there fire only after a clear pattern — several corrections of the same shape within the session — and only when the platform is confident the suggestion is worth your attention. A blank panel during review is normal silence, not a fault.

Tips never change your data — there is no action a tip performs for you, so nothing happens without your own edit. Tips never penalize you for passing them over; ignored tips do not accumulate into a score or a warning. And tips never substitute for configuration — if your environment's required fields, vocabularies, or workflows are out of date, the right fix is to update the configuration, not to lean on tips. Raise that with your environment administrator.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A tip you expected never appears. The trigger was not met — too few similar records to compare against, no repeated correction pattern, or the suggestion was not confident enough to show. Tips may also be turned off for your environment. Confirm the trigger applies; an improvement tip needs at least three similar records in your environment. If tips seem off entirely, contact your environment administrator. The tip panel during import review is blank. No tip cleared the confidence bar for this session, or you have not yet repeated a correction enough times for a pattern to register. Nothing to fix — silence is intentional. A whole kind of tip stopped appearing. Tips were turned off for your environment, or that kind's trigger no longer applies to your records. If tips are gone everywhere, contact your environment administrator; otherwise there is nothing to fix. Tips feel noisy or distracting. The patterns in your data are triggering more suggestions than is helpful to you. Contact your environment administrator — tips can be turned off for the whole environment.

Workspace walkthrough — where tips appear in the workspace. Adding and editing rows — the editing flow tips sit beside. Privacy and safety — how aggregate usage figures are protected. Efficiency tips for environment administrators — turning tips on or off for an environment and reading aggregate figures.

Sometimes a record that has a public page should not be public any more — it was published by mistake, a rights question came up, or it needs substantial rework away from public view. Withdrawing a record takes its public page off the web while leaving the record itself untouched in your workspace. This page explains when withdrawal is the right tool, what it does, what a reader sees afterwards, and how to bring a withdrawn record back. Withdrawal is the reverse of publishing, and like publishing it is held by your environment's administrators. Your data is never deleted by a withdrawal — only the public face is removed.

Whole-record withdrawal — withdrawing a record removes its public page everywhere the record is published, in one action. Maturity: Active. Public search and index removal — a withdrawn record also leaves public search results and the browsable index. Maturity: Active. Limit: the search listing refresh can lag. Workspace data untouched — withdrawal changes nothing inside your workspace: the record stays in your collection, linkable, and editable. Maturity: Active. Reversible — a withdrawn record can be published again; an unchanged record returns at the same web address. Maturity: Active. Withdrawn is remembered as withdrawn — the platform keeps the difference between a record that was withdrawn and one that was never published, and withdrawing the same record twice causes no harm. Maturity: Active.

Withdrawal is for taking a record off the public web entirely. It is not needed for corrections: The public page has an error — edit the record in your workspace and publish again. The public page shows your corrected version after the next publish. See Publish a record. The record should not be public at all — published by mistake, an unresolved rights or permissions question, content that needs review away from public view — withdraw it. If you are unsure, withdraw first: it is reversible, and the record loses nothing while it is withdrawn.
documents.s: When to withdraw — and when to edit and publish again

documents.t: Withdrawing, like publishing, requires publish access, which belongs to your environment's administrators. It is not one of the workspace publishing controls — to withdraw a record: Confirm that withdrawal is what you need, not an edit followed by publishing again (see above). Contact the administrator of your environment and name the record to withdraw. After the withdrawal, open the record's public address and confirm it no longer returns the record. If you do not know who administers your environment, ask the colleague who handles publishing in your project.

When a record is withdrawn: Its public page is removed — everywhere the record was published. If your project publishes the same record on more than one public surface, withdrawal covers all of them together. It leaves public search and the browsable index — readers can no longer find it by searching or browsing. Your workspace is unaffected — the record keeps its place in your collection, its links to other records, and its full editing history. Colleagues can keep working on it as before.

A reader who opens a bookmarked address to a withdrawn record no longer receives the record. The platform stops serving the withdrawn page — its text, its citations, and the links it offered to any media. The address is not reassigned to a different record. One thing withdrawal does not do: recall a media file someone already has. Withdrawal stops the platform from handing out a record's media, but a large file such as a 3D model or a scan is delivered to the reader's browser by a direct file address. Anyone who already saved that exact file address — or a service that cached the file — may still be able to open the file itself, even though the record's page is gone. This matters when you are withdrawing for a rights or permissions reason rather than for editorial rework. Withdrawal is the right first step, but if a file must become genuinely unreachable, tell your environment administrator so the stored file can be dealt with directly. A citation a reader copied earlier keeps its text, but its web address stops resolving while the record is withdrawn. Publishing the record again makes the cited address work again.

A withdrawn record can be published again at any time by anyone with publish access — the same way as any publication. The public page returns, and the record reappears in public search and the index. An unchanged record returns at the same web address, so earlier citations and bookmarks work again. If the record's identifying details were edited while it was withdrawn, its address can change with them — check the address of the new public page after publishing. A whole-table publish includes withdrawn records. When your project next publishes the entire table — for example after a period of internal review — a withdrawn record in that table is published again along with the rest. If a record must stay off the public web, tell whoever runs your project's publishing, so it is not swept back in by the next table-wide publish.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A withdrawn record is back on the public site. The whole table was published since the withdrawal; a table-wide publish includes every ready record, withdrawn ones included. Ask your environment administrator to withdraw it again, and agree with whoever publishes that this record stays out of table-wide publishes. You withdrew a record but its public page still shows. Your browser may be showing a stored copy, or the withdrawal did not cover this record. Reload the page. If it still shows the record, contact your environment administrator. A withdrawn record still appears in public search results. The search listing refreshes when a record is withdrawn, but the refresh can lag. Re-check after a short interval. If the result persists, contact your environment administrator. You want a public page corrected, not removed. Withdrawal is not needed for corrections — the public page updates when the record is published again after your edit. Edit the record and publish again. See Publish a record. You cannot find a withdraw option in your workspace. Withdrawal is held by your environment's administrators; it is not one of the workspace publishing controls. Contact the administrator of your environment. A reader reports that a cited address returns nothing. The record is withdrawn. If the withdrawal was intended, no action is needed — the address works again when the record is re-published. If it was not intended, ask your environment administrator to publish the record again.

Publish a record — the three stages from draft to published, and who can publish. Public reader — what readers see, stable addresses, and how a record reaches the public web. Preview an entry before publishing — check a record's public rendering before committing to publication. Adding and editing rows — how records are created, edited and deleted in the workspace. Entry surface readiness (for environment admins) — the companion surface controlling what gets published to the reader.

Many projects keep their material in more than one form: a native-script form, a transliteration, a translation — sometimes all three on the same record. This page covers how those forms relate to each other, how to enter text in any script, how one search reaches every form at once, and how multi-script records appear to readers. Read it when you start work in a multilingual environment, or when a search behaves differently across scripts than you expect. What is available depends on how your environment is configured. The sections below describe what the platform supports; your project may use all of it or a subset.

Text in any script — every text field stores what you write, in the script you write it. The platform never rewrites your text into another script. Maturity: Active. Side-by-side language forms — a record can carry a native-script field, a transliteration field, and a translation field next to each other; a search term in any of them finds the record, provided those fields are searchable and filled. Maturity: Active. A field that holds several values — a single field can keep more than one value per record — one for each language, register, script, edition, or calendar. All the values are searchable together, and you edit them in the table cell or the record's form. Maturity: Active. Forgiving matching across accents and marks — search sets aside most marks (Greek breathings and iota subscripts, Arabic vowel marks, Hebrew vowel points) while keeping the acute accent and the diaeresis, so a term typed in a modern keyboard layout finds historic spellings. Maturity: Active. Exact matching where a mark makes a different letter — a field can be set to match every mark exactly, for languages where marks are part of a letter's identity. Your environment administrator sets this per field. Maturity: Active. Script-aware browsing for readers — a project can publish more than one index of its entries (by transliteration and by original script, for example), and Greek and Latin index lists group accented entries under their base letter while still displaying the full form. Maturity: Active.

Multilingual records take two shapes, and a project may use either or both: Separate fields side by side. The native-script form, the transliteration, and the translation are each their own field — each with its own column in the table, and each searchable in its own right. One field holding several values. A single field keeps more than one value per record — most often one per language, but a field can instead separate by register, script, edition, or calendar. The Details panel marks these fields with a multilingual badge. Every form you fill is one more way the record can be found: the native script for colleagues who search in it, the transliteration for those who search in Latin script, the translation for finding by meaning. Search reaches a form only when it has a value and its field is searchable — and the platform never invents a transliteration or a translation from another field. What you write is all there is.
documents.s: One entry, several forms — which to fill and why

documents.t: A field that holds several values is set up once, on the field. Its setup has two independent parts: Field setup ├─ This column's language & script ← one language + script for the whole column │ Language code: [ grc ] (use when every value is in one language) │ Script: [ greek ] │ └─ Multiple values ← the column keeps a separate value per entry [✓] This column holds more than one value A separate value for each: [ Language ▾ ] (or Register / Script / Edition / Calendar / Custom) Allowed languages: [ GK ✕ ] [ LA ✕ ] [ AR ✕ ] ← chips: each allowed value Add a language: [________] (Add) ← type a new one; it's tidied to a chip The two parts are independent. This column's language & script stamps a single language on the whole column; Multiple values instead lets the column keep a separate value for each allowed language. Allowed languages is a set of chips, not free text — and the label follows your choice (Allowed registers, Allowed scripts, and so on). For the full walkthrough, see Let a column hold several values. Setting fields up is an administrator task — see Field configuration.
documents.s: Setting a field up to hold several values

documents.t: Type or paste in any script. Keyboard layouts and input methods come from your operating system, not the platform; whatever they produce, the field stores. Ordinary text fields work the same in every script — write as you would anywhere. A field holding several values shows them together in the table cell. Edit the cell and an editor opens: one row per value, each pairing the value with the language (or register, script, edition, or calendar) it belongs to. Choose the language for a row from the dropdown beside it — it lists the languages the field allows, and + new lets you add one the list does not yet offer. + Add language (the wording follows the field's setup — + Add register, + Add script, and so on) adds a row, the × beside a row removes it, Save commits, and Cancel or Esc closes without saving. Rows left empty are dropped when you save. When a row's language is Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu, or Aramaic, its value box writes from right to left. In the record's form, the same field edits the same way: one row per value, the language chosen from the dropdown, + new for one not yet listed, and + Add language for another row. The cell and the form edit the same values — fill them wherever suits you. You pick each row's language from a list rather than typing it freely. That keeps every record's values lining up under the same set of languages, so they group and display consistently across the collection. Which languages a field allows is part of the field's setup — see Field configuration. For the step-by-step, see Add a value in another language.

Quick search and Search & Read match against every searchable field of a record at once — the native form, the transliteration, the translation, and every value of a field that holds several. One query, all forms; there is no language switch to set first. Matching is forgiving about most accents and marks. When text is prepared for search, and again when your typed term is read, these are set aside: breathings and iota subscripts in polytonic Greek, and the circumflex and grave accents; Arabic vowel marks; Hebrew vowel points. Two marks still count: the acute accent and the diaeresis, in Greek and in Latin script alike. A term typed with no accents at all can miss a record whose stored form carries one of these. It does not matter how your keyboard produces an accented letter — as one key or as letter plus accent — search treats both the same. Some languages use marks as part of a letter's identity rather than as accents — the Scandinavian å, the Turkish dotted and dotless i, Vietnamese tone marks. For fields in such languages, your environment can keep every mark significant: search then finds that field's content only when your term carries the same marks as the stored form. This is set per field — the platform suggests a setting from the language it detects in each field, and your environment administrator confirms or changes it. The table's Filter rows… box folds marks the same way search does: the marks listed above are set aside, so a term typed without them reaches both the marked and the unmarked forms, while a term typed with one of them reaches only the rows carrying it; the acute accent and the diaeresis count on both sides. It is no longer stricter than search.
documents.s: How one search covers all the forms

documents.t: Each quick search result shows which fields your term matched. Read that line: it tells you whether the native form, the transliteration, or the translation caught your term — and, when a result surprises you, which form is responsible. When a record you expect does not come back, work through the likely causes in order: an acute accent or diaeresis the stored form carries and your term omits; a form that is empty on that record; a field outside your environment's search configuration; a field set to exact matching. Find a record when search returns nothing walks each case with its fix.
documents.s: Why a search matched — or missed

documents.t: Search matches what is written. If a record's transliteration field is empty, no transliterated term will find it — the native form still works, and the rest of the record is unaffected. The same holds inside a field that holds several values: each value is searchable when it has text, and an empty one is not there to match. Filling the missing form is the whole fix; the record becomes findable that way as soon as the value is saved.

Published pages show your text as you stored it, in its original script — the reader's layout and typography render it; nothing transliterates it for display. A field that holds several values shows them all together on the published page, joined into one line — for example, several translations read as "Genitals, Penis, Sexual organ" and a transliteration alongside its native form as "aidoion · A'da' Al-tnasul". A project can instead set such a field to show one chosen value per record on its published pages — the Greek value on a Greek record, say — but showing them all is the default. A project can publish more than one browsable index of its entries — by transliteration and by original script, for example — and readers switch between them. Index rows can show the transliterated form, the original-script form, and a short gloss together. In Greek and Latin index lists, an entry beginning with an accented letter is grouped under its base letter — an entry starting with an accented alpha lists under Α — while the row still displays the full accented form. Fields set to exact matching keep their marks in browse lists, and other scripts are listed as written. See Public reader and Browse entries by index. Which form serves as an entry's heading, and where translation and transliteration sets sit on the page, is part of your project's publication setup — if the arrangement does not suit your corpus, contact your environment administrator.
documents.s: What readers see on published pages

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A Greek term typed without breathings finds the record, but the same term without its acute accent does not. Breathings are set aside in matching; the acute accent still counts. Retype the term with its acute accent. A transliterated search misses a record you can see in the table. The transliteration field is empty on that record, or it is not searchable. Open the record and check the transliteration field. Find a record when search returns nothing covers each case. Arabic or Hebrew text in a multi-value editor writes left-to-right. The row's language is not set to a right-to-left language. Pick Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu, or Aramaic from the row's dropdown; the value box switches direction. The language you need is not in a row's dropdown. It is not yet among the languages the field allows. Click + new and type it, or ask your environment administrator to add it to the field. A term without marks misses content you know is in a particular field. That field is set to match every mark exactly. Type the term with the marks the stored form carries. If you are unsure which fields match exactly, contact your environment administrator. The Filter rows… box misses a row that quick search finds, when you typed the term with its marks. Typing marks makes the filter exact: it reaches only rows carrying the same marks, not the unmarked ones. Retype the term without the marks, or use quick search.

Let a column hold several values — setting up a field to keep one value per language, register, script, edition, or calendar. Add a value in another language — filling in a record's per-language values. Searching and reading — quick search, Search & Read, and the table filter box in full. Find a record when search returns nothing — the step-by-step diagnosis when a record will not surface. Public reader — the full path from draft to published page, including the browsable indexes. Browse entries by index — switching between a project's published indexes. Field configuration — for environment administrators: per-field language behavior, including exact-mark matching. Making fields searchable — for environment administrators: which fields search, suggest, and filter.

The workspace keeps several kinds of memory working for you at once: a history for edits to a table's records and fields, a separate history for changes to how a saved view is displayed, browser-side memory of where you left off, and account-level memory of how you organized your sidebar. They behave differently. This page explains which is which, so you know what Undo can bring back, why it sometimes refuses, and why your screen may not match a colleague's.

Undo and redo for workspace edits (Active) — Table, Details, and Relations share one chronological history for the active table. It holds up to 50 value, paste, manual row-order, reversible field-definition, and relationship changes while this browser tab keeps the workspace page open. A type conversion that rewrites stored cells starts this history over because configuration snapshots cannot restore those cells. Undo and redo for view changes (Active) — the separate view history steps through filters, sort order, column layout, row color rules, and row density. It holds up to 20 presentation changes. Confirmation for destructive structure changes (Active) — deleting a saved view asks you to confirm and does not enter either history. Creating or deleting a row or field is also outside workspace edit history. Removing a relationship is different: it is an edit to the connection and can be undone. Shared default view wins for first entry (Active) — each table has one shared default saved view, including its view kind: Table, Details, Relations, Publish, or Media where available. Last concrete view remembered per table (Active) — the browser you are using can remember a specific non-default view tab you last opened in a table. That memory does not replace the table's shared default view kind. Sidebar size remembered per browser (Active) — how wide you made the sidebar, and whether you collapsed it to the icon rail. Sidebar organization saved with your account (Active) — pinned tables, named groups, your table order, which groups you collapsed, and your recently opened tables are stored with your sign-in, not in the browser.

The workspace-history Undo and Redo controls appear in Table, Details, and Relations. Their labels name both the surface and the next operation, such as a value edit made in Details or a link removed in Relations. They follow one chronological history for the active table: editing one value in Table or Details pasting values into existing rows, including a batch changing the hand-arranged row order changing a field type or another field definition when the save rewrites no stored cell adding or removing a relationship from Table, Details, or Relations Each press of Undo steps back one saved operation, up to 50 entries; Redo reapplies what you undid. Ctrl/Cmd+Z runs Undo. Redo accepts Ctrl/Cmd+Y and Shift+Ctrl/Cmd+Z. These shortcuts are ignored while you are typing in an editor or while a dialog is open. If a paste review is still waiting for confirmation, Undo cancels that pending paste before it touches saved data. Undo is careful around newer work. Before it replays a value or field-definition change, the workspace checks that the current value or definition still matches the history entry. If another edit has landed since then, Undo refuses, keeps the history entry in place, and explains the conflict instead of overwriting the newer edit. A refused direct save also keeps your draft visible with Retry save and Discard retained edit choices. Some type changes convert stored cells to the new type. The workspace reports the converted and quarantined counts; quarantined values remain as they were and are marked for correction. If at least one cell was converted, the receipt says the conversion cannot be undone and clears this table's Undo and Redo history. Schema-only changes that convert no cell remain ordinary history entries. Undoing an unlink restores the same connection, including its recorded status, provenance, detail, anchor, and attribution. The restore is accepted only for the same signed-in person and environment, within 90 days of the unlink, and only while the current relationship field still permits that connection. A restore that is stale, already used, duplicated, or no longer allowed is refused without consuming the history entry. An import run does not enter this browser history. If an import created an approved connection through a declared relationship field and you later unlink it in the workspace, that later unlink is a workspace edit and can be undone. Imported connections that have no editable relationship field remain read-only.

Workspace Undo does not create or delete rows or fields, reverse an import run, upload or remove a media file, change Appearance, alter citation rules, change field visibility, publish or unpublish records, or change privacy/public scope. Appearance, Publish, and Media do not expose or intercept the workspace-history shortcuts, so pressing Ctrl/Cmd+Z there cannot replay an edit from another panel or change publication state. Creating a new row, duplicating a row, and adding or deleting a field therefore require their own explicit action and confirmation where appropriate. Pasting into existing rows is reversible; extra clipboard lines never create new rows automatically.
documents.s: What workspace Undo deliberately leaves alone

documents.t: The view-history controls cover how the active saved view is displayed: filters — adding a condition, changing one, or removing it sort order column layout — order, visibility, pinning, widths, and the view display column row color rules row density That history holds up to 20 changes. Its command-palette actions are named Undo view change and Redo view change, keeping it distinct from the labelled workspace-operation entries. A restored arrangement is saved back to the shared view, so collaborators see the arrangement you restored.

Saved-view deletion does not enter either history. Deleting a saved view shows a confirmation step on the view's tab itself, and a deleted view is gone for everyone who works in the environment. When you want to experiment with a shared view, Duplicate it first and work on the copy.
documents.s: Why saved-view deletion is confirmed, not undone
